Even with wh=1.0w_h = 1.0wh​=1.0 (the most favorable possible value) and neurons well away from saturation, the gradient reaching step 1 from step 20 is only 10.9% of the original. In realistic settings — with ∣wh∣<1|w_h| < 1∣wh​∣<1 or neurons in saturated regions — the decay is catastrophically faster:

For wh=2.0w_h = 2.0wh​=2.0, x1=2.0x_1 = 2.0x1​=2.0: neurons saturate at step 3 with h3≈0.95h_3 \approx 0.95h3​≈0.95 and f′(z3)≈0.10f'(z_3) \approx 0.10f′(z3​)≈0.10. The per-step product wh⋅f′(z)≈2.0×0.10=0.20w_h \cdot f'(z) \approx 2.0 \times 0.10 = 0.20wh​⋅f′(z)≈2.0×0.10=0.20. After 17 more steps:

0.2017≈1.3×10−120.20^{17} \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-12}0.2017≈1.3×10−12

The gradient is 101210^{12}1012 times smaller than the original signal. This neuron cannot learn anything about x1x_1x1​.

#### 11.1.5 The Gradient Half-Life

Define the **gradient half-life** t1/2t_{1/2}t1/2​: the number of steps for the gradient to decay to 50% of its initial value.

For per-step decay factor α=E[f′(zt)]⋅∣wh∣\alpha = \mathbb{E}[f'(z_t)] \cdot |w_h|α=E[f′(zt​)]⋅∣wh​∣:

t1/2=ln⁡0.5ln⁡α=−0.693ln⁡αt_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 0.5}{\ln \alpha} = \frac{-0.693}{\ln \alpha}t1/2​=lnαln0.5​=lnα−0.693​ Decay factor α\alphaα | Half-life (steps) | Steps to reach 1% of original  
---|---|---  
0.95 | 13.5 | 90  
0.90 | 6.6 | 44  
0.80 | 3.1 | 21  
0.50 | 1.0 | 7  
  
At α=0.90\alpha = 0.90α=0.90 (typical), gradients carry negligible information about events more than ∼\sim∼40 steps in the past. Vanilla RNNs cannot learn long-range dependencies.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> **Impulse response functions in time-series analysis, radioactive decay in physics, and the Lyapunov exponent in dynamical systems** : The gradient half-life concept maps exactly to familiar decay phenomena across disciplines. In **time-series econometrics** , the impulse response function of an AR(1) process yt=ϕyt−1+ϵty_t = \phi y_{t-1} + \epsilon_tyt​=ϕyt−1​+ϵt​ decays as ϕk\phi^kϕk — giving half-life t1/2=−ln⁡2/ln⁡∣ϕ∣t_{1/2} = -\ln 2/\ln|\phi|t1/2​=−ln2/ln∣ϕ∣. The RNN gradient product ∏sf′(zs)wh\prod_s f'(z_s) w_h∏s​f′(zs​)wh​ is mathematically identical, with α\alphaα playing the role of the autoregressive coefficient. In **nuclear physics** , radioactive decay follows N(t)=N0e−λtN(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}N(t)=N0​e−λt; the half-life t1/2=ln⁡2/λt_{1/2} = \ln 2/\lambdat1/2​=ln2/λ is the universal descriptor. In **dynamical systems theory** , the Lyapunov exponent λ=lim⁡T→∞1Tln⁡∥J0→T∥\lambda = \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{T} \ln\|\mathbf{J}_{0\to T}\|λ=limT→∞​T1​ln∥J0→T​∥ exactly captures the average per-step log-amplification of the Jacobian product. Negative Lyapunov exponent → vanishing gradients (contracting dynamics); positive → exploding gradients (chaotic dynamics). All three frameworks describe the same exponential behavior; the vocabulary differs across disciplines.

* * *

### 11.2 Gradient Explosion and Clipping

#### 11.2.1 When Gradients Explode

Gradient explosion occurs when ρ(DWh)>1\rho(\mathbf{D} \mathbf{W}_h) > 1ρ(DWh​)>1. For tanh⁡\tanhtanh, this requires σmax⁡(Wh)>1/∥D∥\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{W}_h) > 1 / \|\mathbf{D}\|σmax​(Wh​)>1/∥D∥. In early training, neurons are often in the linear region (tanh⁡′(z)≈1\tanh'(z) \approx 1tanh′(z)≈1), and if σmax⁡(Wh)>1\sigma_{\max}(\mathbf{W}_h) > 1σmax​(Wh​)>1, gradients grow exponentially.

Explosion causes training to diverge: the parameter update step is so large that weights fly off to large values, after which loss is uncomputable (NaN).

**Coexistence** : in the same training step, gradients can vanish in some directions (eigenvalue components <1< 1<1) and explode in others (>1> 1>1). The optimizer receives contradictory signals.

#### 11.2.2 Gradient Clipping

Gradient explosion has a clean fix: if the gradient norm ∥g∥\|\mathbf{g}\|∥g∥ exceeds threshold τ\tauτ, rescale it:

g←{gif ∥g∥≤ττ∥g∥⋅gif ∥g∥>τ\mathbf{g} \leftarrow \begin{cases} \mathbf{g} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{g}\| \leq \tau \\\ \dfrac{\tau}{\|\mathbf{g}\|} \cdot \mathbf{g} & \text{if } \|\mathbf{g}\| > \tau \end{cases}g←⎩⎨⎧​g∥g∥τ​⋅g​if ∥g∥≤τif ∥g∥>τ​

This preserves the gradient direction while bounding its magnitude. The threshold τ\tauτ (typically 1.0–5.0) is a hyperparameter.

**Why clipping works for explosion but not vanishing** : clipping prevents the update from being too large, maintaining numerical stability. But the vanishing problem is opposite — the gradient signal is too small, not too large. You cannot "amplify" a vanished gradient; amplifying a near-zero gradient means amplifying noise, not signal. Vanishing requires a structural architectural fix, not a numerical one.

* * *

### 11.3 The Gating Idea: Additive vs. Multiplicative Updates

#### 11.3.1 The Root Cause

The fundamental issue is that the vanilla RNN's state update is **multiplicative** : the previous state ht−1\mathbf{h}_{t-1}ht−1​ is multiplied by Wh\mathbf{W}_hWh​ at every step. The gradient of the loss with respect to the state at step ttt involves multiplying by Wh⊤\mathbf{W}_h^\topWh⊤​ at every subsequent step — causing the product to decay or grow exponentially.

**Key insight** : if the state update were **additive** — if the new state were the old state plus a correction — the gradient would include a direct path from the final loss to early states, bypassing the multiplicative decay.

Consider a hypothetical update:

ct=ct−1+updatetc_t = c_{t-1} + \text{update}_tct​=ct−1​+updatet​

The gradient ∂cT/∂ct=1\partial c_T / \partial c_t = 1∂cT​/∂ct​=1 for all t<Tt < Tt<T — the gradient flows backward unchanged, regardless of depth. The additive structure gives the identity Jacobian.

#### 11.3.2 The Problem with Pure Additive Updates

A pure additive update ct=ct−1+updatetc_t = c_{t-1} + \text{update}_tct​=ct−1​+updatet​ cannot forget. Once information is written to the state, it persists indefinitely. For many sequences, this is wrong: early context is often irrelevant to the current step, and retaining it indefinitely pollutes the state.

The LSTM's insight: make the state update **selectively additive**. At each step, a **forget gate** decides what fraction of the previous state to keep (ft∈(0,1)f_t \in (0, 1)ft​∈(0,1)), and an **input gate** decides what fraction of the new information to add (it∈(0,1)i_t \in (0, 1)it​∈(0,1)). The update becomes:

ct=ft⊙ct−1+it⊙c~tc_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_tct​=ft​⊙ct−1​+it​⊙c~t​

When ft≈1f_t \approx 1ft​≈1: the previous state is mostly preserved (long memory). When ft≈0f_t \approx 0ft​≈0: the previous state is mostly discarded (selective forgetting).

The gradient ∂ct/∂ct−1=ft\partial c_t / \partial c_{t-1} = f_t∂ct​/∂ct−1​=ft​ — instead of the matrix product DWh\mathbf{D} \mathbf{W}_hDWh​, the gradient passes through ftf_tft​. When ft≈1f_t \approx 1ft​≈1, the gradient flows essentially unchanged; when ft≈0f_t \approx 0ft​≈0, the gradient is intentionally blocked (the information was intentionally forgotten).

* * *

### 11.4 The Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)

#### 11.4.1 The Cell State: The Constant Error Carousel

The LSTM introduces two state vectors: the **cell state** ct∈Rn\mathbf{c}_t \in \mathbb{R}^nct​∈Rn and the **hidden state** ht∈Rn\mathbf{h}_t \in \mathbb{R}^nht​∈Rn.

The cell state ct\mathbf{c}_tct​ is the "long-term memory" — it flows through time via an additive update. Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) called this the **Constant Error Carousel (CEC)** : a structure designed to maintain gradient magnitude across many steps.

The cell state update:

ct=ft⊙ct−1+it⊙c~t\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_tct​=ft​⊙ct−1​+it​⊙c~t​

where ⊙\odot⊙ denotes element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication.

The gradient through the cell state:

∂ct∂ct−1=diag(ft)\frac{\partial \mathbf{c}_t}{\partial \mathbf{c}_{t-1}} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{f}_t)∂ct−1​∂ct​​=diag(ft​)

For a sequence of steps where ft,j≈1f_{t,j} \approx 1ft,j​≈1 for dimension jjj: ∂cT,j/∂ck,j=∏s=k+1Tfs,j≈1\partial c_{T,j} / \partial c_{k,j} = \prod_{s=k+1}^{T} f_{s,j} \approx 1∂cT,j​/∂ck,j​=∏s=k+1T​fs,j​≈1. The gradient is preserved. This is the mathematical core of the LSTM's long-range memory.

#### 11.4.2 The Three Gates

Three gating vectors, each ∈(0,1)n\in (0, 1)^n∈(0,1)n, control information flow. All gates are computed from the same input: the current input xt\mathbf{x}_txt​ and the previous hidden state ht−1\mathbf{h}_{t-1}ht−1​, followed by a sigmoid activation.

**Forget gate** ft\mathbf{f}_tft​: what fraction of the previous cell state to retain.

ft=σ(Wf[ht−1,xt]+bf)\mathbf{f}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_f [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_f)ft​=σ(Wf​[ht−1​,xt​]+bf​)

**Input gate** it\mathbf{i}_tit​: what fraction of the new candidate information to write.

it=σ(Wi[ht−1,xt]+bi)\mathbf{i}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_i [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_i)it​=σ(Wi​[ht−1​,xt​]+bi​)

**Candidate cell state** c~t\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_tc~t​: the proposed new information to add.

c~t=tanh⁡(Wc[ht−1,xt]+bc)\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}_c [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_c)c~t​=tanh(Wc​[ht−1​,xt​]+bc​)

**Output gate** ot\mathbf{o}_tot​: what part of the cell state to expose as the hidden state.

ot=σ(Wo[ht−1,xt]+bo)\mathbf{o}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_o [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_o)ot​=σ(Wo​[ht−1​,xt​]+bo​)

Here [ht−1,xt][\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t][ht−1​,xt​] denotes the concatenation of ht−1∈Rn\mathbf{h}_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}^nht−1​∈Rn and xt∈Rd\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^dxt​∈Rd into a vector of dimension n+dn + dn+d.

The notation is often written with two separate weight matrices:

ft=σ(Wfhht−1+Wfxxt+bf)\mathbf{f}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_{fh} \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_{fx} \mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}_f)ft​=σ(Wfh​ht−1​+Wfx​xt​+bf​)

#### 11.4.3 The Complete LSTM Equations

The four LSTM equations in standard order:

ft=σ(Wf[ht−1,xt]+bf)(Forget gate)\mathbf{f}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_f [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_f) \tag{Forget gate}ft​=σ(Wf​[ht−1​,xt​]+bf​)(Forget gate) it=σ(Wi[ht−1,xt]+bi)(Input gate)\mathbf{i}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_i [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_i) \tag{Input gate}it​=σ(Wi​[ht−1​,xt​]+bi​)(Input gate) c~t=tanh⁡(Wc[ht−1,xt]+bc)(Candidate)\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}_c [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_c) \tag{Candidate}c~t​=tanh(Wc​[ht−1​,xt​]+bc​)(Candidate) ot=σ(Wo[ht−1,xt]+bo)(Output gate)\mathbf{o}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_o [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_o) \tag{Output gate}ot​=σ(Wo​[ht−1​,xt​]+bo​)(Output gate)

And the state updates:

ct=ft⊙ct−1+it⊙c~t(Cell update)\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t \tag{Cell update}ct​=ft​⊙ct−1​+it​⊙c~t​(Cell update) ht=ot⊙tanh⁡(ct)(Hidden state)\mathbf{h}_t = \mathbf{o}_t \odot \tanh(\mathbf{c}_t) \tag{Hidden state}ht​=ot​⊙tanh(ct​)(Hidden state)

#### 11.4.4 What Each Gate Does

**The forget gate** decides how much of the previous cell state to keep. When the model encounters the phrase "The trophy... it was too large," the subject "trophy" should be retained in the cell state until "it" is resolved. The forget gate keeps relevant context alive.

**The input gate** decides how much of the new candidate information to add. Not every new input is equally important — the input gate filters which new content to incorporate.

**The candidate cell state** is the full proposed update, computed the same way as a vanilla RNN hidden state: a tanh⁡\tanhtanh of a linear function of the current input and previous hidden state.

**The output gate** decides what to read out from the cell state as the hidden state ht\mathbf{h}_tht​. The cell state contains all accumulated information; the output gate selectively exposes only the parts relevant for the current output. For a language model generating the next word, only some of the accumulated context is relevant for each output.

#### 11.4.5 The Constant Error Carousel: Formal Proof

**Claim** : the gradient of the loss with respect to ct\mathbf{c}_tct​ satisfies ∂L/∂ct=diag(ft+1)⋅∂L/∂ct+1\partial L / \partial \mathbf{c}_t = \text{diag}(\mathbf{f}_{t+1}) \cdot \partial L / \partial \mathbf{c}_{t+1}∂L/∂ct​=diag(ft+1​)⋅∂L/∂ct+1​ (approximately, ignoring second-order terms from ft+1\mathbf{f}_{t+1}ft+1​ depending on ct\mathbf{c}_tct​ through ht\mathbf{h}_tht​).

**Derivation** : From ct+1=ft+1⊙ct+it+1⊙c~t+1\mathbf{c}_{t+1} = \mathbf{f}_{t+1} \odot \mathbf{c}_t + \mathbf{i}_{t+1} \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_{t+1}ct+1​=ft+1​⊙ct​+it+1​⊙c~t+1​:

∂ct+1∂ct=diag(ft+1)+(terms from ft+1,it+1 through ht)\frac{\partial \mathbf{c}_{t+1}}{\partial \mathbf{c}_t} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{f}_{t+1}) + \text{(terms from } \mathbf{f}_{t+1}, \mathbf{i}_{t+1} \text{ through } \mathbf{h}_t \text{)}∂ct​∂ct+1​​=diag(ft+1​)+(terms from ft+1​,it+1​ through ht​)

The dominant term is diag(ft+1)\text{diag}(\mathbf{f}_{t+1})diag(ft+1​). For a sequence of steps where a dimension jjj has ft,j≈1f_{t,j} \approx 1ft,j​≈1:

∂cT,j∂ck,j=∏s=k+1Tfs,j≈1T−k=1\frac{\partial c_{T,j}}{\partial c_{k,j}} = \prod_{s=k+1}^{T} f_{s,j} \approx 1^{T-k} = 1∂ck,j​∂cT,j​​=s=k+1∏T​fs,j​≈1T−k=1

The gradient flows backward through these steps with zero attenuation. The LSTM can in principle learn to preserve gradient information for arbitrarily long sequences by learning ft,j≈1f_{t,j} \approx 1ft,j​≈1 for the relevant dimensions.

Contrast with the vanilla RNN, where the analogous product is ∏s=k+1T(f′(zs,j)⋅Wh,jj)\prod_{s=k+1}^{T} (f'(z_{s,j}) \cdot W_{h,jj})∏s=k+1T​(f′(zs,j​)⋅Wh,jj​), which decays exponentially when f′(zs,j)<1f'(z_{s,j}) < 1f′(zs,j​)<1.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> **Leaky integrators in neuroscience, exponentially weighted moving averages in statistics, and persistent storage in computer science** : The LSTM cell state is an instance of a **leaky integrator** : a system that accumulates input over time with a decay factor (the forget gate). In **computational neuroscience** , leaky integrate-and-fire neurons model this behavior exactly: membrane potential Vt=(1−λ)Vt−1+ItV_t = (1-\lambda)V_{t-1} + I_tVt​=(1−λ)Vt−1​+It​, with forgetting rate λ\lambdaλ. When λ=0\lambda = 0λ=0 (no forgetting), the neuron integrates perfectly. The LSTM learns this leak rate from data. In **signal processing and finance** , the exponentially weighted moving average EWMAt=α⋅EWMAt−1+(1−α)xt\text{EWMA}_t = \alpha \cdot \text{EWMA}_{t-1} + (1-\alpha) x_tEWMAt​=α⋅EWMAt−1​+(1−α)xt​ is a fixed-forget-rate version — the LSTM generalizes this to a learned, input-dependent, dimension-specific decay rate. In **computer architecture** , the distinction between volatile memory (RAM, which forgets when power is removed) and persistent storage (disk, which retains information indefinitely) captures the same conceptual split: the cell state is persistent memory, the hidden state is the current working register.

* * *

### 11.5 The Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)

#### 11.5.1 Simplifying the LSTM

Cho et al. (2014) introduced the **Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)** as a simplification of the LSTM. The GRU merges the cell state and hidden state into a single vector, and replaces the three gates with two:

**Update gate** zt\mathbf{z}_tzt​: controls how much of the previous hidden state to retain vs. how much new information to incorporate (combines the LSTM's forget and input gates).

zt=σ(Wz[ht−1,xt]+bz)\mathbf{z}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_z [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_z)zt​=σ(Wz​[ht−1​,xt​]+bz​)

**Reset gate** rt\mathbf{r}_trt​: controls how much of the previous hidden state to use when computing the candidate.

rt=σ(Wr[ht−1,xt]+br)\mathbf{r}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_r [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_r)rt​=σ(Wr​[ht−1​,xt​]+br​)

**Candidate hidden state** :

h~t=tanh⁡(Wh[rt⊙ht−1,xt]+bh)\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}_h [\mathbf{r}_t \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_h)h~t​=tanh(Wh​[rt​⊙ht−1​,xt​]+bh​)

The reset gate rt\mathbf{r}_trt​ modulates how much the candidate depends on the previous hidden state. When rt≈0\mathbf{r}_t \approx 0rt​≈0, the candidate is computed without access to history — the network can learn to produce a new starting state.

**Update** :

ht=(1−zt)⊙ht−1+zt⊙h~t\mathbf{h}_t = (1 - \mathbf{z}_t) \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{z}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_tht​=(1−zt​)⊙ht−1​+zt​⊙h~t​

When zt,j=0z_{t,j} = 0zt,j​=0: ht,j=ht−1,jh_{t,j} = h_{t-1,j}ht,j​=ht−1,j​ — perfect carry-over (analogous to LSTM with f=1f = 1f=1, i=0i = 0i=0). When zt,j=1z_{t,j} = 1zt,j​=1: ht,j=h~t,jh_{t,j} = \tilde{h}_{t,j}ht,j​=h~t,j​ — full replacement (analogous to LSTM with f=0f = 0f=0, i=1i = 1i=1).

The (1−zt)(1 - \mathbf{z}_t)(1−zt​) weight ensures that retaining and updating are complementary: the fraction not updated from the candidate is retained from the previous state.

#### 11.5.2 LSTM vs. GRU

Feature | LSTM | GRU  
---|---|---  
State vectors | Two (ct\mathbf{c}_tct​, ht\mathbf{h}_tht​) | One (ht\mathbf{h}_tht​)  
Gates | Three (forget, input, output) | Two (update, reset)  
Parameters | ~4× vanilla RNN | ~3× vanilla RNN  
Expressive power | Slightly higher | Slightly lower  
Performance (empirical) | Similar | Similar  
Preferred when | Many tasks with careful tuning | Faster training, less memory  
  
Neither architecture uniformly dominates. The LSTM has a richer representational vocabulary (separate cell and hidden state, separate read/write control). The GRU trains faster (fewer parameters, single state) and often achieves comparable accuracy. The GRU is now commonly the default choice in practice when memory efficiency matters.

* * *

### 11.6 What LSTMs Solved and What They Didn't

#### 11.6.1 What LSTMs Solved

**Long-range dependencies** : LSTMs can learn to maintain relevant information for hundreds of steps via the constant error carousel. Tasks like sentiment analysis of long reviews, language modeling, and machine translation all improved dramatically with LSTM-based models.

**Gradient stability** : the CEC provides a guaranteed gradient pathway for dimensions where the forget gate ≈1\approx 1≈1. Gradient explosion is still possible (and is addressed by gradient clipping), but gradient vanishing is architecturally mitigated.

#### 11.6.2 What LSTMs Didn't Solve

**Sequential computation** : an LSTM processes one time step at a time. Computing ht\mathbf{h}_tht​ requires ht−1\mathbf{h}_{t-1}ht−1​, which requires ht−2\mathbf{h}_{t-2}ht−2​, and so on. This sequential dependency means an LSTM on a sequence of length TTT cannot be parallelized across the time dimension. Training on long sequences is slow.

**Fixed context capacity** : even with a large hidden dimension nnn, the cell state ct∈Rn\mathbf{c}_t \in \mathbb{R}^nct​∈Rn must compress all relevant past information into nnn numbers. For tasks requiring simultaneous reference to many past positions (e.g., long-document question answering), this fixed capacity is a bottleneck.

**No direct access to arbitrary past positions** : at step ttt, the LSTM can only access the current cell state — it cannot "look back" to what it was computing at step kkk for some specific k<tk < tk<t. Information about step kkk must have been maintained continuously in the cell state from kkk to ttt. If the forget gate dropped it at step k+5k + 5k+5, it is permanently gone.

These three limitations motivate the attention mechanism: rather than compressing all past information into a single state vector, attention allows the model to directly compute a weighted average over all past positions at each step, with the weights dynamically computed from the current query and past key vectors. This is the subject of Part V.

* * *

### 11.7 Chapter Summary

The vanilla RNN's gradient instability is mathematically precise: the product ∏s=t+1Tdiag(f′(zs))Wh\prod_{s=t+1}^{T} \text{diag}(f'(\mathbf{z}_s)) \mathbf{W}_h∏s=t+1T​diag(f′(zs​))Wh​ has spectral radius ρ\rhoρ that determines whether gradients vanish (ρ<1\rho < 1ρ<1) or explode (ρ>1\rho > 1ρ>1). For tanh⁡\tanhtanh activations, the activation derivative is bounded above by 1, creating a systematic compression that makes stable gradient flow impossible without architectural intervention.

The LSTM solves this through **gating** : by replacing the multiplicative state update with a selective additive update ct=ft⊙ct−1+it⊙c~t\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_tct​=ft​⊙ct−1​+it​⊙c~t​, the gradient through the cell state becomes ∂ct/∂ct−1=diag(ft)\partial \mathbf{c}_t / \partial \mathbf{c}_{t-1} = \text{diag}(\mathbf{f}_t)∂ct​/∂ct−1​=diag(ft​). When ft≈1\mathbf{f}_t \approx 1ft​≈1, gradients flow unchanged through any number of steps — the constant error carousel.

Three gates (forget, input, output) provide separable control: the forget gate decides what to retain, the input gate decides what to write, and the output gate decides what to read. The GRU simplifies this to two gates (update, reset) with comparable empirical performance and lower parameter count.

LSTMs enabled a decade of progress in sequence modeling: speech recognition, machine translation, language modeling, and question answering. Their sequential computation bottleneck — one step at a time — remained a fundamental constraint until the attention mechanism replaced recurrence with direct access to all positions simultaneously.

#### Concept Check

**1.** Write out the gradient product J1→T\mathbf{J}_{1 \to T}J1→T​ for a many-to-one vanilla RNN of depth T=4T = 4T=4. Under what condition on the spectral radius of DWh\mathbf{D} \mathbf{W}_hDWh​ does the gradient reaching step 1 shrink to less than 1% of the loss gradient at step 4?

Answer J1→4=∏s=24DsWh=(D4Wh)(D3Wh)(D2Wh)\mathbf{J}_{1 \to 4} = \prod_{s=2}^{4} \mathbf{D}_s \mathbf{W}_h = (\mathbf{D}_4 \mathbf{W}_h)(\mathbf{D}_3 \mathbf{W}_h)(\mathbf{D}_2 \mathbf{W}_h)J1→4​=s=2∏4​Ds​Wh​=(D4​Wh​)(D3​Wh​)(D2​Wh​)

With Ds\mathbf{D}_sDs​ all equal to D\mathbf{D}D: J1→4≈(DWh)3\mathbf{J}_{1\to4} \approx (\mathbf{D}\mathbf{W}_h)^3J1→4​≈(DWh​)3.

For ∥J1→4∥<0.01\|\mathbf{J}_{1\to4}\| < 0.01∥J1→4​∥<0.01: need ρ(DWh)3<0.01\rho(\mathbf{D}\mathbf{W}_h)^3 < 0.01ρ(DWh​)3<0.01, i.e., ρ<0.011/3≈0.215\rho < 0.01^{1/3} \approx 0.215ρ<0.011/3≈0.215.

More generally for depth TTT: ρ(DWh)<0.011/(T−1)\rho(\mathbf{D}\mathbf{W}_h) < 0.01^{1/(T-1)}ρ(DWh​)<0.011/(T−1). For T=20T = 20T=20: ρ<0.011/19≈0.78\rho < 0.01^{1/19} \approx 0.78ρ<0.011/19≈0.78. Even a spectral radius of 0.78 per step gives less than 1% gradient reach over 20 steps — illustrating how dramatically the threshold tightens with depth.

**2.** In the LSTM cell update ct=ft⊙ct−1+it⊙c~t\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_tct​=ft​⊙ct−1​+it​⊙c~t​, what happens in the two extreme cases: (a) ft=0\mathbf{f}_t = \mathbf{0}ft​=0, it=1\mathbf{i}_t = \mathbf{1}it​=1; (b) ft=1\mathbf{f}_t = \mathbf{1}ft​=1, it=0\mathbf{i}_t = \mathbf{0}it​=0?

Answer

(a) ft=0\mathbf{f}_t = \mathbf{0}ft​=0, it=1\mathbf{i}_t = \mathbf{1}it​=1: ct=0⊙ct−1+1⊙c~t=c~t\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{0} \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{1} \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t = \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_tct​=0⊙ct−1​+1⊙c~t​=c~t​. The previous cell state is completely forgotten; the new candidate completely replaces it. This is a "hard reset" — the cell discards all history at this step.

(b) ft=1\mathbf{f}_t = \mathbf{1}ft​=1, it=0\mathbf{i}_t = \mathbf{0}it​=0: ct=1⊙ct−1+0⊙c~t=ct−1\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{1} \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{0} \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t = \mathbf{c}_{t-1}ct​=1⊙ct−1​+0⊙c~t​=ct−1​. The previous cell state is preserved exactly; no new information is written. This is a "hard memory" — information from however long ago it was written persists unchanged. The gradient through this step: ∂ct/∂ct−1=I\partial \mathbf{c}_t / \partial \mathbf{c}_{t-1} = \mathbf{I}∂ct​/∂ct−1​=I, perfect gradient preservation.

**3.** Compare the parameter counts of a vanilla RNN, LSTM, and GRU, each with hidden dimension n=256n = 256n=256 and input dimension d=128d = 128d=128. How many times larger is the LSTM than the vanilla RNN?

**7.** An LSTM processes a sequence of length T=200T = 200T=200. The forget gate for a particular cell dimension outputs ft=0.95f_t = 0.95ft​=0.95 for all ttt.

(a) What fraction of the gradient signal from step 200 reaches step 1 through this cell dimension? Compare with a vanilla RNN with per-step decay factor α=0.95\alpha = 0.95α=0.95. (b) Now suppose the forget gate is not constant: ft=0.99f_t = 0.99ft​=0.99 for t=1,…,180t = 1, \ldots, 180t=1,…,180 (retaining mode) and ft=0.5f_t = 0.5ft​=0.5 for t=181,…,200t = 181, \ldots, 200t=181,…,200 (actively forgetting). What fraction of the gradient from step 200 reaches step 1? Explain why this selective forgetting is actually beneficial for gradient flow to step 1.

**(a)** LSTM: gradient through cell state = ∏t=2200ft=0.95199≈3.5×10−5\prod_{t=2}^{200} f_t = 0.95^{199} \approx 3.5 \times 10^{-5}∏t=2200​ft​=0.95199≈3.5×10−5. Very small but nonzero. Vanilla RNN: gradient = α199=0.95199≈3.5×10−5\alpha^{199} = 0.95^{199} \approx 3.5 \times 10^{-5}α199=0.95199≈3.5×10−5. **Identical** — when the forget gate is constant at 0.95, the LSTM cell state gradient has the same decay as a vanilla RNN with the same per-step factor. The LSTM's advantage is not in the magnitude of decay per se, but in the ability to **learn** different ftf_tft​ values at different steps.

**(b)** Gradient = ∏t=21800.99×∏t=1812000.5=0.99179×0.520\prod_{t=2}^{180} 0.99 \times \prod_{t=181}^{200} 0.5 = 0.99^{179} \times 0.5^{20}∏t=2180​0.99×∏t=181200​0.5=0.99179×0.520. 0.99179≈0.1660.99^{179} \approx 0.1660.99179≈0.166. 0.520≈9.5×10−70.5^{20} \approx 9.5 \times 10^{-7}0.520≈9.5×10−7. Total ≈1.6×10−7\approx 1.6 \times 10^{-7}≈1.6×10−7. Worse than the constant case because the ft=0.5f_t = 0.5ft​=0.5 segment causes rapid decay.

**(c)** The gradient from step 200 to step 1 is small because the forget gate **intentionally** decided to forget at step 181. This is correct behavior: information before the "forget signal" (e.g., the previous sentence) is no longer relevant to the loss at step 200. The gradient **should** be small — the model is correctly attributing the loss to recent inputs (steps 181-200), not to ancient history (steps 1-180). The LSTM's selective forgetting ensures that gradients flow strongly to the relevant past and weakly to the irrelevant past, which is exactly what efficient credit assignment requires.

#### Think Deeper

**6.** The LSTM was designed to solve the vanishing gradient problem in RNNs. ResNet (Chapter 9) solved the analogous problem in CNNs with skip connections y=F(x)+x\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}y=F(x)+x. Identify the structural parallel between the two solutions, and explain why the LSTM's solution is more complex than ResNet's.

Answer

**The parallel** : Both solutions replace a purely multiplicative transformation with one that includes an additive direct path. ResNet: y=F(x)+x\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}y=F(x)+x — the Jacobian ∂y/∂x=∂F/∂x+I\partial \mathbf{y}/\partial \mathbf{x} = \partial \mathcal{F}/\partial \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{I}∂y/∂x=∂F/∂x+I, guaranteeing the identity term in the gradient. LSTM: ct=ft⊙ct−1+it⊙c~t\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_tct​=ft​⊙ct−1​+it​⊙c~t​ — when ft=1\mathbf{f}_t = \mathbf{1}ft​=1, ∂ct/∂ct−1=I\partial \mathbf{c}_t / \partial \mathbf{c}_{t-1} = \mathbf{I}∂ct​/∂ct−1​=I, same guarantee. Both architectures discovered the same solution: add a direct pathway to preserve gradient flow.

**Why LSTM is more complex** : (1) ResNet's skip connection is a fixed identity — x\mathbf{x}x is always added without modification. The LSTM's skip connection is **gated** : ft⊙ct−1f_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1}ft​⊙ct−1​ can zero out parts of the previous state. This is necessary because unlike ResNet (where we want every layer's input to pass through), the RNN must sometimes **forget** — retaining all past history indefinitely would cause the fixed-size cell state to overflow. (2) ResNet only needs to preserve gradients through depth; the LSTM must also decide what new information to add (the input gate) and what to expose for output (the output gate). ResNet has one purpose; LSTM has three simultaneously controlled information flows. The additional complexity is the price for making selective memory a learnable, data-driven choice.

**8.** The LSTM and the ResNet (Chapter 9) both use additive update paths to preserve gradient flow. Compare them systematically.

(a) Write the LSTM cell state update and the ResNet residual block side by side. Identify the structural parallel. (b) The LSTM has a learnable gate ft\mathbf{f}_tft​ controlling the skip connection; the ResNet has a fixed identity skip. Why does the LSTM need the gate but the ResNet does not? (c) Could you add a learnable gate to the ResNet skip connection (y=g(x)⊙F(x)+(1−g(x))⊙x\mathbf{y} = g(\mathbf{x}) \odot \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + (1 - g(\mathbf{x})) \odot \mathbf{x}y=g(x)⊙F(x)+(1−g(x))⊙x)? This is called a **Highway Network** (Srivastava et al., 2015). Why did Highway Networks fail to match ResNet's performance?

Answer

**(a)** LSTM: ct=ft⊙ct−1+it⊙c~t\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_tct​=ft​⊙ct−1​+it​⊙c~t​ (gated skip + gated update). ResNet: y=x+F(x)\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} + \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})y=x+F(x) (identity skip + learned residual). Both have the form: output = (fraction of old input) + (new information). The skip path provides a gradient highway; the update path provides new computation.

**(b)** The LSTM processes **sequences** where different time steps may require different retention behavior: "remember the subject until the verb appears, then forget." The gate ft\mathbf{f}_tft​ is data-dependent — it decides what to keep based on the input at each step. The ResNet processes **spatial features** at a fixed depth: the skip connection's purpose is always the same (bypass an unhelpful transformation). There is no temporal variation requiring different skip behavior at different layers. A fixed identity is the correct default: if a layer is useless, F(x)≈0\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) \approx 0F(x)≈0 and the input passes through unchanged.

**(c)** Highway Networks add exactly this gate. They underperformed ResNets for two reasons: (1) The gate g(x)g(\mathbf{x})g(x) adds parameters and computation without clear benefit — the model must learn to set g≈0.5g \approx 0.5g≈0.5 (half skip, half transform) at most layers, wasting capacity on learning a near-constant. (2) The gate can **block** the skip connection: if g(x)≈1g(\mathbf{x}) \approx 1g(x)≈1, no skip occurs and gradients vanish. ResNet's fixed identity skip **guarantees** gradient flow by construction, requiring no learning. The lesson: when the skip connection should always be present, making it learnable adds complexity without benefit and introduces a failure mode.

## Chapter 12: Paper Close Read — Long Short-Term Memory (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997)

> **Chapter Learning Objectives**

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  1. Describe the intellectual context of the LSTM paper: why RNNs were nearly abandoned in 1997 and what problem the paper set out to solve.
  2. State the constant error flow requirement precisely and derive why additive self-connections satisfy it.
  3. Reconstruct the derivation of the cell state update from first principles.
  4. Trace the historical evolution: original 1997 LSTM (no forget gate) → Gers et al. (2000) with forget gate → modern LSTM.
  5. Apply the gradient analysis from Chapter 11 to the LSTM cell, quantifying the improvement in gradient retention over a vanilla RNN.
  6. Compare LSTM and GRU across five dimensions: state variables, gate count, parameter count, coupled vs. independent control, and expressive power.
  7. Identify the three residual limitations of gated RNNs and explain which each motivates.

* * *

### 12.1 Historical Context: The Second Winter

#### 12.1.1 The State of Sequence Modeling in 1997

Long Short-Term Memory (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) was published in _Neural Computation_ at one of the lowest points in the history of neural networks. The community had absorbed two years earlier (Bengio et al., 1994) the formal proof that gradient-based learning was fundamentally unable to capture long-range temporal dependencies in standard RNNs. The response was largely abandonment: by 1997, support vector machines, hidden Markov models, and other non-gradient-based methods dominated sequence modeling research.

Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's paper was, at the time, almost entirely ignored. Hochreiter had analyzed the vanishing gradient problem in his 1991 diploma thesis — five years before the paper. The paper would wait a decade for wide recognition, rediscovered when deep learning began producing record-breaking results on tasks like speech recognition (2011) and machine translation (2013–2014) that depended critically on LSTM-based architectures.

The paper is 42 pages long. Its contribution is not the empirical results (which, by today's standards, are small-scale) but its **precise mathematical diagnosis** of what fails and **rigorous construction** of an architecture that, by design, does not fail.

#### 12.1.2 The Paper's Central Question

The opening of the paper is explicit:

> "Recurrent networks or 'simple recurrent networks' suffer from fundamental difficulties with learning to bridge long time lags. Theoretical analysis revealed two problems: (1) the exploding gradient problem and (2) the vanishing gradient problem."

The central question: **Is it possible to design a recurrent architecture that provably avoids the vanishing gradient problem — not as an approximation or with particular initialization, but structurally, by construction?**

The answer is yes, and the construction is the LSTM.

* * *

### 12.2 The Constant Error Flow Analysis

#### 12.2.1 The Requirement

Chapter 11 derived that the gradient product for a vanilla RNN is:

∂hT∂hk=∏t=k+1TDtWh\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_k} = \prod_{t=k+1}^{T} \mathbf{D}_t \mathbf{W}_h∂hk​∂hT​​=t=k+1∏T​Dt​Wh​

where Dt=diag(f′(zt))\mathbf{D}_t = \text{diag}(f'(\mathbf{z}_t))Dt​=diag(f′(zt​)). This product decays exponentially when the spectral radius of DtWh\mathbf{D}_t \mathbf{W}_hDt​Wh​ is less than 1.

Hochreiter and Schmidhuber asked: what minimal modification makes ∂sj(t)/∂sj(t−1)=1\partial s_j(t) / \partial s_j(t-1) = 1∂sj​(t)/∂sj​(t−1)=1 for all ttt? (Here sjs_jsj​ denotes the state of unit jjj.)

**Answer** : replace the multiplicative update sj(t)=fj(⋯ )s_j(t) = f_j(\cdots)sj​(t)=fj​(⋯) with an additive self-connection:

sj(t)=sj(t−1)+gj(⋯ )s_j(t) = s_j(t-1) + g_j(\cdots)sj​(t)=sj​(t−1)+gj​(⋯)

For this structure: ∂sj(t)/∂sj(t−1)=1\partial s_j(t) / \partial s_j(t-1) = 1∂sj​(t)/∂sj​(t−1)=1 identically, for every step and every value of sjs_jsj​. The gradient from any time step flows back to any earlier step with no attenuation at all.

This is the **constant error flow** condition — the mathematical foundation of the LSTM.

#### 12.2.2 From CEC to the Cell State

A pure additive self-connection ct=ct−1+gtc_t = c_{t-1} + g_tct​=ct−1​+gt​ satisfies the constant error flow condition but has two problems:

**Problem 1: No forgetting.** The state accumulates indefinitely. Old, irrelevant information is never cleared. A language model reading "The cat sat on the mat. The dog barked at..." should be able to forget that the previous subject was "cat" once a new subject "dog" appears.

**Problem 2: No input control.** Every new input gtg_tgt​ is unconditionally added. The model cannot decide that some inputs are irrelevant and should not modify the state.

**Solution** : introduce multiplicative gates to control the additive update:

ct=ft⋅ct−1+it⋅c~tc_t = f_t \cdot c_{t-1} + i_t \cdot \tilde{c}_tct​=ft​⋅ct−1​+it​⋅c~t​

where ft,it∈(0,1)f_t, i_t \in (0, 1)ft​,it​∈(0,1) are learned gate activations (one for "how much to forget," one for "how much to write"). This is the cell state equation of the modern LSTM. When ft=1f_t = 1ft​=1 and it=0i_t = 0it​=0, the state is preserved exactly and ∂ct/∂ct−1=1\partial c_t / \partial c_{t-1} = 1∂ct​/∂ct−1​=1. When ft=0f_t = 0ft​=0, the state is cleared — and the gradient is also cleared, which is correct: if information was intentionally discarded at time ttt, there is no meaningful gradient to propagate through that step.

#### 12.2.3 Historical Note: The Forget Gate

The original 1997 paper did not include a forget gate. The 1997 LSTM used:

ct=ct−1+it⋅c~tc_t = c_{t-1} + i_t \cdot \tilde{c}_tct​=ct−1​+it​⋅c~t​

(The self-connection has weight exactly 1; no forget gate multiplies it.) This is the pure constant error carousel: the gradient through ctc_tct​ with respect to ct−1c_{t-1}ct−1​ is always exactly 1.

The forget gate ftf_tft​ was introduced by Gers, Schmidhuber, and Cummins (2000), "Learning to Forget: Continual Prediction with LSTM." They observed that certain tasks require resetting the state — for example, in time series with periodic structure, the model must be able to "start fresh" when a new cycle begins. The 1997 LSTM could never truly forget.

All modern implementations (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX) include the forget gate by default. The forget gate can learn ft≈1f_t \approx 1ft​≈1 everywhere (recovering near-constant error flow), so its inclusion is strictly more general than the original design.

* * *

### 12.3 The Complete LSTM: Six Equations from First Principles

#### 12.3.1 Notation

* xt∈Rd\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^dxt​∈Rd: input at time ttt
* ht−1∈Rn\mathbf{h}_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}^nht−1​∈Rn: previous hidden state (LSTM output)
* ct−1∈Rn\mathbf{c}_{t-1} \in \mathbb{R}^nct−1​∈Rn: previous cell state (long-term memory)
* [ht−1;xt]∈Rn+d[\mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \mathbf{x}_t] \in \mathbb{R}^{n+d}[ht−1​;xt​]∈Rn+d: concatenation
* σ(⋅)\sigma(\cdot)σ(⋅): sigmoid function, output in (0,1)(0,1)(0,1)
* ⊙\odot⊙: element-wise multiplication

#### 12.3.2 Equation 1: Forget Gate

ft=σ(Wf[ht−1;xt]+bf)\mathbf{f}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_f [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_f)ft​=σ(Wf​[ht−1​;xt​]+bf​)

**Dimensions** : Wf∈Rn×(n+d)\mathbf{W}_f \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (n+d)}Wf​∈Rn×(n+d), bf∈Rn\mathbf{b}_f \in \mathbb{R}^nbf​∈Rn, ft∈(0,1)n\mathbf{f}_t \in (0,1)^nft​∈(0,1)n.

**Role** : ft,jf_{t,j}ft,j​ is the fraction of cell state dimension jjj to retain. ft,j≈1f_{t,j} \approx 1ft,j​≈1: keep this memory. ft,j≈0f_{t,j} \approx 0ft,j​≈0: erase this memory.

**Linguistic example** : encountering the word "but" in "The thesis argued X, but the data showed Y." The forget gate should reduce the weight of the previous argument XXX in preparation for the contrasting claim YYY.

#### 12.3.3 Equation 2: Input Gate

it=σ(Wi[ht−1;xt]+bi)\mathbf{i}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_i [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_i)it​=σ(Wi​[ht−1​;xt​]+bi​)

**Role** : it,ji_{t,j}it,j​ is the fraction of the candidate new information to write to dimension jjj. it,j≈1i_{t,j} \approx 1it,j​≈1: this new content is important. it,j≈0i_{t,j} \approx 0it,j​≈0: ignore this input.

#### 12.3.4 Equation 3: Candidate Cell State

c~t=tanh⁡(Wc[ht−1;xt]+bc)\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}_c [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_c)c~t​=tanh(Wc​[ht−1​;xt​]+bc​)

**Role** : the proposed update to the cell state. The tanh⁡\tanhtanh keeps values in (−1,1)(-1, 1)(−1,1) — zero-centered, allowing both positive and negative writes. This is the "what would we write if we wrote everything" signal, filtered by the input gate.

**Why tanh⁡\tanhtanh here but σ\sigmaσ for gates?** Gates must be in (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1) to act as "fractions" (interpolation between keeping and discarding). The candidate c~t\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_tc~t​ represents content that can be positive or negative, so tanh⁡\tanhtanh's output in (−1,1)(-1, 1)(−1,1) is appropriate.

#### 12.3.5 Equation 4: Cell State Update (The Core)

ct=ft⊙ct−1+it⊙c~t\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_tct​=ft​⊙ct−1​+it​⊙c~t​

**This is the mathematical heart of the LSTM.** For dimension jjj:

ct,j=ft,j⋅ct−1,j⏟retained memory+it,j⋅c~t,j⏟new writec_{t,j} = \underbrace{f_{t,j} \cdot c_{t-1,j}}_{\text{retained memory}} + \underbrace{i_{t,j} \cdot \tilde{c}_{t,j}}_{\text{new write}}ct,j​=retained memoryft,j​⋅ct−1,j​​​+new writeit,j​⋅c~t,j​​​

The gradient through this equation:

∂ct,j∂ct−1,j≈ft,j\frac{\partial c_{t,j}}{\partial c_{t-1,j}} \approx f_{t,j}∂ct−1,j​∂ct,j​​≈ft,j​

(ignoring second-order terms through the gate dependence on ht−1\mathbf{h}_{t-1}ht−1​, which depends on ct−1\mathbf{c}_{t-1}ct−1​ through the output gate). For long sequences where ft,j≈1f_{t,j} \approx 1ft,j​≈1 sustained:

∂cT,j∂ck,j=∏t=k+1Tft,j≈1T−k=1\frac{\partial c_{T,j}}{\partial c_{k,j}} = \prod_{t=k+1}^{T} f_{t,j} \approx 1^{T-k} = 1∂ck,j​∂cT,j​​=t=k+1∏T​ft,j​≈1T−k=1

The gradient flows unchanged. This is the constant error carousel in practice.

#### 12.3.6 Equation 5: Output Gate

ot=σ(Wo[ht−1;xt]+bo)\mathbf{o}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_o [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_o)ot​=σ(Wo​[ht−1​;xt​]+bo​)

**Role** : controls which parts of the cell state to expose as the hidden state. The cell state ct\mathbf{c}_tct​ holds all accumulated information; the output gate selectively reads relevant parts.

**Linguistic example** : to generate a verb, the model needs to know whether the subject is singular or plural. The output gate activates the "number" dimension of the cell state when a verb slot is being predicted, while potentially suppressing other dimensions (such as specific lexical properties).

#### 12.3.7 Equation 6: Hidden State Output

ht=ot⊙tanh⁡(ct)\mathbf{h}_t = \mathbf{o}_t \odot \tanh(\mathbf{c}_t)ht​=ot​⊙tanh(ct​)

The tanh⁡\tanhtanh maps the cell state from an unbounded range to (−1,1)(-1, 1)(−1,1), normalizing the representation before the output gate filters it. ht\mathbf{h}_tht​ serves two roles: (1) as the current output used to compute y^t\hat{\mathbf{y}}_ty^​t​ and (2) as the recurrent input to the next step's gate computations.

#### 12.3.8 Parameter Count

Four weight matrices (Wf,Wi,Wc,Wo\mathbf{W}_f, \mathbf{W}_i, \mathbf{W}_c, \mathbf{W}_oWf​,Wi​,Wc​,Wo​), each of shape n×(n+d)n \times (n+d)n×(n+d), plus four bias vectors of shape nnn:

LSTM parameters=4n(n+d+1)\text{LSTM parameters} = 4n(n + d + 1)LSTM parameters=4n(n+d+1)

This is exactly 4×4\times4× the parameter count of a vanilla RNN. The additional parameters are the cost of structural memory control.

### 12.4 Quantifying the Improvement

#### 12.4.1 Memory Retention Comparison

Consider the fraction of a signal written at step kkk that survives to step TTT, measured by the gradient magnitude ∣∂cT,j/∂ck,j∣|\partial c_{T,j} / \partial c_{k,j}|∣∂cT,j​/∂ck,j​∣ vs. ∣∂hT,j/∂hk,j∣|\partial h_{T,j} / \partial h_{k,j}|∣∂hT,j​/∂hk,j​∣ for vanilla RNN.

**Vanilla RNN** : per-step factor α=E[f′(zt,j)]⋅∣wh,jj∣≈0.80\alpha = \mathbb{E}[f'(z_{t,j})] \cdot |w_{h,jj}| \approx 0.80α=E[f′(zt,j​)]⋅∣wh,jj​∣≈0.80 (typical).

**LSTM** : per-step factor ≈ft,j\approx f_{t,j}≈ft,j​. With well-initialized forget gate biases (Jozefowicz et al., 2015 recommend initializing bf\mathbf{b}_fbf​ to 1 or 2 so that σ(bf)≈0.73\sigma(\mathbf{b}_f) \approx 0.73σ(bf​)≈0.73 or 0.880.880.88 initially):

Steps | Vanilla RNN (α=0.80\alpha = 0.80α=0.80) | LSTM (ft=0.95f_t = 0.95ft​=0.95) | LSTM (ft=0.99f_t = 0.99ft​=0.99)  
---|---|---|---  
5 | 32.8% | 77.4% | 95.1%  
10 | 10.7% | 59.9% | 90.4%  
20 | 1.2% | 35.8% | 81.8%  
50 | <0.01%< 0.01\%<0.01% | 7.7% | 60.5%  
100 | ≈0\approx 0≈0 | 0.6% | 36.6%  
  
The LSTM with ft=0.99f_t = 0.99ft​=0.99 retains over a third of the gradient signal after 100 steps. The vanilla RNN retains essentially nothing after 50 steps. This is the quantitative demonstration of the LSTM's core advantage.

#### 12.4.2 The Key Insight: Gates Decouple Forgetting from Gradient Flow

In a vanilla RNN, the gradient decay rate is fixed by the weight matrix and activation derivative — not learnable in any useful sense. Making Wh\mathbf{W}_hWh​ satisfy ρ(DtWh)=1\rho(\mathbf{D}_t \mathbf{W}_h) = 1ρ(Dt​Wh​)=1 requires a precise spectral condition that cannot be maintained as weights evolve.

In the LSTM, the gradient decay rate is ftf_tft​ — a function of the current input and previous hidden state. The network can learn to set ft≈1f_t \approx 1ft​≈1 precisely when a particular memory dimension should be preserved, and ft≈0f_t \approx 0ft​≈0 when it should be cleared. The gradient flow is adaptive, not fixed.

* * *

### 12.5 What LSTM Achieved: The Decade of RNN Dominance

#### 12.5.1 Key Applications (2011–2017)

The LSTM's rediscovery coincided with the availability of large datasets and sufficient compute to train them. Between 2011 and 2017, LSTM-based models achieved state-of-the-art results across nearly every sequence modeling benchmark:

**Speech recognition** (Graves et al., 2013): LSTM combined with CTC (Connectionist Temporal Classification) achieved record low word error rates on TIMIT, eventually enabling the commercial speech recognition products (Siri, Google Voice) that reached millions of users.

**Neural machine translation** (Sutskever, Vinyals, Le 2014): LSTM Seq2Seq models achieved near-phrase-based-SMT performance on English-French translation, a benchmark task that symbolic NLP systems had dominated for years. The encoder-decoder framework they introduced remains the standard.

**Language modeling** : Zaremba et al. (2014) showed LSTM language models dramatically outperform n-gram models on Penn Treebank, achieving then-state-of-the-art perplexity.

**Handwriting recognition and generation** : Graves (2013) demonstrated LSTMs could generate realistic handwriting, including continuation in the style of a particular writer.

#### 12.5.2 The Architecture Refinements

The core LSTM from 1997 (plus forget gate from 2000) has undergone several refinements:

**Peephole connections** (Gers & Schmidhuber, 2000): allow the gates to access the cell state directly, not just through ht−1\mathbf{h}_{t-1}ht−1​. Useful when precise timing is important (e.g., detecting exact durations in time series).

**Coupled input and forget gates** : set it=1−fti_t = 1 - f_tit​=1−ft​ instead of computing separate gates. Reduces parameters by n(n+d+1)n(n+d+1)n(n+d+1). Slightly underperforms full LSTM on most tasks.

**Depth** : stacking 2–4 LSTM layers (where the hidden state of layer lll becomes the input to layer l+1l+1l+1) consistently improves performance. Sutskever et al. (2014) used 4 layers. Google's 2016 production translation system used 8.

**Dropout for RNNs** : standard spatial dropout applied to RNN inputs works; applying it to the recurrent connection ht−1→ht\mathbf{h}_{t-1} \to \mathbf{h}_tht−1​→ht​ destroys long-range memory. Variational Dropout (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016) uses the same mask at every time step, preserving temporal structure.

* * *

### 12.6 The GRU: A Streamlined Alternative

#### 12.6.1 Design Philosophy

Cho et al. (2014) introduced the Gated Recurrent Unit as part of the Seq2Seq translation system. The GRU asks: can we achieve LSTM-level performance with fewer parameters and a single state vector?

The two key simplifications:

  1. **Merge cell state and hidden state** : the single vector ht\mathbf{h}_tht​ serves both roles.
  2. **Couple forget and input gates** : instead of independent ftf_tft​ and iti_tit​, use a single update gate ztz_tzt​ with the constraint that the fractions retained and updated sum to 1.

ht=(1−zt)⊙ht−1+zt⊙h~t\mathbf{h}_t = (1 - \mathbf{z}_t) \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{z}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_tht​=(1−zt​)⊙ht−1​+zt​⊙h~t​

This is a **convex combination** of the previous state and the candidate. (1−zt)(1-z_t)(1−zt​) is the retention fraction and ztz_tzt​ is the update fraction; they always sum to 1. This eliminates one weight matrix compared to the LSTM.

#### 12.6.2 The Reset Gate

The reset gate rt\mathbf{r}_trt​ modifies the candidate computation:

h~t=tanh⁡(W[rt⊙ht−1;xt]+b)\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}[\mathbf{r}_t \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b})h~t​=tanh(W[rt​⊙ht−1​;xt​]+b)

When rt≈0\mathbf{r}_t \approx 0rt​≈0: the candidate is computed without reference to history (rt⊙ht−1≈0\mathbf{r}_t \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1} \approx \mathbf{0}rt​⊙ht−1​≈0). The GRU starts fresh. This allows the model to learn when the past is irrelevant to the current step's candidate.

When rt≈1\mathbf{r}_t \approx 1rt​≈1: the full previous hidden state contributes to the candidate, like a vanilla RNN step.

#### 12.6.3 Complete GRU Equations

zt=σ(Wz[ht−1;xt]+bz)(Update gate)\mathbf{z}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_z [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_z) \tag{Update gate}zt​=σ(Wz​[ht−1​;xt​]+bz​)(Update gate) rt=σ(Wr[ht−1;xt]+br)(Reset gate)\mathbf{r}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_r [\mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_r) \tag{Reset gate}rt​=σ(Wr​[ht−1​;xt​]+br​)(Reset gate) h~t=tanh⁡(W[rt⊙ht−1;xt]+b)(Candidate)\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}[\mathbf{r}_t \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1}; \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}) \tag{Candidate}h~t​=tanh(W[rt​⊙ht−1​;xt​]+b)(Candidate) ht=(1−zt)⊙ht−1+zt⊙h~t(Update)\mathbf{h}_t = (1 - \mathbf{z}_t) \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{z}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t \tag{Update}ht​=(1−zt​)⊙ht−1​+zt​⊙h~t​(Update)

**Parameters** : 3n(n+d+1)3n(n + d + 1)3n(n+d+1) — 75% of the LSTM's 4n(n+d+1)4n(n+d+1)4n(n+d+1).

**Gradient through update** : ∂ht/∂ht−1≈diag(1−zt)\partial \mathbf{h}_t / \partial \mathbf{h}_{t-1} \approx \text{diag}(1 - \mathbf{z}_t)∂ht​/∂ht−1​≈diag(1−zt​) — same structure as LSTM's diag(ft)\text{diag}(\mathbf{f}_t)diag(ft​). When zt≈0z_t \approx 0zt​≈0 (retain mode), (1−zt)≈1(1-z_t) \approx 1(1−zt​)≈1, giving near-perfect gradient flow — exactly as ft≈1f_t \approx 1ft​≈1 in the LSTM. The GRU achieves the same gradient stability through the same mechanism.

#### 12.6.4 LSTM vs. GRU: Structured Comparison

Dimension | LSTM | GRU  
---|---|---  
State variables | ct\mathbf{c}_tct​ (cell) + ht\mathbf{h}_tht​ (hidden) | ht\mathbf{h}_tht​ only  
Gate count | 3 (forget, input, output) | 2 (update, reset)  
Parameters | 4n(n+d+1)4n(n+d+1)4n(n+d+1) | 3n(n+d+1)3n(n+d+1)3n(n+d+1)  
Forget/write coupling | Independent (ftf_tft​ and iti_tit​ are separate) | Coupled (ztz_tzt​ \+ (1−zt)=1(1-z_t) = 1(1−zt​)=1)  
Can simultaneously retain and write | Yes (ft≈1f_t \approx 1ft​≈1, it≈1i_t \approx 1it​≈1 simultaneously) | No (retaining more ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ writing less)  
Gradient stability mechanism | ftf_tft​ acts as per-step gradient scalar | (1−zt)(1-z_t)(1−zt​) acts as per-step gradient scalar  
Expressive power | Strictly richer | Slightly less  
Empirical performance | Similar | Similar  
  
**Critical difference in coupled control** : the LSTM can have ft≈1f_t \approx 1ft​≈1 (retain everything) AND it≈1i_t \approx 1it​≈1 (write a lot of new information), causing the cell state magnitude to grow. This "accumulation" mode is impossible in the GRU: if zt≈0z_t \approx 0zt​≈0 (retain everything, so 1−zt≈11-z_t \approx 11−zt​≈1), then zt≈0z_t \approx 0zt​≈0 (write almost nothing of the new candidate). Conversely, if zt≈1z_t \approx 1zt​≈1 (update fully), then (1−zt)≈0(1-z_t) \approx 0(1−zt​)≈0 (retain almost nothing). The GRU cannot simultaneously retain and write heavily. For tasks requiring accumulation of evidence over many steps without discarding old evidence, LSTM has an architectural advantage.

### 12.7 What the LSTM Left Unresolved

#### 12.7.1 Sequential Computation

The LSTM processes one time step at a time. Computing ht\mathbf{h}_tht​ requires ht−1\mathbf{h}_{t-1}ht−1​, which requires ht−2\mathbf{h}_{t-2}ht−2​. The computation over a sequence of length TTT requires exactly TTT serial steps — no matter how many parallel compute units are available.

For T=512T = 512T=512 (a short paragraph), this is a bottleneck. For T=10,000T = 10{,}000T=10,000 (a long document), training is impractically slow. GPUs are designed for massive parallelism; a sequential computation of length 10,000 uses only a tiny fraction of their capacity.

This is fundamentally different from CNNs, where all spatial positions can be processed simultaneously.

#### 12.7.2 Residual Long-Range Decay

Even with ft=0.99f_t = 0.99ft​=0.99 per step, 500 steps of gradient decay leaves only 0.99500≈0.0070.99^{500} \approx 0.0070.99500≈0.007 — less than 1% of the original signal. Information at step 1 has negligible gradient influence on events at step 500.

Empirically, LSTMs handle dependencies of 200–300 steps effectively. For long-document tasks (e.g., reasoning over a 10,000-word context), even gated recurrence is insufficient.

#### 12.7.3 Fixed Context Capacity

The hidden state hT∈Rn\mathbf{h}_T \in \mathbb{R}^nhT​∈Rn or cell state cT∈Rn\mathbf{c}_T \in \mathbb{R}^ncT​∈Rn must encode all task-relevant information from a sequence of any length. For a 200-word sentence with n=512n = 512n=512, this is reasonable. For a 5,000-word document, every piece of relevant information must fit in 512 numbers — a severe constraint.

These three limitations led directly to the attention mechanism (Part V) and the Transformer (Part VI). The attention mechanism solves the fixed context capacity by allowing the decoder to directly access any encoder hidden state. The Transformer eliminates sequential computation entirely by replacing recurrence with parallel self-attention.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> **Finite automata, working memory in cognitive science, and the Chomsky hierarchy** : The LSTM's computational limitations have formal analogs in theoretical computer science and cognitive science. In **formal language theory** , finite automata (including RNNs) can in principle recognize any regular language but require exponentially large state spaces for certain context-free constructs. The LSTM's fixed hidden dimension limits the "stack depth" it can emulate — it can approximate push-down automata behavior for shallow depths but fails for deeply nested structures. In **cognitive science** , Baddeley's working memory model distinguishes the phonological loop (short-term verbal rehearsal), the visuospatial sketchpad, and the central executive — with each component having finite capacity. The LSTM's fixed-size cell state is a precise computational analog: finite capacity working memory that must be actively managed (via gates) to avoid overflow. In **information theory** , the data processing inequality places a fundamental limit: no matter how sophisticated the processing, the mutual information between the final hidden state and any subset of the input sequence can never exceed the hidden state's entropy bound of nlog⁡2(∣range∣)n \log_2(|\text{range}|)nlog2​(∣range∣) bits. The LSTM respects this bound; the Transformer escapes it by maintaining direct access to all input positions rather than compressing them.

* * *

### 12.8 The Reading Protocol

This is the second paper close read in the series. The reading protocol from Chapter 9 applies:

**Step 1: Historical context.** LSTM was published in 1997, largely ignored for a decade, and became dominant from ~2012 to ~2017. The timing matters: the paper solved a problem that would only become economically important when scale (data + compute) arrived.

**Step 2: Central question.** Can a recurrent architecture provably avoid vanishing gradients? The answer required mathematical derivation (the CEC analysis), not just empirical tuning.

**Step 3: Key innovation.** The cell state with additive updates, gated by sigmoid functions. Not gradient clipping (which addresses explosion, not vanishing), not initialization tricks (which maintain spectral radius only at the start), but a structural change that makes stable gradient flow the architectural default.

**Step 4: Experiments.** The original paper tested on synthetic benchmarks designed to require long-range memory (tasks with minimum time lags of 100+ steps). These are not the tasks LSTM became famous for — they were designed to demonstrate the specific failure mode being fixed.

**Step 5: What remains unresolved.** Sequential computation bottleneck. Residual long-range decay. Fixed context capacity. These are not failures of the 1997 paper — they are different problems that the paper did not claim to solve. The Transformer addresses all three.

* * *

### 12.9 Chapter Summary

The LSTM was designed by asking: what mathematical structure guarantees constant error flow — gradient propagation with no attenuation over arbitrary distances? The answer was an additive self-connection for the cell state, with multiplicative gates controlling what is written, retained, and read.

The forget gate (Gers et al., 2000) added the capacity to selectively discard information, producing the modern LSTM: six equations, 4n(n+d+1)4n(n+d+1)4n(n+d+1) parameters, and gradient flow that depends on the learned forget gate values rather than fixed architectural constants.

The GRU (Cho et al., 2014) achieves comparable gradient stability with 25% fewer parameters by coupling the forget and write decisions (update gate) and eliminating the separate cell state. For most tasks, LSTM and GRU performance is similar; the LSTM has an architectural advantage for tasks requiring simultaneous accumulation and retention.

Three limitations remain unsolved by any gated RNN: sequential computation that cannot be parallelized across time, residual long-range gradient decay (even with ft≈0.99f_t \approx 0.99ft​≈0.99, 500-step sequences lose 99% of the gradient), and a fixed-capacity state vector that cannot scale with sequence length. These limitations are the direct motivation for the attention mechanism and the Transformer, developed in Parts V and VI.

For the vanilla RNN (scalar case for simplicity): ht=tanh⁡(whht−1+wxxt+b)h_t = \tanh(w_h h_{t-1} + w_x x_t + b)ht​=tanh(wh​ht−1​+wx​xt​+b), so ∂ht/∂ht−1=wh⋅tanh⁡′(whht−1+⋯ )\partial h_t / \partial h_{t-1} = w_h \cdot \tanh'(w_h h_{t-1} + \cdots)∂ht​/∂ht−1​=wh​⋅tanh′(wh​ht−1​+⋯).

For this to equal 1 for all ttt and all ht−1h_{t-1}ht−1​, we need wh⋅tanh⁡′(zt)=1w_h \cdot \tanh'(z_t) = 1wh​⋅tanh′(zt​)=1 for all values of ztz_tzt​. But tanh⁡′(zt)=1−tanh⁡2(zt)<1\tanh'(z_t) = 1 - \tanh^2(z_t) < 1tanh′(zt​)=1−tanh2(zt​)<1 for all zt≠0z_t \neq 0zt​=0, and tanh⁡′(zt)→0\tanh'(z_t) \to 0tanh′(zt​)→0 as ∣zt∣→∞|z_t| \to \infty∣zt​∣→∞. So the condition would require wh=1/tanh⁡′(zt)w_h = 1/\tanh'(z_t)wh​=1/tanh′(zt​), which varies with ztz_tzt​ — it cannot be a fixed weight. No constant whw_hwh​ can make this true universally. □\square□

**2.** The original 1997 LSTM had no forget gate. What would ct\mathbf{c}_tct​ simplify to, and what are the consequences for (a) long-term memory retention and (b) gradient flow?

Answer

Without a forget gate: ct=ct−1+it⊙c~t\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_tct​=ct−1​+it​⊙c~t​ (the forget gate multiplier is absent or set to 1).

(a) **Memory retention** : information is never discarded. The cell state can only grow in magnitude (each write adds to it). For tasks where old context is irrelevant (e.g., detecting the beginning of a new topic), the accumulated cell state pollutes the representation with stale information. The model has no mechanism to "start fresh."

(b) **Gradient flow** : ∂ct/∂ct−1≈I\partial \mathbf{c}_t / \partial \mathbf{c}_{t-1} \approx \mathbf{I}∂ct​/∂ct−1​≈I (identity matrix, since the constant self-connection weight is 1). This gives perfect gradient preservation: ∂cT,j/∂ck,j=1\partial c_{T,j} / \partial c_{k,j} = 1∂cT,j​/∂ck,j​=1 for all T>kT > kT>k. The gradient flow is ideal — but at the cost of no forgetting. The addition of the forget gate trades perfect gradient preservation for learnable gradient preservation.

**3.** The GRU uses the constraint ht=(1−zt)⊙ht−1+zt⊙h~th_t = (1-z_t) \odot h_{t-1} + z_t \odot \tilde{h}_tht​=(1−zt​)⊙ht−1​+zt​⊙h~t​. Can the GRU achieve a state where it simultaneously retains 90% of its old state AND adds 90% of a new candidate? Can the LSTM achieve this? What is the implication for sequence tasks?

Answer

**GRU** : No. Retaining 90% of the old state requires (1−zt)=0.9(1-z_t) = 0.9(1−zt​)=0.9, i.e., zt=0.1z_t = 0.1zt​=0.1, which means only zt=0.1z_t = 0.1zt​=0.1 (10%) of the new candidate is added. Simultaneously adding 90% of the new candidate would require zt=0.9z_t = 0.9zt​=0.9, which contradicts zt=0.1z_t = 0.1zt​=0.1 — impossible.

**LSTM** : Yes. If ft=0.9f_t = 0.9ft​=0.9 (retain 90% of old cell state) and it=0.9i_t = 0.9it​=0.9 (add 90% of candidate), then ct=0.9ct−1+0.9c~tc_t = 0.9 c_{t-1} + 0.9 \tilde{c}_tct​=0.9ct−1​+0.9c~t​. The cell state magnitude grows to 0.9∣ct−1∣+0.9∣c~t∣0.9 |c_{t-1}| + 0.9 |\tilde{c}_t|0.9∣ct−1​∣+0.9∣c~t​∣, which may exceed ∣ct−1∣|c_{t-1}|∣ct−1​∣. The tanh⁡(ct)\tanh(c_t)tanh(ct​) in the hidden state output normalizes this, but within the cell, accumulation is possible.

**Implication** : for tasks requiring evidence accumulation (counting occurrences, building up evidence over many steps before deciding), the LSTM has an expressive advantage over the GRU. The GRU's budget constraint — retain + update = 1 — prevents accumulation modes.

#### Application

**4.** A sequence contains a rare triggering event at step k=10k = 10k=10, and the model must produce a correct response at step T=110T = 110T=110 (100 steps later). Compare the fraction of gradient information that flows from step 110 back to step 10 for:

(a) Vanilla RNN with α=0.85\alpha = 0.85α=0.85 per step. (b) LSTM with ft,j=0.97f_{t,j} = 0.97ft,j​=0.97 for the relevant dimension. (c) LSTM with ft,j=0.99f_{t,j} = 0.99ft,j​=0.99 for the relevant dimension.

Answer

Signal retention from step 10 to step 110 = 100 steps.

(a) Vanilla RNN: 0.85100≈8.7×10−80.85^{100} \approx 8.7 \times 10^{-8}0.85100≈8.7×10−8. Essentially zero — the event at step 10 contributes negligibly to the gradient at step 110.

(b) LSTM with f=0.97f = 0.97f=0.97: 0.97100≈0.0480.97^{100} \approx 0.0480.97100≈0.048. About 4.8% of the gradient signal survives — small but nonzero and learnable.

(c) LSTM with f=0.99f = 0.99f=0.99: 0.99100≈0.3660.99^{100} \approx 0.3660.99100≈0.366. About 36.6% of the gradient survives — enough to learn the long-range dependency reliably.

These numbers explain why the forget gate bias initialization matters: initializing bf\mathbf{b}_fbf​ to a large positive value (e.g., 1.0 or 2.0) ensures ft≈σ(1)=0.73f_t \approx \sigma(1) = 0.73ft​≈σ(1)=0.73 or σ(2)=0.88\sigma(2) = 0.88σ(2)=0.88 initially, rather than σ(0)=0.5\sigma(0) = 0.5σ(0)=0.5. The higher initial forget gate reduces gradient decay even before the network has learned the task.

**5.** Verify the parameter count formula for an LSTM with n=256n = 256n=256 (hidden), d=128d = 128d=128 (input). Write down the shape of each weight matrix and bias vector, count all parameters, and confirm against 4n(n+d+1)4n(n+d+1)4n(n+d+1).

Answer

Each gate/candidate uses a weight matrix W∈Rn×(n+d)\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (n+d)}W∈Rn×(n+d) and bias b∈Rn\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^nb∈Rn.

For n=256n = 256n=256, d=128d = 128d=128: each W\mathbf{W}W has shape 256×384256 \times 384256×384, giving 256×384=98,304256 \times 384 = 98{,}304256×384=98,304 weights, plus 256256256 bias terms = 98,56098{,}56098,560 per gate/candidate.

Four components (forget, input, candidate, output): 4×98,560=394,2404 \times 98{,}560 = 394{,}2404×98,560=394,240.

**Check** : 4n(n+d+1)=4×256×(256+128+1)=4×256×385=4×98,560=394,2404n(n+d+1) = 4 \times 256 \times (256 + 128 + 1) = 4 \times 256 \times 385 = 4 \times 98{,}560 = 394{,}2404n(n+d+1)=4×256×(256+128+1)=4×256×385=4×98,560=394,240. ✓\checkmark✓

**8.** Compare the parameter counts of an LSTM and a GRU with the same hidden dimension n=512n = 512n=512 and input dimension d=256d = 256d=256.

(a) Compute the LSTM parameter count using 4n(n+d+1)4n(n + d + 1)4n(n+d+1). (b) Compute the GRU parameter count using 3n(n+d+1)3n(n + d + 1)3n(n+d+1). (c) What is the parameter ratio GRU/LSTM? What does the GRU "save" by having 3 gates instead of 4? (d) Despite having 25% fewer parameters, GRUs often match LSTM performance on many benchmarks. What architectural property might explain this efficiency?

Answer

**(a)** LSTM: 4×512×(512+256+1)=4×512×769=1,574,912≈1.57M4 \times 512 \times (512 + 256 + 1) = 4 \times 512 \times 769 = 1{,}574{,}912 \approx 1.57M4×512×(512+256+1)=4×512×769=1,574,912≈1.57M.

**(b)** GRU: 3×512×(512+256+1)=3×512×769=1,181,184≈1.18M3 \times 512 \times (512 + 256 + 1) = 3 \times 512 \times 769 = 1{,}181{,}184 \approx 1.18M3×512×(512+256+1)=3×512×769=1,181,184≈1.18M.

**(c)** Ratio: 3/4=0.753/4 = 0.753/4=0.75. The GRU saves exactly 25% of parameters by eliminating the output gate and its associated weight matrices. Specifically, the GRU merges the forget and input gates into a single update gate (ztz_tzt​) with the constraint retain+update=1\text{retain} + \text{update} = 1retain+update=1, and eliminates the separate output gate entirely (exposing the full hidden state).

**(d)** The GRU's coupled update gate (1−zt1 - z_t1−zt​ for retention, ztz_tzt​ for update) acts as a regularizer: it prevents the network from independently setting both high retention and high update (which would cause cell state explosion in the LSTM). This built-in constraint reduces the effective hypothesis space, which can improve generalization with limited data. Additionally, with fewer parameters per step, the GRU has a smaller per-step computational cost, allowing more training iterations in the same wall-clock time. For tasks where the LSTM's independent gating (simultaneous high forget and high input) is not needed, the GRU's simpler parameterization is sufficient and potentially better-regularized.

#### Think Deeper

**6.** The LSTM paper was largely ignored for a decade after publication. Identify the three external conditions that had to change before LSTMs could fulfill their potential, and explain what changed in each case around 2011–2013.

Answer

**(1) Training data scale.** In 1997, labeled sequence datasets were small (TIMIT speech corpus: ~4 hours; machine translation corpora: a few million sentence pairs). The LSTM's advantage over shallow models is most pronounced on long sequences with complex long-range dependencies — and learning these requires large amounts of data. By 2011–2013, ImageNet-scale datasets existed for vision, and hundred-million-sentence parallel corpora existed for translation.

**(2) Computational infrastructure (GPUs).** Training deep LSTMs on long sequences requires massive floating point operations. In 1997, CPU-based training of a 2-layer LSTM on a medium dataset could take weeks. The GPU computing revolution (CUDA, 2007; commodity GPU clusters, ~2010) reduced training time by 10–100×, making iterative experimentation possible.

**(3) Algorithmic improvements.** Several improvements to the basic LSTM made it reliably trainable: (a) the forget gate (Gers et al., 2000) — without it, cell states grow unboundedly; (b) proper dropout for RNNs (Zaremba et al., 2014); (c) proper forget gate bias initialization (Jozefowicz et al., 2015); (d) gradient clipping (Pascanu et al., 2013). Together these transformed the LSTM from a theoretically sound but practically finicky architecture into a robust workhorse.

**7.** The Transformer (Chapter 21) addresses all three limitations of gated RNNs. For each limitation — (a) sequential computation, (b) residual long-range decay, (c) fixed context capacity — identify the specific Transformer component that resolves it and explain the mechanism in one sentence.

Answer

(a) **Sequential computation → self-attention**. In self-attention, the output at every position is computed simultaneously as a weighted sum over all input positions — no recurrence, so all positions can be processed in parallel.

(b) **Residual long-range decay → direct attention connections**. Self-attention computes direct weighted sums between any two positions regardless of distance: the attention weight between position 1 and position 500 is computed via a single matrix product, with no intervening multiplicative decay.

(c) **Fixed context capacity → full key-value memory**. Instead of compressing the entire input into a single fixed-size vector, the Transformer stores all TTT encoder representations (keys and values) and allows the decoder to attend to any subset at each step, with total available context scaling as O(T)O(T)O(T) rather than O(n)O(n)O(n).
