## Chapter 13: The Representational Problem — From One-Hot to Distributed Semantics

### 13.1 Why Sequences Alone Are Not Enough

The previous three chapters developed powerful machinery for processing sequential data. RNNs can in principle maintain arbitrary state across time steps; LSTMs solved the gradient problem that prevented learning long-range dependencies. Yet all of this temporal reasoning rests on a foundation we have so far taken for granted: the input representation itself.

Consider the word _equity_. How should a neural network represent it as input? The simplest answer is: assign each word in the vocabulary a unique integer index, then convert that index to a vector using one-hot encoding. If the vocabulary has V=50,000V = 50{,}000V=50,000 words and _equity_ is word number 8,4328{,}4328,432, its representation is a vector in R50000\mathbb{R}^{50000}R50000 that is zero everywhere except position 8,4328{,}4328,432.

This representation is _correct_ in the narrow sense that it uniquely identifies the word. But it is catastrophically uninformative. Two synonyms — _equity_ and _stock_ — are represented by vectors that are perfectly orthogonal:

⟨vequity,vstock⟩=0\langle \mathbf{v}_{\text{equity}}, \mathbf{v}_{\text{stock}} \rangle = 0⟨vequity​,vstock​⟩=0

But so are two words with no semantic relation whatsoever:

⟨vequity,vbanana⟩=0\langle \mathbf{v}_{\text{equity}}, \mathbf{v}_{\text{banana}} \rangle = 0⟨vequity​,vbanana​⟩=0

The representation encodes the index of the word — nothing more. All semantic relationships are invisible. A neural network processing these vectors must _learn_ even the most basic synonymy from scratch, on every new task, from whatever supervision signal is available.

This chapter examines the representational problem in depth, develops the theoretical foundation for dense word representations, and traces the path from bag-of-words models through co-occurrence statistics to Pointwise Mutual Information and Latent Semantic Analysis — the direct predecessors of Word2Vec and GloVe, which Chapter 14 will examine as landmark papers.

> **Chapter Learning Objectives**
> 
> By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
> 
>   1. Explain why one-hot encoding fails to capture semantic similarity and identify its four specific limitations.
>   2. State the distributional hypothesis and explain its computational formalization via context windows.
>   3. Construct a word-word co-occurrence matrix from a small corpus and compute TF-IDF weights.
>   4. Define Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) and PPMI, and explain why PPMI is preferred over raw counts.
>   5. Explain how truncated SVD (LSA) produces dense word representations from sparse co-occurrence matrices.
>   6. Articulate the four desirable properties of a word representation system (compactness, semantic geometry, algebraic structure, transferability).
> 

* * *

### 13.2 The Distributional Hypothesis

The foundation for all modern word representations is a deceptively simple observation, articulated by J.R. Firth in 1957:

> **"You shall know a word by the company it keeps."**
> 
> — J.R. Firth, _A Synopsis of Linguistic Theory_ , 1957

This observation — the **distributional hypothesis** — asserts that words occurring in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. The intuition is intuitive: _doctor_ and _physician_ appear in similar contexts (sentences about hospitals, patients, treatment); _doctor_ and _asteroid_ do not. If we can somehow encode the statistical patterns of contextual co-occurrence, we can build representations that capture semantic similarity without manual annotation.

The distributional hypothesis is more than intuition. It connects to profound ideas in information theory and cognitive science. But let us first be precise about what it means computationally.

**Definition.** Given a text corpus, the **context** of a word www at position iii is the set of words appearing within a window of size kkk around position iii:

Context(w,i)={wi−k,…,wi−1,wi+1,…,wi+k}\text{Context}(w, i) = \\{w_{i-k}, \ldots, w_{i-1}, w_{i+1}, \ldots, w_{i+k}\\}Context(w,i)={wi−k​,…,wi−1​,wi+1​,…,wi+k​}

The distributional hypothesis says: words that share many context words tend to be semantically related.

**Example.** In a large corpus, both _doctor_ and _physician_ frequently appear near: _hospital_ , _patient_ , _treatment_ , _diagnosis_ , _prescription_ , _nurse_ , _surgery_. Their context distributions are similar. Meanwhile, _doctor_ and _banana_ share almost no context words. A representation that captures this statistical structure would naturally place _doctor_ and _physician_ close together and _doctor_ and _banana_ far apart.

* * *

### 13.3 The Failure of Sparse Representations

Before developing dense representations, it is worth understanding precisely why sparse representations fail.

#### 13.3.1 One-Hot Encoding

One-hot encoding represents word wiw_iwi​ as a standard basis vector ei∈RV\mathbf{e}_i \in \mathbb{R}^Vei​∈RV. Given a vocabulary of size VVV, we have:

vwi=ei=[0,…,0,1⏟i,0,…,0]⊤∈RV\mathbf{v}_{w_i} = \mathbf{e}_i = [0, \ldots, 0, \underbrace{1}_{i}, 0, \ldots, 0]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^Vvwi​​=ei​=[0,…,0,i1​​,0,…,0]⊤∈RV

**Problems:**

  1. **No similarity structure.** For any i≠ji \neq ji=j: ⟨ei,ej⟩=0\langle \mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j \rangle = 0⟨ei​,ej​⟩=0. All pairs of distinct words are equidistant. The geometry encodes no semantics.

  2. **Dimensionality explosion.** Modern vocabularies contain V≈50,000V \approx 50{,}000V≈50,000 to 500,000500{,}000500,000 words. Storing a one-hot vector for every token in a billion-word corpus is computationally and spatially prohibitive.

  3. **No generalization.** A model trained to recognize that _the doctor administered the medication_ contains medical content must learn separately that _the physician administered the medication_ means the same thing — the representations share no information.

  4. **Sparsity.** Each vector is 99.998% zeros. Most neural network operations are wasted on multiplying by zero.

#### 13.3.2 Bag of Words

The **Bag-of-Words (BOW)** model represents a document as the unordered multiset of its words — a frequency count vector:

d=[c1,c2,…,cV]⊤\mathbf{d} = [c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_V]^\topd=[c1​,c2​,…,cV​]⊤

where cic_ici​ is the count of word wiw_iwi​ in the document.

BOW preserves word frequency information but discards all positional information. The sentences _"the cat ate the mouse"_ and _"the mouse ate the cat"_ receive identical BOW representations. For many classification tasks, this is acceptable; for sequence understanding, it is not.

**TF-IDF** improves on raw counts by down-weighting words that are common across many documents (low discriminative power):

TF-IDF(w,d)=c(w,d)∣d∣⏟term frequency⋅log⁡N∣{d′:w∈d′}∣⏟inverse document frequency\text{TF-IDF}(w, d) = \underbrace{\frac{c(w, d)}{|d|}}_{\text{term frequency}} \cdot \underbrace{\log \frac{N}{|\\{d' : w \in d'\\}|}}_{\text{inverse document frequency}}TF-IDF(w,d)=term frequency∣d∣c(w,d)​​​⋅inverse document frequencylog∣{d′:w∈d′}∣N​​​

TF-IDF is a useful heuristic for information retrieval but still inherits the fundamental orthogonality problem of one-hot representations. Two documents discussing _equity markets_ and _stock exchanges_ will not be recognized as topically similar.

* * *

### 13.4 Dense Representations: The Design Space

What properties should a good word representation have?

**Definition.** A **word embedding** is a mapping f:V→Rdf: \mathcal{V} \to \mathbb{R}^df:V→Rd where d≪Vd \ll Vd≪V, such that geometric proximity in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd reflects semantic similarity.

The key requirements are:

  1. **Compactness:** ddd is typically 50–300, compared to V∼104V \sim 10^4V∼104–10510^5105. The compression ratio is d/V≈10−3d/V \approx 10^{-3}d/V≈10−3–10−410^{-4}10−4.

  2. **Semantic geometry:** Similar words should be geometrically close. The standard measure is cosine similarity:

sim(u,v)=u⋅v∥u∥⋅∥v∥\text{sim}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\| \cdot \|\mathbf{v}\|}sim(u,v)=∥u∥⋅∥v∥u⋅v​

  3. **Algebraic structure:** The celebrated word2vec results showed that embeddings can encode relational analogies: vking−vman+vwoman≈vqueen\mathbf{v}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{v}_{\text{woman}} \approx \mathbf{v}_{\text{queen}}vking​−vman​+vwoman​≈vqueen​. This suggests that directions in embedding space encode semantic dimensions.

  4. **Transferability:** Embeddings trained on large unsupervised corpora should be useful for downstream tasks — sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, machine translation — with minimal task-specific training.

The question is: how do we _construct_ such representations?

* * *

### 13.5 The Co-Occurrence Matrix

The most direct implementation of the distributional hypothesis is the **co-occurrence matrix**.

**Construction.** Given a corpus and a context window of size kkk, define the co-occurrence matrix C∈RV×V\mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times V}C∈RV×V where:

Cij=number of times word wj appears in a context window around wiC_{ij} = \text{number of times word } w_j \text{ appears in a context window around } w_iCij​=number of times word wj​ appears in a context window around wi​

**Example.** Consider a toy corpus with 5 sentences and vocabulary V={cat, dog, fish, eats, swims, barks, meows}\mathcal{V} = \\{\text{cat, dog, fish, eats, swims, barks, meows}\\}V={cat, dog, fish, eats, swims, barks, meows}. For window size k=1k=1k=1:

| cat | dog | fish | eats | swims | barks | meows  
---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---  
**cat** | 0 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 3  
**dog** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0 | 3 | 0  
**fish** | 1 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 3 | 0 | 0  
**eats** | 2 | 2 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0  
  
The rows of C\mathbf{C}C are now word representations — each word is described by which other words it co-occurs with.

**Observation:** _cat_ and _dog_ have similar co-occurrence patterns (both appear near _eats_ , differ in _meows_ vs _barks_). Their row vectors will be more similar to each other than to _eats_ , which appears near multiple animals but not near itself.

**Problems with raw counts:**

  1. **High dimensionality.** The matrix is V×VV \times VV×V, which is 50,000×50,000=2.5×10950{,}000 \times 50{,}000 = 2.5 \times 10^950,000×50,000=2.5×109 entries. Storing and computing with it is expensive.

  2. **Frequency bias.** Common words like _the_ , _a_ , _of_ appear in virtually every context window. Raw counts overweight these uninformative co-occurrences.

  3. **Sparsity.** Despite the frequency bias of common words, most pairs (wi,wj)(w_i, w_j)(wi​,wj​) have Cij=0C_{ij} = 0Cij​=0. The matrix is extremely sparse.

* * *

### 13.6 Pointwise Mutual Information

To address the frequency bias, we replace raw counts with **Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI)**.

**Definition.** The PMI between words wiw_iwi​ and wjw_jwj​ is:

PMI(wi,wj)=log⁡P(wi,wj)P(wi)⋅P(wj)\text{PMI}(w_i, w_j) = \log \frac{P(w_i, w_j)}{P(w_i) \cdot P(w_j)}PMI(wi​,wj​)=logP(wi​)⋅P(wj​)P(wi​,wj​)​

where:

* P(wi,wj)P(w_i, w_j)P(wi​,wj​) = probability of wjw_jwj​ appearing in a window around wiw_iwi​
* P(wi)P(w_i)P(wi​), P(wj)P(w_j)P(wj​) = marginal probabilities (estimated from corpus frequencies)

**Interpretation.** PMI measures how much more (or less) often two words co-occur than expected under independence.

* PMI(wi,wj)>0\text{PMI}(w_i, w_j) > 0PMI(wi​,wj​)>0: they co-occur more than chance → positive association
* PMI(wi,wj)=0\text{PMI}(w_i, w_j) = 0PMI(wi​,wj​)=0: co-occurrence matches the independence baseline
* PMI(wi,wj)<0\text{PMI}(w_i, w_j) < 0PMI(wi​,wj​)<0: they co-occur less than chance → negative association (or avoidance)

**Worked example.** In a corpus with N=109N = 10^9N=109 tokens:

* _neural_ appears 100,000 times: P(neural)=10−4P(\text{neural}) = 10^{-4}P(neural)=10−4
* _network_ appears 200,000 times: P(network)=2×10−4P(\text{network}) = 2 \times 10^{-4}P(network)=2×10−4
* They co-occur in 50,000 windows: P(neural,network)=5×10−5P(\text{neural}, \text{network}) = 5 \times 10^{-5}P(neural,network)=5×10−5

PMI(neural,network)=log⁡5×10−5(10−4)(2×10−4)=log⁡5×10−52×10−8=log⁡2500≈7.8\text{PMI}(\text{neural}, \text{network}) = \log \frac{5 \times 10^{-5}}{(10^{-4})(2 \times 10^{-4})} = \log \frac{5 \times 10^{-5}}{2 \times 10^{-8}} = \log 2500 \approx 7.8PMI(neural,network)=log(10−4)(2×10−4)5×10−5​=log2×10−85×10−5​=log2500≈7.8

Now compare _neural_ and _the_ :

* _the_ appears 5×1075 \times 10^75×107 times: P(the)=0.05P(\text{the}) = 0.05P(the)=0.05
* Co-occurrence: 500050005000 windows: P(neural,the)=5×10−6P(\text{neural}, \text{the}) = 5 \times 10^{-6}P(neural,the)=5×10−6

PMI(neural,the)=log⁡5×10−6(10−4)(0.05)=log⁡5×10−65×10−6=log⁡1=0\text{PMI}(\text{neural}, \text{the}) = \log \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{(10^{-4})(0.05)} = \log \frac{5 \times 10^{-6}}{5 \times 10^{-6}} = \log 1 = 0PMI(neural,the)=log(10−4)(0.05)5×10−6​=log5×10−65×10−6​=log1=0

PMI correctly identifies that _neural_ – _network_ is a meaningful association while _neural_ – _the_ is merely incidental co-occurrence.

#### 13.6.1 Positive PMI

A practical problem: PMI is −∞-\infty−∞ for word pairs that never co-occur. **Positive PMI (PPMI)** addresses this by clamping negative values:

PPMI(wi,wj)=max⁡(PMI(wi,wj), 0)\text{PPMI}(w_i, w_j) = \max(\text{PMI}(w_i, w_j), \, 0)PPMI(wi​,wj​)=max(PMI(wi​,wj​),0)

PPMI retains positive associations (more co-occurrence than chance) while treating both negative PMI and zero co-occurrence as "no meaningful positive association." Empirically, PPMI representations are competitive with more sophisticated methods on word similarity benchmarks.

#### 13.6.2 Properties of PMI

PMI has a beautiful probabilistic interpretation. Expanding the log:

PMI(wi,wj)=log⁡P(wj∣wi)−log⁡P(wj)\text{PMI}(w_i, w_j) = \log P(w_j \mid w_i) - \log P(w_j)PMI(wi​,wj​)=logP(wj​∣wi​)−logP(wj​)

This is the log ratio between the probability of seeing wjw_jwj​ given wiw_iwi​'s context, and the baseline probability of seeing wjw_jwj​ in any context. PMI thus measures how much context provides above-baseline information about co-occurrence.

* * *

### 13.7 Latent Semantic Analysis

The co-occurrence matrix (or its PPMI variant) gives us semantically meaningful word representations, but they are still high-dimensional and dense. **Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA)** applies the Singular Value Decomposition to compress this matrix into a low-dimensional, dense representation.

#### 13.7.1 The SVD

Any matrix A∈Rm×n\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}A∈Rm×n can be decomposed as:

A=UΣV⊤\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U} \mathbf{\Sigma} \mathbf{V}^\topA=UΣV⊤

where:

* U∈Rm×m\mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}U∈Rm×m — left singular vectors (orthonormal columns)
* Σ∈Rm×n\mathbf{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}Σ∈Rm×n — diagonal matrix of singular values σ1≥σ2≥…≥0\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \ldots \geq 0σ1​≥σ2​≥…≥0
* V∈Rn×n\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}V∈Rn×n — right singular vectors (orthonormal columns)

**Truncated SVD.** Keeping only the top-ddd singular values and vectors:

A≈UdΣdVd⊤\mathbf{A} \approx \mathbf{U}_d \mathbf{\Sigma}_d \mathbf{V}_d^\topA≈Ud​Σd​Vd⊤​

This is the best rank-ddd approximation of A\mathbf{A}A in the Frobenius norm (Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem). The rows of UdΣd1/2\mathbf{U}_d \mathbf{\Sigma}_d^{1/2}Ud​Σd1/2​ are ddd-dimensional word representations.

#### 13.7.2 LSA Applied to Co-Occurrence

LSA applies truncated SVD to the term-document matrix or (more commonly in NLP) to the word co-occurrence matrix:

C≈UdΣdVd⊤\mathbf{C} \approx \mathbf{U}_d \mathbf{\Sigma}_d \mathbf{V}_d^\topC≈Ud​Σd​Vd⊤​

The rows of UdΣd\mathbf{U}_d \mathbf{\Sigma}_dUd​Σd​ are the word embeddings. The ddd latent dimensions can be interpreted as abstract semantic topics — linear combinations of raw co-occurrence patterns that explain the most variance in the data.

**Geometric interpretation.** The singular vectors identify the ddd orthogonal directions in the original VVV-dimensional co-occurrence space that capture the most variance. Words that frequently co-occur with the same words will project similarly onto these directions.

#### 13.7.3 Strengths and Limitations of LSA

Property | Assessment  
---|---  
Handles synonymy | Good — synonyms will have similar rows in C\mathbf{C}C  
Dimensionality reduction | Effective compression from VVV to d≪Vd \ll Vd≪V  
Computational cost | O(V2d)O(V^2 d)O(V2d) SVD — expensive for large VVV  
Online updates | Poor — adding new words requires recomputing SVD  
Semantic arithmetic | Limited — directions do not typically support analogy completion  
Training signal | Unsupervised reconstruction of co-occurrence matrix  
  
LSA was a significant advance in the 1990s and remains competitive on some benchmarks. But its computational cost and inability to scale to V∼106V \sim 10^6V∼106 motivated the next generation of methods.

* * *

### 13.8 The Connection to Neural Word Embeddings

LSA can be understood as the following optimization problem: find a low-rank factorization W∈RV×d\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}W∈RV×d and C′∈RV×d\mathbf{C}' \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}C′∈RV×d such that:

min⁡W,C′∑i,j(Cij−wi⊤cj)2\min_{\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{C}'} \sum_{i,j} (\mathbf{C}_{ij} - \mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{c}_j)^2W,C′min​i,j∑​(Cij​−wi⊤​cj​)2

This is matrix factorization with squared loss. The optimal solution is exactly the truncated SVD.

Word2Vec (Chapter 14) solves a different but related optimization: it finds W\mathbf{W}W and C′\mathbf{C}'C′ such that:

min⁡W,C′∑(i,j)∈corpus−log⁡σ(wi⊤cj)\min_{\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{C}'} \sum_{(i,j) \in \text{corpus}} -\log \sigma(\mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{c}_j)W,C′min​(i,j)∈corpus∑​−logσ(wi⊤​cj​)

Levy and Goldberg (2014) proved that the Skip-gram with negative sampling objective is _implicitly_ factorizing the shifted PMI matrix:

wi⊤cj≈PMI(wi,wj)−log⁡k\mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{c}_j \approx \text{PMI}(w_i, w_j) - \log kwi⊤​cj​≈PMI(wi​,wj​)−logk

where kkk is the number of negative samples. This is a profound result: Word2Vec's neural network training procedure is — up to the loss function — doing approximately the same thing as SVD on the PMI matrix. The two approaches that seemed entirely different (matrix factorization vs. neural language models) turn out to be instances of the same underlying idea.

GloVe (Chapter 15) makes this connection explicit by directly optimizing a weighted least-squares factorization of the log co-occurrence matrix.

* * *

### 13.9 Why Distributed Representations Work

#### 13.9.1 Distributed vs. Local Representations

A **local representation** encodes each concept in a single, dedicated unit. One-hot encoding is the extreme case: each word activates exactly one dimension.

A **distributed representation** encodes each concept across many dimensions, and each dimension participates in representing many concepts. Dense word embeddings are distributed: the vector for _king_ uses all d=300d = 300d=300 dimensions, and each dimension contributes to encoding multiple words.

Hinton (1986) argued that distributed representations are fundamentally more powerful because they allow exponential representational capacity: nnn binary features can encode 2n2^n2n distinct patterns, whereas nnn local units can encode only nnn distinct patterns.

#### 13.9.2 Semantic Directions

One of the most striking properties of learned dense embeddings is that _directions_ in embedding space correspond to semantic dimensions:

Direction | Semantic Content  
---|---  
vking−vqueen\mathbf{v}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{queen}}vking​−vqueen​ | Gender (male/female)  
vParis−vFrance\mathbf{v}_{\text{Paris}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{France}}vParis​−vFrance​ | Capital-country relationship  
vwalked−vwalk\mathbf{v}_{\text{walked}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{walk}}vwalked​−vwalk​ | Past tense morphology  
vbiggest−vbig\mathbf{v}_{\text{biggest}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{big}}vbiggest​−vbig​ | Superlative form  
  
These directions are not hand-engineered — they emerge from distributional statistics. This suggests that the geometry of language is latently structured, and that optimization pressure to predict context words is sufficient to recover that structure.

#### 13.9.3 The Analogy Arithmetic

The famous word2vec analogy result:

vking−vman+vwoman≈vqueen\mathbf{v}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{v}_{\text{woman}} \approx \mathbf{v}_{\text{queen}}vking​−vman​+vwoman​≈vqueen​

can be understood geometrically. If the direction vking−vqueen\mathbf{v}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{queen}}vking​−vqueen​ encodes gender, and vman−vwoman\mathbf{v}_{\text{man}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{woman}}vman​−vwoman​ encodes the same direction in a different semantic neighborhood, then subtracting one and adding the other should navigate across the gender direction while preserving the "royalty" dimension.

This arithmetic is imperfect and fails for many analogies. But its success for regularized analogies suggests that learned embeddings have captured genuine semantic geometry.

* * *

### 13.10 Worked Example: Computing PPMI Vectors

Let us compute PPMI representations for a toy vocabulary.

**Corpus** (5 sentences):

  1. _the cat eats fish_
  2. _the dog eats meat_
  3. _the cat meows loudly_
  4. _the dog barks loudly_
  5. _the fish swims quietly_

**Vocabulary:** {cat, dog, fish, eats, swims, meows, barks} (excluding _the_ , _loudly_ , _quietly_ , _meat_ for clarity)

**Step 1: Count co-occurrences (window k=1k=1k=1)**

From sentence 1: (cat, eats), (eats, cat), (eats, fish), (fish, eats) From sentence 2: (dog, eats), (eats, dog) From sentence 3: (cat, meows) From sentence 4: (dog, barks) From sentence 5: (fish, swims)

Co-occurrence matrix C\mathbf{C}C (symmetric pairs counted once each direction):

| cat | dog | fish | eats | swims | meows | barks  
---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---  
**cat** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0 | 1 | 0  
**dog** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1  
**fish** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0  
**eats** | 2 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0  
**swims** | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0  
**meows** | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0  
**barks** | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0  
  
**Step 2: Compute marginal and joint probabilities**

Total co-occurrence count =2+1+1+2+1+1+1+1+1+1=12= 2+1+1+2+1+1+1+1+1+1 = 12=2+1+1+2+1+1+1+1+1+1=12 (counting each directed pair once)

P(eats)=(2+1+1)/12=4/12=1/3P(\text{eats}) = (2+1+1)/12 = 4/12 = 1/3P(eats)=(2+1+1)/12=4/12=1/3 P(cat)=(2+1)/12=3/12=1/4P(\text{cat}) = (2+1)/12 = 3/12 = 1/4P(cat)=(2+1)/12=3/12=1/4 P(cat,eats)=2/12=1/6P(\text{cat}, \text{eats}) = 2/12 = 1/6P(cat,eats)=2/12=1/6

PMI(cat,eats)=log⁡1/6(1/4)(1/3)=log⁡1/61/12=log⁡2≈0.69\text{PMI}(\text{cat}, \text{eats}) = \log \frac{1/6}{(1/4)(1/3)} = \log \frac{1/6}{1/12} = \log 2 \approx 0.69PMI(cat,eats)=log(1/4)(1/3)1/6​=log1/121/6​=log2≈0.69

**Step 3: PPMI vectors**

For _cat_ : [PPMI(cat, cat),PPMI(cat, dog),…]=[0,0,0,0.69,0,large,0][\text{PPMI}(\text{cat, cat}), \text{PPMI}(\text{cat, dog}), \ldots] = [0, 0, 0, 0.69, 0, \text{large}, 0][PPMI(cat, cat),PPMI(cat, dog),…]=[0,0,0,0.69,0,large,0]

For _dog_ : [0,0,0,moderate,0,0,large][0, 0, 0, \text{moderate}, 0, 0, \text{large}][0,0,0,moderate,0,0,large]

**Observation:** The PPMI vectors for _cat_ and _dog_ are both non-zero in the _eats_ dimension but differ in the _meows_ vs. _barks_ dimension — correctly capturing that both are pets that eat, but have different vocalizations. Their cosine similarity will be positive (they share a context) but less than 1 (they differ in some contexts).

* * *

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> The distributional hypothesis connects to measurement theory in multiple scientific domains.
> 
> **Spectroscopy.** Spectroscopists identify chemical compounds by their spectral signatures — patterns of wavelengths absorbed or emitted. The spectral fingerprint of a molecule _is_ its context in the space of electromagnetic wavelengths. Two molecules with similar spectra have similar chemical structures, even if we do not know their explicit structure. Distributional word representation is analogous: the "spectrum" of a word is its co-occurrence pattern across the vocabulary.
> 
> **Ecology.** Niche theory characterizes species by their ecological interactions — what they eat, what eats them, what habitats they occupy. The ecological niche is a distributional representation: species occupying similar niches will have similar co-occurrence patterns with other species in community surveys. This is exactly the distributional hypothesis applied to organisms instead of words.
> 
> **Physics: Renormalization.** In condensed matter physics, coarse-graining operations (renormalization group) identify which microscopic degrees of freedom are relevant at different scales. PMI-based compression does something similar: it identifies which co-occurrence patterns carry genuine information (above-baseline association) and discards the rest. Both are principled dimensionality reduction based on information content rather than raw magnitude.

* * *

### 13.11 Limitations of Count-Based Methods

Count-based methods (co-occurrence matrix + PPMI + SVD) have several persistent limitations that motivated the prediction-based approaches of the next chapter.

#### 13.11.1 Computational Scale

Computing the full co-occurrence matrix over a corpus with V=100,000V = 100{,}000V=100,000 unique words requires a 101010^{10}1010-entry matrix — 80 GB at float32. Performing SVD on this matrix requires O(V2d)O(V^2 d)O(V2d) operations. Both the storage and computation are prohibitive for modern corpora (billions of words, millions of vocabulary items).

#### 13.11.2 Incremental Updates

When new text arrives, the co-occurrence matrix must be rebuilt and the SVD recomputed. There is no natural online update procedure. In contrast, neural methods can update embeddings incrementally via gradient descent on each new sentence.

#### 13.11.3 Weighting Function

The choice of context window size kkk and weighting scheme (flat vs. distance-decayed) significantly impacts results but has no principled justification from the model itself. Practitioners tune these hyperparameters empirically.

#### 13.11.4 Polysemy

A single word type (_bank_ meaning financial institution or riverbank) is mapped to a single embedding vector — the average of its co-occurrence patterns across all senses. The vector for _bank_ will sit somewhere between its financial and geographical senses, accurately representing neither. Count-based methods have no mechanism for disambiguating word senses.

This limitation motivates the move to **contextualized representations** (Chapter 16): ELMo, GPT, and BERT produce different representations for the same word type depending on its context — allowing _bank_ to have different representations in "river bank" vs. "World Bank".

* * *

### 13.12 Evaluating Word Representations

How do we know if a word representation is good? Several standard evaluation paradigms exist.

#### 13.12.1 Intrinsic Evaluation: Word Similarity

Datasets like **WordSim-353** and **SimLex-999** provide human-annotated similarity judgments for word pairs. The evaluation is Spearman rank correlation between the cosine similarity of embeddings and human similarity ratings:

ρ=Spearman({ui⋅vi∥ui∥∥vi∥},{sihuman})\rho = \text{Spearman}\left(\left\\{\frac{\mathbf{u}_i \cdot \mathbf{v}_i}{\|\mathbf{u}_i\|\|\mathbf{v}_i\|}\right\\}, \left\\{s_i^{\text{human}}\right\\}\right)ρ=Spearman({∥ui​∥∥vi​∥ui​⋅vi​​},{sihuman​})

#### 13.12.2 Intrinsic Evaluation: Analogy

Given pairs (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) and query ccc, find ddd such that a:b::c:da:b :: c:da:b::c:d. The standard approach is:

d^=arg⁡max⁡w≠a,b,ccos⁡(vw,vb−va+vc)\hat{d} = \arg\max_{w \neq a,b,c} \cos(\mathbf{v}_w, \mathbf{v}_b - \mathbf{v}_a + \mathbf{v}_c)d^=argw=a,b,cmax​cos(vw​,vb​−va​+vc​)

The Google Analogy Dataset contains 19,544 pairs covering semantic (capital cities, currencies) and syntactic (verb tenses, adjective forms) analogies.

#### 13.12.3 Extrinsic Evaluation: Downstream Tasks

More informative but more expensive: use the embeddings as features in named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, or question answering, and measure performance on labeled test sets. Good embeddings should improve downstream performance over random initialization.

**The evaluation gap.** Intrinsic evaluations are fast and reproducible but may not predict downstream performance. Faruqui et al. (2016) showed that models optimizing intrinsic similarity benchmarks do not reliably achieve better extrinsic task performance. This has led to skepticism about similarity-based benchmarks as the primary evaluation target.

* * *

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> The evaluation problem for word representations echoes a fundamental tension in measurement theory.
> 
> **Psychometrics.** Intelligence tests face the same construct validity problem: a test score is an intrinsic evaluation metric, but the quantity of interest is real-world cognitive performance (extrinsic). Charles Spearman's ggg factor (1904) was an early attempt to find latent dimensions underlying correlated test performance — directly analogous to the latent semantic dimensions found by SVD/LSA applied to word co-occurrence.
> 
> **Physics: Operational definitions.** Physicists define temperature operationally through the behavior of thermometers. There is a known gap between operational definitions (intrinsic) and the theoretical quantity they measure (extrinsic). PMI-based similarity is an operational definition of semantic relatedness — it measures distributional overlap rather than "true" meaning, with a similar validity gap.
> 
> **Dimensionality reduction in genomics.** Principal Component Analysis of genetic variation data (a technique analogous to SVD/LSA) reduces millions of SNPs to a few principal components. Population geneticists use these components as proxies for ancestry, then validate them against known population histories. The two-stage process — compress and then validate against an external criterion — mirrors the intrinsic/extrinsic evaluation pipeline for word embeddings.

* * *

### 13.13 The Bottleneck Problem

Section 13.8 noted that Word2Vec is implicitly factorizing the PMI matrix. But Word2Vec uses a different _training procedure_ : rather than explicitly computing the co-occurrence matrix and performing SVD, it trains a shallow neural network to _predict_ context words from target words (or vice versa), using gradient descent on individual word pairs.

This prediction-based training has a crucial advantage: the network can be trained on raw text without ever materializing the full V×VV \times VV×V co-occurrence matrix. The vocabulary terms are processed in streaming fashion. Modern corpora with billions of words and millions of vocabulary items become computationally feasible.

But prediction-based training introduces its own bottleneck. To predict which word appears in context, the model must compute a probability over all VVV vocabulary items:

P(wj∣wi)=exp⁡(wi⊤cj)∑k=1Vexp⁡(wi⊤ck)P(w_j \mid w_i) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{c}_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^V \exp(\mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{c}_k)}P(wj​∣wi​)=∑k=1V​exp(wi⊤​ck​)exp(wi⊤​cj​)​

The denominator — the **partition function** — requires VVV dot products per training step. With V=50,000V = 50{,}000V=50,000 words and billions of training pairs, this is O(V×corpus size)O(V \times \text{corpus size})O(V×corpus size) total operations — computationally infeasible.

Chapter 14 examines how Word2Vec solved this **softmax bottleneck** through two approximations: **hierarchical softmax** (replacing the flat softmax with a binary tree) and **negative sampling** (replacing the full normalization with a binary discrimination task). These approximations enabled training on billion-word corpora and transformed NLP.

* * *

### 13.14 Summary

This chapter established the theoretical foundation for dense word representations:

  1. **The representational problem:** One-hot encoding is orthogonal and uninformative. Dense representations are required to encode semantic similarity.

  2. **The distributional hypothesis:** Words that appear in similar contexts have similar meanings (Firth 1957). This hypothesis grounds all count-based and prediction-based word representation methods.

  3. **Co-occurrence matrix:** Direct implementation of the distributional hypothesis. Row iii = context profile of word wiw_iwi​. Problems: high dimensionality, frequency bias, sparsity.

  4. **PMI and PPMI:** Replacing raw counts with log-ratio statistics removes frequency bias. PMI(wi,wj)=log⁡P(wi,wj)/[P(wi)P(wj)]\text{PMI}(w_i, w_j) = \log P(w_i, w_j)/[P(w_i)P(w_j)]PMI(wi​,wj​)=logP(wi​,wj​)/[P(wi​)P(wj​)] measures above-chance co-occurrence. PPMI = max(PMI, 0).

  5. **LSA:** SVD on the co-occurrence (or PPMI) matrix gives dense, low-dimensional representations. Optimal rank-ddd approximation in Frobenius norm. Scalability limits: O(V2d)O(V^2 d)O(V2d) computation.

  6. **The PMI-Word2Vec connection:** Word2Vec implicitly factorizes the shifted PMI matrix (Levy & Goldberg 2014). Count-based and prediction-based methods share the same theoretical foundation.

  7. **The softmax bottleneck:** Prediction-based methods must normalize over the full vocabulary at each training step. This O(V)O(V)O(V) operation per step blocks scaling. Negative sampling solves this, as we see in Chapter 14.

The key table:

Method | Training Signal | Dimensionality | Scalability | Polysemy  
---|---|---|---|---  
One-hot | None | VVV | Good | N/A  
BOW / TF-IDF | Document labels | VVV | Good | None  
Co-occurrence + PPMI | Co-occurrence | VVV | Poor | None  
LSA (SVD) | Reconstruction | d≪Vd \ll Vd≪V | Poor | None  
Word2Vec | Context prediction | d≪Vd \ll Vd≪V | Good | None  
GloVe | Log co-occurrence | d≪Vd \ll Vd≪V | Good | None  
ELMo / BERT | Language modeling | ddd per context | Good | Good  
  
* * *

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> The progression from local to distributed representations parallels transitions in multiple fields.
> 
> **Cognitive neuroscience.** Early theories of brain organization proposed local, "grandmother cell" representations — individual neurons specifically responding to specific concepts. Contemporary neuroscience favors population coding: concepts are represented by patterns of activity across large neural populations. fMRI studies show that semantic categories are encoded in distributed, overlapping activation patterns across cortex — not in localized regions. Dense word embeddings match this population-coding model; one-hot encodings correspond to the discredited grandmother cell hypothesis.
> 
> **Coding theory.** Error-correcting codes (Reed-Solomon, LDPC) distribute information about a message across many bits so that any individual bit can be corrupted without losing the full message. Distributed representations have an analogous robustness: corrupting or perturbing individual dimensions of an embedding does not destroy the semantic content, because that content is spread across many dimensions. One-hot codes have no such robustness — perturbing the single active bit destroys all information.
> 
> **Thermodynamics.** Macroscopic thermodynamic quantities (temperature, pressure) are distributed summaries of microscopic degrees of freedom. No individual molecule "is" the temperature; temperature is a collective property. Word embeddings are similarly collective: no single dimension "is" the gender of a word; gender is a distributed pattern across many dimensions. The analogy extends to the SVD compression step, which mirrors the coarse-graining that produces macroscopic thermodynamic descriptions from microscopic particle dynamics.

### Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Exercise 13.1.** A vocabulary has V=10V = 10V=10 words: {apple, orange, fruit, dog, cat, animal, red, green, run, jump}. Design (by hand) a co-occurrence matrix for a plausible small corpus. Compute the cosine similarity between _apple_ and _orange_ , and between _apple_ and _dog_. Verify that semantically related words have higher cosine similarity.

Answer

To construct the co-occurrence matrix, first write a small corpus such as: "apple is a red fruit", "orange is a green fruit", "dog and cat are animal", "cat can run and jump", "dog can run". Using a symmetric context window of size k=1k = 1k=1, scan each word and record its neighbors. For instance, _apple_ co-occurs with _red_ and _fruit_ ; _orange_ co-occurs with _green_ and _fruit_. Fill in CijC_{ij}Cij​ by counting each context pair in both directions. The resulting matrix is symmetric when using symmetric windows. Now compute cosine similarity: cos⁡(vapple,vorange)=vapple⋅vorange∥vapple∥∥vorange∥\cos(\mathbf{v}_{\text{apple}}, \mathbf{v}_{\text{orange}}) = \frac{\mathbf{v}_{\text{apple}} \cdot \mathbf{v}_{\text{orange}}}{\|\mathbf{v}_{\text{apple}}\| \|\mathbf{v}_{\text{orange}}\|}cos(vapple​,vorange​)=∥vapple​∥∥vorange​∥vapple​⋅vorange​​. Both _apple_ and _orange_ share a non-zero entry in the _fruit_ column, so their dot product is positive. In contrast, _apple_ and _dog_ share no context words (one co-occurs with _fruit_ /_red_ , the other with _animal_ /_run_), so their dot product is zero or near-zero. This confirms the distributional hypothesis: semantically related words (_apple_ , _orange_ — both fruits) have higher cosine similarity than unrelated words (_apple_ , _dog_).

* * *

**Exercise 13.2.** Show algebraically that if two words wiw_iwi​ and wjw_jwj​ have identical context distributions (i.e., P(wk∣wi)=P(wk∣wj)P(w_k \mid w_i) = P(w_k \mid w_j)P(wk​∣wi​)=P(wk​∣wj​) for all kkk), then their PMI vectors are identical. (Hint: express P(wi,wk)P(w_i, w_k)P(wi​,wk​) in terms of P(wk∣wi)P(w_k \mid w_i)P(wk​∣wi​) and P(wi)P(w_i)P(wi​).)

Answer

Recall that PMI(w,c)=log⁡P(w,c)P(w)P(c)\text{PMI}(w, c) = \log \frac{P(w, c)}{P(w) P(c)}PMI(w,c)=logP(w)P(c)P(w,c)​. We can rewrite the joint probability as P(w,c)=P(c∣w)⋅P(w)P(w, c) = P(c \mid w) \cdot P(w)P(w,c)=P(c∣w)⋅P(w), so PMI(w,c)=log⁡P(c∣w)⋅P(w)P(w)⋅P(c)=log⁡P(c∣w)P(c)\text{PMI}(w, c) = \log \frac{P(c \mid w) \cdot P(w)}{P(w) \cdot P(c)} = \log \frac{P(c \mid w)}{P(c)}PMI(w,c)=logP(w)⋅P(c)P(c∣w)⋅P(w)​=logP(c)P(c∣w)​. Now if P(c∣wi)=P(c∣wj)P(c \mid w_i) = P(c \mid w_j)P(c∣wi​)=P(c∣wj​) for all context words ccc, then PMI(wi,c)=log⁡P(c∣wi)P(c)=log⁡P(c∣wj)P(c)=PMI(wj,c)\text{PMI}(w_i, c) = \log \frac{P(c \mid w_i)}{P(c)} = \log \frac{P(c \mid w_j)}{P(c)} = \text{PMI}(w_j, c)PMI(wi​,c)=logP(c)P(c∣wi​)​=logP(c)P(c∣wj​)​=PMI(wj​,c) for every ccc. This means the PMI row vectors of wiw_iwi​ and wjw_jwj​ are identical entry-by-entry. Note that the marginal probabilities P(wi)P(w_i)P(wi​) and P(wj)P(w_j)P(wj​) cancel entirely — only the conditional context distributions matter. This result is a precise formalization of the distributional hypothesis: identical context distributions imply identical representations in PMI space, regardless of how frequent the two words are individually.

* * *

**Exercise 13.6.** Consider the polysemy problem for the word _bank_. (a) In a corpus containing both financial and geographical uses of _bank_ , sketch what the co-occurrence vector for _bank_ would look like (which words would have high co-occurrence counts?). (b) Explain why a single embedding vector cannot simultaneously represent both senses well. (c) What architectural change (described briefly in Section 13.11.4) is needed to handle polysemy? What additional information does it require that count-based methods do not use?

Answer

(a) The co-occurrence vector for _bank_ would have elevated counts for both financial-context words (_money_ , _account_ , _loan_ , _deposit_ , _interest_ , _financial_) and geographical-context words (_river_ , _water_ , _shore_ , _flood_ , _erosion_). The single row in the co-occurrence matrix aggregates all occurrences regardless of sense. (b) A single embedding vector for _bank_ is effectively a weighted average of its two sense vectors, with weights proportional to corpus frequency of each sense. If 80% of occurrences are financial, the vector sits close to the financial sense but far from the river sense. Cosine similarity with _money_ will be moderate (not high), and with _river_ also moderate — the vector faithfully represents neither sense. Geometrically, the averaged vector occupies a region of embedding space between two sense clusters, a location that may not correspond to any coherent meaning. (c) Contextualized embeddings (ELMo, BERT, as described in Chapter 16) solve this by producing a different vector for _bank_ in each sentence, conditioned on the surrounding words. They require the full sentential context at inference time — information that count-based methods discard by aggregating over all occurrences of a word type.

#### Application

**Exercise 13.3 (PMI calculation).** Suppose a corpus of N=106N = 10^6N=106 tokens has the following statistics:

* P(machine)=10−3P(\text{machine}) = 10^{-3}P(machine)=10−3, P(learning)=8×10−4P(\text{learning}) = 8 \times 10^{-4}P(learning)=8×10−4
* P(machine,learning)=2×10−4P(\text{machine}, \text{learning}) = 2 \times 10^{-4}P(machine,learning)=2×10−4 (within window k=3k=3k=3)
* P(machine,the)=5×10−4P(\text{machine}, \text{the}) = 5 \times 10^{-4}P(machine,the)=5×10−4, P(the)=0.06P(\text{the}) = 0.06P(the)=0.06

(a) Compute PMI(machine,learning)\text{PMI}(\text{machine}, \text{learning})PMI(machine,learning) and PMI(machine,the)\text{PMI}(\text{machine}, \text{the})PMI(machine,the). (b) Compute PPMI\text{PPMI}PPMI for both pairs. (c) Explain intuitively why _machine_ – _learning_ should have high PMI and _machine_ – _the_ should have low PMI.

Answer

(a) Using PMI(w,c)=log⁡2P(w,c)P(w)P(c)\text{PMI}(w, c) = \log_2 \frac{P(w, c)}{P(w) P(c)}PMI(w,c)=log2​P(w)P(c)P(w,c)​:

PMI(machine,learning)=log⁡22×10−4(10−3)(8×10−4)=log⁡22×10−48×10−7=log⁡2250≈7.97\text{PMI}(\text{machine}, \text{learning}) = \log_2 \frac{2 \times 10^{-4}}{(10^{-3})(8 \times 10^{-4})} = \log_2 \frac{2 \times 10^{-4}}{8 \times 10^{-7}} = \log_2 250 \approx 7.97PMI(machine,learning)=log2​(10−3)(8×10−4)2×10−4​=log2​8×10−72×10−4​=log2​250≈7.97

PMI(machine,the)=log⁡25×10−4(10−3)(0.06)=log⁡25×10−46×10−5=log⁡28.33≈3.06\text{PMI}(\text{machine}, \text{the}) = \log_2 \frac{5 \times 10^{-4}}{(10^{-3})(0.06)} = \log_2 \frac{5 \times 10^{-4}}{6 \times 10^{-5}} = \log_2 8.33 \approx 3.06PMI(machine,the)=log2​(10−3)(0.06)5×10−4​=log2​6×10−55×10−4​=log2​8.33≈3.06

(b) Both PMI values are positive, so PPMI(machine,learning)≈7.97\text{PPMI}(\text{machine}, \text{learning}) \approx 7.97PPMI(machine,learning)≈7.97 and PPMI(machine,the)≈3.06\text{PPMI}(\text{machine}, \text{the}) \approx 3.06PPMI(machine,the)≈3.06.

(c) _Machine_ and _learning_ form a compound term — they co-occur far more than independent frequencies predict, producing high PMI. _Machine_ and _the_ co-occur frequently in absolute terms because _the_ appears in nearly every sentence, but this high co-occurrence is almost entirely explained by the high marginal frequency of _the_. PMI normalizes for this baseline, correctly assigning a much lower (though still positive) score. If the corpus were larger and the co-occurrence rate matched independence more closely, this PMI would approach zero. This illustrates why PMI is preferred over raw counts: it distinguishes genuine semantic association from frequency-driven coincidence.

**Exercise 13.4.** The Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem states that the truncated SVD Ad=UdΣdVd⊤\mathbf{A}_d = \mathbf{U}_d \mathbf{\Sigma}_d \mathbf{V}_d^\topAd​=Ud​Σd​Vd⊤​ minimizes ∥A−B∥F\|\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}\|_F∥A−B∥F​ over all rank-ddd matrices B\mathbf{B}B. Prove that ∥A−Ad∥F2=∑i=d+1min⁡(m,n)σi2\|\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}_d\|_F^2 = \sum_{i=d+1}^{\min(m,n)} \sigma_i^2∥A−Ad​∥F2​=∑i=d+1min(m,n)​σi2​. What does this tell us about the error of LSA as a function of retained dimensions?

Answer

Write the full SVD as A=∑i=1rσiuivi⊤\mathbf{A} = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\topA=∑i=1r​σi​ui​vi⊤​ where r=rank(A)r = \text{rank}(\mathbf{A})r=rank(A). The truncated SVD keeps only the first ddd terms: Ad=∑i=1dσiuivi⊤\mathbf{A}_d = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \sigma_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\topAd​=∑i=1d​σi​ui​vi⊤​. The residual is A−Ad=∑i=d+1rσiuivi⊤\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}_d = \sum_{i=d+1}^{r} \sigma_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\topA−Ad​=∑i=d+1r​σi​ui​vi⊤​. Since the uivi⊤\mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\topui​vi⊤​ matrices are orthonormal under the Frobenius inner product (i.e., ⟨uivi⊤,ujvj⊤⟩F=δij\langle \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\top, \mathbf{u}_j \mathbf{v}_j^\top \rangle_F = \delta_{ij}⟨ui​vi⊤​,uj​vj⊤​⟩F​=δij​), the squared Frobenius norm decomposes as ∥A−Ad∥F2=∑i=d+1rσi2\|\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}_d\|_F^2 = \sum_{i=d+1}^{r} \sigma_i^2∥A−Ad​∥F2​=∑i=d+1r​σi2​. The Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem guarantees no other rank-ddd matrix achieves a smaller residual. For LSA, this means the approximation error equals the sum of squared discarded singular values. If the singular value spectrum decays rapidly (as it does for natural language co-occurrence matrices), most variance is captured by the first few hundred dimensions, and the error from truncation is small. Each additional retained dimension reduces the error by exactly σd+12\sigma_{d+1}^2σd+12​, giving a principled criterion for choosing ddd: retain enough dimensions to capture a target fraction of total variance ∑iσi2\sum_i \sigma_i^2∑i​σi2​.

**Exercise 13.5 (Analogy arithmetic).** Word2Vec embeddings satisfy vParis−vFrance+vGermany≈vBerlin\mathbf{v}_{\text{Paris}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{France}} + \mathbf{v}_{\text{Germany}} \approx \mathbf{v}_{\text{Berlin}}vParis​−vFrance​+vGermany​≈vBerlin​. Suppose you observe that the direction vParis−vFrance\mathbf{v}_{\text{Paris}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{France}}vParis​−vFrance​ also applies to: (Rome,Italy)(\text{Rome}, \text{Italy})(Rome,Italy), (Madrid,Spain)(\text{Madrid}, \text{Spain})(Madrid,Spain), (Tokyo,Japan)(\text{Tokyo}, \text{Japan})(Tokyo,Japan).

(a) What semantic dimension does this direction encode? (b) If embeddings were local (one-hot), could any such arithmetic work? Explain. (c) Describe one failure case where the analogy arithmetic likely breaks down, and explain why.

Answer

(a) The direction vParis−vFrance\mathbf{v}_{\text{Paris}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{France}}vParis​−vFrance​ encodes the "capital-of" relationship — it is the vector offset that transforms a country into its capital city. The consistency across multiple country-capital pairs confirms this is a stable semantic direction in the embedding space.

(b) In one-hot space, vParis−vFrance=eParis−eFrance\mathbf{v}_{\text{Paris}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{France}} = \mathbf{e}_{\text{Paris}} - \mathbf{e}_{\text{France}}vParis​−vFrance​=eParis​−eFrance​, which is a vector with +1+1+1 at the Paris index and −1-1−1 at the France index. Adding this to eGermany\mathbf{e}_{\text{Germany}}eGermany​ yields a vector with +1+1+1 at Paris, +1+1+1 at Germany, and −1-1−1 at France — this is not close to eBerlin\mathbf{e}_{\text{Berlin}}eBerlin​ or any valid one-hot vector. The arithmetic fails because one-hot vectors encode no relational structure; each word occupies an isolated axis.

(c) The analogy arithmetic breaks down for non-parallel semantic shifts. For example, vking−vqueen+vwaiter\mathbf{v}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{queen}} + \mathbf{v}_{\text{waiter}}vking​−vqueen​+vwaiter​ should yield _waitress_ , but this assumes the gender direction is identical across royalty and occupation domains. In practice, the PMI difference PMI(king,c)−PMI(queen,c)≈PMI(waiter,c)−PMI(waitress,c)\text{PMI}(\text{king}, c) - \text{PMI}(\text{queen}, c) \approx \text{PMI}(\text{waiter}, c) - \text{PMI}(\text{waitress}, c)PMI(king,c)−PMI(queen,c)≈PMI(waiter,c)−PMI(waitress,c) need not hold for all contexts ccc, because gender interacts differently with different social roles. The linear relationship assumption breaks whenever the semantic shift is not a consistent, context-independent offset across the relevant word pairs.

* * *

#### Think Deeper

**Exercise 13.7.** The **curse of dimensionality** affects co-occurrence matrix estimation. Suppose we want reliable estimates of P(wi,wj)P(w_i, w_j)P(wi​,wj​) for all V2=4×109V^2 = 4 \times 10^9V2=4×109 word pairs (with V=63,000V = 63{,}000V=63,000). (a) How many corpus tokens are needed to observe each pair at least 10 times, assuming pairs are uniformly distributed? (b) Is this a realistic corpus size? What is the practical consequence for PMI estimates of rare pairs? (c) How does PPMI partially mitigate this problem?

Answer

(a) If co-occurrence pairs were uniformly distributed over V2=4×109V^2 = 4 \times 10^9V2=4×109 cells, each pair would need 10 observations, requiring approximately 4×10104 \times 10^{10}4×1010 co-occurrence events. Since each token generates O(k)O(k)O(k) co-occurrence pairs (for window size kkk), the corpus would need on the order of 4×1010/k4 \times 10^{10} / k4×1010/k tokens — roughly 101010^{10}1010 tokens for k=5k = 5k=5. This is 10 billion tokens.

(b) While corpora of this size exist (Common Crawl, etc.), the uniform distribution assumption is wildly unrealistic. Word frequencies follow a Zipfian distribution: a few words are extremely common, and the vast majority are rare. Most word pairs involve at least one rare word and will have zero or very few co-occurrences even in a 10-billion-token corpus. The practical consequence is that PMI estimates for rare pairs are extremely noisy: PMI(wi,wj)=log⁡P(wi,wj)P(wi)P(wj)\text{PMI}(w_i, w_j) = \log \frac{P(w_i, w_j)}{P(w_i)P(w_j)}PMI(wi​,wj​)=logP(wi​)P(wj​)P(wi​,wj​)​ can be arbitrarily large when the denominator is tiny and the numerator reflects a single chance co-occurrence.

(c) PPMI mitigates this by clamping negative values to zero: PPMI(w,c)=max⁡(0,PMI(w,c))\text{PPMI}(w, c) = \max(0, \text{PMI}(w, c))PPMI(w,c)=max(0,PMI(w,c)). Rare pairs that never co-occur get PMI =−∞= -\infty=−∞, which PPMI maps to 0 — a safe default. More importantly, rare pairs that co-occur once or twice by chance can produce spuriously high PMI values, but PPMI does not fix this directly. The real mitigation comes from the fact that in high-dimensional one-hot space (V≈50,000V \approx 50{,}000V≈50,000), every word is equidistant (Euclidean distance =2= \sqrt{2}=2​, cosine similarity =0= 0=0) from every other word, so no neighborhood structure exists. Dense low-dimensional representations (d≈300d \approx 300d≈300) produced by SVD on the PPMI matrix smooth over sparse estimates by projecting onto the principal variance directions, effectively averaging out noise from rare pairs.

* * *

**Exercise 13.8 (Conceptual).** Levy and Goldberg (2014) proved that the Skip-gram with negative sampling objective implicitly factorizes the shifted PMI matrix: wi⊤cj≈PMI(wi,wj)−log⁡k\mathbf{w}_i^\top \mathbf{c}_j \approx \text{PMI}(w_i, w_j) - \log kwi⊤​cj​≈PMI(wi​,wj​)−logk where kkk is the number of negative samples. (a) What does this result tell us about the relationship between count-based and prediction-based approaches? (b) If the two approaches are theoretically equivalent, what practical advantages does Word2Vec have over LSA that explain its widespread adoption? (c) GloVe (Chapter 15) directly optimizes a weighted factorization of the log co-occurrence matrix. How does this relate to the Levy-Goldberg result?

Answer

(a) The Levy-Goldberg result reveals that count-based and prediction-based methods are not fundamentally different paradigms — they are two algorithmic approaches to the same underlying objective. Word2Vec's skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix: Mij=PMI(wi,cj)−log⁡kM_{ij} = \text{PMI}(w_i, c_j) - \log kMij​=PMI(wi​,cj​)−logk. LSA factorizes the co-occurrence or PPMI matrix via SVD. Both methods discover the same latent structure — distributional co-occurrence statistics — through different optimization procedures. The geometry of the resulting embedding spaces converges because both capture the same statistical signal.

(b) Word2Vec's practical advantages are computational, not theoretical. It processes raw text in a single streaming pass without ever materializing the V×VV \times VV×V co-occurrence matrix, enabling training on billion-word corpora with modest memory. SVD requires O(V2)O(V^2)O(V2) storage and O(V2d)O(V^2 d)O(V2d) computation. Word2Vec also supports easy incremental updates via additional gradient steps on new data, while SVD must be recomputed from scratch. Finally, negative sampling reduces the per-step cost from O(V)O(V)O(V) (full softmax normalization) to O(k)O(k)O(k) where k≈5k \approx 5k≈5–151515.

(c) GloVe explicitly factorizes log⁡Xij\log X_{ij}logXij​ (the log of the co-occurrence matrix) with a weighted least-squares objective that down-weights rare pairs. This sits between LSA and Word2Vec: like LSA, it works directly with co-occurrence statistics; like Word2Vec, it optimizes via stochastic gradient descent. The Levy-Goldberg result implies all three methods — LSA on PPMI, Word2Vec skip-gram, and GloVe — are factorizing closely related matrices (PPMI, shifted PMI, and log co-occurrence respectively). Their empirical similarity on downstream tasks is therefore expected: the underlying statistical structure they capture is the same, and differences in performance stem from implementation details (weighting, optimization, hyperparameters) rather than fundamental representational differences.

## Chapter 14: Paper Close Read — Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013)

> **Chapter Learning Objectives**
>

> 
>   1. Describe the CBOW and Skip-gram architectures, explain their prediction tasks, and articulate why Skip-gram performs better on rare words.
>   2. Identify the computational bottleneck in the full softmax and explain why it scales as O(V) per training example.
>   3. Derive the negative sampling objective from noise contrastive estimation and explain what matrix SGNS implicitly factorizes (Levy-Goldberg theorem).
>   4. Explain hierarchical softmax using a binary tree and prove that path probabilities sum to 1 via the identity σ(x) + σ(−x) = 1.
>   5. Compute the subsampling discard probability for a given word frequency and explain its effect on co-occurrence statistics.
>   6. Apply the five-section paper reading methodology to analyze the Word2Vec papers' contributions and limitations.

### 14.1 Reading Strategy

This chapter performs a close reading of two landmark papers:

  1. **Mikolov, T., Chen, K., Corrado, G., & Dean, J. (2013).** _Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space._ ICLR.
  2. **Mikolov, T., Sutskever, I., Chen, K., Corrado, G., & Dean, J. (2013).** _Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality._ NeurIPS.

The first paper introduced the CBOW and Skip-gram architectures. The second introduced negative sampling and demonstrated the analogy arithmetic at scale. Together they constitute the Word2Vec contribution that transformed NLP.

Our reading protocol follows the five-section structure introduced in Chapter 9: (1) What problem does the paper solve? (2) What is the key insight? (3) What is the mathematical formulation? (4) What experiments support the claims? (5) What did it leave unsolved?

* * *

### 14.2 What Problem Does Word2Vec Solve?

Chapter 13 established that co-occurrence matrices + PMI + SVD can produce semantically meaningful word representations. The Levy-Goldberg (2014) result — which we will derive in this chapter — later showed that Word2Vec is _implicitly_ doing the same thing. So what was the actual problem Word2Vec solved?

**The answer is scale.**

LSA on a V=50,000V = 50{,}000V=50,000 vocabulary requires:

* Storing a 50,000×50,00050{,}000 \times 50{,}00050,000×50,000 co-occurrence matrix: 2.5×1092.5 \times 10^92.5×109 entries = 10 GB at float32
* Computing truncated SVD: O(V2d)O(V^2 d)O(V2d) operations ≈ 101210^{12}1012 operations for d=300d = 300d=300

With modern corpora containing billions of words and vocabularies of 10510^5105–10610^6106 terms, explicit matrix factorization was computationally infeasible.

Word2Vec's key contribution was showing that high-quality word representations could be learned from raw text using a shallow neural network trained with gradient descent — _without ever materializing the full co-occurrence matrix_. Training on a billion-word corpus took minutes to hours on a single machine.

The **softmax bottleneck** remained: computing P(wj∣wi)∝exp⁡(vwj⊤vwi)P(w_j \mid w_i) \propto \exp(\mathbf{v}_{w_j}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_i})P(wj​∣wi​)∝exp(vwj​⊤​vwi​​) requires normalizing over all VVV vocabulary items, a O(V)O(V)O(V) operation per training step. The papers solved this with two complementary approximations: hierarchical softmax and negative sampling.

* * *

### 14.3 The Two Architectures

Word2Vec introduces two architectures for learning word embeddings from context prediction.

#### 14.3.1 Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW)

CBOW predicts the center word from its context:

P(wt∣wt−k,…,wt−1,wt+1,…,wt+k)P(w_t \mid w_{t-k}, \ldots, w_{t-1}, w_{t+1}, \ldots, w_{t+k})P(wt​∣wt−k​,…,wt−1​,wt+1​,…,wt+k​)

**Architecture:** The context word embeddings are averaged (not concatenated), then fed through a linear layer to produce a distribution over the vocabulary:

v^=12k∑−k≤j≤k,j≠0vwt+j\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{1}{2k} \sum_{-k \leq j \leq k, j \neq 0} \mathbf{v}_{w_{t+j}}v^=2k1​−k≤j≤k,j=0∑​vwt+j​​ P(wt∣context)=exp⁡(uwt⊤v^)∑w∈Vexp⁡(uw⊤v^)P(w_t \mid \text{context}) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{u}_{w_t}^\top \hat{\mathbf{v}})}{\sum_{w \in \mathcal{V}} \exp(\mathbf{u}_w^\top \hat{\mathbf{v}})}P(wt​∣context)=∑w∈V​exp(uw⊤​v^)exp(uwt​⊤​v^)​

Here vw\mathbf{v}_wvw​ are the input embeddings (one per word) and uw\mathbf{u}_wuw​ are the output embeddings (one per word). The vocabulary has two embedding matrices.

**Key design choice: averaging, not concatenating.** Averaging the context vectors makes the model position-invariant — the context words can appear in any order and produce the same prediction. This is computationally efficient but throws away word order information. The "Bag" in CBOW refers to this position-invariance.

#### 14.3.2 Skip-gram

Skip-gram inverts the CBOW objective: predict context words from the center word.

max⁡θ∑t=1T∑−k≤j≤k,j≠0log⁡P(wt+j∣wt)\max_\theta \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{-k \leq j \leq k, j \neq 0} \log P(w_{t+j} \mid w_t)θmax​t=1∑T​−k≤j≤k,j=0∑​logP(wt+j​∣wt​)

For each center word wtw_twt​, Skip-gram tries to predict all words within a window of radius kkk.

**Softmax formulation:**

P(wO∣wI)=exp⁡(vwO′⊤vwI)∑w=1Vexp⁡(vw′⊤vwI)P(w_O \mid w_I) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{v}'_{w_O}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I})}{\sum_{w=1}^V \exp(\mathbf{v}'_w{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I})}P(wO​∣wI​)=∑w=1V​exp(vw′​⊤vwI​​)exp(vwO​′​⊤vwI​​)​

where vwI\mathbf{v}_{w_I}vwI​​ is the input embedding of the center word and vwO′\mathbf{v}'_{w_O}vwO​′​ is the output embedding of the context word. (Notation: this chapter follows the Word2Vec papers' convention of using primes v′\mathbf{v}'v′ for output embeddings. Chapter 15, following the GloVe paper, uses tildes w~\tilde{\mathbf{w}}w~ for the same role. Both denote the second embedding matrix; the different notation reflects each paper's original convention.)

#### 14.3.3 CBOW vs. Skip-gram: Asymmetry

Property | CBOW | Skip-gram  
---|---|---  
Prediction task | Context → Center | Center → Context  
Training signal per step | 1 center word from 2k contexts | 2k context words from 1 center  
Frequency sensitivity | Smooths context, good for frequent words | Oversamples rare words more  
Empirical performance | Faster training | Better on rare words and analogies  
  
The asymmetry matters: Skip-gram generates 2k2k2k training pairs per token (one for each context word), giving rare words more gradient signal relative to their corpus frequency. CBOW averages 2k2k2k contexts per step, giving frequent words more stable gradient estimates.

* * *

### 14.4 The Softmax Bottleneck

Both architectures require computing the full softmax:

P(wO∣wI)=exp⁡(vwO′⊤vwI)∑w=1Vexp⁡(vw′⊤vwI)⏟partition function Z(vwI)P(w_O \mid w_I) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{v}'_{w_O}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I})}{\underbrace{\sum_{w=1}^V \exp(\mathbf{v}'_w{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I})}_{\text{partition function } Z(\mathbf{v}_{w_I})}}P(wO​∣wI​)=partition function Z(vwI​​)w=1∑V​exp(vw′​⊤vwI​​)​​exp(vwO​′​⊤vwI​​)​

The partition function ZZZ requires VVV dot products. With V=50,000V = 50{,}000V=50,000:

* Each training step requires 50,000 dot products of dimension d=300d = 300d=300: 1.5×1071.5 \times 10^71.5×107 multiplications
* A billion-word corpus with average window k=5k = 5k=5 generates 101010^{10}1010 training pairs
* Total: 1.5×10171.5 \times 10^{17}1.5×1017 multiplications — infeasible

The papers offer two solutions.

* * *

### 14.5 Hierarchical Softmax

Hierarchical softmax replaces the flat vocabulary softmax with a binary tree, reducing normalization cost from O(V)O(V)O(V) to O(log⁡V)O(\log V)O(logV).

**Construction.** Build a binary tree with VVV leaves, one per vocabulary word. Each internal node contains a parameter vector θn∈Rd\mathbf{\theta}_n \in \mathbb{R}^dθn​∈Rd. Define a path from root to word www as n(w,1),n(w,2),…,n(w,L(w))n(w, 1), n(w, 2), \ldots, n(w, L(w))n(w,1),n(w,2),…,n(w,L(w)) where L(w)L(w)L(w) is the path length.

**Probability decomposition.** At each internal node nnn, a binary decision determines whether to go left or right. The probability of word www given context vwI\mathbf{v}_{w_I}vwI​​:

P(w∣wI)=∏ℓ=1L(w)−1σ(⟦n(w,ℓ+1)=ch(n(w,ℓ))⟧⋅θn(w,ℓ)⊤vwI)P(w \mid w_I) = \prod_{\ell=1}^{L(w)-1} \sigma\left(\llbracket n(w, \ell+1) = \text{ch}(n(w, \ell)) \rrbracket \cdot \mathbf{\theta}_{n(w,\ell)}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I}\right)P(w∣wI​)=ℓ=1∏L(w)−1​σ([[n(w,ℓ+1)=ch(n(w,ℓ))]]⋅θn(w,ℓ)⊤​vwI​​)

where ch(n)\text{ch}(n)ch(n) is the left child of node nnn and ⟦⋅⟧\llbracket \cdot \rrbracket[[⋅]] is 1 if true, -1 if false.

**Verification:** The product over all paths sums to 1 (each leaf is reached by exactly one path, and at each node the two child probabilities sum to 1 via the sigmoid identity σ(x)+σ(−x)=1\sigma(x) + \sigma(-x) = 1σ(x)+σ(−x)=1).

**Complexity.** Computing P(w∣wI)P(w \mid w_I)P(w∣wI​) requires L(w)−1L(w)-1L(w)−1 sigmoid evaluations and dot products. For a balanced binary tree, L(w)=O(log⁡2V)L(w) = O(\log_2 V)L(w)=O(log2​V). With V=50,000V = 50{,}000V=50,000, this is log⁡2(50,000)≈16\log_2(50{,}000) \approx 16log2​(50,000)≈16 operations instead of 50,000.

**Huffman tree optimization.** Word2Vec uses a Huffman tree rather than a balanced tree. Huffman coding assigns shorter paths to more frequent words and longer paths to rare words. For natural language, which follows Zipf's law (frequency∝rank−1\text{frequency} \propto \text{rank}^{-1}frequency∝rank−1), this achieves average path length ≈log⁡2(perplexity)≈\approx \log_2(\text{perplexity}) \approx≈log2​(perplexity)≈ 10–12, roughly twice as fast as a balanced tree.

* * *

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> Hierarchical softmax applies a structural insight from information theory: the expected code length of an optimal prefix-free code equals the entropy of the source (Shannon's source coding theorem). The Huffman tree is the optimal prefix-free code, so it minimizes the expected number of binary decisions needed to identify a word.
> 
> This principle appears across disciplines. **Probability decision trees** in machine learning partition the hypothesis space hierarchically — each split reduces uncertainty (information gain), exactly as each step down the hierarchical softmax tree reduces the set of candidate words. **Phylogenetic trees** in evolutionary biology organize species hierarchically such that closely related species share subtrees; searching for an ancestor is O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) in depth. **Radix trees** in computer science store strings in a compressed trie, reducing lookup cost from O(n)O(n)O(n) to O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn) by exploiting shared prefixes — the same structural compression that hierarchical softmax exploits in vocabulary space.

* * *

### 14.6 Negative Sampling: Complete Derivation

Negative sampling is Word2Vec's more practically important contribution. Rather than computing the full softmax, it frames vocabulary prediction as a binary classification task.

#### 14.6.1 From NCE to Negative Sampling

**Noise Contrastive Estimation (NCE)** (Gutmann & Hyvärinen, 2012) provides the theoretical foundation. The core idea: a good probability model should be able to distinguish real data from noise via logistic regression.

**Step 1: Binary classification setup.**

Define two classes:

* **Positive sample:** (wO,wI)(w_O, w_I)(wO​,wI​) — a word pair that actually co-occurs in the corpus. Label D=1D = 1D=1.
* **Negative sample:** (wneg,wI)(w_{\text{neg}}, w_I)(wneg​,wI​) — a word wnegw_{\text{neg}}wneg​ sampled from noise distribution Pn(w)P_n(w)Pn​(w), paired with wIw_IwI​. Label D=0D = 0D=0.

For each positive pair, we sample kkk negative pairs. Prior probabilities:

P(D=1)=1k+1,P(D=0)=kk+1P(D=1) = \frac{1}{k+1}, \qquad P(D=0) = \frac{k}{k+1}P(D=1)=k+11​,P(D=0)=k+1k​

**Step 2: Posterior probability via Bayes' rule.**

The probability that observed pair (w,wI)(w, w_I)(w,wI​) comes from the data rather than noise:

P(D=1∣w,wI)=Pdata(w∣wI;θ)⋅1k+1Pdata(w∣wI;θ)⋅1k+1+Pn(w)⋅kk+1P(D=1 \mid w, w_I) = \frac{P_{\text{data}}(w \mid w_I; \theta) \cdot \frac{1}{k+1}}{P_{\text{data}}(w \mid w_I; \theta) \cdot \frac{1}{k+1} + P_n(w) \cdot \frac{k}{k+1}}P(D=1∣w,wI​)=Pdata​(w∣wI​;θ)⋅k+11​+Pn​(w)⋅k+1k​Pdata​(w∣wI​;θ)⋅k+11​​

Multiplying numerator and denominator by (k+1)(k+1)(k+1):

P(D=1∣w,wI)=Pdata(w∣wI;θ)Pdata(w∣wI;θ)+k⋅Pn(w)P(D=1 \mid w, w_I) = \frac{P_{\text{data}}(w \mid w_I; \theta)}{P_{\text{data}}(w \mid w_I; \theta) + k \cdot P_n(w)}P(D=1∣w,wI​)=Pdata​(w∣wI​;θ)+k⋅Pn​(w)Pdata​(w∣wI​;θ)​

**Step 3: NCE objective.**

Maximize the log-likelihood of correctly classifying both positive and negative samples:

LNCE=log⁡P(D=1∣wO,wI)+∑i=1kEwi∼Pn[log⁡P(D=0∣wi,wI)]\mathcal{L}_{\text{NCE}} = \log P(D=1 \mid w_O, w_I) + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \mathbb{E}_{w_i \sim P_n} \left[\log P(D=0 \mid w_i, w_I)\right]LNCE​=logP(D=1∣wO​,wI​)+i=1∑k​Ewi​∼Pn​​[logP(D=0∣wi​,wI​)]

**Step 4: Parameterization.**

Substitute the Skip-gram parameterization: Pdata(wO∣wI;θ)∝exp⁡(vwO′⊤vwI)P_{\text{data}}(w_O \mid w_I; \theta) \propto \exp(\mathbf{v}'_{w_O}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I})Pdata​(wO​∣wI​;θ)∝exp(vwO​′​⊤vwI​​). Using unnormalized scores s(w,wI)=exp⁡(vw′⊤vwI)s(w, w_I) = \exp(\mathbf{v}'_w{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I})s(w,wI​)=exp(vw′​⊤vwI​​):

P(D=1∣w,wI)=s(w,wI)s(w,wI)+k⋅Pn(w)=σ(vw′⊤vwI−log⁡k−log⁡Pn(w))P(D=1 \mid w, w_I) = \frac{s(w, w_I)}{s(w, w_I) + k \cdot P_n(w)} = \sigma\left(\mathbf{v}'_w{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I} - \log k - \log P_n(w)\right)P(D=1∣w,wI​)=s(w,wI​)+k⋅Pn​(w)s(w,wI​)​=σ(vw′​⊤vwI​​−logk−logPn​(w))

**Step 5: Mikolov's simplification.**

Mikolov et al. observe that Skip-gram's goal is not to learn a precise probability distribution — it is to learn useful representations. They drop the log⁡k\log klogk and log⁡Pn(w)\log P_n(w)logPn​(w) normalization terms:

P(D=1∣w,wI)≈σ(vw′⊤vwI)P(D=1 \mid w, w_I) \approx \sigma\left(\mathbf{v}'_w{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I}\right)P(D=1∣w,wI​)≈σ(vw′​⊤vwI​​)

**Final negative sampling objective.** For positive pair (wO,wI)(w_O, w_I)(wO​,wI​) and kkk negative samples {wi}i=1k∼Pn(w)\\{w_i\\}_{i=1}^k \sim P_n(w){wi​}i=1k​∼Pn​(w):

LNEG=log⁡σ(vwO′⊤vwI)+∑i=1kEwi∼Pn(w)[log⁡σ(−vwi′⊤vwI)]\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\text{NEG}} = \log \sigma(\mathbf{v}'_{w_O}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I}) + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \mathbb{E}_{w_i \sim P_n(w)}\left[\log \sigma(-\mathbf{v}'_{w_i}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I})\right]}LNEG​=logσ(vwO​′​⊤vwI​​)+i=1∑k​Ewi​∼Pn​(w)​[logσ(−vwi​′​⊤vwI​​)]​

**Term-by-term interpretation:**

* **First term** log⁡σ(vwO′⊤vwI)\log \sigma(\mathbf{v}'_{w_O}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I})logσ(vwO​′​⊤vwI​​): maximize the dot product between the center word and its true context → _pull_ the positive pair closer
* **Second term** ∑log⁡σ(−vwi′⊤vwI)\sum \log \sigma(-\mathbf{v}'_{w_i}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I})∑logσ(−vwi​′​⊤vwI​​): using σ(−x)=1−σ(x)\sigma(-x) = 1 - \sigma(x)σ(−x)=1−σ(x), this is ∑log⁡(1−σ(vwi′⊤vwI))\sum \log(1 - \sigma(\mathbf{v}'_{w_i}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I}))∑log(1−σ(vwi​′​⊤vwI​​)) → minimize the dot product between the center word and noise words → _push_ negative pairs apart

Negative sampling is a **contrastive learning** objective: attract positive pairs, repel negative pairs. This reformulation reduces per-step cost from O(V)O(V)O(V) to O(k)O(k)O(k) — a speedup of V/k≈10,000×V/k \approx 10{,}000 \timesV/k≈10,000× for k=5k = 5k=5, V=50,000V = 50{,}000V=50,000.

#### 14.6.2 Computing the Gradient

For completeness, the gradient of LNEG\mathcal{L}_{\text{NEG}}LNEG​ with respect to the center word embedding vwI\mathbf{v}_{w_I}vwI​​:

∇vwILNEG=σ(−vwO′⊤vwI)⋅vwO′⏟positive gradient+∑i=1kσ(vwi′⊤vwI)⋅(−vwi′)⏟negative gradient\nabla_{\mathbf{v}_{w_I}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{NEG}} = \underbrace{\sigma(-\mathbf{v}'_{w_O}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I}) \cdot \mathbf{v}'_{w_O}}_{\text{positive gradient}} + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \underbrace{\sigma(\mathbf{v}'_{w_i}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I}) \cdot (-\mathbf{v}'_{w_i})}_{\text{negative gradient}}∇vwI​​​LNEG​=positive gradientσ(−vwO​′​⊤vwI​​)⋅vwO​′​​​+i=1∑k​negative gradientσ(vwi​′​⊤vwI​​)⋅(−vwi​′​)​​

The positive gradient σ(−vwO′⊤vwI)\sigma(-\mathbf{v}'_{w_O}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I})σ(−vwO​′​⊤vwI​​) is large when the positive pair has low dot product (model is uncertain or wrong) — similar to the "observed minus expected" form from Chapter 13's Skip-gram gradient derivation.

The negative gradient pushes vwI\mathbf{v}_{w_I}vwI​​ away from negative samples vwi′\mathbf{v}'_{w_i}vwi​′​ in proportion to σ(vwi′⊤vwI)\sigma(\mathbf{v}'_{w_i}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_{w_I})σ(vwi​′​⊤vwI​​) — the model's current (erroneous) confidence that wiw_iwi​ is a valid context.

### 14.7 The Noise Distribution: Why U(w)3/4U(w)^{3/4}U(w)3/4?

Mikolov et al. tried several noise distributions and found that the **3/4-power unigram distribution** worked best:

Pn(w)=U(w)3/4Z,Z=∑w′U(w′)3/4P_n(w) = \frac{U(w)^{3/4}}{Z}, \qquad Z = \sum_{w'} U(w')^{3/4}Pn​(w)=ZU(w)3/4​,Z=w′∑​U(w′)3/4

where U(w)=count(w)/∑w′count(w′)U(w) = \text{count}(w) / \sum_{w'} \text{count}(w')U(w)=count(w)/∑w′​count(w′) is the standard unigram frequency.

**Why not plain unigram U(w)U(w)U(w)?** High-frequency words like _the_ , _is_ , _a_ dominate the vocabulary. If Pn=UP_n = UPn​=U, then 30–40% of negative samples are function words — they provide little semantic discriminative signal. The model learns mainly to distinguish content words from _the_ , which is not the goal.

**Why not uniform Pn=1/VP_n = 1/VPn​=1/V?** Extremely rare words (hapax legomena, misspellings) would be over-sampled. These words have unreliable embeddings due to sparse training signal.

**The 3/4 power as a smooth interpolation.**

Define the α\alphaα-power smoothing: Pnα(w)∝U(w)αP_n^\alpha(w) \propto U(w)^\alphaPnα​(w)∝U(w)α.

* α=1\alpha = 1α=1: plain unigram (biased toward high-frequency words)
* α=0\alpha = 0α=0: uniform (ignores frequency entirely)
* α<1\alpha < 1α<1: intermediate — compresses the frequency range

For α=3/4\alpha = 3/4α=3/4, relative to α=1\alpha = 1α=1:

Word | U(w)U(w)U(w) | U(w)3/4U(w)^{3/4}U(w)3/4 | Relative sampling boost  
---|---|---|---  
_the_ | 0.50 | 0.595 | 0.88×  
_economy_ | 0.01 | 0.0316 | 2.3×  
_deflation_ | 0.0001 | 0.00056 | 4.0×  
  
The 3/4 power modestly reduces the dominance of high-frequency words while substantially increasing the sampling probability of rare words. The practical justification is empirical: it works better on word similarity and analogy benchmarks. A theoretical justification: natural language follows Zipf's law (U(w)∝rank−1U(w) \propto \text{rank}^{-1}U(w)∝rank−1), and the 3/4 power preserves this power-law character while rebalancing it toward lower frequencies.

**Number of negative samples kkk.** The papers recommend k=5k = 5k=5–202020 for small datasets, k=2k = 2k=2–555 for large datasets. The intuition: with more data, each positive pair is seen many times, providing stable gradient signal. Negative samples serve to break symmetry early in training; once the model is well-trained, fewer negative samples suffice.

* * *

### 14.8 Subsampling of Frequent Words

A separate technique — **frequency-based subsampling** — addresses the imbalance between frequent and rare words from the input side.

Each word wtw_twt​ in the training corpus is discarded independently with probability:

P(discard wt)=1−tf(wt)P(\text{discard } w_t) = 1 - \sqrt{\frac{t}{f(w_t)}}P(discard wt​)=1−f(wt​)t​​

where f(wt)f(w_t)f(wt​) is the word's corpus frequency and ttt is a threshold (typically t=10−5t = 10^{-5}t=10−5).

**Effect:** High-frequency words (below the threshold) are almost always discarded; low-frequency words are almost never discarded. This achieves two goals:

  1. **Speed:** Fewer tokens → fewer training steps
  2. **Quality:** The model focuses on informative co-occurrences. The co-occurrence between _France_ and _Paris_ is semantically rich; the co-occurrence between _the_ and _Paris_ is not. Downsampling _the_ allows more training steps on meaningful pairs.

Subsampling and the 3/4-power noise distribution work complementarily: subsampling reduces the effective contribution of high-frequency words as positive samples; the noise distribution adjusts their contribution as negative samples.

* * *

### 14.9 The Levy-Goldberg Connection: SGNS ≈ Shifted PMI Factorization

Levy and Goldberg (2014) proved a result that fundamentally changed how NLP researchers understood Word2Vec: **Skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) implicitly factorizes the shifted PMI matrix.**

**Theorem.** At the global optimum of the SGNS objective, the dot product between word and context embeddings satisfies:

vc′⊤vw=PMI(w,c)−log⁡k\mathbf{v}'_{c}{}^\top \mathbf{v}_w = \text{PMI}(w, c) - \log kvc′​⊤vw​=PMI(w,c)−logk

**Proof sketch.** For fixed word pair (w,c)(w, c)(w,c), the per-pair SGNS contribution to the objective is:

J(w,c)=#(w,c)⋅log⁡σ(x)+k⋅#(w)⋅Pn(c)⋅log⁡σ(−x)J(w, c) = \\#(w, c) \cdot \log \sigma(x) + k \cdot \\#(w) \cdot P_n(c) \cdot \log \sigma(-x)J(w,c)=#(w,c)⋅logσ(x)+k⋅#(w)⋅Pn​(c)⋅logσ(−x)

where x=vc′⊤vwx = \mathbf{v}'_c{}^\top \mathbf{v}_wx=vc′​⊤vw​ and #(w,c)\\#(w, c)#(w,c) is the co-occurrence count of the pair.

Setting ∂J/∂x=0\partial J / \partial x = 0∂J/∂x=0:

#(w,c)⋅σ(−x)=k⋅#(w)⋅Pn(c)⋅σ(x)\\#(w, c) \cdot \sigma(-x) = k \cdot \\#(w) \cdot P_n(c) \cdot \sigma(x)#(w,c)⋅σ(−x)=k⋅#(w)⋅Pn​(c)⋅σ(x)

Using σ(−x)/σ(x)=e−x\sigma(-x)/\sigma(x) = e^{-x}σ(−x)/σ(x)=e−x:

e−x=k⋅#(w)⋅Pn(c)#(w,c)e^{-x} = \frac{k \cdot \\#(w) \cdot P_n(c)}{\\#(w, c)}e−x=#(w,c)k⋅#(w)⋅Pn​(c)​

Therefore:

x=log⁡#(w,c)k⋅#(w)⋅Pn(c)x = \log \frac{\\#(w, c)}{k \cdot \\#(w) \cdot P_n(c)}x=logk⋅#(w)⋅Pn​(c)#(w,c)​

With unigram noise distribution Pn(c)=#(c)/∣D∣P_n(c) = \\#(c) / |D|Pn​(c)=#(c)/∣D∣:

x=log⁡#(w,c)⋅∣D∣#(w)⋅#(c)−log⁡k=PMI(w,c)−log⁡k■x = \log \frac{\\#(w, c) \cdot |D|}{\\#(w) \cdot \\#(c)} - \log k = \text{PMI}(w, c) - \log k \quad \blacksquarex=log#(w)⋅#(c)#(w,c)⋅∣D∣​−logk=PMI(w,c)−logk■

**Implications:**

  1. **Theoretical unification.** Word2Vec and LSA are not fundamentally different approaches — they are both approximating the PMI matrix with a low-rank factorization. The difference is in the loss function (cross-entropy vs. squared error) and optimization (gradient descent on individual pairs vs. batch SVD).

  2. **The role of kkk.** Increasing the number of negative samples kkk shifts the target matrix by log⁡k\log klogk. More negative samples effectively apply PPMI (truncation at −log⁡k-\log k−logk rather than 0).

  3. **Design space.** The Levy-Goldberg result reveals that several design choices in Word2Vec (normalization, noise distribution) are essentially choices about _which_ variant of the PMI matrix to factorize.

* * *

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> Negative sampling is an instance of **contrastive learning** — a paradigm with deep roots in perceptual science and physics.
> 
> **Neuroscience: Lateral inhibition.** In the retina and early visual cortex, neurons representing similar stimuli inhibit each other, sharpening contrast. A cell responding to a vertical edge suppresses nearby cells that would respond to slightly tilted edges. Negative sampling implements the same mechanism computationally: the update rule pushes the center word _away from_ words that the model incorrectly believes are in its context, sharpening the word's semantic "boundary."
> 
> **Statistical mechanics: Contrastive Divergence.** Boltzmann machines (Hinton & Sejnowski, 1986) are energy-based models where learning involves comparing statistics from real data ("positive phase") against statistics from the model's own samples ("negative phase"). Contrastive Divergence (Hinton, 2002) approximates this by running short MCMC chains for the negative phase — mathematically analogous to the kkk negative samples in SGNS, where each negative sample contributes one gradient update to the "push apart" phase.
> 
> **Information theory: Sufficient statistics.** The NCE framework (from which negative sampling derives) estimates density ratios Pdata/PnoiseP_{\text{data}} / P_{\text{noise}}Pdata​/Pnoise​ rather than absolute densities. This is sufficient for the downstream task (representation learning) because the _ratio_ captures all the information about which features distinguish data from noise — analogous to how likelihood ratios are sufficient statistics for hypothesis testing in the Neyman-Pearson framework.
