## Chapter 16: From Static to Contextualized Representations

> **Chapter Learning Objectives**
> 
> By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
> 
>   1. Identify the polysemy problem as the fundamental limitation of static word embeddings and explain why a single vector per word type cannot capture context-dependent meaning.
>   2. Evaluate three attempted static-embedding patches (sense disambiguation, subword models, retrofitting) and explain why each is insufficient.
>   3. Define contextualized embeddings formally: a function from (word, context) pairs to vectors, producing different representations for different occurrences of the same word.
>   4. Describe ELMo's architecture (bidirectional LSTM + task-specific layer combination) and explain why layer weights are task-dependent.
>   5. Articulate why RNN-based contextualization (ELMo) inherits the sequential computation and fixed-context-capacity limitations of LSTMs, motivating the Transformer.
> 

### 16.1 A Bridge Chapter

The preceding four chapters developed the theory and practice of static word representations: how the distributional hypothesis motivates dense embeddings, and how two landmark methods (Word2Vec and GloVe) learn them efficiently from large corpora. These methods transformed NLP. Between 2013 and 2017, essentially every state-of-the-art NLP system used pretrained word embeddings as its input layer.

But Word2Vec and GloVe share a fundamental limitation that no engineering improvement can fix. This chapter identifies that limitation precisely, traces the chain of ideas that addresses it, and previews the architecture — the Transformer — that makes the solution computationally viable.

This chapter serves a structural role in the book. Part V (Chapters 17–20) develops the encoder-decoder architecture and attention mechanism. Part VI (Chapters 21–26) introduces the Transformer. The limitation identified here is the _reason_ those architectures were built.

* * *

### 16.2 The Single-Vector Constraint

The core limitation of Word2Vec and GloVe is architectural: both methods assign each word type exactly one vector, regardless of context.

**Formally:** A word embedding is a function f:V→Rdf: \mathcal{V} \to \mathbb{R}^df:V→Rd mapping each vocabulary item to a fixed vector. The same vector is used everywhere the word appears.

This is what we mean by "static" or "type-level" representations. The word _bank_ is not represented as an occurrence in a sentence — it is represented as an entry in a lookup table:
    
    
    embedding_matrix["bank"] = [0.34, -0.12, 0.87, ..., 0.23]   # same vector always
    

Contrast this with what we actually need: a representation of _this occurrence of bank, in this sentence, meaning this specific thing_.

* * *

### 16.3 The Polysemy Problem

**Polysemy** — multiple distinct meanings for one word form — is ubiquitous in natural language. Consider the word _bank_ :

  1. _"I went to the**bank** to deposit money."_ (financial institution)
  2. _"We sat on the**bank** of the river."_ (river bank)
  3. _"You can**bank** on me to show up."_ (rely on)

In Word2Vec or GloVe, _bank_ has exactly one vector e(bank)∈Rd\mathbf{e}(\text{bank}) \in \mathbb{R}^de(bank)∈Rd. What value does this vector take?

**Theorem (informal, Arora et al. 2018).** Under mild distributional assumptions, the Word2Vec/GloVe vector for a polysemous word is approximately a frequency-weighted average of its sense vectors:

e(w)≈∑k=1Kαk vsk\mathbf{e}(w) \approx \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_k \, \mathbf{v}_{s_k}e(w)≈k=1∑K​αk​vsk​​

where KKK is the number of senses, αk\alpha_kαk​ is the frequency with which sense sks_ksk​ is used, and vsk\mathbf{v}_{s_k}vsk​​ is the "ideal" representation of that sense.

**Consequence:** The actual vector e(bank)\mathbf{e}(\text{bank})e(bank) is a weighted average of the financial, geographical, and idiomatic senses. If the financial sense is most common (say, α1=0.7\alpha_1 = 0.7α1​=0.7), the vector is pulled strongly toward the financial sense cluster. A model reading the sentence _"We sat on the bank of the river"_ receives the average vector — a representation that is 70% about finance and only 30% about geography.

This is not a small-data problem. Training on more data will not fix it — it simply produces a better estimate of the _average_ vector. The problem is architectural: one vector per type cannot represent type-level variation.

#### 16.3.1 The Scope of Polysemy

Polysemy is not an edge case. Many of the most frequent words in English are highly polysemous:

Word | Senses (partial)  
---|---  
_run_ | physical movement; manage; execute (code); elapsed duration; score in baseball  
_interest_ | intellectual curiosity; financial interest rate; stake or claim  
_spring_ | season; coiled elastic; water source; to leap  
_cell_ | biological unit; battery; prison room; spreadsheet unit  
_play_ | game; theatrical performance; musical performance; strategic maneuver  
  
Even words that appear semantically stable exhibit **sense modulation** — subtle context-dependent meaning shifts:

* _"run a company"_ vs. _"run an experiment"_ vs. _"run a marathon"_ vs. _"run out of time"_

All four are uses of the same word, yet the semantic content differs in ways that matter for downstream tasks. Static vectors represent all four uses identically.

* * *

### 16.4 Why Static Patches Fail

Before contextualized embeddings, researchers tried several approaches to patch the polysemy problem within the static framework.

#### 16.4.1 Multiple Prototype Models

Reisinger and Mooney (2010) and Huang et al. (2012) proposed learning KKK separate vectors per word — one per sense:

  1. Cluster all occurrences of word www by their context vectors
  2. Train a separate embedding vw,k\mathbf{v}_{w,k}vw,k​ for each cluster kkk
  3. At inference time, select vw,k∗\mathbf{v}_{w,k^*}vw,k∗​ where k∗=arg⁡min⁡kd(context,clusterk)k^* = \arg\min_k d(\text{context}, \text{cluster}_k)k∗=argmink​d(context,clusterk​)

This approach has irreducible problems:

* **K KK must be pre-specified.** Different words have different numbers of senses. _The_ has essentially one meaning; _bank_ has three clearly distinct ones; _run_ has dozens. No fixed KKK works for all words.
* **Hard cluster boundaries.** Senses often form a continuum rather than discrete clusters. The word _interest_ in "strategic interest in the region" lies between the intellectual-curiosity and financial-stake senses. Any hard boundary misrepresents these cases.
* **No compositional generalization.** Multiple prototypes cannot represent novel sense combinations that arise from new word-word interactions.

#### 16.4.2 Sense Disambiguation as a Pre-Processing Step

An alternative: run a word sense disambiguation (WSD) system to identify the intended sense, then select the corresponding embedding. The problem is circular — WSD itself requires good representations of word meaning to work well.

#### 16.4.3 The Fundamental Limitation

Both patches share a deeper problem: they operate on static embeddings and try to introduce context sensitivity as a post-hoc correction. The correct solution is to build context sensitivity into the representation architecture from the beginning. Context is not an afterthought; it is the fundamental input from which meaning is determined.

The distributional hypothesis says: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps." But Word2Vec and GloVe operationalize this only at training time — they use context to train fixed vectors, then throw the context away. A representation system that is truly faithful to the distributional hypothesis should use context _at every use_ , not only during training.

* * *

### 16.5 Contextualized Embeddings: The Core Idea

**Definition.** A **contextualized word embedding** is a mapping:

f:(word,context)→Rdf: (\text{word}, \text{context}) \to \mathbb{R}^df:(word,context)→Rd

that produces a different vector for each occurrence of a word, depending on the surrounding sentence.

The contrast with static embeddings:

| Static | Contextualized  
---|---|---  
Input | word type | (word, sentence) pair  
Output | single vector per type | different vector per token  
Representation of _bank_ | same vector everywhere | different vectors in financial vs. geographical contexts  
Analogy | lookup table | function call  
  
The key insight: to produce a contextualized representation, the model must _read the entire sentence_ before producing the representation for any word. This requires a sequence model — either an RNN (as in ELMo) or a Transformer (as in BERT and GPT).

* * *

### 16.6 ELMo: The First Widely Successful Contextualized Embeddings

**Peters, M.E., Neumann, M., Iyyer, M., et al. (2018).** _Deep contextualized word representations._ NAACL.

ELMo (_Embeddings from Language Models_) was the first method to demonstrate that contextualized embeddings could produce large, consistent gains across a wide range of NLP tasks without task-specific architecture changes.

#### 16.6.1 Architecture

ELMo uses a **bidirectional LSTM language model** (biLM):

* A forward LSTM reads the sentence left-to-right and predicts each word from its preceding context
* A backward LSTM reads right-to-left and predicts each word from its following context
* L=2L = 2L=2 layers of bidirectional LSTM are stacked

For a sentence of nnn tokens, the biLM produces 2L+12L + 12L+1 representations per token: the token embedding layer plus LLL forward-LSTM layers plus LLL backward-LSTM layers (the +1+1+1 counts the initial embedding).

Rk={xkemb,h→k,j,h←k,j∣j=1,…,L}\mathbf{R}_k = \left\\{ \mathbf{x}_k^{\text{emb}}, \overrightarrow{\mathbf{h}}_{k,j}, \overleftarrow{\mathbf{h}}_{k,j} \mid j = 1, \ldots, L \right\\}Rk​={xkemb​,hk,j​,hk,j​∣j=1,…,L}

#### 16.6.2 Task-Specific Combination

For a downstream task, ELMo computes a _learned linear combination_ of all layers for each token:

ELMoktask=γtask∑j=0Lsjtaskhk,jLM\text{ELMo}_k^{\text{task}} = \gamma^{\text{task}} \sum_{j=0}^{L} s_j^{\text{task}} \mathbf{h}_{k,j}^{\text{LM}}ELMoktask​=γtaskj=0∑L​sjtask​hk,jLM​

where γtask\gamma^{\text{task}}γtask and {sjtask}\\{s_j^{\text{task}}\\}{sjtask​} are task-specific parameters learned during fine-tuning.

**Why different layers?** Peters et al. showed that different layers encode different types of information:

* Lower layers (layer 1): syntactic information — POS tags, dependency structure
* Higher layers (layer 2): semantic information — word sense, semantic role

This is the same hierarchical specialization observed in CNNs (Chapter 8): lower layers capture local structure, higher layers capture abstract semantics.

#### 16.6.3 ELMo Results

Peters et al. evaluated ELMo across six diverse NLP benchmarks. In every case, simply adding ELMo representations to an existing task-specific architecture — with no other changes — produced substantial improvements:

Task | Baseline F1/Acc | \+ ELMo | Absolute Gain  
---|---|---|---  
SQuAD 1.1 (F1) | 81.1 | 85.8 | +4.7  
Named Entity Recognition, CoNLL 2003 (F1) | 90.15 | 92.22 | +2.06  
Semantic Role Labeling (F1) | 81.4 | 84.6 | +3.2  
Sentiment Analysis, SST-5 (Acc) | 51.4 | 54.7 | +1.0*  
Coreference Resolution (Avg F1) | 67.2 | 70.4 | +3.2  
Textual Entailment, SNLI (Acc) | 88.0 | 88.7 | +0.7  
  
* _SST-5 is five-class fine-grained sentiment, where even small accuracy gains are significant._

**The key result is not any single number — it is the pattern.** ELMo improved _every_ downstream task using the _same_ pretrained representations. The biLM was trained once on a large text corpus; no task-specific modification was made to the language model itself. This was the first convincing demonstration that a single pretrained language model transfers broadly across NLP tasks — the core idea behind the pretraining revolution that followed with BERT and GPT.

**Layer weighting analysis.** The task-specific layer weights sjtasks_j^{\text{task}}sjtask​ (from §16.6.2) revealed a striking pattern: syntactic tasks such as POS tagging and NER assigned higher weight to the lower (first) LSTM layer, while semantic tasks such as SRL and sentiment analysis assigned higher weight to the upper (second) layer. This confirmed that different layers of the biLM encode different levels of linguistic abstraction — shallow layers capture syntax, deeper layers capture semantics — and that the optimal combination depends on what the downstream task requires.

#### 16.6.4 Why Does ELMo Work?

ELMo's language modeling objective (predict the next word) is the same task as a classic language model, but applied to a very large corpus. To predict the next word accurately, the model must:

  1. Track syntactic structure (subject-verb agreement, pronoun binding)
  2. Resolve word sense from context (is _bank_ the financial or geographic meaning?)
  3. Model discourse-level information (what topic is being discussed?)

These capabilities emerge from the prediction objective without explicit supervision — an early demonstration of the pretraining principle: if you make the model predict text well, it develops rich representations of language structure as a by-product.

* * *

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> The distinction between static and contextualized representations maps onto a fundamental divide in measurement theory.
> 
> **Physics: State vs. property.** Classical mechanics distinguishes a particle's intrinsic properties (mass, charge — fixed) from its state (position, momentum — context-dependent). A word's morphological form is an intrinsic property; its meaning is a state that depends on context. Static embeddings treat word meaning as an intrinsic property; contextualized embeddings treat it as a state.
> 
> **Genetics: Genotype vs. phenotype.** An organism's genotype is fixed (its DNA sequence); its phenotype — how those genes are expressed — depends on the environment. The same gene can produce different outcomes in different cellular contexts (gene regulation, epigenetics). Word types are like genotypes (fixed sequences); their contextualized representations are like phenotypes (context-dependent expressions). The word _run_ has one "genotype" (its form) but many "phenotypes" (its meanings in context).
> 
> **Psychology: Semantic priming.** In cognitive psychology, the context in which a word is encountered changes subsequent processing — reading _doctor_ activates _hospital_ , _nurse_ , _medicine_. This priming effect shows that human lexical access is contextualized: the same word evokes different activation patterns in different contexts. ELMo's bidirectional LSTM approximates this context-sensitive activation; BERT's attention mechanism models it more directly.

* * *

### 16.7 The ELMo Limitation: Bidirectional LSTMs

ELMo produces stronger representations than static embeddings — but it inherits all the limitations of the LSTM architecture analyzed in Chapters 10–12.

#### 16.7.1 Sequential Processing

The LSTM processes tokens one at a time. Even with modern hardware that parallelizes matrix operations within a single time step, the _sequence_ of operations is inherently serial. Computing ht\mathbf{h}_tht​ requires ht−1\mathbf{h}_{t-1}ht−1​; there is no way to compute all hidden states simultaneously.

**Consequence for training.** Training ELMo on a large corpus requires many sequential steps. The training wall-clock time grows linearly with sequence length, limiting the size of corpora and sequences that can be processed efficiently.

**Consequence for very long contexts.** Even with LSTM's constant error carousel (CEC), the effective receptive field is limited. For a sentence of length 100, the hidden state h100\mathbf{h}_{100}h100​ nominally encodes the entire history — but in practice the most recent tokens dominate. Distant dependencies are harder to learn.

#### 16.7.2 Fixed Hidden State Capacity

At each time step, the LSTM must compress _all information needed for future predictions_ into a hidden state vector of fixed dimension dhd_hdh​. This is a hard capacity constraint. For a complex sentence, this vector must simultaneously encode:

* The word currently being processed
* The relevant syntactic structure built so far
* The referents of pronouns and anaphora
* The broader semantic topic

For a sufficiently complex sentence, some of this information will be lost.

#### 16.7.3 Limited Context Integration

ELMo's forward LSTM at position ttt can only use context from positions {1,…,t−1}\\{1, \ldots, t-1\\}{1,…,t−1}; the backward LSTM at position ttt can only use context from positions {t+1,…,n}\\{t+1, \ldots, n\\}{t+1,…,n}. While ELMo concatenates both directions, neither component of the LSTM actually "sees" the full bidirectional context simultaneously at a single position. The full context is only accessible by combining both LSTM outputs — a coarse approximation of true bidirectional context.

* * *

### 16.8 The Transformer Solution (Preview)

The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) replaces recurrent computation with **self-attention** — a mechanism that allows _any position_ to attend to _any other position_ in the sequence, with learned attention weights, in a single computational step.

**The key contrast:**

Architecture | Context access | Sequential steps | Per-step cost  
---|---|---|---  
LSTM (ELMo) | O(n)O(n)O(n) steps to propagate context from position 1 to position nnn | O(n)O(n)O(n) | O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2)  
Transformer | Direct access to all positions simultaneously | O(1)O(1)O(1) | O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d)  
  
The Transformer's O(1)O(1)O(1) sequential step count means: the representation at position ttt can be computed using full context from all positions simultaneously, without information loss from sequential propagation. For typical sequences (n≪dn \ll dn≪d, where d=512d = 512d=512 in the original Transformer), the O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d) attention cost is manageable.

**BERT and GPT.** With the Transformer as the backbone, two architectures emerged that solved ELMo's remaining limitations:

* **BERT** (Devlin et al., 2019): a Transformer _encoder_ pretrained on Masked Language Modeling — randomly masking 15% of tokens and training the model to predict the masked tokens from the full bidirectional context. Because the encoder reads the entire sequence in both directions simultaneously (not sequentially), every token's representation is computed from its full context. BERT solved the "bidirectionality approximation" problem in ELMo.

* **GPT** (Radford et al., 2018): a Transformer _decoder_ trained on autoregressive language modeling — predict the next token from all preceding tokens. GPT demonstrated that the pretraining → fine-tuning paradigm could scale dramatically, eventually producing models (GPT-3, GPT-4) capable of few-shot learning across arbitrary tasks.

These models and their descendants — the large language models that define the current state of AI — are conceptually introduced in Chapter 25 and developed in detail in Volume II.

* * *

### 16.9 The Technical Prerequisite: Attention

Why does the Transformer enable contextualized representations so effectively? The answer is the **attention mechanism** : a mathematical operation that computes, for each position in a sequence, a weighted sum of all other positions' representations, where the weights are determined by learned compatibility functions.

Attention was not invented for the Transformer — it originated in machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015), where it was used to allow the decoder of a Seq2Seq model to selectively attend to different parts of the input sequence when generating each output word.

Part V (Chapters 17–20) derives the attention mechanism from scratch:

* Chapter 17: the Encoder-Decoder framework and why it fails for long sequences
* Chapter 18: Paper close read on the Seq2Seq model (Sutskever et al., 2014)
* Chapter 19: The mathematics of attention — query-key-value framework, additive vs. dot-product attention
* Chapter 20: Paper close read on Bahdanau attention

Part VI then applies attention as the _sole_ building block of a sequence model — removing the LSTM entirely:

* Chapters 21–23: Self-attention, multi-head attention, and the complete Transformer
* Chapter 24: Paper close read on "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017)
* Chapters 25–26: The pretraining paradigm and language model mathematics

* * *

### 16.10 The Development Arc: A Retrospective

The development of word representations from 1990 to 2020 follows a coherent progression, each step motivated by the failure mode of the previous one:

One-hot→sparsityLSA/SVD→scaleWord2Vec→global statsGloVe→polysemyELMo→sequentialBERT/GPT\text{One-hot} \xrightarrow{\text{sparsity}} \text{LSA/SVD} \xrightarrow{\text{scale}} \text{Word2Vec} \xrightarrow{\text{global stats}} \text{GloVe} \xrightarrow{\text{polysemy}} \text{ELMo} \xrightarrow{\text{sequential}} \text{BERT/GPT}One-hotsparsity​LSA/SVDscale​Word2Vecglobal stats​GloVepolysemy​ELMosequential​BERT/GPT

Each arrow represents a specific problem:

  1. One-hot → LSA: one-hot encodes no semantic similarity; SVD compresses the co-occurrence matrix into a dense semantic space
  2. LSA → Word2Vec: explicit matrix factorization doesn't scale; prediction-based training handles billion-word corpora
  3. Word2Vec → GloVe: local context windows miss global statistics; GloVe explicitly optimizes over the full co-occurrence matrix
  4. Static → ELMo: one vector per type cannot represent polysemy; bidirectional LSTM produces context-dependent representations
  5. ELMo → BERT/GPT: sequential LSTM limits training speed and context integration; Transformer processes all positions simultaneously

**The key insight:** each method is not merely "better" — it solves a _specific_ problem that the previous approach had in principle. Understanding this chain is understanding why modern language models look the way they do.

* * *

### 16.11 Mathematical Summary: From Lookup Tables to Functions

The progression from static to contextualized representations is a progression in mathematical complexity:

**Static embedding:**

fstatic:V→Rdf_{\text{static}}: \mathcal{V} \to \mathbb{R}^dfstatic​:V→Rd

A simple lookup table. Index a matrix by word ID.

**ELMo-style contextualized embedding:**

fELMo:Vn×{1,…,n}→Rdf_{\text{ELMo}}: \mathcal{V}^n \times \\{1, \ldots, n\\} \to \mathbb{R}^dfELMo​:Vn×{1,…,n}→Rd

Given the full sentence [w1,…,wn][w_1, \ldots, w_n][w1​,…,wn​], returns the representation of the ttt-th word. Computed by running a biLM over the sequence.

**Transformer-style contextualized embedding:**

fTransformer:Vn→Rn×df_{\text{Transformer}}: \mathcal{V}^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}fTransformer​:Vn→Rn×d

Computes all nnn token representations simultaneously, with each token's representation attending to all other positions. The entire output matrix is computed as a function of the entire input matrix — no sequential dependency.

The move from lookup tables to sequence functions is what enables polysemy resolution. The move from sequential to parallel processing (LSTM to Transformer) is what enables the scale of pretraining that produces powerful general-purpose representations.

* * *

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> The distinction between static and contextualized representations parallels a fundamental shift in how systems encode information.
> 
> **Fixed effects vs. random coefficient models.** In panel data econometrics, the fixed effects model assigns each entity a single fixed intercept: yit=αi+xit⊤β+ϵity_{it} = \alpha_i + \mathbf{x}_{it}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta} + \epsilon_{it}yit​=αi​+xit⊤​β+ϵit​. This is the static embedding approach — one parameter per entity regardless of context. The random coefficient model allows βi\boldsymbol{\beta}_iβi​ to vary by entity and, in the Correlated Random Coefficients model, depend on observable covariates: βi=γzi+ui\boldsymbol{\beta}_i = \boldsymbol{\gamma}\mathbf{z}_i + \mathbf{u}_iβi​=γzi​+ui​. Contextualized embeddings are the NLP analogue of random coefficient models: the "coefficient" (word representation) depends on the observable context variables (the surrounding sentence).
> 
> **Protein folding: Sequence vs. structure.** A protein's amino acid sequence is its static representation — the same for every molecule of that protein, in any environment. Its three-dimensional structure is its contextualized representation — it depends on the local molecular environment, post-translational modifications, and binding partners. AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021) predicts protein structure from sequence using a Transformer architecture (Evoformer) that attends over both the amino acid sequence and evolutionary co-variation data — a contextualized representation of each residue's role in the structure. The architectural parallel is not coincidental: self-attention over sequences is a general mechanism for computing context-dependent representations in any domain.

* * *

### 16.12 Summary

Concept | Details  
---|---  
Static embedding | One vector per word type: f:V→Rdf: \mathcal{V} \to \mathbb{R}^df:V→Rd  
The polysemy problem | Polysemous words receive a frequency-weighted average of their sense vectors  
Formal statement | e(w)≈∑kαkvsk\mathbf{e}(w) \approx \sum_k \alpha_k \mathbf{v}_{s_k}e(w)≈∑k​αk​vsk​​ — a model averaging distinct senses  
Multi-prototype patch | Multiple vectors per word, one per sense cluster — fails on KKK-selection and hard boundaries  
Contextualized embedding | f:(sentence,position)→Rdf: (\text{sentence}, \text{position}) \to \mathbb{R}^df:(sentence,position)→Rd — different vector per occurrence  
ELMo | Bidirectional LSTM; different layers capture syntax vs. semantics; task-specific layer weighting  
ELMo limitation | Sequential computation; fixed hidden state capacity; approximate bidirectionality  
Transformer solution | Self-attention allows all positions to interact in O(1)O(1)O(1) sequential steps  
BERT | Bidirectional Transformer encoder; Masked Language Model pretraining  
GPT | Causal Transformer decoder; autoregressive pretraining  
  
**The forward pointer:** Part V builds up to attention, and Part VI builds the Transformer. Every component developed in those chapters — encoder-decoder architecture, attention weights, multi-head attention, positional encoding — is a direct consequence of the limitation identified in this chapter: that sequential, fixed-capacity architectures cannot efficiently produce rich, contextualized representations at scale.

### Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Exercise 16.1.** The word _run_ in English has dozens of distinct uses. For each of the following sentences, describe what a contextualized embedding at the position of _run_ should represent — and explain why a static embedding would fail to capture it. (a) _"She can run a four-minute mile."_ (b) _"The play had a run of three years on Broadway."_ (c) _"He decided to run for Senate."_ (d) _"The database query will run for about 10 minutes."_

Answer

Four senses: "run a marathon" (physical locomotion), "run a company" (manage), "run a program" (execute software), "the colors run" (bleed/spread). A single vector averages all four senses weighted by corpus frequency. The vector is close to the most frequent sense but poorly represents rare senses. Cosine similarity with related words (e.g., "jog") reflects only the dominant sense.

Specifically: (a) physical locomotion — the embedding should be near vectors for _sprint_ , _jog_ , _race_ ; (b) extended duration of performance — near _duration_ , _engagement_ , _showing_ ; (c) political candidacy — near _campaign_ , _compete_ , _election_ ; (d) software execution — near _execute_ , _process_ , _compute_. A static embedding produces the same vector for all four, dominated by whichever sense is most frequent in the training corpus.

* * *

**Exercise 16.5.** The chapter claims that ELMo's bidirectionality is "approximate" because the forward and backward LSTMs are trained separately and their outputs are concatenated (not jointly optimized). Explain what "true" bidirectionality would mean. How does BERT's masked language modeling objective achieve true bidirectionality?

Answer

ELMo concatenates independently trained forward and backward LSTMs: [h→k;h←k][\overrightarrow{\mathbf{h}}_k; \overleftarrow{\mathbf{h}}_k][hk​;hk​]. Each direction processes the sequence independently — the forward LSTM at position kkk knows only tokens 1..k1..k1..k, the backward knows only tokens k..Tk..Tk..T. This is "approximate" bidirectionality. "True" bidirectionality (as in BERT's Transformer encoder) allows every position to attend to every other position simultaneously. The practical difference: in ELMo, the forward representation at position 5 doesn't benefit from rightward context until concatenation, and even then the two directions don't interact within the LSTM computation.

BERT achieves true bidirectionality through the masked language modeling (MLM) objective: by masking a token and asking the model to predict it from _all_ surrounding context (both left and right simultaneously), the Transformer encoder learns representations where every position's hidden state is a function of the entire sequence. There is no separate "forward" and "backward" — there is a single unified computation where all positions attend to all other positions in each layer.

* * *

**Exercise 16.6 (Conceptual).** The progression from Word2Vec to ELMo to BERT can be described as moving from _type-level_ to _token-level_ representations. (a) Define _word type_ and _word token_ precisely. (b) A corpus contains the sentence _"The bank called the bank."_ This sentence has 5 tokens. How many distinct word types does it contain? (c) What does a static embedding system produce for the two occurrences of _bank_? What does a contextualized embedding system produce? In what sense are the contextualized embeddings more faithful to the distributional hypothesis?

Answer

"Type" = unique word in the vocabulary (the abstract concept "bank"); "token" = specific occurrence in a sentence (this particular "bank" in "river bank"). Static embeddings are type-level (one vector per type); contextualized embeddings are token-level (different vector for each occurrence). The distinction matters because NLP tasks operate on tokens (this sentence, this context), not types. A system that assigns the same representation to all occurrences of "bank" cannot distinguish financial from geographical contexts.

Specifically: (a) A _word type_ is a unique entry in the vocabulary — the abstract lexical item regardless of how many times it appears. A _word token_ is a specific occurrence of a word in a specific position in a specific sentence. (b) The sentence has 5 tokens (_The_ , _bank_ , _called_ , _the_ , _bank_) but only 3 distinct types (_the_ , _bank_ , _called_) — noting that "The" and "the" may or may not be the same type depending on case normalization. (c) A static system produces the identical vector for both occurrences of _bank_. A contextualized system produces two different vectors — the first _bank_ is contextualized by "called" (subject), and the second by the full sentence (object). The contextualized embeddings are more faithful to the distributional hypothesis because they use the _actual local context_ of each occurrence, not just aggregate statistics over all occurrences.

* * *

#### Application

**Exercise 16.2.** According to the Arora et al. (2018) result, the static embedding of a polysemous word is approximately a frequency-weighted average of its sense vectors: e(w)≈∑kαkvsk\mathbf{e}(w) \approx \sum_k \alpha_k \mathbf{v}_{s_k}e(w)≈∑k​αk​vsk​​. (a) If w=w = w= _spring_ has four senses with frequencies α1=0.4\alpha_1 = 0.4α1​=0.4 (season), α2=0.3\alpha_2 = 0.3α2​=0.3 (coil), α3=0.2\alpha_3 = 0.2α3​=0.2 (water source), α4=0.1\alpha_4 = 0.1α4​=0.1 (jump), what does the static embedding represent geometrically? (b) A user query is about spring-loaded mechanisms. They encode the query using the static embedding of _spring_. Qualitatively, how accurate will this encoding be? What is the information loss? (c) ELMo processes the sentence _"The spring in the mechanism was broken."_ Explain what additional information (beyond the static embedding) ELMo has access to when computing the representation of _spring_.

Answer

The result that static word vectors are approximately a weighted sum of sense vectors (vw≈∑kαkvsk\mathbf{v}_w \approx \sum_k \alpha_k \mathbf{v}_{s_k}vw​≈∑k​αk​vsk​​) implies: (1) the vector captures a blurred average of senses; (2) for a dominant sense (α1≫\alpha_1 \ggα1​≫ others), the vector is a good approximation; (3) for balanced polysemy (α1≈α2\alpha_1 \approx \alpha_2α1​≈α2​), the vector is equidistant from both senses and may be near neither — maximally unhelpful. Computationally, recovering sense vectors requires knowing the mixing weights, which depends on the very context information that static embeddings discard.

Specifically: (a) Geometrically, the static embedding is a point in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd located at 0.4vseason+0.3vcoil+0.2vwater+0.1vjump0.4\mathbf{v}_{\text{season}} + 0.3\mathbf{v}_{\text{coil}} + 0.2\mathbf{v}_{\text{water}} + 0.1\mathbf{v}_{\text{jump}}0.4vseason​+0.3vcoil​+0.2vwater​+0.1vjump​ — pulled most strongly toward the "season" sense cluster. (b) The query about spring-loaded mechanisms needs the coil sense (α2=0.3\alpha_2 = 0.3α2​=0.3), but the static embedding is 40% season, so the encoding is substantially contaminated by the wrong sense. The information loss is the 70% of the vector that represents non-coil senses. (c) ELMo reads "mechanism was broken" — context words that strongly signal the mechanical/coil sense — and produces a representation shifted toward the coil sense vector, effectively performing implicit disambiguation.

* * *

**Exercise 16.4.** ELMo uses task-specific weighted combination of layers: ELMoktask=γtask∑jsjtaskhk,j\text{ELMo}_k^{\text{task}} = \gamma^{\text{task}} \sum_j s_j^{\text{task}} \mathbf{h}_{k,j}ELMoktask​=γtask∑j​sjtask​hk,j​. (a) Peters et al. found that for POS tagging (a syntactic task), the lower LSTM layers are upweighted; for question answering (a semantic task), the higher layers are upweighted. Explain why this makes sense given what you know about how representations evolve across layers (see Chapter 8 for the CNN analogy). (b) Why do we need separate weights sjtasks_j^{\text{task}}sjtask​ for each task, rather than using a single fixed combination? Give a concrete example of two tasks where you would expect different optimal weightings.

Answer

Syntactic tasks (POS tagging, NER) weight lower LSTM layers more heavily because these layers encode local morphological and syntactic patterns. Semantic tasks (sentiment analysis, textual entailment) weight higher layers because these encode sentence-level semantic composition. The task-specific scalar weights sjtasks_j^{\text{task}}sjtask​ learn this automatically during fine-tuning. This layer-wise specialization is evidence that different LSTM layers encode different levels of linguistic abstraction.

Specifically: (a) Lower layers are closer to the input and capture local patterns (morphology, syntax) — analogous to how early CNN layers detect edges and textures. Higher layers compose these patterns into more abstract representations (semantics, discourse) — analogous to how deeper CNN layers detect objects and scenes. POS tagging is a local syntactic task, so it benefits from lower-layer representations; QA requires understanding meaning and relationships across the sentence, so it benefits from higher-layer representations. (b) A single fixed combination would be suboptimal for at least one task. Example: POS tagging (optimal: s0≫s2s_0 \gg s_2s0​≫s2​) vs. sentiment analysis (optimal: s2≫s0s_2 \gg s_0s2​≫s0​). These two tasks need opposite layer weightings because they operate at different levels of linguistic abstraction.

* * *

**Exercise 16.7.** This chapter previews the Transformer as the solution to ELMo's sequential processing limitation. The Transformer's self-attention has computational complexity O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d) per layer, while an LSTM has O(nd2)O(nd^2)O(nd2) per layer. (a) For a sequence of length n=64n = 64n=64 and dimension d=512d = 512d=512, compute the approximate FLOP count for one layer of self-attention and one layer of LSTM. (b) For n=2048n = 2048n=2048 and d=512d = 512d=512, recompute. At what value of nnn (for fixed d=512d = 512d=512) do self-attention and LSTM have equal complexity? (c) Given that modern language models use sequences of length 4096–128000, does the O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) scaling of attention become a problem? What is the currently active research area that addresses this?

Answer

Self-attention: O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d) per layer — the n×nn \times nn×n attention matrix is the bottleneck, but all positions are computed in parallel (O(1)O(1)O(1) sequential depth). LSTM: O(nd2)O(nd^2)O(nd2) per layer — the matrix-vector multiplication at each step costs O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2), and nnn steps must be sequential (O(n)O(n)O(n) sequential depth). For typical NLP: n≈100n \approx 100n≈100, d≈512d \approx 512d≈512 → attention is 100×512=51,200100 \times 512 = 51{,}200100×512=51,200 per position vs LSTM is 5122=262,144512^2 = 262{,}1445122=262,144 per step. Attention is cheaper per position when n<dn < dn<d, which holds for most NLP tasks. The sequential bottleneck is the more important difference: attention processes all positions simultaneously.

Specifically: (a) For n=64n=64n=64, d=512d=512d=512: Self-attention ≈n2d=642×512=2,097,152≈2.1M\approx n^2 d = 64^2 \times 512 = 2{,}097{,}152 \approx 2.1\text{M}≈n2d=642×512=2,097,152≈2.1M FLOPs. LSTM ≈nd2=64×5122=16,777,216≈16.8M\approx nd^2 = 64 \times 512^2 = 16{,}777{,}216 \approx 16.8\text{M}≈nd2=64×5122=16,777,216≈16.8M FLOPs. Attention is ~8x cheaper. (b) For n=2048n=2048n=2048, d=512d=512d=512: Self-attention ≈20482×512≈2.15G\approx 2048^2 \times 512 \approx 2.15\text{G}≈20482×512≈2.15G FLOPs. LSTM ≈2048×5122≈537M\approx 2048 \times 512^2 \approx 537\text{M}≈2048×5122≈537M FLOPs. Now LSTM is ~4x cheaper in raw FLOPs (but still sequential). Equal complexity when n2d=nd2n^2 d = nd^2n2d=nd2, i.e., n=d=512n = d = 512n=d=512. (c) Yes, O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) becomes prohibitive for long sequences. This motivates efficient attention research: linear attention, sparse attention (Longformer, BigBird), FlashAttention (hardware-aware), and state-space models (Mamba) that achieve O(n)O(n)O(n) scaling.

#### Think Deeper

**Exercise 16.3 (Architecture comparison).** Compare static word embeddings, ELMo, and a Transformer-based model (BERT) on the following properties. For each cell, give a brief explanation (1–2 sentences).

Property | Word2Vec/GloVe | ELMo | BERT  
---|---|---|---  
Polysemy handling |  |  |   
Training speed |  |  |   
Inference speed |  |  |   
Context window |  |  |   
Requires sentence context |  |  |   
Answer

Static embeddings: train once, look up (O(1)O(1)O(1) per word, no context); ELMo: run full bidirectional LSTM over sentence (O(n⋅d2)O(n \cdot d^2)O(n⋅d2) sequential, context from both directions but compressed through hidden state); BERT-style: run full Transformer encoder (O(n2⋅d)O(n^2 \cdot d)O(n2⋅d) parallelizable, direct attention between all positions). Key tradeoff: static is fastest but context-blind; ELMo is context-aware but sequential; Transformer is context-aware and parallelizable but O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) in sequence length.

Property | Word2Vec/GloVe | ELMo | BERT  
---|---|---|---  
Polysemy handling | None — one vector per type regardless of context | Context-dependent via biLSTM; different occurrences get different vectors | Full bidirectional context via self-attention; strongest polysemy resolution  
Training speed | Fast — shallow model, simple objective | Slow — sequential LSTM over large corpus | Moderate — parallelizable but very large model  
Inference speed | O(1)O(1)O(1) lookup | O(n⋅d2)O(n \cdot d^2)O(n⋅d2) sequential per sentence | O(n2⋅d)O(n^2 \cdot d)O(n2⋅d) parallel per sentence  
Context window | None (training uses local windows, but inference is context-free) | Full sentence, but compressed through fixed-size hidden state | Full sentence with direct attention (up to max sequence length)  
Requires sentence context | No | Yes | Yes  
  
* * *

**Exercise 16.8.** The chapter described the historical progression: One-hot → LSA → Word2Vec → GloVe → ELMo → BERT/GPT. (a) For each arrow in this chain, identify the _specific failure mode_ of the left-hand method that motivated the right-hand method. (b) What failure mode of BERT/GPT is motivating current research (beyond Volume I of this textbook)? (c) All methods in this chain share one thing in common: they all train on text using some form of _prediction objective_. What does this suggest about the relationship between _prediction_ and _representation_?

Answer

Word2Vec (2013): solved efficiency of training word vectors, failed on polysemy. GloVe (2014): solved global vs local statistics debate, confirmed distributional structure, same polysemy limitation. ELMo (2018): solved polysemy via context, failed on parallelism (sequential LSTM). BERT/GPT (2018): solved parallelism via Transformer, introduced pre-training paradigm. Each generation's solution created the conditions for discovering the next limitation — this is the "limitation chain" that structures the entire book.

Specifically: (a) One-hot → LSA: one-hot vectors are sparse and encode no semantic similarity; LSA compresses co-occurrence into dense semantic space. LSA → Word2Vec: explicit SVD doesn't scale to billion-word corpora; prediction-based training handles massive data efficiently. Word2Vec → GloVe: local context windows miss global co-occurrence statistics; GloVe optimizes over the full co-occurrence matrix. GloVe → ELMo: one vector per type cannot represent polysemy; biLSTM produces context-dependent representations. ELMo → BERT/GPT: sequential LSTM limits training speed and context integration; Transformer processes all positions simultaneously. (b) Current failure modes of BERT/GPT include: quadratic attention scaling limiting context length, hallucination (generating plausible but false text), lack of grounding in non-textual reality, difficulty with precise reasoning and arithmetic, and the enormous computational cost of training and inference. (c) The consistent use of prediction objectives across all methods suggests that _learning to predict is learning to represent_ — a model that can predict well must have learned the statistical structure of language, and that structure _is_ the representation. Prediction is not just a training trick; it is the mechanism by which distributional structure is internalized.

## Chapter 17: The Encoder-Decoder Framework and the Information Bottleneck

> **Chapter Learning Objectives**
> 
> By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
> 
>   1. Describe the encoder-decoder framework and explain why it is the natural architecture for variable-length input-to-output sequence tasks.
>   2. Trace the information flow from input tokens through the LSTM encoder to the context vector and explain the compression that occurs.
>   3. Derive the autoregressive factorization P(y∣x)=∏tP(yt∣y<t,x)P(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x}) = \prod_t P(y_t \mid y_{<t}, \mathbf{x})P(y∣x)=∏t​P(yt​∣y<t​,x) from the chain rule of probability.
>   4. Explain teacher forcing, identify the exposure bias problem it creates, and describe how scheduled sampling addresses it.
>   5. Quantify the information bottleneck: explain why a fixed-size context vector becomes a performance ceiling for long sequences.
>   6. Describe beam search, compute beam scores with length normalization, and explain why large beam widths produce degenerate outputs.
> 

### 17.1 A New Class of Problems

The first four parts of this book developed tools for two types of tasks: (1) mapping fixed-size inputs to fixed-size outputs (feedforward networks), and (2) mapping variable-length sequences to fixed-size outputs or element-wise labels (RNNs). Chapter 16 added a third capability: mapping any position in a sequence to a context-dependent embedding.

A fourth type of problem remains: **mapping a variable-length input sequence to a variable-length output sequence** , where the two lengths need not be equal.

Formally, given x=(x1,…,xTx)\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_{T_x})x=(x1​,…,xTx​​), produce y=(y1,…,yTy)\mathbf{y} = (y_1, \ldots, y_{T_y})y=(y1​,…,yTy​​), where TxT_xTx​ and TyT_yTy​ are generally different and TyT_yTy​ may not be known in advance.

**Sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) tasks:**

Task | Input | Output | Length relationship  
---|---|---|---  
Machine translation | English sentence | French sentence | Variable  
Summarization | Long article | Short summary | Ty≪TxT_y \ll T_xTy​≪Tx​  
Dialogue | User utterance | System response | Variable  
Speech recognition | Audio frame sequence | Text tokens | Variable  
Code generation | Natural language description | Program code | Variable  
  
None of the architectures developed so far can handle this class of problems. A fixed-output network cannot produce variable-length sequences. An RNN language model can generate sequences, but not sequences conditioned on an arbitrary input sequence of different length.

The **encoder-decoder** (or Seq2Seq) framework is the natural solution. This chapter derives it in full, identifies its fundamental limitation — the information bottleneck — and sets up the motivation for attention.

* * *

### 17.2 Before Neural Seq2Seq: Statistical Machine Translation

The history of machine translation illuminates what the encoder-decoder framework replaced. Before 2014, the dominant approach was **Phrase-Based Statistical Machine Translation (PBSMT)**. A PBSMT system decomposes translation into separately trained components:

  1. **Word alignment model:** estimate which source words correspond to which target words (IBM Models 1–5)
  2. **Phrase extraction:** build a table of translated phrase pairs from aligned sentences
  3. **Language model:** ensure the output sounds fluent in the target language (nnn-gram LM, typically 5-gram)
  4. **Reordering model:** handle different word orders between languages
  5. **Parameter tuning:** optimize the combination weights using MERT

The Seq2Seq framework replaced this entire pipeline with a single end-to-end neural network. No hand-engineered alignment rules, no phrase tables, no separately trained components — one model, one training procedure, one loss function.

The price of this simplicity was initially paid in quality (early neural MT was worse than PBSMT) and ultimately recovered through scale (deep LSTMs with enough data surpassed PBSMT by 2015-2016).

* * *

### 17.3 The Encoder

#### 17.3.1 Function

The encoder reads the entire input sequence and compresses it into a fixed-dimensional representation:

c=fenc(x1,x2,…,xTx)\mathbf{c} = f_{\text{enc}}(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{T_x})c=fenc​(x1​,x2​,…,xTx​​)

where c∈Rn\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^nc∈Rn is the **context vector**.

#### 17.3.2 LSTM Encoder

In the original Seq2Seq papers (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014), the encoder is an LSTM (or GRU). It processes tokens sequentially:

htenc=fLSTM(ht−1enc,e(xt))\mathbf{h}_t^{\text{enc}} = f_{\text{LSTM}}(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{\text{enc}}, \mathbf{e}(x_t))htenc​=fLSTM​(ht−1enc​,e(xt​))

where e(xt)∈Rd\mathbf{e}(x_t) \in \mathbb{R}^de(xt​)∈Rd is the word embedding of token xtx_txt​.

After processing all TxT_xTx​ tokens, the context vector is set to the final hidden state:

c=hTxenc\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{h}_{T_x}^{\text{enc}}c=hTx​enc​

(If the encoder uses an LSTM, both the hidden state and memory cell are included: c=(hTxenc,CTxenc)\mathbf{c} = (\mathbf{h}_{T_x}^{\text{enc}}, \mathbf{C}_{T_x}^{\text{enc}})c=(hTx​enc​,CTx​enc​).)

#### 17.3.3 Progressive Information Accumulation

The encoder progressively builds up a representation of the input. For the sentence _"The stock market crashed yesterday"_ :

Step ttt | Token xtx_txt​ | Information in htenc\mathbf{h}_t^{\text{enc}}htenc​  
---|---|---  
1 | _The_ | Definite article; anticipates a noun phrase  
2 | _stock_ | The stock [?] — ambiguous (inventory or equity)  
3 | _market_ | **The stock market** — disambiguated to equity market  
4 | _crashed_ | The stock market crashed — event established, negative valence  
5 | _yesterday_ | Temporal specification: this happened in the past  
  
After t=5t = 5t=5, the context vector c=h5enc\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{h}_5^{\text{enc}}c=h5enc​ must simultaneously encode: the subject (_stock market_), the predicate (_crashed_), the tense (_past_), and the emotional valence (_negative event_). All of this is compressed into nnn numbers.

* * *

### 17.4 The Decoder

#### 17.4.1 Function

The decoder takes the context vector c\mathbf{c}c and generates the output sequence token by token. It is also an LSTM (or GRU), initialized with c\mathbf{c}c:

s0=cs_0 = \mathbf{c}s0​=c

At each step ttt, the decoder updates its hidden state and computes a distribution over the output vocabulary:

st=fdec(st−1,e(yt−1),c)s_t = f_{\text{dec}}(s_{t-1}, \mathbf{e}(y_{t-1}), \mathbf{c})st​=fdec​(st−1​,e(yt−1​),c) P(yt∣y1,…,yt−1,x)=softmax(Woutst+bout)P(y_t \mid y_1, \ldots, y_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}) = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{out}} s_t + \mathbf{b}_{\text{out}})P(yt​∣y1​,…,yt−1​,x)=softmax(Wout​st​+bout​)

The output token yty_tyt​ is either sampled from this distribution or selected as the argmax (greedy decoding).

#### 17.4.2 Autoregressive Generation

The decoder generates sequences **autoregressively** : each token depends on all previously generated tokens.

P(y∣x)=∏t=1TyP(yt∣y1,…,yt−1,x)P(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x}) = \prod_{t=1}^{T_y} P(y_t \mid y_1, \ldots, y_{t-1}, \mathbf{x})P(y∣x)=t=1∏Ty​​P(yt​∣y1​,…,yt−1​,x)

The chain rule decomposition means:

* Generating y1y_1y1​ depends only on c\mathbf{c}c (initialized from the encoder)
* Generating yty_tyt​ depends on c\mathbf{c}c and the previously generated tokens y1,…,yt−1y_1, \ldots, y_{t-1}y1​,…,yt−1​
* Generation terminates when the special end-of-sequence token ⟨EOS⟩\langle \text{EOS} \rangle⟨EOS⟩ is produced

**Error propagation.** The autoregressive structure creates a cascading failure mode: an error in y1y_1y1​ affects the state s1s_1s1​, which affects y2y_2y2​, which affects s2s_2s2​, and so on. Early errors corrupt all subsequent generation. This is sometimes called **error propagation** or **exposure bias**.

#### 17.4.3 Teacher Forcing vs. Free Generation

**At training time:** the decoder receives the _ground-truth_ previous token as input, regardless of what it actually generated:

sttrain=fdec(st−1,e(yt−1true),c)s_t^{\text{train}} = f_{\text{dec}}(s_{t-1}, \mathbf{e}(y_{t-1}^{\text{true}}), \mathbf{c})sttrain​=fdec​(st−1​,e(yt−1true​),c)

This is **teacher forcing** — the "teacher" (ground truth) guides each step. Advantages: stable training, parallelizable loss computation across time steps. Disadvantage: **train-test mismatch** — during inference the model must condition on its own (potentially erroneous) outputs, a distribution it never saw during training.

**At inference time:** the model uses its own previous prediction:

stinfer=fdec(st−1,e(y^t−1),c)s_t^{\text{infer}} = f_{\text{dec}}(s_{t-1}, \mathbf{e}(\hat{y}_{t-1}), \mathbf{c})stinfer​=fdec​(st−1​,e(y^​t−1​),c)

The discrepancy between training and inference distributions is a known weakness of standard teacher forcing. Scheduled Sampling (Bengio et al., 2015) addresses it by gradually mixing ground-truth and model-generated inputs during training.

* * *

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> Autoregressive generation appears across multiple scientific domains under different names.
> 
> **Econometrics: Iterated forecasting.** In a VAR (Vector Autoregression) model, multi-step forecasts are produced by feeding the previous forecast as input for the next step: y^t+1=Ay^t+u^\hat{y}_{t+1} = A\hat{y}_t + \hat{u}y^​t+1​=Ay^​t​+u^. Forecast errors compound — a single-step forecast error biases all subsequent forecasts. Decoder error propagation is the same phenomenon. The exposure bias fix (mixing true and predicted tokens during training) is analogous to closed-loop vs. open-loop control in control theory.
> 
> **Physics: Discrete dynamical systems.** The decoder's recurrence st=f(st−1,yt−1,c)s_t = f(s_{t-1}, y_{t-1}, \mathbf{c})st​=f(st−1​,yt−1​,c) is a driven dynamical system — the hidden state evolves under the influence of the context and the generated sequence. The stability of this system (whether errors grow or decay) determines whether long sequences can be generated reliably. This connects to the spectral radius analysis of Chapter 11: if the Jacobian of fff has spectral radius >1> 1>1, errors amplify; if <1< 1<1, they decay.
> 
> **Information theory: Source coding with side information.** The context vector c\mathbf{c}c plays the role of _side information_ available to the decoder (but not in the input stream). Shannon's rate-distortion theory with side information (Wyner-Ziv coding) bounds the achievable compression at each side-information rate. The encoder's task is analogous to rate-distortion coding: compress x\mathbf{x}x into c\mathbf{c}c as efficiently as possible. The bottleneck is exactly the rate constraint.

* * *

### 17.5 The Information Bottleneck

#### 17.5.1 The Fundamental Constraint

The encoder-decoder framework requires all information about the input sequence to pass through the single vector c∈Rn\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^nc∈Rn. This is the **information bottleneck**.

The problem is not architectural complexity or insufficient parameters — it is geometric. Information about a sequence of TxT_xTx​ tokens scales with TxT_xTx​, but the context vector has fixed dimension nnn regardless of sequence length.

**Formal analysis.** Let each token encode approximately bbb bits of information (lexical, syntactic, semantic). A sequence of length TxT_xTx​ contains Ω(Tx⋅b)\Omega(T_x \cdot b)Ω(Tx​⋅b) bits of information. A continuous vector c∈Rn\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^nc∈Rn can encode at most O(nlog⁡(1/ϵ))O(n \log(1/\epsilon))O(nlog(1/ϵ)) bits at precision ϵ\epsilonϵ. When:

Tx⋅b>nlog⁡(1/ϵ)T_x \cdot b > n \log(1/\epsilon)Tx​⋅b>nlog(1/ϵ)

information loss is mathematically unavoidable. For typical parameters (n=1024n = 1024n=1024, b≈10b \approx 10b≈10 bits/token), the bottleneck begins to bind around Tx≈100T_x \approx 100Tx​≈100 tokens — roughly a paragraph.

#### 17.5.2 Empirical Evidence

Cho et al. (2014b) measured BLEU score as a function of sentence length for their RNN encoder-decoder:
    
    
    Translation quality (BLEU)
        ↑
        |___________
        |            \
        |             \_______ ← Seq2Seq without attention
        |
        +–––––––––––––––––––––→ Input sequence length
                  20   30   40
    

Performance is competitive with PBSMT for short sentences (length ≤ 20) and degrades sharply for longer sentences. The degradation is faster than the baseline — the bottleneck is a Seq2Seq-specific problem, not a general difficulty of long-range processing.

**The intuitive explanation.** Imagine being required to read a 50-page document, return the document, and then write a full translation from memory. Even with excellent recall, details — precise numbers, logical chains, specific terminology — will be lost. The encoder faces exactly this constraint.

The fix is obvious in the human analogy: allow the translator to look back at the source document while writing each section. This is precisely what attention mechanisms implement.

#### 17.5.3 Information Requirements for Decoding

The decoder must recover from c\mathbf{c}c at least the following information to produce correct output:

  1. **Lexical information:** the meaning of each input token
  2. **Syntactic structure:** subject-verb-object relationships, clause structure
  3. **Semantic relations:** reference, causation, modification
  4. **Pragmatic information:** tone, implied meaning, discourse context
  5. **Global context:** the topic and register of the full input

For a 100-token input sequence, compressing all five dimensions into a 1024-dimensional vector requires an average of 1024/100≈101024/100 \approx 101024/100≈10 dimensions per token — before accounting for compositional and structural information. This is geometrically impossible to do without loss.

* * *

### 17.6 Beam Search Decoding

Regardless of the information bottleneck, the decoder requires a decoding strategy at inference time. **Greedy decoding** selects the argmax at each step:

y^t=arg⁡max⁡wP(w∣y^1,…,y^t−1,x)\hat{y}_t = \arg\max_w P(w \mid \hat{y}_1, \ldots, \hat{y}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x})y^​t​=argwmax​P(w∣y^​1​,…,y^​t−1​,x)

This is fast but suboptimal: a locally less likely token may open a globally more likely sequence.

**Beam search** maintains the BBB most probable partial sequences (beams) at each step:

  1. **Initialize:** take the BBB highest-probability first tokens
  2. **Expand:** for each beam, consider all VVV possible next tokens → B×VB \times VB×V candidates
  3. **Prune:** keep only the BBB highest-probability prefixes
  4. **Terminate:** a beam stops when it produces ⟨EOS⟩\langle \text{EOS} \rangle⟨EOS⟩
  5. **Select:** after all beams terminate, return the highest-scoring complete sequence

To prevent bias toward short sequences, scores are normalized by length:

score(y)=1Tyα∑t=1Tylog⁡P(yt∣y1,…,yt−1,x)\text{score}(\mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{T_y^\alpha} \sum_{t=1}^{T_y} \log P(y_t \mid y_1, \ldots, y_{t-1}, \mathbf{x})score(y)=Tyα​1​t=1∑Ty​​logP(yt​∣y1​,…,yt−1​,x)

where α∈[0.6,1.0]\alpha \in [0.6, 1.0]α∈[0.6,1.0] is a length penalty. Sutskever et al. used B=2B = 2B=2; typical values in production MT systems are B=4B = 4B=4–101010.

**Computational cost.** Beam search requires O(B⋅V)O(B \cdot V)O(B⋅V) work per step rather than O(V)O(V)O(V) for greedy. With V=50,000V = 50{,}000V=50,000 and B=5B = 5B=5, this is 5× more expensive — tractable for moderate sequence lengths.

* * *

### 17.7 A Complete Worked Example

#### Setup

* **Task:** Translate _"I love you"_ to French _"Je t'aime"_
* **Encoder:** single-layer RNN with tanh⁡\tanhtanh, hidden dimension n=4n = 4n=4
* **Decoder:** single-layer RNN, same dimension
* **Vocabulary:** {I, love, you, Je, t'aime, ⟨\langle⟨BOS⟩\rangle⟩, ⟨\langle⟨EOS⟩\rangle⟩}

#### Encoding

Assume word embeddings (dimension d=3d = 3d=3):

The bottleneck is not visible here because the input is only 3 tokens. Scale to 50 tokens and the same 4-dimensional context vector cannot retain all of the source information.

* * *

### 17.8 What Attention Will Fix

The bottleneck has a natural solution: instead of the decoder reading from a single fixed vector c\mathbf{c}c, allow it to read directly from all encoder hidden states h1enc,…,hTxenc\mathbf{h}_1^{\text{enc}}, \ldots, \mathbf{h}_{T_x}^{\text{enc}}h1enc​,…,hTx​enc​, with different weights at each decoding step.

**Original decoder:** st=f(st−1,yt−1,c⏟fixed)s_t = f(s_{t-1}, y_{t-1}, \underbrace{\mathbf{c}}_{\text{fixed}})st​=f(st−1​,yt−1​,fixedc​​)

**Attention decoder:** st=f(st−1,yt−1,ct⏟dynamic)s_t = f(s_{t-1}, y_{t-1}, \underbrace{\mathbf{c}_t}_{\text{dynamic}})st​=f(st−1​,yt−1​,dynamicct​​​)

where ct=∑i=1Txαt,ihienc\mathbf{c}_t = \sum_{i=1}^{T_x} \alpha_{t,i} \mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}}ct​=∑i=1Tx​​αt,i​hienc​ is a weighted sum of encoder states, with weights αt,i\alpha_{t,i}αt,i​ computed from the decoder's current state and the encoder states.

This moves from a single compressed bottleneck to a differentiable read operation over the full encoder memory. The encoder no longer needs to compress everything into a single vector — it only needs to represent each position well locally. The decoder can then selectively read from the positions relevant to the current generation step.

The intuition matches human translation: a translator does not memorize a document and then write from memory. They read each source segment as needed while producing the target.

Chapter 18 reads the paper that first demonstrated this idea at scale (Sutskever et al., 2014 — the bottleneck paper). Chapter 19 derives the mathematics of attention. Chapter 20 reads the paper that introduced attention for machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015).

* * *

### 17.9 Summary

Component | Formula | Purpose  
---|---|---  
Encoder | htenc=fLSTM(ht−1enc,e(xt))\mathbf{h}_t^{\text{enc}} = f_{\text{LSTM}}(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}^{\text{enc}}, \mathbf{e}(x_t))htenc​=fLSTM​(ht−1enc​,e(xt​)) | Read input, update state  
Context vector | c=hTxenc\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{h}_{T_x}^{\text{enc}}c=hTx​enc​ | Compress entire input  
Decoder hidden state | st=fdec(st−1,e(yt−1),c)s_t = f_{\text{dec}}(s_{t-1}, \mathbf{e}(y_{t-1}), \mathbf{c})st​=fdec​(st−1​,e(yt−1​),c) | Condition output on input  
Output distribution | P(yt∣⋅)=softmax(Woutst)P(y_t \mid \cdot) = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{out}} s_t)P(yt​∣⋅)=softmax(Wout​st​) | Predict next token  
Autoregressive likelihood | P(y∣x)=∏tP(yt∣y<t,x)P(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x}) = \prod_t P(y_t \mid y_{<t}, \mathbf{x})P(y∣x)=∏t​P(yt​∣y<t​,x) | Training objective  
Information bottleneck | c∈Rn\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^nc∈Rn, nnn fixed | Architectural limitation  
  
**The central limitation:** All information about the input sequence must pass through a fixed-size vector c\mathbf{c}c. For short sequences this is acceptable; for long sequences it causes measurable quality degradation. Attention mechanisms resolve this limitation by replacing the fixed bottleneck with a dynamic, weighted reading mechanism over all encoder states.

### Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Exercise 17.1.** The encoder-decoder architecture processes an input sequence of length Tx=50T_x = 50Tx​=50 with encoder hidden dimension n=256n = 256n=256. (a) What is the compression ratio (bits available / bits needed) assuming each token requires 10 bits? (b) If the hidden dimension were doubled to n=512n = 512n=512, does this resolve the information bottleneck for arbitrarily long sequences? Why or why not? (c) What is the fundamental difference between the bottleneck caused by a fixed hidden dimension and the bottleneck caused by gradient vanishing?

Answer

**(a)** The input carries Tx⋅b=50×10=500T_x \cdot b = 50 \times 10 = 500Tx​⋅b=50×10=500 bits of information. The context vector c∈R256\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{256}c∈R256 has 256 real-valued dimensions. If each float32 dimension encodes up to 32 bits, the raw capacity is 256×32=8,192256 \times 32 = 8{,}192256×32=8,192 bits, giving a ratio of 8192/500≈16.48192 / 500 \approx 16.48192/500≈16.4. However, effective information capacity is much less than 32 bits per dimension due to correlations between dimensions and limited dynamic range. A more realistic estimate of ∼5{\sim}5∼5–101010 effective bits per dimension gives 1,2801{,}2801,280–2,5602{,}5602,560 bits capacity, so the effective ratio is ≈2.6\approx 2.6≈2.6–5.15.15.1.

**(b)** Doubling nnn to 512 doubles the capacity of c\mathbf{c}c, but does not resolve the bottleneck for arbitrarily long sequences. The capacity of a fixed-dimension vector grows as O(n)O(n)O(n), while the information content of the input grows as O(Tx)O(T_x)O(Tx​). For Tx→∞T_x \to \inftyTx​→∞, any fixed nnn is insufficient — the condition Tx⋅b>nlog⁡(1/ϵ)T_x \cdot b > n \log(1/\epsilon)Tx​⋅b>nlog(1/ϵ) from Section 17.5.1 will eventually be violated.

**(c)** The fixed-dimension bottleneck is a **capacity problem** : all information about x\mathbf{x}x must fit into nnn numbers, regardless of input length. Gradient vanishing is an **optimization problem** : the information may be present in htenc\mathbf{h}_t^{\text{enc}}htenc​, but gradients cannot propagate back to early time steps to update their contributions. Attention (Chapter 19) solves the bottleneck by giving the decoder direct access to all encoder states h1enc,…,hTxenc\mathbf{h}_1^{\text{enc}}, \ldots, \mathbf{h}_{T_x}^{\text{enc}}h1enc​,…,hTx​enc​; gating mechanisms (Chapter 11) solve the gradient problem by providing shortcut paths for gradient flow.

#### Concept Check

**Exercise 17.2 (Autoregressive chain rule).** Show that the joint probability of a sequence P(y1,y2,…,yTy∣x)P(y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_{T_y} \mid \mathbf{x})P(y1​,y2​,…,yTy​​∣x) is equal to ∏t=1TyP(yt∣y1,…,yt−1,x)\prod_{t=1}^{T_y} P(y_t \mid y_1, \ldots, y_{t-1}, \mathbf{x})∏t=1Ty​​P(yt​∣y1​,…,yt−1​,x) by applying the chain rule of probability. What independence assumption allows this decomposition?

Answer

By the chain rule of conditional probability:

P(y1,…,yTy∣x)=P(y1∣x)⋅P(y2∣y1,x)⋅P(y3∣y1,y2,x)⋯=∏t=1TyP(yt∣y1,…,yt−1,x)P(y_1, \ldots, y_{T_y} \mid \mathbf{x}) = P(y_1 \mid \mathbf{x}) \cdot P(y_2 \mid y_1, \mathbf{x}) \cdot P(y_3 \mid y_1, y_2, \mathbf{x}) \cdots = \prod_{t=1}^{T_y} P(y_t \mid y_1, \ldots, y_{t-1}, \mathbf{x})P(y1​,…,yTy​​∣x)=P(y1​∣x)⋅P(y2​∣y1​,x)⋅P(y3​∣y1​,y2​,x)⋯=t=1∏Ty​​P(yt​∣y1​,…,yt−1​,x)

**No independence assumption is needed** — this is an identity, not an approximation. The chain rule holds for any joint distribution. The autoregressive model parameterizes each conditional P(yt∣y<t,x)P(y_t \mid y_{<t}, \mathbf{x})P(yt​∣y<t​,x) using the decoder RNN, which compresses the history y<ty_{<t}y<t​ into the hidden state sts_tst​. The only approximation is in the parameterization (the decoder's finite capacity to represent the true conditional), not in the factorization itself.

#### Application

**Exercise 17.3.** Beam search with width B=3B = 3B=3 maintains 3 partial hypotheses at each step. (a) For a vocabulary of V=50,000V = 50{,}000V=50,000 and B=3B = 3B=3, how many candidate extensions are evaluated at each step? (b) The total sequence probability under beam search is score(y)=1Ty0.7∑t=1Tylog⁡P(yt∣y<t,x)\text{score}(\mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{T_y^{0.7}} \sum_{t=1}^{T_y} \log P(y_t \mid y_{<t}, \mathbf{x})score(y)=Ty0.7​1​∑t=1Ty​​logP(yt​∣y<t​,x). If a beam of length 5 has ∑log⁡P=−12.3\sum \log P = -12.3∑logP=−12.3 and a beam of length 8 has ∑log⁡P=−14.1\sum \log P = -14.1∑logP=−14.1, which beam is selected? (c) Why does beam search with very large BBB tend to produce short, generic translations rather than long, accurate ones?

Answer

**(a)** At each step, each of the B=3B = 3B=3 beams is extended by all V=50,000V = 50{,}000V=50,000 vocabulary items: 3×50,000=150,0003 \times 50{,}000 = 150{,}0003×50,000=150,000 candidates are evaluated, then the top-3 are kept.

**(b)** Length-5 beam: score=150.7×(−12.3)=−12.33.09≈−3.98\text{score} = \frac{1}{5^{0.7}} \times (-12.3) = \frac{-12.3}{3.09} \approx -3.98score=50.71​×(−12.3)=3.09−12.3​≈−3.98. Length-8 beam: score=180.7×(−14.1)=−14.14.59≈−3.07\text{score} = \frac{1}{8^{0.7}} \times (-14.1) = \frac{-14.1}{4.59} \approx -3.07score=80.71​×(−14.1)=4.59−14.1​≈−3.07. The length-8 beam has a higher (less negative) normalized score, so **the length-8 beam is selected**. Length normalization prevents the systematic bias toward shorter sequences that would otherwise result from multiplying more probabilities (each ≤1\leq 1≤1).

**(c)** Very large BBB approximates exact search, which finds the sequence that maximizes P(y∣x)P(\mathbf{y} \mid \mathbf{x})P(y∣x). But the maximum-probability sequence is often short and generic (e.g., "I don't know") because the model assigns high probability to safe, common responses. The length normalization partially addresses this but cannot fully overcome the model's conservative probability assignments. This is a fundamental mismatch between the MAP (maximum a posteriori) objective and the desired output quality.

#### Concept Check

**Exercise 17.4.** Teacher forcing trains the decoder using ground-truth previous tokens rather than its own predictions. (a) During teacher-forced training, are the TyT_yTy​ loss terms for positions t=1,…,Tyt = 1, \ldots, T_yt=1,…,Ty​ independent (can they be computed in parallel)? Explain. (b) During inference (without teacher forcing), can the TyT_yTy​ predictions be parallelized? Why or why not? (c) This asymmetry between training and inference is eliminated by the Transformer architecture (Chapter 23). What architectural property of the Transformer enables this?

Answer

**(a)** Yes, they can be computed in parallel during teacher forcing. At training time, all TyT_yTy​ ground-truth tokens y1true,…,yTytruey_1^{\text{true}}, \ldots, y_{T_y}^{\text{true}}y1true​,…,yTy​true​ are known in advance. Each conditional P(yt∣y<ttrue,x)P(y_t \mid y_{<t}^{\text{true}}, \mathbf{x})P(yt​∣y<ttrue​,x) depends only on the ground-truth prefix (not on the model's predictions), so the TyT_yTy​ softmax computations can be batched. (Note: for RNNs the hidden states sts_tst​ still depend sequentially on st−1s_{t-1}st−1​, so full parallelism requires architectural changes — but the loss terms themselves are independent given the hidden states.)

**(b)** No. During inference the model uses its own previous prediction: stinfer=fdec(st−1,e(y^t−1),c)s_t^{\text{infer}} = f_{\text{dec}}(s_{t-1}, \mathbf{e}(\hat{y}_{t-1}), \mathbf{c})stinfer​=fdec​(st−1​,e(y^​t−1​),c). Since y^t−1\hat{y}_{t-1}y^​t−1​ must be generated before step ttt can proceed, generation is inherently sequential: O(Ty)O(T_y)O(Ty​) serial steps.

**(c)** The Transformer uses **masked self-attention** during training, which allows all positions to be computed simultaneously (the mask prevents position ttt from attending to positions >t> t>t, enforcing the autoregressive constraint without sequential computation). During inference, generation remains sequential (each token depends on the previous), but the Transformer's training parallelism — all positions computed in one forward pass — is a crucial efficiency advantage over LSTM decoders, which require sequential hidden-state computation even during training.

#### Application

**Exercise 17.5.** Consider translating the sentence _"The Federal Reserve raised interest rates by 25 basis points, citing persistent inflation above the 2% target and strong labor market conditions, despite slowing consumer spending growth."_ (approximately 30 tokens) into French.

(a) List five categories of information the decoder would need from the context vector c\mathbf{c}c to produce an accurate translation. (b) Assuming n=1024n = 1024n=1024 dimensions and 10 bits per token, compute the theoretical information capacity of c\mathbf{c}c and compare it to the information content of the input. (c) If you had to prioritize what information to retain in c\mathbf{c}c (given the bottleneck), what would you keep and what would you discard? How does attention solve this prioritization problem dynamically?

Answer

**(a)** Five categories: (1) **Entity identities** — Federal Reserve, interest rates, basis points; (2) **Numerical values** — 25 basis points, 2% target; (3) **Causal relationships** — "citing" links the rate increase to its justification; (4) **Temporal and discourse markers** — "despite" signals a concurrent contrast; (5) **Domain knowledge** — monetary policy terminology, inflation targets.

**(b)** Input information: 30×10=30030 \times 10 = 30030×10=300 bits. Context vector capacity: c∈R1024\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^{1024}c∈R1024. At ∼5{\sim}5∼5–101010 effective bits per dimension (accounting for correlations and limited dynamic range), capacity ≈5,120\approx 5{,}120≈5,120–10,24010{,}24010,240 bits. Ratio ≈17\approx 17≈17–34×34\times34×. For this 30-token sentence, the bottleneck is manageable — there is ample capacity. For sentences exceeding ∼100{\sim}100∼100 tokens, the ratio drops below 5×5\times5× and quality degrades (consistent with the empirical evidence in Section 17.5.2).

**(c)** Priority: **entity identities and relationships** (structural meaning), then **numerical values** (precision-sensitive), then **temporal/discourse markers** (grammatical structure). Discard: redundant function words, stylistic choices that can be reconstructed from target-language conventions. Attention solves this dynamically: at each decoder step ttt, the attention weights αt,i\alpha_{t,i}αt,i​ select the relevant subset of encoder positions hienc\mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}}hienc​, so the decoder reads entity names when translating nouns, numerical values when translating quantities, and discourse markers when generating connectives — avoiding the need to compress everything into one vector c\mathbf{c}c.

#### Think Deeper

**Exercise 17.6.** In Sutskever et al. (2014), the context vector initializes all layers of the decoder LSTM. In Cho et al. (2014), the context vector is fed as input at every decoder step. Analyze the tradeoffs: which approach provides more persistent access to the input information? Which is more prone to the information bottleneck?

Answer

**Sutskever (context vector initializes decoder):** c\mathbf{c}c is used once to set s0=cs_0 = \mathbf{c}s0​=c, then the decoder runs autonomously via st=fdec(st−1,e(yt−1))s_t = f_{\text{dec}}(s_{t-1}, \mathbf{e}(y_{t-1}))st​=fdec​(st−1​,e(yt−1​)). Access to input information decays with decoder steps as sts_tst​ evolves away from s0s_0s0​. More prone to the information bottleneck for long decoder sequences because late decoder steps have no direct access to input information.

**Cho (context vector fed at every step):** c\mathbf{c}c is concatenated with the input at every decoder step: st=fdec(st−1,[e(yt−1);c])s_t = f_{\text{dec}}(s_{t-1}, [\mathbf{e}(y_{t-1}); \mathbf{c}])st​=fdec​(st−1​,[e(yt−1​);c]). This provides **persistent access** to the source information — c\mathbf{c}c is re-injected at every time step, so even late decoder steps can read from it directly. Less prone to information loss over long decoder sequences.

**Tradeoff:** Cho's approach is more robust to long decoder sequences but adds computation (larger input dimension at each step due to concatenation). However, both approaches still suffer from the fundamental fixed-size c\mathbf{c}c problem: regardless of how the decoder uses c\mathbf{c}c, the encoder must still compress the entire input into a single vector. Attention eliminates this limitation entirely by replacing the fixed c\mathbf{c}c with dynamic ct=∑iαt,ihienc\mathbf{c}_t = \sum_i \alpha_{t,i} \mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}}ct​=∑i​αt,i​hienc​.

#### Think Deeper

**Exercise 17.7 (Conceptual).** The information bottleneck theorem (Tishby et al., 2000) states that the optimal compressed representation c\mathbf{c}c of input x\mathbf{x}x for predicting output y\mathbf{y}y maximizes I(c;y)−βI(c;x)I(\mathbf{c}; \mathbf{y}) - \beta I(\mathbf{c}; \mathbf{x})I(c;y)−βI(c;x), where I(⋅;⋅)I(\cdot; \cdot)I(⋅;⋅) denotes mutual information and β>0\beta > 0β>0 controls the compression rate. (a) Interpret this objective in the context of the encoder-decoder framework. (b) What does setting β→0\beta \to 0β→0 correspond to architecturally? (c) What does setting β→∞\beta \to \inftyβ→∞ correspond to? (d) How does the attention mechanism relate to this tradeoff?

Answer

**(a)** The encoder minimizes I(c;x)I(\mathbf{c}; \mathbf{x})I(c;x) (compress the input — discard information not needed for the task) while maximizing I(c;y)I(\mathbf{c}; \mathbf{y})I(c;y) (retain information useful for the decoder to produce the correct output). The parameter β\betaβ controls this tradeoff: high β\betaβ favors compression over utility. In the encoder-decoder framework, the fixed dimension nnn of c\mathbf{c}c implicitly sets an upper bound on I(c;x)I(\mathbf{c}; \mathbf{x})I(c;x), forcing the encoder to learn which information to retain and which to discard.

**(b)** β→0\beta \to 0β→0: the objective becomes max⁡I(c;y)\max I(\mathbf{c}; \mathbf{y})maxI(c;y) with no compression penalty. The encoder should encode everything about x\mathbf{x}x that could possibly help predict y\mathbf{y}y — effectively c\mathbf{c}c encodes all of x\mathbf{x}x (no bottleneck). Architecturally, this corresponds to the **attention mechanism** , which gives the decoder access to all encoder states h1enc,…,hTxenc\mathbf{h}_1^{\text{enc}}, \ldots, \mathbf{h}_{T_x}^{\text{enc}}h1enc​,…,hTx​enc​ rather than a single compressed vector.

**(c)** β→∞\beta \to \inftyβ→∞: the objective is dominated by −βI(c;x)-\beta I(\mathbf{c}; \mathbf{x})−βI(c;x), so the encoder maximizes compression — c\mathbf{c}c retains nothing about x\mathbf{x}x, becoming independent of the input. Architecturally, this corresponds to a **decoder that ignores the input entirely** — an unconditional language model P(y)P(\mathbf{y})P(y) with no conditioning on x\mathbf{x}x.

**(d)** Attention dynamically adjusts the effective β\betaβ per decoder step. For steps requiring specific source information (e.g., translating a proper noun), the attention weights αt,i\alpha_{t,i}αt,i​ concentrate on the relevant encoder position — low effective β\betaβ, high I(ct;x)I(\mathbf{c}_t; \mathbf{x})I(ct​;x). For steps requiring only general context (e.g., generating a function word like "the"), the attention distributes broadly — higher effective β\betaβ. This dynamic, per-step control is impossible with a single fixed c\mathbf{c}c.
