> **Chapter Goal** : Read _Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate_ with full technical depth — understanding its motivation, architectural innovations (bidirectional encoder, additive attention), complete mathematics, the landmark Figure 3 visualization, experimental results, and its place as the founding paper of attention mechanisms in deep learning.
> 
> **Paper** : Bahdanau, D., Cho, K., & Bengio, Y. (2014/2015). Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate. _arXiv:1409.0473_. Published at ICLR 2015.

> **Chapter Learning Objectives**
> 
> By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
> 
>   1. Explain why Bahdanau et al. use s_{i-1} (not s_i) to compute alignment scores and identify the circular dependency that would arise otherwise.
>   2. Derive the complete Bahdanau attention computation: alignment scores → softmax weights → context vector → decoder state update.
>   3. Compute the parameter count of the additive alignment model given encoder dimension 2n, decoder dimension m, and attention dimension d_a.
>   4. Interpret an attention weight matrix (alignment plot) and identify patterns such as monotonic alignment, reordering, and many-to-one mappings.
>   5. Compare the bidirectional GRU encoder with the deep unidirectional LSTM encoder on informational richness, efficiency, and compatibility with attention.
>   6. Articulate what the paper left unresolved (sequential computation bottleneck) and how this motivates the Transformer.
> 

* * *

### 20.1 Historical Position

#### A Paper That Changed Everything

If one were to select the ten most consequential papers in deep learning history, Bahdanau et al. (2014) would appear on virtually every such list. This paper introduced the **attention mechanism** to deep sequence models for the first time, broke the fixed-length bottleneck of the encoder-decoder framework, and achieved breakthrough results in machine translation.

More importantly, the attention idea it pioneered subsequently evolved into:

* **Luong attention** (2015): simplified and generalized attention variants
* **Self-attention** (2016–2017): sequences attending to themselves
* **Transformer** (Vaswani et al., 2017): fully attention-based architecture
* **BERT, GPT, and beyond** (2018–): attention as the core of all modern large language models

From Bahdanau's additive attention to GPT-4's multi-head self-attention, the core mathematical logic has not changed — it is always "compute similarity → normalize → take weighted sum." The Bahdanau paper is the origin of this entire evolutionary chain.

#### The Paper's Immediate Predecessors

The introduction explicitly cites two direct predecessors (covered in Chapters 17–18):

  1. **Cho et al. (2014)** : proposed the RNN Encoder-Decoder framework and GRU
  2. **Sutskever et al. (2014)** : achieved end-to-end translation with deep LSTMs

Bahdanau et al. identify the **shared weakness** of both:

> _"A potential issue with this encoder-decoder approach is that a neural network needs to be able to compress all the necessary information of a source sentence into a fixed-length vector."_

This is exactly the information bottleneck we analyzed formally in Chapter 17. The Bahdanau paper is the direct answer to that problem.

#### Academic Context

An interesting historical footnote: this paper was first posted on arXiv in September 2014, before Sutskever et al.'s formal NeurIPS 2014 publication (December). It was accepted at ICLR 2015. First author Dzmitry Bahdanau was a PhD student in Yoshua Bengio's lab (Bengio received the 2018 Turing Award). Second author Kyunghyun Cho was the first author of the RNN Encoder-Decoder paper — the collaboration united Cho's encoder-decoder framework with Bahdanau's attention idea.

* * *

### 20.2 Core Innovation: Let the Decoder Look Back

#### From Fixed Vector to Dynamic Lookup

The core insight of Bahdanau et al. can be stated in one sentence: **do not compress all information into a single vector; instead, let the decoder consult the encoder's full state at every position at each decoding step.**

In the original Seq2Seq model:

c=hTxenc(fixed — all decoding steps share one context)\mathbf{c} = h_{T_x}^{\text{enc}} \qquad \text{(fixed — all decoding steps share one context)}c=hTx​enc​(fixed — all decoding steps share one context)

In Bahdanau's model:

ci=∑j=1Txαij hj(dynamic — each decoding step has its own context)\mathbf{c}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{T_x} \alpha_{ij}\, h_j \qquad \text{(dynamic — each decoding step has its own context)}ci​=j=1∑Tx​​αij​hj​(dynamic — each decoding step has its own context)

This seemingly simple change carries three deep consequences:

  1. **No information loss** : every encoder position's hidden state is retained and accessible, not just the final state
  2. **On-demand retrieval** : the decoder dynamically selects which positions to attend based on current needs
  3. **Interpretability** : attention weights αij\alpha_{ij}αij​ provide a window into the model's "reasoning process"

#### The Paper's Precise Formulation

Section 3 of the paper gives the complete model definition. Working through the mathematics step by step:

**Conditional probability decomposition** :

p(yi∣y1,…,yi−1,x)=g(yi−1,si,ci)p(y_i | y_1, \dots, y_{i-1}, \mathbf{x}) = g(y_{i-1}, s_i, c_i)p(yi​∣y1​,…,yi−1​,x)=g(yi−1​,si​,ci​)

where sis_isi​ is the decoder hidden state at step iii:

si=f(si−1,yi−1,ci)s_i = f(s_{i-1}, y_{i-1}, c_i)si​=f(si−1​,yi−1​,ci​)

Note: in Bahdanau's design, the context vector cic_ici​ participates in hidden-state **updating** — not just output computation. This differs from Sutskever's design, where the context vector only initialized s0s_0s0​ and was unused thereafter.

**Context vector** :

ci=∑j=1Txαijhjc_i = \sum_{j=1}^{T_x} \alpha_{ij} h_jci​=j=1∑Tx​​αij​hj​

**Attention weights** :

αij=exp⁡(eij)∑k=1Txexp⁡(eik)\alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(e_{ij})}{\sum_{k=1}^{T_x} \exp(e_{ik})}αij​=∑k=1Tx​​exp(eik​)exp(eij​)​

**Alignment score** :

eij=a(si−1,hj)e_{ij} = a(s_{i-1}, h_j)eij​=a(si−1​,hj​)

where a(⋅,⋅)a(\cdot,\cdot)a(⋅,⋅) is an **alignment model** — a small feedforward neural network:

a(si−1,hj)=va⊤tanh⁡(Wasi−1+Uahj)a(s_{i-1}, h_j) = \mathbf{v}_a^\top \tanh(\mathbf{W}_a s_{i-1} + \mathbf{U}_a h_j)a(si−1​,hj​)=va⊤​tanh(Wa​si−1​+Ua​hj​)

This is the additive attention we derived in Chapter 19.

#### A Critical Design Detail

The paper uses si−1s_{i-1}si−1​ (the previous decoder state) rather than sis_isi​ (the current state) to compute attention. This is because a circular dependency would otherwise arise: sis_isi​ depends on cic_ici​, which depends on the attention weights, which would depend on sis_isi​ — forming a cycle. Using si−1s_{i-1}si−1​ breaks the cycle cleanly:

si−1 ⟶ αij ⟶ ci ⟶ sis_{i-1} \;\longrightarrow\; \alpha_{ij} \;\longrightarrow\; c_i \;\longrightarrow\; s_isi−1​⟶αij​⟶ci​⟶si​

This causal chain is unambiguous and computable sequentially from left to right.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Causal Ordering in Complex Systems**
> 
> The circular dependency problem that arises when using sis_isi​ instead of si−1s_{i-1}si−1​ appears across many disciplines under different names. In **thermodynamics and chemical kinetics** , implicit systems of equations — where the state at time ttt depends on quantities that themselves depend on that state — require iterative solvers (Newton-Raphson, fixed-point iteration) to resolve. The Prandtl boundary-layer equations in **fluid mechanics** exhibit analogous coupling between velocity and pressure, necessitating splitting schemes (SIMPLE algorithm) to advance the solution. In **control engineering** , algebraic loops in block diagrams — where a signal feeds back instantaneously — must be broken by inserting a unit delay or solved via implicit integration. Bahdanau's choice of si−1s_{i-1}si−1​ is the neural-network equivalent of inserting a unit delay: it transforms an implicit algebraic problem into an explicit sequential computation, trading a marginal loss of "synchrony" for guaranteed computability. The Luong (2015) attention later addressed this by computing an initial sis_isi​ without attention, then using it to compute cic_ici​ and refining sis_isi​ — closer to the predictor-corrector methods used in numerical ODE solvers.

* * *

### 20.3 Bidirectional Encoder

#### Why Bidirectionality?

The other major design decision in Bahdanau et al. is the use of a **Bidirectional RNN (BiRNN)** encoder. With a unidirectional encoder, the hidden state at position jjj only contains information from positions 1,2,…,j1, 2, \dots, j1,2,…,j (leftward context). This means words in the latter half of the sentence cannot influence the representations of earlier positions.

In an attention model, the decoder consults **every position's** hidden state. If hjh_jhj​ encodes only leftward context, information about words after position jjj is unavailable when the decoder attends to position jjj. For example, when processing "stock" in "The stock market crashed," if h2h_2h2​ ("stock") does not know that "market" follows, it cannot correctly disambiguate the sense — inventory or equity?

#### Mathematics of the Bidirectional Encoder

The bidirectional encoder runs two independent GRUs:

**Forward GRU** (processing x1x_1x1​ to xTxx_{T_x}xTx​​):

hj→=GRU→(e(xj), hj−1→)\overrightarrow{h_j} = \overrightarrow{\text{GRU}}(e(x_j),\, \overrightarrow{h_{j-1}})hj​​=GRU(e(xj​),hj−1​​)

**Backward GRU** (processing xTxx_{T_x}xTx​​ to x1x_1x1​):

hj←=GRU←(e(xj), hj+1←)\overleftarrow{h_j} = \overleftarrow{\text{GRU}}(e(x_j),\, \overleftarrow{h_{j+1}})hj​​=GRU(e(xj​),hj+1​​)

**Concatenation** :

hj=[hj→; hj←] ∈ R2nh_j = [\overrightarrow{h_j};\, \overleftarrow{h_j}] \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{2n}hj​=[hj​​;hj​​]∈R2n

Every position jjj thus encodes simultaneously:

* Leftward context x1,…,xjx_1, \dots, x_jx1​,…,xj​ (via hj→\overrightarrow{h_j}hj​​)
* Rightward context xj,…,xTxx_j, \dots, x_{T_x}xj​,…,xTx​​ (via hj←\overleftarrow{h_j}hj​​)

The paper states it succinctly:

> _"In this way, the annotation hjh_jhj​ contains information about the whole input sequence with a strong focus on the parts surrounding the jjj-th word."_

#### Synergy Between Bidirectional Encoding and Attention

The two innovations work in concert:

* The **bidirectional encoder** ensures each position's representation captures rich contextual information
* The **attention mechanism** lets the decoder selectively extract from those rich representations on demand

Without the bidirectional encoder, attention would query impoverished representations (each position missing half its context). Without attention, the bidirectional encoder's detailed local representations would still be compressed into a single vector — the rich local information would ultimately be discarded.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Bidirectional Information Flow in Physical and Biological Systems**
> 
> The principle that a meaningful local representation requires information from both directions appears throughout physics and biology. In **quantum mechanics** , solving the Schrödinger equation for a particle in a potential well requires matching wavefunctions and their derivatives at boundaries from both directions (shooting method); solutions that look locally correct from the left often fail to be physically admissible when continuity from the right is imposed. In **neuroscience** , visual cortex neurons have receptive fields with both excitatory and inhibitory surrounds — classical center-surround organization processes both leftward and rightward stimulus context simultaneously, not sequentially. In **signal processing** , zero-phase digital filters achieve bidirectional symmetry by forward-filtering and then backward-filtering, achieving linear phase at the cost of offline (non-causal) processing — exactly the trade-off bidirectional RNNs make: they gain full context but cannot run in real time. In **genomics** , protein secondary structure prediction from sequence is dramatically improved by bidirectional models (e.g., bidirectional LSTMs in ProteinBERT) because a residue's fold depends on residues both upstream and downstream in the primary sequence.

* * *

### 20.4 Complete Model Architecture

#### Architecture Overview

The full model can be summarized as:

**Encoder** :

* Bidirectional GRU (forward + backward)
* 1,000 hidden units per direction
* Encoder hidden state dimension: 2×1000=20002 \times 1000 = 20002×1000=2000 (concatenated)

**Alignment model (attention)** :

* Additive attention: a(si−1,hj)=va⊤tanh⁡(Wasi−1+Uahj)a(s_{i-1}, h_j) = \mathbf{v}_a^\top \tanh(\mathbf{W}_a s_{i-1} + \mathbf{U}_a h_j)a(si−1​,hj​)=va⊤​tanh(Wa​si−1​+Ua​hj​)
* Attention hidden dimension dad_ada​: matched to decoder hidden dimension

**Decoder** :

* Unidirectional GRU
* 1,000 hidden units
* Receives context vector cic_ici​ as additional input at every step

**Output layer** :

* Maxout layer (Goodfellow et al., 2013) + softmax
* Target vocabulary size: 30,000

#### Architecture Comparison: Bahdanau vs. Sutskever

Design Decision | Sutskever (2014) | Bahdanau (2014)  
---|---|---  
Encoder type | 4-layer unidirectional LSTM | **1-layer bidirectional GRU**  
Decoder type | 4-layer LSTM | 1-layer GRU  
Attention | None | **Additive attention**  
Context vector | Fixed (hTxh_{T_x}hTx​​) | **Dynamic ( cic_ici​ per step)**  
Parameter count | 384M | Significantly fewer  
Input processing | Input reversal trick | Not needed (BiRNN)  
Vocabulary size | 80,000 | 30,000  
  
Two design choices deserve emphasis. First, Bahdanau's model is shallower (1 layer vs. 4 layers) yet achieves superior results — demonstrating that attention provides a qualitatively more efficient form of information utilization, not merely an additive computational cost. Second, Sutskever required input reversal as a heuristic workaround for the information bottleneck; Bahdanau does not need it, because the bidirectional encoder already processes both directions and attention gives the decoder direct access to any position. The reversal trick is a patch; attention is a fundamental architectural fix.

* * *

### 20.5 Figure 3: Visualizing Alignment

#### The Most Influential Visualization in Early NLP

Figure 3 of the Bahdanau paper is one of the most reproduced figures in deep learning history. It displays a heatmap of attention weights αij\alpha_{ij}αij​, with English source words on the horizontal axis and French target words on the vertical axis; each cell's intensity represents αij\alpha_{ij}αij​ — brighter means stronger attention.

#### Patterns Revealed by the Figure

**Pattern 1 — Near-diagonal structure**. For English and French, which share largely parallel word order, the attention heatmap exhibits a pronounced near-diagonal pattern: the iii-th English word broadly corresponds to the iii-th French word. This confirms that attention weights learn linguistically meaningful alignment, not noise.

**Pattern 2 — Off-diagonal bright cells**. More revealing are the off-diagonal cells, corresponding to **word-order divergences** between the two languages. French adjectives typically follow the noun they modify: "the European Economic Area" → "la zone économique européenne." In the heatmap, "économique" attends strongly to "Economic" and "européenne" attends strongly to "European" — but these two words' positions are reversed relative to "zone"/"Area." The off-diagonal bright cells are the model's learned representation of reordering.

**Pattern 3 — Many-to-one and one-to-many correspondences**. Some target words distribute attention across multiple source positions (many-to-one phrase translation); others concentrate attention sharply on one source word (one-to-one). The continuous, differentiable nature of softmax attention allows these graded relationships to be expressed without hard alignment decisions.

#### Why This Figure Mattered Beyond the Numbers

Figure 3 had impact at three levels:

**1\. Validation of correctness**. Attention weights recover linguistically meaningful alignment without ever being trained on word-alignment labels. The model jointly learned "where to look" and "what to say" from translation examples alone — confirming the method is not fitting arbitrary patterns.

**2\. Opening "attention as interpretability"**. Before this figure, neural networks were widely regarded as black boxes. Figure 3 demonstrated a method for inspecting a model's internal computation — visualizing attention weights to understand "what the model attended to." This paradigm spread rapidly across NLP, computer vision, and beyond.

**3\. Building trust**. Seeing the model "do the right thing" (attending to corresponding words) convinced researchers to adopt and extend the method in ways that no BLEU score alone would have. Quantitative improvement is necessary; qualitative coherence is what builds institutional confidence.

#### An Important Caveat on Interpretability

While attention weights provide valuable visualization, subsequent work (Jain & Wallace, 2019; Wiegreffe & Pinter, 2019) established that **attention weights are not reliably causal explanations**. They reflect the direction of information flow during computation, but do not necessarily identify which inputs causally determined the output. High attention weight at position jjj means the model drew information from position jjj — not that position jjj's content was the counterfactual cause of the prediction. Attention ablation experiments (zeroing out specific weights and observing output changes) are needed to approach causal claims. This is the standard correlation-vs.-causation caveat applied to neural network interpretability.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Visualization, Interpretability, and Trust in Science**
> 
> The role that Figure 3 played in building trust in attention mechanisms parallels similar episodes across science. In **astronomy** , false-color maps of cosmic microwave background anisotropies (COBE, WMAP, Planck missions) were scientifically redundant given the power spectra, yet they became the primary vehicle for building public and scientific trust in Big Bang cosmology — the visual made the abstract empirically tangible. In **crystallography** , electron density maps from X-ray diffraction allowed biochemists to "see" protein structures for the first time; the visual credibility of a 3D model at atomic resolution was essential for the Watson-Crick double helix and every subsequent structural biology paper. In **functional MRI** , BOLD activation maps serve as the primary communication medium despite well-known statistical concerns (voxel-wise testing, double-dipping); neuroimagers and clinicians alike require spatial visualization before accepting findings. The common thread is that scientific communities require **visualizations that make internal process legible** before trusting quantitative metrics — a principle that predates deep learning by centuries.

* * *

### 20.6 Experimental Results

#### Dataset and Evaluation

* **Dataset** : WMT'14 English-French translation (348M English words)
* **Evaluation metric** : BLEU — an automatic metric based on n-gram precision
* **Vocabulary constraint** : 30,000 most frequent words for each language

#### Main Results

Model | BLEU  
---|---  
RNN Encoder-Decoder (Cho et al., 2014) | 26.71  
RNNsearch-30 (Bahdanau, trained on shorter sentences) | 28.45  
RNNsearch-50 (Bahdanau, trained on longer sentences) | **30.97**  
Moses (best phrase-based SMT) | 33.30  
  
#### Reading the Results

**Attention substantially outperforms the no-attention baseline**. RNNsearch-50 (30.97) improves over RNN Encoder-Decoder (26.71) by 4.26 BLEU points — a large margin that unambiguously attributes the gain to the attention mechanism.

**The critical finding: long-sentence performance**. Figure 2 of the paper (performance vs. sentence length) is arguably more important than the headline BLEU numbers. In models without attention, BLEU drops sharply as sentence length increases, directly reflecting the information bottleneck. In RNNsearch-50, performance is nearly flat across sentence lengths. The paper states:

> _"The performance of RNNsearch is as good as that of the conventional phrase-based translation system (Moses) on sentences of known lengths... The most significant improvement by the proposed RNNsearch model is on long sentences."_

**Moses still leads overall**. The Bahdanau model (30.97) has not yet surpassed Moses (33.30). But given that Bahdanau uses only 30K vocabulary (vs. Moses's full vocabulary) and a smaller model, the result is already compelling. Subsequent work — particularly Luong et al. (2015) at larger scale — quickly surpassed phrase-based systems entirely.

#### The Implicit Ablation

The comparison between RNNsearch and RNN Encoder-Decoder constitutes a clean **ablation study** : the only difference is the presence of the attention mechanism. The 4.26 BLEU gain is attributable solely to attention (jointly with bidirectional encoding, since both innovations are introduced together).

### 20.7 Complete Mathematical Summary

The full mathematical framework of the paper, assembled in one place:

#### Encoder

Bidirectional GRU encoder:

hj→=GRU→(e(xj), hj−1→)\overrightarrow{h_j} = \overrightarrow{\text{GRU}}(e(x_j),\, \overrightarrow{h_{j-1}})hj​​=GRU(e(xj​),hj−1​​) hj←=GRU←(e(xj), hj+1←)\overleftarrow{h_j} = \overleftarrow{\text{GRU}}(e(x_j),\, \overleftarrow{h_{j+1}})hj​​=GRU(e(xj​),hj+1​​) hj=[hj→; hj←] ∈ R2nh_j = [\overrightarrow{h_j};\, \overleftarrow{h_j}] \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{2n}hj​=[hj​​;hj​​]∈R2n

#### Alignment Model

eij=va⊤tanh⁡(Wasi−1+Uahj)e_{ij} = \mathbf{v}_a^\top \tanh(\mathbf{W}_a s_{i-1} + \mathbf{U}_a h_j)eij​=va⊤​tanh(Wa​si−1​+Ua​hj​) αij=exp⁡(eij)∑k=1Txexp⁡(eik)\alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(e_{ij})}{\sum_{k=1}^{T_x} \exp(e_{ik})}αij​=∑k=1Tx​​exp(eik​)exp(eij​)​

#### Context Vector

ci=∑j=1Txαijhjc_i = \sum_{j=1}^{T_x} \alpha_{ij} h_jci​=j=1∑Tx​​αij​hj​

#### Decoder

si=f(si−1,yi−1,ci)=GRU([e(yi−1); ci], si−1)s_i = f(s_{i-1}, y_{i-1}, c_i) = \text{GRU}([e(y_{i-1});\, c_i],\; s_{i-1})si​=f(si−1​,yi−1​,ci​)=GRU([e(yi−1​);ci​],si−1​)

#### Output

p(yi∣y1,…,yi−1,x)=g(si,yi−1,ci)p(y_i \mid y_1, \dots, y_{i-1}, \mathbf{x}) = g(s_i, y_{i-1}, c_i)p(yi​∣y1​,…,yi−1​,x)=g(si​,yi−1​,ci​)

where g(⋅)g(\cdot)g(⋅) is implemented by a maxout hidden layer followed by softmax.

#### Training

End-to-end maximum likelihood estimation. Minimize negative log-likelihood over the training corpus:

L(θ)=−∑n=1Nlog⁡pθ(y(n)∣x(n))\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\sum_{n=1}^{N} \log p_\theta(\mathbf{y}^{(n)} \mid \mathbf{x}^{(n)})L(θ)=−n=1∑N​logpθ​(y(n)∣x(n))

All parameters — encoder, decoder, alignment model — are **jointly** trained via stochastic gradient descent. The "Jointly" in the paper's title carries precise meaning: alignment parameters are not pre-trained or estimated in a separate stage (as in traditional SMT's EM-based word alignment). Instead, "what to attend to" and "what to translate" are learned simultaneously from the same translation objective. The alignment emerges as a latent variable that is discovered because it is useful for translation, not because it matches any pre-specified alignment criterion.

* * *

### 20.8 Historical Significance and Evolutionary Chain

#### From Bahdanau to Transformer

Bahdanau attention initiated a clear technology evolution:

Year | Milestone | Key Advance  
---|---|---  
2014 | **Bahdanau attention** | Encoder-decoder with additive attention  
2015 | Luong attention | Dot-product attention, global/local variants  
2016 | Pointer networks | Attention for copying from input  
2017 | **Transformer** | Self-attention replaces RNN entirely  
2018 | BERT / GPT | Pre-trained Transformers  
2020+ | GPT-3, PaLM, etc. | Large-scale language models  
  
The core mathematics did not change: from Bahdanau to GPT-4, attention is always "score → softmax → weighted sum." What changed:

* Score function: additive → scaled dot-product
* Single-head → multi-head
* Cross-sequence attention → self-attention
* Attention as RNN supplement → attention as the full architecture

#### Propagation Across Fields

Bahdanau's attention idea spread almost immediately to every area of deep learning:

* **Computer vision** : spatial attention for image captioning (Xu et al., 2015, _Show, Attend and Tell_)
* **Speech recognition** : Listen, Attend and Spell (Chan et al., 2016)
* **Graph neural networks** : Graph Attention Networks (Velickovic et al., 2018)
* **Protein structure prediction** : attention mechanisms central to AlphaFold2
* **Reinforcement learning** : attention-based architectures for long-horizon planning

#### Joint Estimation vs. Sequential Estimation

The title phrase "Jointly Learning to Align and Translate" has deep methodological significance. Traditional SMT estimated alignment and translation models in separate stages — first run EM to learn word alignments, then estimate translation probabilities conditioned on those alignments. This sequential estimation means each component's parameters do not account for the other component's presence.

Bahdanau's approach is **joint estimation** : alignment (attention weights) and translation (decoder output) are optimized simultaneously through the same loss function. The alignment model does not learn "correct" alignment in isolation — it learns "alignment that helps translation." These two objectives need not coincide. A word alignment that maximizes translation quality may look different from one that maximizes alignment accuracy on human-labeled data. Joint estimation allows the model to discover this task-useful alignment autonomously.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Joint vs. Sequential Estimation Across Scientific Disciplines**
> 
> The tension between joint and sequential estimation is a recurring theme in statistics, physics, and engineering. In **structural equation modeling** (psychometrics and social science), joint maximum likelihood estimation of latent variable models is computationally harder than two-step estimation but statistically efficient under correct specification — an analog to Bahdanau's joint training vs. SMT's sequential pipeline. In **quantum field theory** , renormalization requires simultaneously updating all coupling constants in a theory rather than adjusting them one at a time; sequential updates can destabilize the vacuum. In **control systems engineering** , the Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) regulator famously separates the estimation problem (Kalman filter) from the control problem (LQR) via the separation principle — a case where sequential solution is provably optimal under Gaussian noise. The key insight is that separation works when the two sub-problems are **conditionally independent** given the shared variable; when they are not (as in alignment and translation), joint optimization is strictly superior. Bahdanau's result can be read as an empirical demonstration that word alignment and translation are not conditionally independent in the way traditional SMT assumed.

### 20.9 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**1.** Explain precisely why Bahdanau uses si−1s_{i-1}si−1​ rather than sis_isi​ to compute the alignment score. Draw the causal dependency graph for both cases and identify the cycle that arises from using sis_isi​.

Answer

In the aligned decoder, step iii proceeds as:

  1. Compute eij=va⊤tanh⁡(Wasi−1+Uahj)e_{ij} = \mathbf{v}_a^\top\tanh(\mathbf{W}_a s_{i-1} + \mathbf{U}_a h_j)eij​=va⊤​tanh(Wa​si−1​+Ua​hj​)
  2. Compute αij=softmaxj(eij)\alpha_{ij} = \text{softmax}_j(e_{ij})αij​=softmaxj​(eij​)
  3. Compute ci=∑jαijhjc_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} h_jci​=∑j​αij​hj​
  4. Compute si=GRU([e(yi−1);ci], si−1)s_i = \text{GRU}([e(y_{i-1}); c_i],\; s_{i-1})si​=GRU([e(yi−1​);ci​],si−1​)

With si−1s_{i-1}si−1​ (already computed at step i−1i-1i−1), the chain si−1→eij→αij→ci→sis_{i-1} \to e_{ij} \to \alpha_{ij} \to c_i \to s_isi−1​→eij​→αij​→ci​→si​ is acyclic and computable left-to-right.

If instead sis_isi​ were used in step 1, the dependency graph becomes:

si ⟶ eij ⟶ αij ⟶ ci ⟶ sis_i \;\longrightarrow\; e_{ij} \;\longrightarrow\; \alpha_{ij} \;\longrightarrow\; c_i \;\longrightarrow\; s_isi​⟶eij​⟶αij​⟶ci​⟶si​

This cycle means no closed-form sequential computation exists. One could in principle solve for sis_isi​ iteratively (fixed-point iteration), but this dramatically increases per-step cost and complicates backpropagation. Using si−1s_{i-1}si−1​ eliminates the cycle at the cost of a one-step delay — the attention is computed based on "what the decoder knew before receiving the context," which is conceptually consistent with the sequential generation process.

Luong (2015) later proposed a predictor-corrector variant: compute an initial s~i\tilde{s}_is~i​ without attention, use it to compute αij\alpha_{ij}αij​ and cic_ici​, then compute a refined sis_isi​ incorporating cic_ici​. This is closer to iterative resolution but remains computationally tractable by performing only one correction step.

#### Application

**2.** Compare bidirectional GRU (Bahdanau) and deep unidirectional LSTM (Sutskever) on four dimensions: (a) informational richness of each encoder position; (b) computational efficiency; (c) need for input reversal; (d) compatibility with attention. Which design choices are complementary, and why?

Answer

**(a) Informational richness**

BiGRU: hj=[h→j;h←j]h_j = [\overrightarrow{h}_j; \overleftarrow{h}_j]hj​=[hj​;hj​] contains both left and right context for position jjj — full global context awareness.

Deep unidirectional LSTM: hjh_jhj​ encodes only x1,…,xjx_1, \dots, x_jx1​,…,xj​; positions later in the sequence have no influence on earlier representations regardless of depth.

Advantage: BiGRU. Depth alone cannot substitute for bidirectional information flow.

**(b) Computational efficiency**

BiGRU: two passes over the sequence (parallelizable), one layer, GRU's 3-gate structure. Total operations roughly O(Tx×2×3n(n+d))O(T_x \times 2 \times 3n(n+d))O(Tx​×2×3n(n+d)).

Deep unidirectional LSTM: four sequential layers, LSTM's 4-gate structure. Layers are serially dependent. Total operations roughly O(Tx×4×4n(n+d))O(T_x \times 4 \times 4n(n+d))O(Tx​×4×4n(n+d)) with depth penalty from serial layer dependency.

Advantage: BiGRU. Fewer parameters; two passes are parallelizable.

**(c) Need for input reversal**

Sutskever requires reversal: it brings source-sentence positions 1,2,3,... closer to the context vector in the unrolled computation, improving initial-token translation (gains ~4.7 BLEU). This is a heuristic workaround, not a principled fix.

Bahdanau does not require reversal: the backward GRU already provides access to the full rightward context from every position, and attention allows the decoder to directly access any position regardless of distance.

**(d) Compatibility with attention**

BiGRU: excellent. Each position has a rich, globally-aware representation — exactly what the decoder's attention queries need to find. The "value" returned at each position is informationally complete.

Deep unidirectional LSTM: suboptimal. Attending to an early position retrieves only leftward context. Attending to a late position retrieves richer context but earlier positions may carry outdated representations by the time attention queries them.

The bidirectional encoder and attention mechanism are **mutually reinforcing** : attention needs informationally rich per-position representations; bidirectional encoding provides them. Neither innovation is as effective without the other.

**4.** State the dimensions of all learnable parameters in the Bahdanau alignment model. Assume encoder hidden dimension nnn (bidirectional, so hj∈R2nh_j \in \mathbb{R}^{2n}hj​∈R2n), decoder hidden dimension mmm, and attention hidden dimension dad_ada​. Compute total parameter count for the alignment model.

Answer

The alignment model is:

eij=va⊤tanh⁡(Wasi−1+Uahj)e_{ij} = \mathbf{v}_a^\top \tanh(\mathbf{W}_a s_{i-1} + \mathbf{U}_a h_j)eij​=va⊤​tanh(Wa​si−1​+Ua​hj​)

Parameters:

Parameter | Shape | Count

#### Think Deeper

**3.** The paper uses vocabulary size 30,000 vs. Sutskever's 80,000. Explain why attention allows smaller vocabulary size without proportional performance loss. Consider the role of ⟨UNK⟩\langle\text{UNK}\rangle⟨UNK⟩ handling and local context retrieval.

Answer

With vocabulary size 30K, more rare words map to ⟨UNK⟩\langle\text{UNK}\rangle⟨UNK⟩. In Sutskever's model, ⟨UNK⟩\langle\text{UNK}\rangle⟨UNK⟩ is catastrophic: the encoder creates an uninformative embedding for that position, and the decoder must reconstruct the meaning from a compressed global context vector that already contains minimal information about the unknown word. Hence 80K vocabulary is needed.

In Bahdanau's model, attention provides several compensating mechanisms:

  1. **Contextual disambiguation** : when the decoder encounters a position with ⟨UNK⟩\langle\text{UNK}\rangle⟨UNK⟩, it can attend to _surrounding_ positions — accessing words before and after the unknown word provides strong disambiguation cues.

  2. **Implicit copying** : high attention weight on a ⟨UNK⟩\langle\text{UNK}\rangle⟨UNK⟩ position serves as a pointer to that source location. Post-processing can replace ⟨UNK⟩\langle\text{UNK}\rangle⟨UNK⟩ in the output with the source word at the highest-attention position (this was later formalized as pointer networks and copy mechanisms).

  3. **Shorter information paths** : instead of routing all information through a fixed bottleneck, attention creates direct paths from any source position to the decoder. Even if one position is ⟨UNK⟩\langle\text{UNK}\rangle⟨UNK⟩, its neighboring positions' full representations remain directly accessible.

  4. **Parameter reallocation** : the embedding matrix shrinks from 80000×100080000 \times 100080000×1000 (80M parameters) to 30000×100030000 \times 100030000×1000 (30M parameters), saving 50M parameters that can be allocated to the attention mechanism and bidirectional encoder — increasing effective model capacity for the same total parameter budget.

The 30K vocabulary performs comparably to 80K because attention makes the model more robust to missing vocabulary: the loss from UNK is offset by richer context retrieval.

**6.** The Bahdanau paper's Figure 3 is widely cited as evidence that attention learns "interpretable alignment." But Jain & Wallace (2019) challenge this claim. Articulate precisely what attention weights _do_ and _do not_ tell us, and describe what experimental design would be needed to establish that a particular attention pattern is causally responsible for a model's output.

Answer

**What attention weights tell us** : The weight αij\alpha_{ij}αij​ records how much the computation at decoding step iii drew on encoder position jjj when forming the context vector cic_ici​. High αij\alpha_{ij}αij​ means position jjj's hidden state hjh_jhj​ contributed substantially to cic_ici​ at step iii. This is a factual statement about information routing during the forward pass.

**What attention weights do not tell us** : αij\alpha_{ij}αij​ does not establish that removing position jjj's information would change the model's output. The model may have multiple redundant pathways (through hidden state recurrence, through other attended positions, through the decoder's own hidden state) that carry the same information. High attention can coexist with low causal effect if the information is available via other channels.

Jain & Wallace (2019) showed that many different attention distributions can produce nearly identical model outputs — implying the particular distribution is not uniquely determined by causal necessity. Wiegreffe & Pinter (2019) showed that adversarially trained alternative attention distributions can maintain accuracy, again suggesting the specific weights are underdetermined.

**Experimental design for causal claims** : To establish that a particular attention pattern causally determines the output:

  1. **Attention ablation** : force αij=0\alpha_{ij} = 0αij​=0 for a specific position jjj and observe output change. If output is unchanged, position jjj's attention was not causally necessary.

  2. **Input deletion with attention constraint** : remove or mask input position jjj entirely. If the model's attention then shifts to compensate and output is preserved, attention weights were serving a redundant function.

  3. **Counterfactual intervention** : independently vary the content of position jjj while holding all other positions fixed. Does the output change in a way consistent with the attention weight? If the model "claims" to attend heavily to position jjj but its output is unaffected by changes to jjj's content, the attention is decorative, not causal.

  4. **Integrated gradients** : compute attribution scores using gradient-based methods (Sundararajan et al., 2017) and compare with attention weights. If they disagree, at least one is a poor causal indicator.

The appropriate interpretation of Figure 3 is: "the model's attention weights are _consistent with_ linguistically meaningful alignment" — a necessary but not sufficient condition for attention-as-explanation.

**7.** Trace the evolution from Bahdanau attention (2014) to the Transformer (2017). Identify at each step: (a) what was preserved, (b) what was generalized or simplified, and (c) what was removed. What does this evolutionary trajectory reveal about how architectural progress typically occurs in deep learning?

Answer

**Bahdanau (2014) → Luong (2015)**

* Preserved: attention as "score → softmax → weighted sum"; encoder-decoder structure; context vector as weighted sum of encoder states
* Generalized: score function moved from additive (v⊤tanh⁡(W1q+W2k)\mathbf{v}^\top\tanh(\mathbf{W}_1 q + \mathbf{W}_2 k)v⊤tanh(W1​q+W2​k)) to dot-product (q⊤kq^\top kq⊤k) and general bilinear (q⊤Wkq^\top\mathbf{W}kq⊤Wk); introduced global vs. local attention variants
* Removed: restriction to additive score function; use of si−1s_{i-1}si−1​ for attention (Luong uses sis_isi​ with a corrector step)

**Luong (2015) → Self-Attention (2016)**

* Preserved: dot-product score function; weighted-sum aggregation
* Generalized: queries and keys can come from the _same_ sequence (self-attention); no longer restricted to cross-sequence alignment
* Removed: dependence on a separate encoder and decoder sequence; RNN hidden states as the mandatory carrier

**Self-Attention → Transformer (2017)**

* Preserved: scaled dot-product attention; self-attention as the core operation; encoder-decoder structure for translation
* Generalized: multi-head attention (multiple attention patterns in parallel); positional encoding replaces sequential RNN position information; feed-forward sublayers added
* Removed: RNN entirely — the Transformer has no recurrence, no sequential dependency in computation; sequence is processed in parallel

**What this trajectory reveals** :

  1. **Preservation of the mathematical core** : score → softmax → weighted sum was never replaced, only instantiated differently. This is characteristic of paradigm-level ideas in science — the insight is more durable than any specific implementation.

  2. **Simplification enables generalization** : each step replaced a more complex component (additive scoring, RNN hidden states, single-head) with a simpler version (dot-product, positional embeddings, then multi-head). Simplification is not regression — it exposes the essential structure by removing scaffolding.

  3. **Removal of the scaffolding** : the Transformer's most radical move was removing RNNs entirely. Bahdanau's attention was conceived as a _supplement_ to RNN; Vaswani et al. (2017) showed that the RNN scaffold was not necessary and was in fact the bottleneck (sequential computation prevents parallelization). Major architectural transitions often involve recognizing that a component introduced for historical reasons is now a constraint.

  4. **Combinatorial recombination** : none of the steps from Bahdanau to Transformer introduced wholly new mathematical primitives. Dot-product similarity, softmax, weighted averaging, multi-head ensemble, positional encoding — all existed before. The Transformer's innovation was the specific combination and the architectural commitment to rely solely on attention. Progress frequently comes from systematic recombination rather than discovery of new primitives.

### Preliminary Note

If the entire 26-chapter book has a single center of gravity, this is it.

The Transformer architecture, introduced in 2017, has fundamentally restructured artificial intelligence. GPT, BERT, Claude, Gemini, LLaMA — every large language model you have heard of is built on the Transformer. Its influence has spread far beyond NLP to computer vision (Vision Transformer), protein structure prediction (AlphaFold2), time-series forecasting, mathematical reasoning, and drug discovery.

The Transformer's core is the self-attention mechanism. This chapter derives it from scratch, with every mathematical step made explicit.

### 21.1 From Attention to "Self"-Attention

#### Review: The Query-Key-Value Framework

In Chapter 19 we established the Q-K-V framework for attention. In Bahdanau attention (Chapter 20), the decoder's current hidden state serves as the Query, while the encoder's hidden states serve as Keys and Values. The decoder queries the encoder, dynamically extracting relevant information from the input sequence. This is **cross-sequence attention** : Queries come from one sequence, Keys/Values from another.

#### The Key Leap: Attending to Oneself

Self-attention's defining move is: **Queries, Keys, and Values all come from the same sequence.**

Every position in the sequence simultaneously plays three roles:

* It is the **Query** posing a question: "Which positions should I attend to?"
* It is a **Key** being queried: "What kind of information do I contain?"
* It is a **Value** to be extracted: "If attended to, what do I contribute?"

In other words, every element in the sequence examines every other element (including itself) to decide where to gather information. This self-referential character is precisely what "self"-attention names.

#### Formal Definition

Given input sequence X∈Rn×dmodelX \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}X∈Rn×dmodel​, where nnn is sequence length and dmodeld_{\text{model}}dmodel​ is the embedding dimension per token, self-attention maps XXX to Queries, Keys, and Values via three learnable linear projections:

Q=XWQ,K=XWK,V=XWVQ = XW^Q, \qquad K = XW^K, \qquad V = XW^VQ=XWQ,K=XWK,V=XWV

where:

* WQ∈Rdmodel×dkW^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}WQ∈Rdmodel​×dk​ — Query projection matrix
* WK∈Rdmodel×dkW^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}WK∈Rdmodel​×dk​ — Key projection matrix
* WV∈Rdmodel×dvW^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_v}WV∈Rdmodel​×dv​ — Value projection matrix

Resulting dimensions:

* Q∈Rn×dkQ \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}Q∈Rn×dk​ — each token has a dkd_kdk​-dimensional Query vector
* K∈Rn×dkK \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}K∈Rn×dk​ — each token has a dkd_kdk​-dimensional Key vector
* V∈Rn×dvV \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v}V∈Rn×dv​ — each token has a dvd_vdv​-dimensional Value vector

In the standard Transformer, dk=dv=dmodel/hd_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}} / hdk​=dv​=dmodel​/h, where hhh is the number of attention heads (Chapter 22).

### 21.2 Scaled Dot-Product Attention: Complete Derivation

#### The Formula

The core computation of self-attention is expressed by a single formula:

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax ⁣(QK⊤dk)V\boxed{\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V}Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤​)V​

This may be the single most important formula in the book. We dissect it step by step.

#### Step 1: Similarity Matrix S=QK⊤S = QK^\topS=QK⊤

**Dimension accounting** :

Q∈Rn×dk,K⊤∈Rdk×n⟹S=QK⊤∈Rn×nQ \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}, \quad K^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k \times n} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad S = QK^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}Q∈Rn×dk​,K⊤∈Rdk​×n⟹S=QK⊤∈Rn×n

The (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) entry of SSS is the dot product of the iii-th Query and the jjj-th Key:

Sij=qi⊤kj=∑ℓ=1dkqi,ℓ⋅kj,ℓS_{ij} = q_i^\top k_j = \sum_{\ell=1}^{d_k} q_{i,\ell}\cdot k_{j,\ell}Sij​=qi⊤​kj​=ℓ=1∑dk​​qi,ℓ​⋅kj,ℓ​

**Geometric interpretation** : SijS_{ij}Sij​ measures the "affinity" between positions iii and jjj. Two vectors with similar direction have a larger dot product, indicating that position iii semantically benefits from attending to position jjj.

**Key observation** : SSS is an n×nn \times nn×n matrix, explicitly computing the relationship between **every pair** of positions. For n=1000n = 1000n=1000, this matrix has 10610^6106 entries — this is the origin of self-attention's O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) complexity.

#### Step 2: Scaling — Dividing by dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​

S^=Sdk=QK⊤dk\hat{S} = \frac{S}{\sqrt{d_k}} = \frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}S^=dk​​S​=dk​​QK⊤​

This step appears minor but is critical. Section 21.3 provides a complete variance-analysis proof of its necessity.

#### Step 3: Row-Wise Softmax Normalization

Apply softmax to each **row** of S^\hat{S}S^:

αij=exp⁡(S^ij)∑ℓ=1nexp⁡(S^iℓ)\alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(\hat{S}_{ij})}{\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{n} \exp(\hat{S}_{i\ell})}αij​=ℓ=1∑n​exp(S^iℓ​)exp(S^ij​)​

This ensures every row sums to one:

∀ i:∑j=1nαij=1,αij≥0\forall\, i: \quad \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_{ij} = 1, \quad \alpha_{ij} \geq 0∀i:j=1∑n​αij​=1,αij​≥0

The matrix A=[αij]∈Rn×nA = [\alpha_{ij}] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A=[αij​]∈Rn×n is the **attention weight matrix**. Each row is a probability distribution describing how position iii should distribute "attention" across all positions in the sequence.

#### Step 4: Weighted Aggregation

Compute the weighted sum of Value vectors:

Outputi=∑j=1nαij vj\text{Output}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_{ij}\, v_jOutputi​=j=1∑n​αij​vj​

In matrix form:

Output=AV∈Rn×dv\text{Output} = AV \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v}Output=AV∈Rn×dv​

**Key recognition** : each position iii's output is a **convex combination** of all Value vectors — coefficients αij≥0\alpha_{ij} \geq 0αij​≥0 with ∑jαij=1\sum_j \alpha_{ij} = 1∑j​αij​=1. The output lies within the convex hull of all Value vectors, mixing context from the entire sequence in proportions determined by Query-Key compatibility.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Weighted Aggregation in Physics and Statistics**
> 
> The operation Outputi=∑jαijvj\text{Output}_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} v_jOutputi​=∑j​αij​vj​ with αij≥0\alpha_{ij} \geq 0αij​≥0, ∑jαij=1\sum_j \alpha_{ij} = 1∑j​αij​=1 is formally a **convex combination** , a construction that appears throughout quantitative science. In **statistical mechanics** , the canonical ensemble expectation value ⟨O⟩=∑sP(s)O(s)\langle O \rangle = \sum_s P(s) O(s)⟨O⟩=∑s​P(s)O(s) with Boltzmann weights P(s)=e−Es/kBT/ZP(s) = e^{-E_s/k_BT}/ZP(s)=e−Es​/kB​T/Z has exactly this structure: softmax with the role of energy played by −S^ij-\hat{S}_{ij}−S^ij​ and temperature kBT=1k_BT = 1kB​T=1 (scaling by dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ plays the role of adjusting temperature). In **kernel density estimation** (Parzen-Rosenblatt), the estimated density at point xxx is a weighted average of kernel values centered at each data point — the same convex-combination structure. In **Bayesian model averaging** , posterior predictions under model uncertainty weight each model's prediction by its posterior probability p(Mk∣data)p(M_k \mid \text{data})p(Mk​∣data), again a softmax-type weighted combination. The universality of this operation reflects a deep principle: when multiple sources of information must be integrated, soft weighting by compatibility is the minimum-assumption aggregation rule consistent with probabilistic coherence.

### 21.3 Why Divide by dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​? — Variance Analysis

The scaling factor embodies careful probabilistic reasoning. Here is the complete proof.

#### Setup

**Assumption** : every component of QQQ and KKK is independently sampled from a distribution with mean 0 and variance 1. That is, for all i,ℓi, \elli,ℓ:

qi,ℓ∼(0,1),kj,ℓ∼(0,1),qi,ℓ⊥kj,ℓq_{i,\ell} \sim (0, 1), \quad k_{j,\ell} \sim (0, 1), \quad q_{i,\ell} \perp k_{j,\ell}qi,ℓ​∼(0,1),kj,ℓ​∼(0,1),qi,ℓ​⊥kj,ℓ​

This holds approximately at initialization (Xavier/Kaiming initialization is designed to keep per-layer output variance stable).

#### Computing the Mean

The dot product Sij=qi⊤kj=∑ℓ=1dkqi,ℓ⋅kj,ℓS_{ij} = q_i^\top k_j = \sum_{\ell=1}^{d_k} q_{i,\ell}\cdot k_{j,\ell}Sij​=qi⊤​kj​=∑ℓ=1dk​​qi,ℓ​⋅kj,ℓ​.

Since qi,ℓq_{i,\ell}qi,ℓ​ and kj,ℓk_{j,\ell}kj,ℓ​ are independent with mean zero:

E[qi,ℓ⋅kj,ℓ]=E[qi,ℓ]⋅E[kj,ℓ]=0E[q_{i,\ell}\cdot k_{j,\ell}] = E[q_{i,\ell}]\cdot E[k_{j,\ell}] = 0E[qi,ℓ​⋅kj,ℓ​]=E[qi,ℓ​]⋅E[kj,ℓ​]=0

Therefore: E[Sij]=0E[S_{ij}] = 0E[Sij​]=0.

#### Computing the Variance (Core Derivation)

The variance of each product term qi,ℓ⋅kj,ℓq_{i,\ell}\cdot k_{j,\ell}qi,ℓ​⋅kj,ℓ​:

Var(qi,ℓ⋅kj,ℓ)=E[(qi,ℓ⋅kj,ℓ)2]−0\text{Var}(q_{i,\ell}\cdot k_{j,\ell}) = E[(q_{i,\ell}\cdot k_{j,\ell})^2] - 0Var(qi,ℓ​⋅kj,ℓ​)=E[(qi,ℓ​⋅kj,ℓ​)2]−0

By independence: E[(qi,ℓ⋅kj,ℓ)2]=E[qi,ℓ2]⋅E[kj,ℓ2]=1⋅1=1E[(q_{i,\ell}\cdot k_{j,\ell})^2] = E[q_{i,\ell}^2]\cdot E[k_{j,\ell}^2] = 1 \cdot 1 = 1E[(qi,ℓ​⋅kj,ℓ​)2]=E[qi,ℓ2​]⋅E[kj,ℓ2​]=1⋅1=1.

Summing over dkd_kdk​ independent terms:

Var(Sij)=∑ℓ=1dkVar(qi,ℓ⋅kj,ℓ)=dk\boxed{\text{Var}(S_{ij}) = \sum_{\ell=1}^{d_k} \text{Var}(q_{i,\ell}\cdot k_{j,\ell}) = d_k}Var(Sij​)=ℓ=1∑dk​​Var(qi,ℓ​⋅kj,ℓ​)=dk​​

**Conclusion** : the dot product SijS_{ij}Sij​ has standard deviation dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​.

#### The Problem

As dkd_kdk​ grows, the magnitude of SijS_{ij}Sij​ grows proportionally:

dkd_kdk​ | Std(Sij)=dk\text{Std}(S_{ij}) = \sqrt{d_k}Std(Sij​)=dk​​ | Typical range (±2σ\pm 2\sigma±2σ)  
---|---|---  
16 | 4.0 | [−8, +8][-8,\;+8][−8,+8]  
64 | 8.0 | [−16, +16][-16,\;+16][−16,+16]  
256 | 16.0 | [−32, +32][-32,\;+32][−32,+32]  
512 | 22.6 | [−45, +45][-45,\;+45][−45,+45]  
  
**Softmax behavior with large inputs** : when some element zmax⁡z_{\max}zmax​ greatly exceeds the others,

σ(zmax⁡)≈1,σ(zj)≈0 ∀j≠max⁡\sigma(z_{\max}) \approx 1, \qquad \sigma(z_j) \approx 0 \;\; \forall j \neq \maxσ(zmax​)≈1,σ(zj​)≈0∀j=max

Softmax degenerates to an approximate one-hot distribution. Two severe consequences follow:

**Consequence 1 — Vanishing Gradients**. The softmax gradient is:

∂αi∂zj=αi(δij−αj)\frac{\partial \alpha_i}{\partial z_j} = \alpha_i(\delta_{ij} - \alpha_j)∂zj​∂αi​​=αi​(δij​−αj​)

When αi≈0\alpha_i \approx 0αi​≈0 or αi≈1\alpha_i \approx 1αi​≈1, the gradient αi(1−αi)≈0\alpha_i(1-\alpha_i) \approx 0αi​(1−αi​)≈0. Backpropagation receives nearly zero gradient signal; parameters cannot update effectively.

**Consequence 2 — Attention Over-Concentration**. The model is forced to attend to one position, losing the core advantage of soft attention — aggregating information from multiple positions simultaneously.

#### The Scaling Solution

After dividing by dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​:

Var ⁣(Sijdk)=Var(Sij)dk=dkdk=1\text{Var}\\!\left(\frac{S_{ij}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) = \frac{\text{Var}(S_{ij})}{d_k} = \frac{d_k}{d_k} = 1Var(dk​​Sij​​)=dk​Var(Sij​)​=dk​dk​​=1

**Variance is normalized to 1** , independent of dkd_kdk​. Softmax inputs return to a reasonable range (roughly [−2,+2][-2, +2][−2,+2]), neither saturating nor becoming flat — exactly the regime where soft attention functions as intended.

#### Why Additive Attention Does Not Need Scaling

Bahdanau's additive attention uses:

eij=v⊤tanh⁡(W1si+W2hj)e_{ij} = \mathbf{v}^\top \tanh(\mathbf{W}_1 s_i + \mathbf{W}_2 h_j)eij​=v⊤tanh(W1​si​+W2​hj​)

The tanh⁡\tanhtanh non-linearity constrains values to [−1,+1][-1, +1][−1,+1], naturally preventing softmax saturation. Scaling is unnecessary. The cost is extra parameters (W1,W2,v\mathbf{W}_1, \mathbf{W}_2, \mathbf{v}W1​,W2​,v) and an additional non-linear transform. The dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ scaling lets dot-product attention achieve both computational efficiency and numerical stability simultaneously.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Variance Normalization Across Disciplines**
> 
> The dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ scaling is fundamentally a **variance normalization** step, a procedure that appears under many names across science and engineering. In **signal processing** , matched filter theory derives that the optimal linear detector for a signal of length ddd in white Gaussian noise scales its output by 1/d1/\sqrt{d}1/d​; without this normalization, the detection threshold would need to grow with signal length, making the system scale-dependent. In **quantum mechanics** , the inner product of two ddd-dimensional state vectors ⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩=∑iϕi∗ψi\langle \phi | \psi \rangle = \sum_i \phi_i^* \psi_i⟨ϕ∣ψ⟩=∑i​ϕi∗​ψi​ also grows in expectation as dimensions increase when components are random, necessitating normalization in numerical quantum simulation. In **random matrix theory** (Wigner semicircle law), eigenvalue distributions of large random matrices are studied after rescaling by 1/d1/\sqrt{d}1/d​; without this rescaling, the spectral radius diverges with dimension, obscuring universal structure. The recurring theme is: **dot-product-type statistics grow with dimensionality, and any downstream non-linearity applied to them must be protected by a O(d−1/2)O(d^{-1/2})O(d−1/2) normalization**. Vaswani et al.'s dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ factor is a clean instance of this principle derived from variance analysis.

**Information mixing** : token 1 was (1,0,1)(1,0,1)(1,0,1); it becomes (0.640,0.359,0.640)(0.640, 0.359, 0.640)(0.640,0.359,0.640). The second component changed from 0 to 0.359 — because token 1 "borrowed" information from tokens 2 and 3, which have nonzero second components. Self-attention makes representations context-aware.

**Self-weight preservation** : diagonal entries of AAA are the largest in each row, so each token retains similarity with its original representation while absorbing context from others.

**Representation smoothing** : after self-attention, token representations become more similar to each other (reduced variance). This smoothing effect accumulates in deep Transformers and is counteracted by residual connections (Chapter 23).

### 21.5 Self-Attention vs. RNN: Systematic Comparison

#### Computational Complexity

Metric | Self-Attention | RNN  
---|---|---  
Operations per layer | O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d) | O(nd2)O(n d^2)O(nd2)  
Sequential operations | O(1)O(1)O(1) | O(n)O(n)O(n)  
Maximum path length | O(1)O(1)O(1) | O(n)O(n)O(n)  
  
**Interpreting each metric** :

**Operations per layer** : the bottleneck in self-attention is the O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d) cost of computing QK⊤QK^\topQK⊤. An RNN performs one d×dd \times dd×d matrix multiplication per step for nnn steps: O(nd2)O(nd^2)O(nd2). When n<dn < dn<d (sequence length shorter than hidden dimension — common in many settings), self-attention is actually cheaper. When n>dn > dn>d (long sequences), the n2n^2n2 factor dominates.

**Sequential operations** : self-attention computes all positions simultaneously (one matrix multiplication); an RNN must execute step ttt after step t−1t-1t−1 completes, serializing computation. This is the primary reason Transformers train far faster than RNNs on GPUs.

**Maximum path length** : the number of steps for information to travel from position 1 to position nnn. In self-attention, any two positions interact directly in one step (O(1)O(1)O(1)); in an RNN, information must traverse n−1n-1n−1 steps sequentially (O(n)O(n)O(n)). Shorter paths mean gradient signals decay less over long-range dependencies.

#### Parallelism

**RNN's serial bottleneck** :
    
    
    h_1 = f(x_1, h_0) → h_2 = f(x_2, h_1) → h_3 = f(x_3, h_2) → ... → h_n
    

Each step must await the previous one. No amount of GPU parallelism can accelerate this chain.

**Self-attention's full parallelism** :
    
    
    All (q_i^T k_j) pairs computed simultaneously → all softmax rows simultaneously → all output rows simultaneously
    

GPUs have thousands of cores; matrix multiplication fully exploits all cores at once.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Sequential vs. Parallel Computation in Physical and Biological Systems**
> 
> The contrast between RNN's sequential dependency and self-attention's full parallelism mirrors a fundamental distinction in computation across physics and biology. In **pipelining and parallel processor design** (computer architecture), Flynn's taxonomy distinguishes SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data) from SISD pipelines — self-attention is the SIMD paradigm applied to sequence modeling, while RNNs are essentially SISD. In **DNA replication** , the replication fork proceeds sequentially along a chromosome, but eukaryotes circumvent the speed limit by initiating replication at multiple origins simultaneously (hundreds of replicons in parallel), reducing replication time from months to hours — exactly analogous to how self-attention parallelizes over all positions. In **ant colony foraging** , ants using stigmergic pheromone trails must sequentially visit locations to update the shared information field; in contrast, bees perform a form of parallel "attention" during the waggle dance, broadcasting spatial attention weights to all receivers simultaneously. In **optical computing** , holographic associative memories implement a form of matrix multiplication in parallel using interference patterns — providing O(1)O(1)O(1) associative lookup time regardless of memory size, the same O(1)O(1)O(1) path-length advantage that self-attention provides over sequential RNN traversal.

#### Long-Range Dependencies

**RNN's telephone game problem** : for position 1's information to reach position nnn, it must pass through n−1n-1n−1 sequential time steps. Each step involves a matrix multiplication and a non-linearity; information inevitably degrades or distorts in transit. Even LSTM gating only mitigates, not eliminates, this path-length problem.

**Self-attention's direct connection** : positions 1 and nnn interact directly via α1,n\alpha_{1,n}α1,n​ (or αn,1\alpha_{n,1}αn,1​). One step suffices for information from any position to reach any other.

#### Self-Attention's Cost

Self-attention is not without disadvantages. Its primary cost is O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) time and space complexity:

* The attention matrix A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}A∈Rn×n stores n2n^2n2 elements
* At n=10,000n = 10{,}000n=10,000: single-layer attention matrix ≈108\approx 10^8≈108 entries (≈\approx≈400 MB in float32)
* At n=100,000n = 100{,}000n=100,000: ≈\approx≈40 GB — exceeds single-GPU memory

This quadratic scaling is why processing long sequences (long documents, codebases, genomic sequences) has been a persistent challenge for Transformers, motivating a rich body of follow-up work: Sparse Attention (Child et al., 2019), Linear Attention (Katharopoulos et al., 2020), Flash Attention (Dao et al., 2022), and ring-attention methods for very long contexts.

### 21.6 Permutation Equivariance

A mathematical property deserves dedicated treatment.

**Theorem** : Self-attention is **permutation equivariant**. If we permute the input token order by permutation matrix PPP, the output permutes identically:

SelfAttn(PX)=P⋅SelfAttn(X)\text{SelfAttn}(PX) = P \cdot \text{SelfAttn}(X)SelfAttn(PX)=P⋅SelfAttn(X)

**Proof sketch** : with Q′=PXWQ=PQQ' = PXW^Q = PQQ′=PXWQ=PQ, K′=PKK' = PKK′=PK, V′=PVV' = PVV′=PV:

Q′K′⊤=(PQ)(PK)⊤=PQK⊤P⊤=PSP⊤Q'K'^\top = (PQ)(PK)^\top = PQK^\top P^\top = PSP^\topQ′K′⊤=(PQ)(PK)⊤=PQK⊤P⊤=PSP⊤

Row-wise softmax on PSP⊤PSP^\topPSP⊤ permutes rows and columns simultaneously, preserving the softmax normalization structure. The output becomes:

A′V′=(PAP⊤)(PV)=P(AV)□A'V' = (PAP^\top)(PV) = P(AV) \qquad \squareA′V′=(PAP⊤)(PV)=P(AV)□

**Implication** : pure self-attention is **completely order-blind**. "The cat chased the dog" and "the dog chased the cat" produce identical self-attention outputs if the two noun tokens are simply exchanged. This is why **positional encoding is indispensable** — without it, the Transformer cannot distinguish any two permutations of the same token multiset. Chapter 22 develops positional encoding in full.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Symmetry, Equivariance, and the Need for Symmetry Breaking**
> 
> Permutation equivariance is a form of **global symmetry** — the model treats all orderings equally. In physics, symmetries are foundational: Noether's theorem establishes that every continuous symmetry corresponds to a conservation law. But symmetries must sometimes be **broken** to produce physical reality. In **ferromagnetism** , the Heisenberg model is rotationally symmetric, but below the Curie temperature the ground state spontaneously breaks this symmetry, selecting a preferred magnetization direction — the system "chooses" an ordering from a symmetric set of equally valid options. In **crystallography** , a liquid is translationally symmetric (invariant to position shifts), while a crystal breaks translational symmetry by choosing specific lattice positions — analogous to how positional encoding breaks the permutation symmetry of self-attention to allow position-sensitive reasoning. In **group theory** applied to molecular chemistry, permutation-equivariant functions over atomic positions (like those in AlphaFold2 and SchNet) are precisely the correct inductive bias for molecular modeling, since molecules have no preferred atom ordering — a deliberate preservation of permutation equivariance rather than its breaking. The lesson: **symmetry is a constraint on what functions can be represented; whether to preserve or break it is a modeling choice with profound consequences.**

**(e)** Tokens 1 and 3 share a high dot product (both contain "1" in position 1). Tokens 1 and 2, originally orthogonal, exchange information: token 1's output gains a positive second component; token 2's output gains a positive first component. Self-attention has blended each token's representation with context from the others, weighted by similarity.

**2.** Suppose q,k∈Rdkq, k \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}q,k∈Rdk​ with i.i.d. components from N(0,σ2)\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)N(0,σ2) (variance σ2≠1\sigma^2 \neq 1σ2=1).

(a) Prove E[q⊤k]=0E[q^\top k] = 0E[q⊤k]=0. (b) Prove Var(q⊤k)=dkσ4\text{Var}(q^\top k) = d_k \sigma^4Var(q⊤k)=dk​σ4. (c) What divisor makes the scaled dot product have variance 1? (d) What does this imply for initialization strategies in practice?

Answer

**(a)** E[q⊤k]=∑iE[qiki]=∑iE[qi]E[ki]=0E[q^\top k] = \sum_i E[q_i k_i] = \sum_i E[q_i]E[k_i] = 0E[q⊤k]=∑i​E[qi​ki​]=∑i​E[qi​]E[ki​]=0.

**(b)** Since E[q⊤k]=0E[q^\top k] = 0E[q⊤k]=0, Var(q⊤k)=E[(q⊤k)2]=E[(∑iqiki)2]\text{Var}(q^\top k) = E[(q^\top k)^2] = E[(\sum_i q_i k_i)^2]Var(q⊤k)=E[(q⊤k)2]=E[(∑i​qi​ki​)2].

Expanding: =∑iE[qi2ki2]+∑i≠jE[qikiqjkj]= \sum_i E[q_i^2 k_i^2] + \sum_{i \neq j} E[q_i k_i q_j k_j]=∑i​E[qi2​ki2​]+∑i=j​E[qi​ki​qj​kj​].

Cross terms: by independence and zero mean, E[qikiqjkj]=E[qi]E[ki]E[qj]E[kj]=0E[q_i k_i q_j k_j] = E[q_i]E[k_i]E[q_j]E[k_j] = 0E[qi​ki​qj​kj​]=E[qi​]E[ki​]E[qj​]E[kj​]=0.

Diagonal terms: E[qi2ki2]=E[qi2]E[ki2]=σ2⋅σ2=σ4E[q_i^2 k_i^2] = E[q_i^2]E[k_i^2] = \sigma^2 \cdot \sigma^2 = \sigma^4E[qi2​ki2​]=E[qi2​]E[ki2​]=σ2⋅σ2=σ4.

Therefore Var(q⊤k)=dkσ4\text{Var}(q^\top k) = d_k \sigma^4Var(q⊤k)=dk​σ4.

**(c)** To make Var(q⊤k/c)=1\text{Var}(q^\top k / c) = 1Var(q⊤k/c)=1: dkσ4/c2=1⇒c=σ2dkd_k \sigma^4 / c^2 = 1 \Rightarrow c = \sigma^2\sqrt{d_k}dk​σ4/c2=1⇒c=σ2dk​​.

**(d)** The standard dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ scaling implicitly assumes σ2=1\sigma^2 = 1σ2=1 (unit variance initialization). With Xavier initialization for a linear layer mapping from dimension dind_{\text{in}}din​ to doutd_{\text{out}}dout​, each weight has variance 2/(din+dout)2/(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})2/(din​+dout​), not 1. The effective σ2\sigma^2σ2 for the projected Q and K vectors may differ from 1, meaning the dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ factor is approximate. In practice this rarely causes problems because training quickly adapts; but theoretically, initialization schemes that guarantee σ2=1\sigma^2 = 1σ2=1 at the Q/K output (before projection) would make the dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ scaling exactly correct from the first forward pass.

**3.** For sequence length n=1000n = 1000n=1000, model dimension d=512d = 512d=512:

(a) Compute the FLOPs for one self-attention layer and one RNN step (total nnn steps). (b) Under what conditions (nnn vs. ddd) is the RNN cheaper? (c) Despite potentially higher FLOPs, why is self-attention typically faster on GPUs?

Answer

**(a)** Self-attention: QK⊤QK^\topQK⊤ costs O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d) — specifically ≈10002×512=5.12×108\approx 1000^2 \times 512 = 5.12 \times 10^8≈10002×512=5.12×108 FLOPs. AVAVAV costs another O(n2d)O(n^2 d)O(n2d). Total: ≈109\approx 10^9≈109 FLOPs.

RNN (LSTM): each step computes Wht−1W h_{t-1}Wht−1​ with W∈Rd×dW \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}W∈Rd×d: O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2) FLOPs per step; nnn steps total: O(nd2)≈1000×5122≈2.6×108O(nd^2) \approx 1000 \times 512^2 \approx 2.6 \times 10^8O(nd2)≈1000×5122≈2.6×108 FLOPs.

**(b)** RNN is cheaper when O(nd2)<O(n2d)O(nd^2) < O(n^2 d)O(nd2)<O(n2d), i.e., d<nd < nd<n. For n=1000n = 1000n=1000, d=512d = 512d=512: RNN is cheaper (d<nd < nd<n). For n=64n = 64n=64, d=512d = 512d=512: self-attention is cheaper (n<dn < dn<d). Modern LLMs with context lengths n>104n > 10^4n>104 have n≫dn \gg dn≫d, making the quadratic n2n^2n2 term the dominant bottleneck.

**(c)** Despite more FLOPs, self-attention is faster due to:

  1. **Full parallelism** : QK⊤QK^\topQK⊤ is one GEMM (general matrix multiply) call that fully utilizes thousands of GPU cores simultaneously. RNN's nnn sequential matrix-vector multiplications serialize and cannot exploit GPU parallelism.
  2. **Memory access pattern** : GEMM operations have high arithmetic intensity and exploit GPU cache hierarchy efficiently (coalesced memory access). Small iterative matrix-vector products (RNN steps) are often memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound.
  3. **Gradient path length** : O(1)O(1)O(1) path length means backpropagation through self-attention involves far fewer sequential chain-rule steps than through an RNN's O(n)O(n)O(n) unrolled graph.

**4.** Prove formally that self-attention is permutation equivariant: SelfAttn(PX)=P⋅SelfAttn(X)\text{SelfAttn}(PX) = P \cdot \text{SelfAttn}(X)SelfAttn(PX)=P⋅SelfAttn(X) for any permutation matrix PPP.

Answer

Let Q=XWQQ = XW^QQ=XWQ, K=XWKK = XW^KK=XWK, V=XWVV = XW^VV=XWV.

For permuted input PXPXPX: Q′=PXWQ=PQQ' = PXW^Q = PQQ′=PXWQ=PQ, K′=PKK' = PKK′=PK, V′=PVV' = PVV′=PV.

Score matrix: S′=Q′K′⊤=(PQ)(PK)⊤=PQK⊤P⊤=PSP⊤S' = Q'K'^\top = (PQ)(PK)^\top = PQ K^\top P^\top = PSP^\topS′=Q′K′⊤=(PQ)(PK)⊤=PQK⊤P⊤=PSP⊤.

Softmax (row-wise): A′=softmax(PSP⊤/dk)A' = \text{softmax}(PSP^\top / \sqrt{d_k})A′=softmax(PSP⊤/dk​​).

For any permutation matrix PPP, row-wise softmax satisfies softmax(PMP⊤)ij=softmax(M)P−1(i),P−1(j)\text{softmax}(PMP^\top)_{ij} = \text{softmax}(M)_{P^{-1}(i),P^{-1}(j)}softmax(PMP⊤)ij​=softmax(M)P−1(i),P−1(j)​. Therefore:

A′=PAP⊤A' = PA P^\topA′=PAP⊤

Output: A′V′=(PAP⊤)(PV)=PA(P⊤P)V=PAV=P⋅SelfAttn(X)A'V' = (PAP^\top)(PV) = PA(P^\top P)V = PAV = P \cdot \text{SelfAttn}(X)A′V′=(PAP⊤)(PV)=PA(P⊤P)V=PAV=P⋅SelfAttn(X).

Hence SelfAttn(PX)=P⋅SelfAttn(X)\text{SelfAttn}(PX) = P \cdot \text{SelfAttn}(X)SelfAttn(PX)=P⋅SelfAttn(X). □\square□

The implication is that self-attention can be applied identically to any permutation of the same tokens and produce correspondingly permuted outputs — it carries no notion of token order. Positional encoding breaks this symmetry by adding order-dependent signals to XXX before computing QQQ, KKK, VVV.

#### Think Deeper

**5.** Define Attentionτ(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK⊤/τ)V\text{Attention}_\tau(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}(QK^\top / \tau) VAttentionτ​(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK⊤/τ)V for a temperature parameter τ>0\tau > 0τ>0.

(a) What does the attention distribution approach as τ→0\tau \to 0τ→0? (b) What does it approach as τ→∞\tau \to \inftyτ→∞? (c) Explain the connection between temperature and the dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ scaling factor. (d) In what practical scenarios might a temperature different from dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ be preferable?

Answer

**(a)** As τ→0\tau \to 0τ→0: softmax(S/τ)\text{softmax}(S/\tau)softmax(S/τ) becomes increasingly peaked. In the limit, the distribution concentrates entirely on the position(s) with maximum score — a hard argmax. Attention becomes a "winner-take-all" retrieval that ignores all positions except the single most-compatible one.

**(b)** As τ→∞\tau \to \inftyτ→∞: S/τ→0S/\tau \to 0S/τ→0 component-wise. softmax(0)=(1/n,…,1/n)\text{softmax}(0) = (1/n, \ldots, 1/n)softmax(0)=(1/n,…,1/n) — a uniform distribution. Attention ignores all score differences and averages all Value vectors equally.

**(c)** The dk\sqrt{d_k}dk​​ scaling corresponds to setting τ=dk\tau = \sqrt{d_k}τ=dk​​ in the temperature parameterization. This is a data-driven choice of temperature that keeps the variance of inputs to softmax at approximately 1, independent of the model dimension dkd_kdk​. Choosing τ=dk\tau = \sqrt{d_k}τ=dk​​ is therefore equivalent to performing variance normalization before softmax.

**(d)** Lower temperature (sharper attention) may be preferable when the model should perform near-hard retrieval — e.g., in pointer networks that copy specific positions, or in tasks requiring exact matching (table lookup). Higher temperature (softer attention) may be preferable during early training when attention patterns are not yet reliable, or in tasks requiring broad context integration. Some works (e.g., ALiBi, grouped-query attention) effectively use learnable or task-specific temperature adjustments.

**(c)** In self-attention, the gradient path from any output position to any input position has length **1** (a single matrix multiplication through the attention weights). ### 22.1 Multi-Head Attention: Why Multiple Heads?

#### The Limitation of Single-Head Attention

Consider the sentence:

> "The central bank didn't raise the interest rate because **it** was concerned about recession."

The word "it" simultaneously participates in multiple distinct relationships:

* **Coreference** : it refers to "central bank"
* **Semantic** : it is the subject of "concerned"
* **Causal** : it appears in a causal clause linking non-action (no rate hike) to reason (recession concern)
* **Syntactic** : it occupies the subject position of the subordinate clause

A single attention head must use one set of projection matrices WQ,WK,WVW^Q, W^K, W^VWQ,WK,WV to capture all these relationship types simultaneously. These relationships occupy different directions in semantic space; a single head tends to capture none of them well.

#### The Solution: Multiple Subspaces

Multi-Head Attention's solution is direct: **let multiple independent attention heads each learn different relationship types in different subspaces, then combine their outputs**.

Each head has its own projection matrices WiQ,WiK,WiVW_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^VWiQ​,WiK​,WiV​, projecting input into a low-dimensional subspace where it independently computes attention. Different heads naturally learn different "attention patterns."

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Ensemble Methods and Sensor Fusion**
> 
> The multi-head design instantiates a general principle from **ensemble learning** and **multi-sensor fusion** : combining weak or partial estimators into a richer composite. In **sensor fusion** for autonomous systems (LIDAR + camera + radar), each sensor captures a different aspect of the scene — LIDAR provides precise range but poor color; cameras provide rich texture but no depth; radar penetrates fog but has low resolution. Combining sensors after projection into a common representation space (analogous to the WOW^OWO output projection) produces a representation superior to any single sensor. In **random forests** , individual trees are intentionally uncorrelated by restricting each tree to a random feature subset — the enforced diversity increases ensemble accuracy beyond any single tree. Multi-head attention enforces diversity by projecting into different subspaces (WiQ,WiK,WiVW_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^VWiQ​,WiK​,WiV​ differ across iii), ensuring each head captures complementary information. In **EEG source localization** (neuroscience), multiple electrode channels with different spatial sensitivity are combined to localize brain activity — a direct analog of combining hhh heads that each specialize in different "spatial" relationships within the token space.

* * *

### 22.2 Complete Mathematics of Multi-Head Attention

#### Setup

Given input matrices (in self-attention, Q=K=V=XQ = K = V = XQ=K=V=X):

* Q∈Rn×dmodelQ \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}Q∈Rn×dmodel​ — Query matrix
* K∈Rn×dmodelK \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}K∈Rn×dmodel​ — Key matrix
* V∈Rn×dmodelV \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}V∈Rn×dmodel​ — Value matrix

#### Step 1: Project into Multiple Subspaces

For each head i=1,2,…,hi = 1, 2, \ldots, hi=1,2,…,h, define three learnable projection matrices:

* WiQ∈Rdmodel×dkW_i^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}WiQ​∈Rdmodel​×dk​
* WiK∈Rdmodel×dkW_i^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}WiK​∈Rdmodel​×dk​
* WiV∈Rdmodel×dvW_i^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_v}WiV​∈Rdmodel​×dv​

Execute projections:

Qi=QWiQ∈Rn×dk,Ki=KWiK∈Rn×dk,Vi=VWiV∈Rn×dvQ_i = Q W_i^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}, \quad K_i = K W_i^K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}, \quad V_i = V W_i^V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v}Qi​=QWiQ​∈Rn×dk​,Ki​=KWiK​∈Rn×dk​,Vi​=VWiV​∈Rn×dv​

Each head works in an independent low-dimensional subspace.

#### Step 2: Compute Scaled Dot-Product Attention in Each Subspace

For head iii:

headi=Attention(Qi,Ki,Vi)=softmax ⁣(QiKi⊤dk)Vi∈Rn×dv\text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(Q_i, K_i, V_i) = \text{softmax}\\!\left(\frac{Q_i K_i^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v}headi​=Attention(Qi​,Ki​,Vi​)=softmax(dk​​Qi​Ki⊤​​)Vi​∈Rn×dv​

The score matrix for head iii: Si=QiKi⊤∈Rn×nS_i = Q_i K_i^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}Si​=Qi​Ki⊤​∈Rn×n, with entry:

Si,tj=qi,t⊤ki,j=(∑pQtp(WiQ)p)⊤ ⁣(∑pKjp(WiK)p)S_{i,tj} = q_{i,t}^\top k_{i,j} = \left(\sum_p Q_{tp}(W_i^Q)_{p}\right)^\top\\!\left(\sum_p K_{jp}(W_i^K)_{p}\right)Si,tj​=qi,t⊤​ki,j​=(p∑​Qtp​(WiQ​)p​)⊤(p∑​Kjp​(WiK​)p​)

This n×nn \times nn×n matrix captures, in head iii's subspace, how much each position ttt should attend to each position jjj.

#### Step 3: Concatenate All Head Outputs

Concatenate the hhh head outputs along the feature dimension:

Concat(head1,…,headh)∈Rn×(h⋅dv)\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (h \cdot d_v)}Concat(head1​,…,headh​)∈Rn×(h⋅dv​)

For position ttt: Concatt=[head1,t; head2,t; …; headh,t]∈Rh⋅dv\text{Concat}_t = [\text{head}_{1,t};\; \text{head}_{2,t};\; \ldots;\; \text{head}_{h,t}] \in \mathbb{R}^{h \cdot d_v}Concatt​=[head1,t​;head2,t​;…;headh,t​]∈Rh⋅dv​.

#### Step 4: Output Projection

Project the concatenated representation back to dmodeld_{\text{model}}dmodel​ dimensions:

MultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(head1, …, headh) WO\boxed{\text{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\; \ldots,\; \text{head}_h)\; W^O}MultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(head1​,…,headh​)WO​

where WO∈R(h⋅dv)×dmodelW^O \in \mathbb{R}^{(h \cdot d_v) \times d_{\text{model}}}WO∈R(h⋅dv​)×dmodel​.

**Final output** : Output∈Rn×dmodel\text{Output} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}Output∈Rn×dmodel​ — same shape as input, enabling residual connections:

LayerNorm(X+MultiHead(X,X,X))\text{LayerNorm}(X + \text{MultiHead}(X, X, X))LayerNorm(X+MultiHead(X,X,X))

### 22.3 Parameter Efficiency: Why dk=dmodel/hd_k = d_{\text{model}} / hdk​=dmodel​/h?

One of the most elegant design choices in the original Transformer paper is:

dk=dv=dmodelh\boxed{d_k = d_v = \frac{d_{\text{model}}}{h}}dk​=dv​=hdmodel​​​

#### Parameter Count Comparison

**Setting** : dmodel=512d_{\text{model}} = 512dmodel​=512, h=8h = 8h=8, dk=dv=64d_k = d_v = 64dk​=dv​=64.

**Single-head full-dimensional attention** : WQ,WK,WV∈R512×512W^Q, W^K, W^V \in \mathbb{R}^{512 \times 512}WQ,WK,WV∈R512×512

Parameters=3×512×512=786,432\text{Parameters} = 3 \times 512 \times 512 = 786{,}432Parameters=3×512×512=786,432

**Multi-head attention with dk=dmodel/h=64d_k = d_{\text{model}}/h = 64dk​=dmodel​/h=64**:

Per-head projections for all hhh heads:

h×3×(dmodel×dk)=8×3×(512×64)=786,432h \times 3 \times (d_{\text{model}} \times d_k) = 8 \times 3 \times (512 \times 64) = 786{,}432h×3×(dmodel​×dk​)=8×3×(512×64)=786,432

Output projection WO∈R(h⋅dv)×dmodel=R512×512W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{(h \cdot d_v) \times d_{\text{model}}} = \mathbb{R}^{512 \times 512}WO∈R(h⋅dv​)×dmodel​=R512×512:

512×512=262,144512 \times 512 = 262{,}144512×512=262,144

Total multi-head parameters: 786,432+262,144=1,048,576786{,}432 + 262{,}144 = 1{,}048{,}576786,432+262,144=1,048,576

#### Computation Cost Comparison

Core attention computation across all hhh heads with dk=dmodel/hd_k = d_{\text{model}}/hdk​=dmodel​/h:

h×O(n2dk)=h×O ⁣(n2⋅dmodelh)=O(n2dmodel)h \times O(n^2 d_k) = h \times O\\!\left(n^2 \cdot \frac{d_{\text{model}}}{h}\right) = O(n^2 d_{\text{model}})h×O(n2dk​)=h×O(n2⋅hdmodel​​)=O(n2dmodel​)

**The total computation is the same as single-head attention.** The hhh factor in the number of heads exactly cancels the 1/h1/h1/h reduction in dkd_kdk​. Multi-head attention gains hhh independent attention patterns at essentially no additional computation cost in the core attention step.

#### Dimension Matching Verification

With dv=dmodel/hd_v = d_{\text{model}}/hdv​=dmodel​/h:

Concat output dimension=h⋅dv=h⋅dmodelh=dmodel\text{Concat output dimension} = h \cdot d_v = h \cdot \frac{d_{\text{model}}}{h} = d_{\text{model}}Concat output dimension=h⋅dv​=h⋅hdmodel​​=dmodel​

So WOW^OWO is dmodel×dmodeld_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}dmodel​×dmodel​ — a square matrix, and the output matches the input dimension for residual connections.

#### Ablation Results from the Original Paper

Vaswani et al. (2017) compared (h,dk)(h, d_k)(h,dk​) configurations at fixed total parameter budget:

Configuration | hhh | dkd_kdk​ | EN-DE BLEU  
---|---|---|---  
Single-head | 1 | 512 | 25.3  
Multi-head | 8 | 64 | **27.3**  
Multi-head | 16 | 32 | 26.8  
Multi-head | 32 | 16 | 26.0  
  
h=8h = 8h=8, dk=64d_k = 64dk​=64 is optimal. Too many heads (h=32h = 32h=32) gives each head a subspace too small (dk=16d_k = 16dk​=16) to capture meaningful patterns.

#### What Different Heads Actually Learn

In trained Transformers, different heads specialize automatically. Clark et al. (2019) found in BERT:

* Some heads attend strongly to the **immediately preceding token** (local/positional attention)
* Some heads attend to **sentence separator tokens** `[SEP]` (default/"no-op" attention)
* Some heads learn **syntactic dependencies** : subject-verb, adjective-noun
* Some heads perform **coreference resolution** : pronouns attending to antecedents

This emergent specialization — never explicitly programmed, arising purely from gradient descent — is one of multi-head attention's most striking properties.
