Computing head 1:

Q1=XW1Q=(200211),K1=XW1K=(022011)Q_1 = XW_1^Q = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\\ 0 & 2 \\\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad K_1 = XW_1^K = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 \\\ 2 & 0 \\\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}Q1​=XW1Q​=​201​021​​,K1​=XW1K​=​021​201​​

Score matrix:

S1=Q1K1⊤=(042402222)S_1 = Q_1 K_1^\top = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 4 & 2 \\\ 4 & 0 & 2 \\\ 2 & 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}S1​=Q1​K1⊤​=​042​402​222​​

Scaled (÷2\div\sqrt{2}÷2​) and softmaxed:

* Row 1: S^1=(0,2.83,1.41)⇒α1=(0.045,0.769,0.186)\hat{S}_1 = (0, 2.83, 1.41) \Rightarrow \alpha_1 = (0.045, 0.769, 0.186)S^1​=(0,2.83,1.41)⇒α1​=(0.045,0.769,0.186)
* Row 2: S^2=(2.83,0,1.41)⇒α2=(0.769,0.045,0.186)\hat{S}_2 = (2.83, 0, 1.41) \Rightarrow \alpha_2 = (0.769, 0.045, 0.186)S^2​=(2.83,0,1.41)⇒α2​=(0.769,0.045,0.186)

**Observation** : tokens 1 and 2 have sharply peaked attention on each other (weights ~0.77), while token 3 attends uniformly. Head 1 has learned to detect the asymmetric relationship between positions 1 and 2 (their query and key vectors align strongly with each other but not with themselves — a pattern resembling coreference or syntactic dependency).

This example demonstrates the key feature of multi-head attention: **different heads, using different projection matrices, discover different relationship patterns within the same input sequence**.

### 22.5 Positional Encoding

#### The Problem: Permutation Equivariance

Chapter 21 proved that self-attention is permutation equivariant — completely order-blind. This is catastrophic for natural language:

* "The cat chased the dog" and "the dog chased the cat" would be processed identically (swapping the nouns)
* "A because B" and "B because A" produce the same representation

RNNs acquire positional awareness inherently — processing token ttt at step ttt naturally embeds "this is the ttt-th position" into the computation. The Transformer must **explicitly inject** position information.

#### The Basic Strategy

Positional encoding PE∈Rn×dmodelPE \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}PE∈Rn×dmodel​ is **added** to token embeddings (not concatenated):

Inputi=TokenEmbedding(xi)+PEi\text{Input}_i = \text{TokenEmbedding}(x_i) + PE_iInputi​=TokenEmbedding(xi​)+PEi​

Addition preserves vector dimension, introducing no extra parameters in the core architecture and allowing position and semantic information to mix freely in the same representation space.

#### Sinusoidal Positional Encoding

Vaswani et al. define:

PE(pos, 2i)=sin⁡ ⁣(pos100002i/dmodel)\boxed{PE_{(pos,\, 2i)} = \sin\\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)}PE(pos,2i)​=sin(100002i/dmodel​pos​)​ PE(pos, 2i+1)=cos⁡ ⁣(pos100002i/dmodel)\boxed{PE_{(pos,\, 2i+1)} = \cos\\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)}PE(pos,2i+1)​=cos(100002i/dmodel​pos​)​

where pos∈{0,1,…,n−1}pos \in \\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\\}pos∈{0,1,…,n−1} is the token position and i∈{0,1,…,dmodel/2−1}i \in \\{0,1,\ldots,d_{\text{model}}/2 - 1\\}i∈{0,1,…,dmodel​/2−1} indexes the dimension pair.

**Frequency analysis** : defining ωi=1/100002i/dmodel\omega_i = 1/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}ωi​=1/100002i/dmodel​,

PE(pos, 2i)=sin⁡(ωi⋅pos),PE(pos, 2i+1)=cos⁡(ωi⋅pos)PE_{(pos,\, 2i)} = \sin(\omega_i \cdot pos), \qquad PE_{(pos,\, 2i+1)} = \cos(\omega_i \cdot pos)PE(pos,2i)​=sin(ωi​⋅pos),PE(pos,2i+1)​=cos(ωi​⋅pos)

* Low dimensions (iii small): ωi\omega_iωi​ large (high frequency), wavelength ≈2π\approx 2\pi≈2π — adjacent positions differ substantially → captures **local position**
* High dimensions (iii large): ωi\omega_iωi​ small (low frequency), wavelength ≈2π×10000\approx 2\pi \times 10000≈2π×10000 — only distant positions differ → captures **global position structure**

This multi-scale decomposition is precisely a spatial Fourier basis: the position encoding of each token is a superposition of sinusoids at different frequencies, creating a unique "fingerprint" for every position.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Multi-Scale Representations in Science**
> 
> The sinusoidal PE's design — high frequency at low dimensions, low frequency at high dimensions — mirrors multi-scale representations across many quantitative fields. In **wavelet analysis** (signal processing, geophysics), the continuous wavelet transform decomposes a signal into contributions at different scales simultaneously; shallow wavelets capture local transients while deep wavelets capture global structure — exactly the role played by high-frequency and low-frequency PE components. In **GPS navigation** , timing signals use multiple carrier frequencies: the L1 frequency (≈1.575\approx 1.575≈1.575 GHz) provides high precision over short distances, while code phase differences at L2 (≈1.227\approx 1.227≈1.227 GHz) resolve ambiguity at coarser scale — a physical instantiation of multi-frequency position encoding. In **astronomical imaging** (interferometry), the uvuvuv-plane coverage samples spatial frequencies from short baselines (large-scale structure) to long baselines (fine detail); a full synthesis image requires all frequency scales, analogous to needing all dmodel/2d_{\text{model}}/2dmodel​/2 sinusoidal components to uniquely identify a position. In **neuroscience** , grid cells in the entorhinal cortex encode spatial position using a multi-scale hexagonal grid system — different grid cell modules fire at different spatial frequencies, and the combination uniquely identifies position over ranges far exceeding any single module's period, using essentially the same principle as sinusoidal PE.

#### The Relative Position Linearity Theorem

The deepest mathematical property of sinusoidal PE is:

**Theorem** : For any fixed offset kkk, there exists a linear transformation matrix MkM_kMk​ (depending only on kkk, not on the absolute position pospospos) such that:

PEpos+k=Mk⋅PEpos\boxed{PE_{pos+k} = M_k \cdot PE_{pos}}PEpos+k​=Mk​⋅PEpos​​

This means the model can learn to represent relative position relationships via simple linear transformations.

**Proof** :

**Step 1** : Focus on a single dimension pair (2i,2i+1)(2i, 2i+1)(2i,2i+1) with frequency ωi\omega_iωi​. Let θ=ωi⋅pos\theta = \omega_i \cdot posθ=ωi​⋅pos, δ=ωi⋅k\delta = \omega_i \cdot kδ=ωi​⋅k:

PE(pos, 2i)=sin⁡(θ),PE(pos, 2i+1)=cos⁡(θ)PE_{(pos,\, 2i)} = \sin(\theta), \qquad PE_{(pos,\, 2i+1)} = \cos(\theta)PE(pos,2i)​=sin(θ),PE(pos,2i+1)​=cos(θ)

**Step 2** : Position pos+kpos + kpos+k has angle θ+δ\theta + \deltaθ+δ:

PE(pos+k, 2i)=sin⁡(θ+δ),PE(pos+k, 2i+1)=cos⁡(θ+δ)PE_{(pos+k,\, 2i)} = \sin(\theta + \delta), \qquad PE_{(pos+k,\, 2i+1)} = \cos(\theta + \delta)PE(pos+k,2i)​=sin(θ+δ),PE(pos+k,2i+1)​=cos(θ+δ)

**Step 3** : Apply the trigonometric angle addition formulas:

sin⁡(θ+δ)=sin⁡θcos⁡δ+cos⁡θsin⁡δ\sin(\theta + \delta) = \sin\theta\cos\delta + \cos\theta\sin\deltasin(θ+δ)=sinθcosδ+cosθsinδ cos⁡(θ+δ)=cos⁡θcos⁡δ−sin⁡θsin⁡δ\cos(\theta + \delta) = \cos\theta\cos\delta - \sin\theta\sin\deltacos(θ+δ)=cosθcosδ−sinθsinδ

**Step 4** : Write as a matrix equation:

(sin⁡(θ+δ)cos⁡(θ+δ))=(cos⁡δsin⁡δ−sin⁡δcos⁡δ)⏟Ri(δ)(sin⁡θcos⁡θ)\begin{pmatrix} \sin(\theta+\delta) \\\ \cos(\theta+\delta) \end{pmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \cos\delta & \sin\delta \\\ -\sin\delta & \cos\delta \end{pmatrix}}_{R_i(\delta)} \begin{pmatrix} \sin\theta \\\ \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}(sin(θ+δ)cos(θ+δ)​)=Ri​(δ)(cosδ−sinδ​sinδcosδ​)​​(sinθcosθ​)

**Verification** : row 1: cos⁡δ⋅sin⁡θ+sin⁡δ⋅cos⁡θ=sin⁡(θ+δ)\cos\delta \cdot\sin\theta + \sin\delta\cdot\cos\theta = \sin(\theta+\delta)cosδ⋅sinθ+sinδ⋅cosθ=sin(θ+δ) ✓. Row 2: −sin⁡δ⋅sin⁡θ+cos⁡δ⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡(θ+δ)-\sin\delta\cdot\sin\theta + \cos\delta\cdot\cos\theta = \cos(\theta+\delta)−sinδ⋅sinθ+cosδ⋅cosθ=cos(θ+δ) ✓.

**Step 5** : Ri(δ)=(cos⁡δsin⁡δ−sin⁡δcos⁡δ)R_i(\delta) = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\delta & \sin\delta \\\ -\sin\delta & \cos\delta\end{pmatrix}Ri​(δ)=(cosδ−sinδ​sinδcosδ​) is a **2D rotation matrix** , rotating by angle δ=ωik\delta = \omega_i kδ=ωi​k. Key properties:

* Ri(δ)R_i(\delta)Ri​(δ) depends only on kkk (through δ=ωik\delta = \omega_i kδ=ωi​k), **not on the absolute position pospospos**
* RiR_iRi​ is orthogonal: Ri⊤Ri=IR_i^\top R_i = IRi⊤​Ri​=I, det⁡(Ri)=1\det(R_i) = 1det(Ri​)=1
* Composition law: Ri(δ1)Ri(δ2)=Ri(δ1+δ2)R_i(\delta_1) R_i(\delta_2) = R_i(\delta_1 + \delta_2)Ri​(δ1​)Ri​(δ2​)=Ri​(δ1​+δ2​) (rotation group structure)

**Step 6** : Across all dmodel/2d_{\text{model}}/2dmodel​/2 dimension pairs, the full transformation is a block-diagonal matrix:

Mk=(R0(ω0k)R1(ω1k)⋱Rdmodel/2−1(ωdmodel/2−1k))∈Rdmodel×dmodelM_k = \begin{pmatrix} R_0(\omega_0 k) & & \\\ & R_1(\omega_1 k) & \\\ & & \ddots \\\ & & & R_{d_{\text{model}}/2-1}(\omega_{d_{\text{model}}/2-1} k) \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}}Mk​=​R0​(ω0​k)​R1​(ω1​k)​⋱​Rdmodel​/2−1​(ωdmodel​/2−1​k)​​∈Rdmodel​×dmodel​

Then PEpos+k=Mk⋅PEposPE_{pos+k} = M_k \cdot PE_{pos}PEpos+k​=Mk​⋅PEpos​ for all pospospos and kkk. □\square□

#### Numerical Verification

Let dmodel=4d_{\text{model}} = 4dmodel​=4, pos=10pos = 10pos=10, k=5k = 5k=5. Frequencies: ω0=1\omega_0 = 1ω0​=1, ω1=0.01\omega_1 = 0.01ω1​=0.01.

PE10=(sin⁡(10),cos⁡(10),sin⁡(0.1),cos⁡(0.1))≈(−0.544,−0.839,0.0998,0.995)PE_{10} = (\sin(10), \cos(10), \sin(0.1), \cos(0.1)) \approx (-0.544, -0.839, 0.0998, 0.995)PE10​=(sin(10),cos(10),sin(0.1),cos(0.1))≈(−0.544,−0.839,0.0998,0.995)

Rotation for k=5k = 5k=5: δ0=5\delta_0 = 5δ0​=5, δ1=0.05\delta_1 = 0.05δ1​=0.05.

R0(5)≈(0.284−0.9590.9590.284)R_0(5) \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.284 & -0.959 \\\ 0.959 & 0.284 \end{pmatrix}R0​(5)≈(0.2840.959​−0.9590.284​) R0(5)(−0.544−0.839)=(0.284(−0.544)+(−0.959)(−0.839)0.959(−0.544)+0.284(−0.839))≈(0.650−0.760)R_0(5) \begin{pmatrix}-0.544\\\\-0.839\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.284(-0.544) + (-0.959)(-0.839) \\\ 0.959(-0.544) + 0.284(-0.839) \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.650 \\\ -0.760 \end{pmatrix}R0​(5)(−0.544−0.839​)=(0.284(−0.544)+(−0.959)(−0.839)0.959(−0.544)+0.284(−0.839)​)≈(0.650−0.760​)

Direct computation: PE(15,0)=sin⁡(15)≈0.650PE_{(15, 0)} = \sin(15) \approx 0.650PE(15,0)​=sin(15)≈0.650, PE(15,1)=cos⁡(15)≈−0.759PE_{(15, 1)} = \cos(15) \approx -0.759PE(15,1)​=cos(15)≈−0.759. ✓

#### Why This Property Matters

In self-attention, position ttt's query interacts with position jjj's key:

scoretj∝(xt+PEt)⊤WQWK⊤(xj+PEj)\text{score}_{tj} \propto (x_t + PE_t)^\top W^Q {W^K}^\top (x_j + PE_j)scoretj​∝(xt​+PEt​)⊤WQWK⊤(xj​+PEj​)

The cross term PEt⊤WQWK⊤PEj=PEt⊤WQWK⊤Mj−tPEtPE_t^\top W^Q{W^K}^\top PE_j = PE_t^\top W^Q{W^K}^\top M_{j-t} PE_tPEt⊤​WQWK⊤PEj​=PEt⊤​WQWK⊤Mj−t​PEt​ depends only on the **relative position** j−tj - tj−t (because Mj−tM_{j-t}Mj−t​ is determined solely by the offset). This means that through attention, the model can implicitly represent relative positional relationships without explicit relative position biases — the sinusoidal structure bakes the representation in algebraically.

The composition law Mk1Mk2=Mk1+k2M_{k_1} M_{k_2} = M_{k_1+k_2}Mk1​​Mk2​​=Mk1​+k2​​ further implies: if the model learns "offset 1" and "offset 2" transformations, it automatically has access to "offset 3."

#### Learned Positional Embeddings

An alternative: treat position encoding as learnable parameters, one vector per position:

PE=Embedding(position_ids)∈Rnmax⁡×dmodelPE = \text{Embedding}(\text{position\\_ids}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\max} \times d_{\text{model}}}PE=Embedding(position_ids)∈Rnmax​×dmodel​

**Advantages** : simple to implement; no structural assumptions; used by BERT and GPT-1.

**Disadvantages** : cannot generalize to sequence lengths beyond nmax⁡n_{\max}nmax​ seen during training; requires nmax⁡×dmodeln_{\max} \times d_{\text{model}}nmax​×dmodel​ extra parameters.

Vaswani et al. found sinusoidal and learned PEs perform similarly — but sinusoidal PE can handle sequences longer than those seen during training (extrapolation).

#### Modern Variant: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)

The most widely adopted positional encoding in modern LLMs is **Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)** (Su et al., 2021). Rather than adding PE to token embeddings, RoPE encodes position via **rotation of Query and Key vectors** themselves. For position mmm in dimension pair (2i,2i+1)(2i, 2i+1)(2i,2i+1):

(q2i(m)q2i+1(m))=(cos⁡mθi−sin⁡mθisin⁡mθicos⁡mθi)(q2iq2i+1)\begin{pmatrix} q_{2i}^{(m)} \\\ q_{2i+1}^{(m)} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos m\theta_i & -\sin m\theta_i \\\ \sin m\theta_i & \cos m\theta_i \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} q_{2i} \\\ q_{2i+1} \end{pmatrix}(q2i(m)​q2i+1(m)​​)=(cosmθi​sinmθi​​−sinmθi​cosmθi​​)(q2i​q2i+1​​)

The dot product of rotated query at position mmm and rotated key at position nnn depends only on the relative position m−nm - nm−n:

qm⊤kn=f(q,k,m−n)q_m^\top k_n = f(q, k, m - n)qm⊤​kn​=f(q,k,m−n)

RoPE is adopted by LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, and most modern open-weight LLMs because it naturally encodes relative positions and offers better length generalization than absolute PE.

### 22.6 Layer Normalization vs. Batch Normalization

#### Why Transformer Uses LayerNorm

Batch Normalization (introduced in Chapter 4) is the standard for vision models. The Transformer uses Layer Normalization instead. This is not arbitrary.

#### Batch Normalization Recap

BatchNorm normalizes over the **batch dimension** for each feature:

x^i,j=xi,j−μj(B)(σj(B))2+ϵ,μj(B)=1∣B∣∑i∈Bxi,j\hat{x}_{i,j} = \frac{x_{i,j} - \mu_j^{(B)}}{\sqrt{(\sigma_j^{(B)})^2 + \epsilon}}, \qquad \mu_j^{(B)} = \frac{1}{|B|} \sum_{i \in B} x_{i,j}x^i,j​=(σj(B)​)2+ϵ​xi,j​−μj(B)​​,μj(B)​=∣B∣1​i∈B∑​xi,j​

**Problem 1 — Batch size sensitivity** : with small batch sizes, μj(B)\mu_j^{(B)}μj(B)​ and σj(B)\sigma_j^{(B)}σj(B)​ are unstable estimates. In NLP, GPU memory limits batch size, making this instability significant.

**Problem 2 — Variable-length sequences** : in a single batch, sequences have different lengths. Computing statistics at position 100 uses only sequences of length ≥100\geq 100≥100 — batch statistics change across positions, creating inconsistent behavior.

**Problem 3 — Train/inference mismatch** : training uses mini-batch statistics; inference uses running averages. These can diverge.

#### Layer Normalization

LayerNorm normalizes over the **feature dimension** for each individual token:

μi=1d∑j=1dxi,j,σi2=1d∑j=1d(xi,j−μi)2\mu_i = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{j=1}^{d} x_{i,j}, \quad \sigma_i^2 = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{j=1}^{d}(x_{i,j} - \mu_i)^2μi​=d1​j=1∑d​xi,j​,σi2​=d1​j=1∑d​(xi,j​−μi​)2 LayerNorm(xi)=γ⊙xi−μiσi2+ϵ+β\text{LayerNorm}(x_i) = \gamma \odot \frac{x_i - \mu_i}{\sqrt{\sigma_i^2 + \epsilon}} + \betaLayerNorm(xi​)=γ⊙σi2​+ϵ​xi​−μi​​+β

where γ,β∈Rd\gamma, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^dγ,β∈Rd are learnable gain and bias parameters.

**Key properties** :

* Completely independent of other samples in the batch (each token normalizes itself)
* Completely independent of sequence length (each position normalized independently)
* Identical behavior at training and inference (no running average)

#### Schematic Comparison

For X∈RB×n×dX \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times n \times d}X∈RB×n×d (batch ×\times× sequence ×\times× features):

* **BatchNorm** : normalizes along BBB and nnn for each feature dimension ddd
* **LayerNorm** : normalizes along ddd for each (sample, position) pair (b,t)(b, t)(b,t)

    
    
    BatchNorm:  ←──── across batch and sequence positions ────→ (per feature)
    LayerNorm:  ←──── across feature dimensions ────→           (per sample, per position)
    

#### Pre-Norm vs. Post-Norm

The original Transformer uses **Post-Norm** :

Post-Norm:LayerNorm(x+SubLayer(x))\text{Post-Norm:} \quad \text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{SubLayer}(x))Post-Norm:LayerNorm(x+SubLayer(x))

Subsequent research established that **Pre-Norm** trains more stably:

Pre-Norm:x+SubLayer(LayerNorm(x))\text{Pre-Norm:} \quad x + \text{SubLayer}(\text{LayerNorm}(x))Pre-Norm:x+SubLayer(LayerNorm(x))

Pre-Norm normalizes inputs before they enter each sublayer, preventing numerical values from accumulating along the residual pathway across layers. Modern LLMs (GPT series, LLaMA series) use Pre-Norm universally.

**RMSNorm** : LLaMA and related models further simplify to Root Mean Square Normalization, which removes mean centering:

RMSNorm(x)=γ⊙xRMS(x),RMS(x)=1d∑jxj2\text{RMSNorm}(x) = \gamma \odot \frac{x}{\text{RMS}(x)}, \qquad \text{RMS}(x) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_j x_j^2}RMSNorm(x)=γ⊙RMS(x)x​,RMS(x)=d1​j∑​xj2​​

RMSNorm is computationally cheaper (one fewer subtraction) with comparable empirical performance.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Normalization as Variance Control in Science and Engineering**
> 
> The Layer vs. Batch normalization distinction is a special case of a general design question: **along which dimensions should variance be controlled?** This question appears across engineering and science under different names. In **adaptive optics** (astronomy), wavefront correction systems normalize wavefront distortions measured across the telescope aperture (spatial dimension) rather than across independent sky observations (analogous to batch dimension), because atmospheric turbulence is consistent per observation but variable across the aperture — the "LayerNorm" choice. In **signal processing for EEG** , z-scoring is applied per electrode across time (LayerNorm analog) rather than per time point across electrodes (BatchNorm analog), because neural oscillation statistics are stable within an electrode but highly variable across electrodes. In **mass spectrometry proteomics** , per-sample quantile normalization (bringing each sample's distribution to a reference) is analogous to LayerNorm, while across-sample normalization is analogous to BatchNorm; the choice depends on whether systematic variation is primarily within-sample or between-sample. The theoretical justification is the same in all cases: **normalize along the dimension whose statistics are most reliably estimated and most likely to be consistent across the application context**.

**2.** Prove the relative-position linearity property PEpos+k=Mk⋅PEposPE_{pos+k} = M_k \cdot PE_{pos}PEpos+k​=Mk​⋅PEpos​ for the sinusoidal encoding, with MkM_kMk​ being a block-diagonal matrix of 2×22 \times 22×2 rotation matrices. State precisely what properties of MkM_kMk​ allow the composition law Mk1Mk2=Mk1+k2M_{k_1} M_{k_2} = M_{k_1+k_2}Mk1​​Mk2​​=Mk1​+k2​​.

Answer

The proof is given in Section 22.5. The composition law follows from the rotation group structure: for dimension pair iii, Ri(δ1)Ri(δ2)=Ri(δ1+δ2)R_i(\delta_1) R_i(\delta_2) = R_i(\delta_1 + \delta_2)Ri​(δ1​)Ri​(δ2​)=Ri​(δ1​+δ2​) by the angle addition formula for 2D rotations. Since MkM_kMk​ is block-diagonal with blocks Ri(ωik)R_i(\omega_i k)Ri​(ωi​k):

Mk1Mk2=diag(R0(ω0k1),…)⋅diag(R0(ω0k2),…)=diag(R0(ω0(k1+k2)),…)=Mk1+k2M_{k_1} M_{k_2} = \text{diag}(R_0(\omega_0 k_1), \ldots) \cdot \text{diag}(R_0(\omega_0 k_2), \ldots) = \text{diag}(R_0(\omega_0(k_1+k_2)), \ldots) = M_{k_1+k_2}Mk1​​Mk2​​=diag(R0​(ω0​k1​),…)⋅diag(R0​(ω0​k2​),…)=diag(R0​(ω0​(k1​+k2​)),…)=Mk1​+k2​​

The composition law holds because:

  1. SO(2)SO(2)SO(2) (the group of 2D rotations) is closed under composition
  2. Block-diagonal structure preserves this closure
  3. The rotation angle ωik\omega_i kωi​k is linear in kkk, so offsets add: ωik1+ωik2=ωi(k1+k2)\omega_i k_1 + \omega_i k_2 = \omega_i(k_1+k_2)ωi​k1​+ωi​k2​=ωi​(k1​+k2​)

This means: if a model learns transformations for offsets k1k_1k1​ and k2k_2k2​, it automatically can represent offset k1+k2k_1 + k_2k1​+k2​ by composing the learned transformations — a form of systematic generalization.

**5.** Compare the information-retrieval semantics of Multi-Head Attention to single-head attention in terms of: (a) the function class expressible; (b) representational diversity; (c) the practical implication of emergent head specialization.

Answer

**(a) Function class** : Both compute softmax(QK⊤/dk)V\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})Vsoftmax(QK⊤/dk​​)V with learned projections. Single-head attention in a dmodeld_{\text{model}}dmodel​-dimensional space searches for patterns in one dmodeld_{\text{model}}dmodel​-dimensional subspace. Multi-head attention searches in hhh independent dkd_kdk​-dimensional subspaces simultaneously. Since h⋅dk=dmodelh \cdot d_k = d_{\text{model}}h⋅dk​=dmodel​ (with dk=dmodel/hd_k = d_{\text{model}}/hdk​=dmodel​/h), the total representational capacity is preserved, but distributed across subspaces. Any function computable by multi-head attention is also computable by single-head attention with the same total parameters — the advantage is not expressiveness in the worst case, but **inductive bias** toward decomposing structure into multiple independent patterns.

**(b) Representational diversity** : Single-head attention produces one attention distribution per token, reflecting one learned "viewpoint." Multi-head attention produces hhh distributions per token. Different heads can simultaneously learn short-range syntactic patterns (often high-frequency, local attention) and long-range semantic patterns (often more distributed attention) — something that a single head must trade off. The diversity is enforced by parameter independence: each head's WiQ,WiK,WiVW_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^VWiQ​,WiK​,WiV​ are updated independently by gradient descent, allowing them to converge to different minima.

**(c) Emergent specialization** : Clark et al. (2019) and Michel et al. (2019) ("Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?") found that most heads in trained BERT are redundant — at inference time, 80%+ of heads can be removed with minimal performance loss, and only a few "key heads" are essential for specific tasks. This suggests multi-head attention acts as an **implicit ensemble** with self-organized specialization: gradient descent routes different linguistic computations to different heads, but the architecture doesn't enforce or guarantee equal contribution. The practical implication is that head pruning can yield significant inference speedups without retraining, and that the hhh hyperparameter trades compute for robustness more than pure representational capacity.

M1⋅[0,1]⊤=[0.841,0.540]⊤=[PE1,0,PE1,1]M_1 \cdot [0, 1]^\top = [0.841, 0.540]^\top = [PE_{1,0}, PE_{1,1}]M1​⋅[0,1]⊤=[0.841,0.540]⊤=[PE1,0​,PE1,1​]. ✓ Confirmed.

**7.** Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) applies the rotation directly to the query and key vectors rather than adding PE to the input.

(a) In standard sinusoidal PE, the position signal is added: xpos′=xpos+PEposx'_{\text{pos}} = x_{\text{pos}} + PE_{\text{pos}}xpos′​=xpos​+PEpos​. What happens to the position signal after the linear projection q=WQx′q = W^Q x'q=WQx′? Is the position information preserved, attenuated, or potentially destroyed? (b) In RoPE, the query and key are rotated: qpos′=Rposqposq'_{\text{pos}} = R_{\text{pos}} q_{\text{pos}}qpos′​=Rpos​qpos​, kpos′=Rposkposk'_{\text{pos}} = R_{\text{pos}} k_{\text{pos}}kpos′​=Rpos​kpos​, where RRR is a block-diagonal rotation matrix. Show that the dot product qi′⊤kj′=qi⊤Ri−jkjq'_i{}^\top k'_j = q_i^\top R_{i-j} k_jqi′​⊤kj′​=qi⊤​Ri−j​kj​ depends only on the relative position i−ji - ji−j. (c) Why is relative position dependence desirable for language modeling? Give an example where absolute position would be misleading.

Answer

**(a)** After projection: q=WQ(x+PE)=WQx+WQPEq = W^Q(x + PE) = W^Q x + W^Q PEq=WQ(x+PE)=WQx+WQPE. The position signal WQPEW^Q PEWQPE is linearly mixed with the content signal WQxW^Q xWQx. The projection can attenuate or rotate the position signal depending on WQW^QWQ. In the worst case, if WQW^QWQ has a null space that includes the PE direction, position information is destroyed. In practice, the model learns WQW^QWQ to preserve useful position information, but the mixing is not guaranteed to be clean.

**(b)** qi′⊤kj′=(Riqi)⊤(Rjkj)=qi⊤Ri⊤Rjkj=qi⊤Rj−i⊤kjq'_i{}^\top k'_j = (R_i q_i)^\top (R_j k_j) = q_i^\top R_i^\top R_j k_j = q_i^\top R_{j-i}^\top k_jqi′​⊤kj′​=(Ri​qi​)⊤(Rj​kj​)=qi⊤​Ri⊤​Rj​kj​=qi⊤​Rj−i⊤​kj​. Since rotation matrices satisfy Ra⊤Rb=Rb−aR_a^\top R_b = R_{b-a}Ra⊤​Rb​=Rb−a​, we get qi⊤Ri−jkjq_i^\top R_{i-j} k_jqi⊤​Ri−j​kj​, which depends only on the content vectors qi,kjq_i, k_jqi​,kj​ and the relative offset i−ji - ji−j, not on absolute positions iii or jjj individually. This is a form of **relative positional encoding** built into the attention score.

**(c)** Relative position matters because linguistic relationships are position-invariant: "the cat sat" has the same syntactic structure whether it starts at position 1 or position 501. Absolute position would be misleading for: a model trained on sequences of length ≤512 encountering a length-1024 sequence at inference — positions 513–1024 have never-seen absolute encodings, but relative relationships (adjacent words, clause boundaries) are the same as in training. RoPE's relative encoding generalizes better to unseen lengths.

#### Think Deeper

**8.** A Transformer layer contains multi-head attention (MHA) and a feed-forward network (FFN). For the base model (dmodel=512d_{\text{model}} = 512dmodel​=512, h=8h = 8h=8, dk=64d_k = 64dk​=64, dff=2048d_{ff} = 2048dff​=2048):

(a) Compute the parameter count for one MHA sublayer (all heads' WQ,WK,WVW^Q, W^K, W^VWQ,WK,WV plus WOW^OWO). (b) Compute the parameter count for one FFN sublayer (W1,b1,W2,b2W_1, b_1, W_2, b_2W1​,b1​,W2​,b2​). (c) What fraction of the layer's parameters are in the FFN? Does this surprise you, given that attention is the "signature" component of the Transformer? (d) Compute the FLOPs for MHA vs FFN on a sequence of length n=100n = 100n=100. Which sublayer is more expensive computationally?

Answer

**(a)** MHA: Per-head Q/K/V projections: h×3×(dmodel×dk)=8×3×(512×64)=786,432h \times 3 \times (d_{\text{model}} \times d_k) = 8 \times 3 \times (512 \times 64) = 786{,}432h×3×(dmodel​×dk​)=8×3×(512×64)=786,432. Output projection WOW^OWO: (h⋅dv)×dmodel=512×512=262,144(h \cdot d_v) \times d_{\text{model}} = 512 \times 512 = 262{,}144(h⋅dv​)×dmodel​=512×512=262,144. Total MHA: 786,432+262,144=1,048,576≈1.05M786{,}432 + 262{,}144 = 1{,}048{,}576 \approx 1.05M786,432+262,144=1,048,576≈1.05M.

**(b)** FFN: W1∈Rdff×dmodel=2048×512=1,048,576W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{ff} \times d_{\text{model}}} = 2048 \times 512 = 1{,}048{,}576W1​∈Rdff​×dmodel​=2048×512=1,048,576. b1∈Rdff=2048b_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{ff}} = 2048b1​∈Rdff​=2048. W2∈Rdmodel×dff=512×2048=1,048,576W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{ff}} = 512 \times 2048 = 1{,}048{,}576W2​∈Rdmodel​×dff​=512×2048=1,048,576. b2∈Rdmodel=512b_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}} = 512b2​∈Rdmodel​=512. Total FFN: 1,048,576+2048+1,048,576+512=2,099,712≈2.10M1{,}048{,}576 + 2048 + 1{,}048{,}576 + 512 = 2{,}099{,}712 \approx 2.10M1,048,576+2048+1,048,576+512=2,099,712≈2.10M.

**(c)** FFN fraction: 2.10/(1.05+2.10)=2.10/3.15≈66.7%2.10 / (1.05 + 2.10) = 2.10 / 3.15 \approx 66.7\%2.10/(1.05+2.10)=2.10/3.15≈66.7%. Two-thirds of the parameters are in the FFN, not in attention. This is surprising but makes sense: attention aggregates information across positions (a routing function), while the FFN processes the aggregated information at each position (a transformation function). The FFN's role as a "key-value memory" (storing factual knowledge in its weight matrices) requires substantial parameter capacity.

**(d)** MHA FLOPs (dominant terms): QK⊤QK^\topQK⊤ computation: n×n×dk×h=100×100×64×8=5.12Mn \times n \times d_k \times h = 100 \times 100 \times 64 \times 8 = 5.12Mn×n×dk​×h=100×100×64×8=5.12M. AVAVAV computation: same =5.12M= 5.12M=5.12M. Projections: 4×n×dmodel×dmodel=4×100×5122=104.9M4 \times n \times d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}} = 4 \times 100 \times 512^2 = 104.9M4×n×dmodel​×dmodel​=4×100×5122=104.9M. Total MHA ≈115M\approx 115M≈115M FLOPs. FFN FLOPs: 2×n×dmodel×dff=2×100×512×2048=209.7M2 \times n \times d_{\text{model}} \times d_{ff} = 2 \times 100 \times 512 \times 2048 = 209.7M2×n×dmodel​×dff​=2×100×512×2048=209.7M FLOPs. FFN is roughly 2×2\times2× more expensive than MHA for n=100n = 100n=100. The attention matrix (n2dkh=5.12Mn^2 d_k h = 5.12Mn2dk​h=5.12M) is a small fraction of total compute at this sequence length.

### Chapter Summary

Concept | Key Point  
---|---  
Multi-head motivation | Single head cannot capture multiple relationship types simultaneously  
Core formula | MultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(head1,…,headh)WO\text{MultiHead}(Q,K,V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\ldots,\text{head}_h)W^OMultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(head1​,…,headh​)WO  
Parameter efficiency | dk=dmodel/hd_k = d_{\text{model}}/hdk​=dmodel​/h keeps computation constant: h×O(n2dk)=O(n2dmodel)h \times O(n^2 d_k) = O(n^2 d_{\text{model}})h×O(n2dk​)=O(n2dmodel​)  
Emergent specialization | Heads spontaneously learn coreference, syntax, local attention — no explicit supervision  
Sinusoidal PE | PE(pos,2i)=sin⁡(pos/100002i/d)PE_{(pos,2i)} = \sin(pos/10000^{2i/d})PE(pos,2i)​=sin(pos/100002i/d); multi-scale frequency basis  
Relative position theorem | PEpos+k=MkPEposPE_{pos+k} = M_k PE_{pos}PEpos+k​=Mk​PEpos​ with block-diagonal rotation matrix; model can learn relative offsets via linear transformations  
RoPE | Modern alternative: rotates Q and K by position-dependent angles; qm⊤knq_m^\top k_nqm⊤​kn​ depends only on m−nm - nm−n  
LayerNorm vs. BatchNorm | LayerNorm normalizes per sample per position across feature dimension — handles variable-length sequences without batch-size sensitivity

### 23.1 Global Architecture Overview

The original Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) uses an **Encoder-Decoder** structure designed for sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) tasks such as machine translation.

**Base model core parameters** :

Parameter | Symbol | Value  
---|---|---  
Model dimension | dmodeld_{\text{model}}dmodel​ | 512  
Attention heads | hhh | 8  
Per-head dimension | dk=dvd_k = d_vdk​=dv​ | 64  
FFN hidden dimension | dffd_{ff}dff​ | 2048  
Encoder layers | NencN_{\text{enc}}Nenc​ | 6  
Decoder layers | NdecN_{\text{dec}}Ndec​ | 6  
Vocabulary size | ∥V∥\|V\|∥V∥ | ~37,000  
Dropout rate | ppp | 0.1  
  
What follows traces a complete forward pass through every component in sequence.

* * *

### 23.2 Encoder

#### Input Processing

**Step 1 — Token Embedding**

The input sequence (e.g., "I love mathematics") is tokenized to a sequence of token IDs [t1,…,tn][t_1, \ldots, t_n][t1​,…,tn​]. An embedding matrix Wemb∈R∣V∣×dmodelW_{\text{emb}} \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d_{\text{model}}}Wemb​∈R∣V∣×dmodel​ maps each token to a dense vector:

E=Embedding([t1,…,tn])∈Rn×dmodelE = \text{Embedding}([t_1, \ldots, t_n]) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}E=Embedding([t1​,…,tn​])∈Rn×dmodel​

The paper scales embeddings by dmodel\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}dmodel​​:

Escaled=E⋅dmodelE_{\text{scaled}} = E \cdot \sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}Escaled​=E⋅dmodel​​

Why? Embedding matrices are typically initialized so that each component has variance ∼1/dmodel\sim 1/d_{\text{model}}∼1/dmodel​, giving each embedding vector a small L2 norm. Multiplying by dmodel\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}dmodel​​ brings the embedding magnitude into the same range as the positional encoding values (which lie in [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1]), preventing one from drowning out the other when added.

**Step 2 — Add Positional Encoding**

X(0)=Escaled+PE∈Rn×dmodelX^{(0)} = E_{\text{scaled}} + PE \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}X(0)=Escaled​+PE∈Rn×dmodel​

**Step 3 — Dropout**

X(0)=Dropout(X(0),p=0.1)X^{(0)} = \text{Dropout}(X^{(0)}, p = 0.1)X(0)=Dropout(X(0),p=0.1)

At this point X(0)∈Rn×512X^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 512}X(0)∈Rn×512 is the encoder's layer-0 representation.

#### Single Encoder Layer

Each encoder layer contains two sublayers. Precise formulas for layer ℓ\ellℓ (ℓ=1,…,Nenc\ell = 1, \ldots, N_{\text{enc}}ℓ=1,…,Nenc​):

**Sublayer 1 — Multi-Head Self-Attention + Add & Norm**

MHAout=MultiHead(X(ℓ−1),X(ℓ−1),X(ℓ−1))\text{MHA}_{\text{out}} = \text{MultiHead}(X^{(\ell-1)}, X^{(\ell-1)}, X^{(\ell-1)})MHAout​=MultiHead(X(ℓ−1),X(ℓ−1),X(ℓ−1)) Z(ℓ)=LayerNorm ⁣(X(ℓ−1)+Dropout(MHAout))Z^{(\ell)} = \text{LayerNorm}\\!\left(X^{(\ell-1)} + \text{Dropout}(\text{MHA}_{\text{out}})\right)Z(ℓ)=LayerNorm(X(ℓ−1)+Dropout(MHAout​))

All three arguments are X(ℓ−1)X^{(\ell-1)}X(ℓ−1) — this is "self"-attention.

Dimension tracking: X(ℓ−1)∈Rn×512→MHAout∈Rn×512→Z(ℓ)∈Rn×512X^{(\ell-1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 512} \to \text{MHA}_{\text{out}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 512} \to Z^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 512}X(ℓ−1)∈Rn×512→MHAout​∈Rn×512→Z(ℓ)∈Rn×512.

**Sublayer 2 — Feed-Forward Network + Add & Norm**

FFNout=FFN(Z(ℓ))\text{FFN}_{\text{out}} = \text{FFN}(Z^{(\ell)})FFNout​=FFN(Z(ℓ)) X(ℓ)=LayerNorm ⁣(Z(ℓ)+Dropout(FFNout))X^{(\ell)} = \text{LayerNorm}\\!\left(Z^{(\ell)} + \text{Dropout}(\text{FFN}_{\text{out}})\right)X(ℓ)=LayerNorm(Z(ℓ)+Dropout(FFNout​))

Dimension tracking: Z(ℓ)∈Rn×512→FFNout∈Rn×512→X(ℓ)∈Rn×512Z^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 512} \to \text{FFN}_{\text{out}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 512} \to X^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 512}Z(ℓ)∈Rn×512→FFNout​∈Rn×512→X(ℓ)∈Rn×512.

**Key observation** : every layer's input and output have identical dimensions (n×dmodeln \times d_{\text{model}}n×dmodel​). The residual connection requires this — addition demands matching shapes. This design makes the layer count NNN a free hyperparameter: stacking more layers requires no architectural changes.

#### Encoder Architecture (with Dimensions)
    
    
    Input tokens: [t_1, t_2, ..., t_n]
          │
          ▼
    Token Embedding × √d_model           [n × 512]
          │
          + Positional Encoding           [n × 512]
          │
          ▼ Dropout(0.1)
          │
          ▼ ═══════════════ Encoder Layer 1 ════════════════
          │
          ├──→ MultiHead Self-Attention ──→ Dropout ──┐
          │    Q,K,V = X; h=8, d_k=64                 │ (+) residual
          │    internal: [n×512]→[n×64]×8→[n×512]      │
          └───────────────────────────────────────────┘
          │
          ▼ LayerNorm                     [n × 512]
          │
          ├──→ FFN: W₁[512→2048]→ReLU→W₂[2048→512] → Dropout ──┐
          │                                                        │ (+) residual
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          │
          ▼ LayerNorm                     [n × 512]
          │
          ▼ ═══════════════ Encoder Layers 2–6 ════════════════
          │
          ▼
    Encoder output H_enc                  [n × 512]
    

After 6 encoder layers, Henc∈Rn×512H_{\text{enc}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 512}Henc​∈Rn×512. Each position's vector has been enriched by six rounds of self-attention — every position now contains globally integrated context from the entire input sequence.

### 23.3 Decoder

The decoder is more complex: each layer has **three** sublayers instead of two. The additional sublayer is **Cross-Attention** — the bridge between encoder and decoder.

#### Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention

**Why masking?** During training, teacher forcing provides the complete target sequence [⟨BOS⟩,y1,y2,…,ym−1][\langle\text{BOS}\rangle, y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_{m-1}][⟨BOS⟩,y1​,y2​,…,ym−1​] as decoder input to predict the right-shifted sequence [y1,y2,…,ym,⟨EOS⟩][y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_m, \langle\text{EOS}\rangle][y1​,y2​,…,ym​,⟨EOS⟩]. The constraint: **when generating token ttt, the model must not see positions t+1,t+2,…t+1, t+2, \ldotst+1,t+2,…** — these tokens are not yet generated at inference time. Allowing the model to see them during training would constitute information leakage.

**Mask matrix design** : an upper-triangular mask sets future positions to −∞-\infty−∞ in the attention score matrix:

Maskij={0if i≥j(current and past: allowed)−∞if i<j(future: blocked)\text{Mask}_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i \geq j \quad \text{(current and past: allowed)} \\\ -\infty & \text{if } i < j \quad \text{(future: blocked)} \end{cases}Maskij​={0−∞​if i≥j(current and past: allowed)if i<j(future: blocked)​

Applied to the attention computation:

MaskedAttention(Q,K,V)=softmax ⁣(QK⊤dk+Mask)V\text{MaskedAttention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + \text{Mask}\right) VMaskedAttention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤​+Mask)V

Since e−∞=0e^{-\infty} = 0e−∞=0, masked positions receive exactly zero weight after softmax.

For a length-4 sequence, the masked score matrix and resulting attention weights:

QK⊤dk+Mask=(s11−∞−∞−∞s21s22−∞−∞s31s32s33−∞s41s42s43s44)⇒A=(1000α21α2200α31α32α330α41α42α43α44)\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + \text{Mask} = \begin{pmatrix} s_{11} & -\infty & -\infty & -\infty \\\ s_{21} & s_{22} & -\infty & -\infty \\\ s_{31} & s_{32} & s_{33} & -\infty \\\ s_{41} & s_{42} & s_{43} & s_{44} \end{pmatrix} \quad \Rightarrow \quad A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\\ \alpha_{21} & \alpha_{22} & 0 & 0 \\\ \alpha_{31} & \alpha_{32} & \alpha_{33} & 0 \\\ \alpha_{41} & \alpha_{42} & \alpha_{43} & \alpha_{44} \end{pmatrix}dk​​QK⊤​+Mask=​s11​s21​s31​s41​​−∞s22​s32​s42​​−∞−∞s33​s43​​−∞−∞−∞s44​​​⇒A=​1α21​α31​α41​​0α22​α32​α42​​00α33​α43​​000α44​​​

Position 1 attends only to itself; position 2 attends to positions 1–2; position ttt attends to positions 111 through ttt. This lower-triangular structure is the mathematical realization of **autoregressive generation** — each position depends only on its predecessors.

#### Cross-Attention: The Encoder-Decoder Bridge

Cross-attention is where the encoder's representation enters the decoder.

**Key distinction from self-attention** :

* Self-attention: Q,K,VQ, K, VQ,K,V all come from the same sequence
* Cross-attention: QQQ comes from the **decoder** , KKK and VVV come from the **encoder**

CrossAttn(Y,Henc)=MultiHead(Q=YWQ, K=HencWK, V=HencWV)\text{CrossAttn}(Y, H_{\text{enc}}) = \text{MultiHead}(Q = YW^Q,\; K = H_{\text{enc}}W^K,\; V = H_{\text{enc}}W^V)CrossAttn(Y,Henc​)=MultiHead(Q=YWQ,K=Henc​WK,V=Henc​WV)

where YYY is the decoder's current representation and HencH_{\text{enc}}Henc​ is the final encoder output.

**Dimension tracking** (single head, dk=64d_k = 64dk​=64):

* Q=YWQ∈Rm×64Q = YW^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times 64}Q=YWQ∈Rm×64 (mmm = target sequence length)
* K=HencWK∈Rn×64K = H_{\text{enc}}W^K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 64}K=Henc​WK∈Rn×64 (nnn = source sequence length)
* Attention matrix: A=softmax(QK⊤/dk)∈Rm×nA = \text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}A=softmax(QK⊤/dk​​)∈Rm×n

The attention matrix is m×nm \times nm×n — not square. Row ttt is a probability distribution over all nnn source positions, describing how decoder position ttt weights each source position. This is precisely Bahdanau attention (Chapter 20) implemented through the unified Multi-Head Attention primitive.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Information Integration from Multiple Sources**
> 
> Cross-attention implements a fundamental operation in information theory and systems biology: **querying one information source using queries derived from another**. In **molecular biology** , transcription factor binding is a physical analog — a protein (the query, from one sequence space) searches for specific DNA motifs (the keys/values, from another sequence space), binding where complementarity is highest. In **radar and sonar systems** , matched filtering correlates a transmitted signal (query) with received echoes (keys/values from the environment), extracting target information with maximal signal-to-noise ratio; this is mathematically identical to dot-product attention. In **control systems** , the Kalman filter's update step integrates prediction (prior from the dynamic model — analogous to the decoder state) with measurements (from the sensor — analogous to encoder representations) by weighting each source by its estimated reliability (αij\alpha_{ij}αij​ plays the role of the Kalman gain KtK_tKt​). Cross-attention generalizes this principle: the decoder "asks questions" of the encoder "memory," and the strength of each answer is determined by learned compatibility.

#### Complete Single Decoder Layer

Layer ℓ\ellℓ computation (input Y(ℓ−1)Y^{(\ell-1)}Y(ℓ−1), encoder output HencH_{\text{enc}}Henc​):

**Sublayer 1 — Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention + Add & Norm**

MMHAout=MaskedMultiHead(Y(ℓ−1),Y(ℓ−1),Y(ℓ−1))\text{MMHA}_{\text{out}} = \text{MaskedMultiHead}(Y^{(\ell-1)}, Y^{(\ell-1)}, Y^{(\ell-1)})MMHAout​=MaskedMultiHead(Y(ℓ−1),Y(ℓ−1),Y(ℓ−1)) Z1(ℓ)=LayerNorm ⁣(Y(ℓ−1)+Dropout(MMHAout))Z_1^{(\ell)} = \text{LayerNorm}\\!\left(Y^{(\ell-1)} + \text{Dropout}(\text{MMHA}_{\text{out}})\right)Z1(ℓ)​=LayerNorm(Y(ℓ−1)+Dropout(MMHAout​))

**Sublayer 2 — Multi-Head Cross-Attention + Add & Norm**

CAout=MultiHead(Z1(ℓ),Henc,Henc)\text{CA}_{\text{out}} = \text{MultiHead}(Z_1^{(\ell)}, H_{\text{enc}}, H_{\text{enc}})CAout​=MultiHead(Z1(ℓ)​,Henc​,Henc​) Z2(ℓ)=LayerNorm ⁣(Z1(ℓ)+Dropout(CAout))Z_2^{(\ell)} = \text{LayerNorm}\\!\left(Z_1^{(\ell)} + \text{Dropout}(\text{CA}_{\text{out}})\right)Z2(ℓ)​=LayerNorm(Z1(ℓ)​+Dropout(CAout​))

QQQ from Z1(ℓ)Z_1^{(\ell)}Z1(ℓ)​ (decoder current), KKK and VVV from HencH_{\text{enc}}Henc​ (encoder output).

**Sublayer 3 — Feed-Forward Network + Add & Norm**

FFNout=FFN(Z2(ℓ))\text{FFN}_{\text{out}} = \text{FFN}(Z_2^{(\ell)})FFNout​=FFN(Z2(ℓ)​) Y(ℓ)=LayerNorm ⁣(Z2(ℓ)+Dropout(FFNout))Y^{(\ell)} = \text{LayerNorm}\\!\left(Z_2^{(\ell)} + \text{Dropout}(\text{FFN}_{\text{out}})\right)Y(ℓ)=LayerNorm(Z2(ℓ)​+Dropout(FFNout​))

#### Decoder Architecture (with Dimensions)
    
    
    Target tokens: [<BOS>, y_1, y_2, ..., y_{m-1}]
          │
          ▼
    Token Embedding × √d_model           [m × 512]
          + Positional Encoding
          │
          ▼ Dropout(0.1)
          │
          ▼ ═════════════ Decoder Layer 1 ════════════════
          │
          ├──→ Masked MultiHead Self-Attention ──→ Dropout ──┐
          │    Q,K,V = Y; upper-triangular mask               │ (+) residual
          │    attention matrix: [m × m] (lower triangular)   │
          └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          │
          ▼ LayerNorm                     [m × 512]
          │                                          H_enc [n × 512]
          │                                                ↓
          ├──→ MultiHead Cross-Attention ────→ Dropout ──┐
          │    Q from decoder [m × 64]                   │ (+) residual
          │    K,V from encoder [n × 64]                 │
          │    attention matrix: [m × n]                 │
          └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          │
          ▼ LayerNorm                     [m × 512]
          │
          ├──→ FFN: W₁[512→2048]→ReLU→W₂[2048→512] → Dropout ──┐
          │                                                        │ (+) residual
          └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          │
          ▼ LayerNorm                     [m × 512]
          │
          ▼ ═════════════ Decoder Layers 2–6 ═════════════
          │
          ▼
    Decoder output                        [m × 512]
          │
          ▼ Linear W_out [512 × |V|]
          │
          ▼ Softmax → probability distribution   [m × |V|]

### 23.4 Feed-Forward Network (FFN)

#### Structure

Each Transformer layer (encoder and decoder) contains a **position-wise** two-layer fully-connected network:

FFN(x)=W2⋅ReLU(W1x+b1)+b2\boxed{\text{FFN}(x) = W_2 \cdot \text{ReLU}(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2}FFN(x)=W2​⋅ReLU(W1​x+b1​)+b2​​

where:

* W1∈Rdmodel×dffW_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{ff}}W1​∈Rdmodel​×dff​: upsample, 512→2048512 \to 2048512→2048
* W2∈Rdff×dmodelW_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{ff} \times d_{\text{model}}}W2​∈Rdff​×dmodel​: downsample, 2048→5122048 \to 5122048→512

**"Position-wise" meaning** : the FFN applies the same transformation independently to each position. Position 1's FFN computation and position 2's FFN computation use identical parameters W1,W2,b1,b2W_1, W_2, b_1, b_2W1​,W2​,b1​,b2​ with no information exchange between positions.

FFN(x1) and FFN(x2) are completely independent\text{FFN}(x_1) \text{ and } \text{FFN}(x_2) \text{ are completely independent}FFN(x1​) and FFN(x2​) are completely independent

**Architectural division of labor** : inter-position information exchange occurs only in the attention layers. The attention layer handles "routing" — deciding which positions should exchange information. The FFN handles "processing" — applying non-linear transformation to each position's aggregated representation.

#### The Bottleneck-Expansion Design

The FFN's dimensional progression is:

dmodel→W1dff→ReLUdff→W2dmodel=512→2048→2048→512d_{\text{model}} \xrightarrow{W_1} d_{ff} \xrightarrow{\text{ReLU}} d_{ff} \xrightarrow{W_2} d_{\text{model}} \quad = \quad 512 \to 2048 \to 2048 \to 512dmodel​W1​​dff​ReLU​dff​W2​​dmodel​=512→2048→2048→512

The ratio dff=4×dmodeld_{ff} = 4 \times d_{\text{model}}dff​=4×dmodel​ is an **expand-then-compress** structure. The intermediate high-dimensional space (dff=2048d_{ff} = 2048dff​=2048) provides a large "computational workspace" — the 2048 neurons each define a half-space in the input space, and their combinations approximate complex non-linear functions. The subsequent projection back to 512 dimensions compresses the computation's output.

#### FFN as Key-Value Memory

Geva et al. (2021) revealed an unexpected role: **the FFN is the primary component in Transformer for storing factual knowledge**.

Write the FFN computation as:

FFN(x)=∑i=1dffai⋅vi+b2\text{FFN}(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{d_{ff}} a_i \cdot v_i + b_2FFN(x)=i=1∑dff​​ai​⋅vi​+b2​

where ki=W1[i,:]∈Rdmodelk_i = W_1[i, :] \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}ki​=W1​[i,:]∈Rdmodel​ is row iii of W1W_1W1​ (a "key" vector), vi=W2[:,i]∈Rdmodelv_i = W_2[:, i] \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}vi​=W2​[:,i]∈Rdmodel​ is column iii of W2W_2W2​ (a "value" vector), and ai=ReLU(ki⊤x+b1,i)a_i = \text{ReLU}(k_i^\top x + b_{1,i})ai​=ReLU(ki⊤​x+b1,i​) is the activation.

This interpretation:

* kik_iki​ is a **pattern detector** — when input xxx aligns with kik_iki​, ai>0a_i > 0ai​>0 and the associated "value" viv_ivi​ is activated
* viv_ivi​ is the **stored knowledge** for that pattern
* FFN output is a weighted combination of all activated value vectors

The FFN behaves as a **differentiable soft key-value memory** — a lookup table learned from data. Probing experiments find that individual neurons in FFN layers encode specific factual associations: particular neurons activate for "Paris is the capital of" contexts, or "the chemical symbol for gold is," and the corresponding value vectors nudge the output distribution toward "France" or "Au" respectively.

#### Modern Improvement: SwiGLU

The original Transformer uses ReLU. Later work found **SwiGLU** (Shazeer, 2020) consistently improves performance:

SwiGLU(x)=(Swish(xW1))⊙(xW3)\text{SwiGLU}(x) = (\text{Swish}(xW_1)) \odot (xW_3)SwiGLU(x)=(Swish(xW1​))⊙(xW3​)

where Swish(z)=z⋅σ(z)\text{Swish}(z) = z \cdot \sigma(z)Swish(z)=z⋅σ(z), σ\sigmaσ is sigmoid, and ⊙\odot⊙ is element-wise multiplication. The gating matrix W3W_3W3​ adds a multiplicative gate that can suppress (gate value ≈0\approx 0≈0) or pass (gate value ≈1\approx 1≈1) individual dimensions. LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, and most modern open-weight LLMs use SwiGLU.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Localized Pattern Activation in Neural and Physical Systems**
> 
> The FFN's pattern-detector interpretation (each neuron = one key/value pair activated when input matches the key) has analogs across neuroscience and chemistry. In **Hopfield networks** (associative memory), stored patterns are embedded as fixed points; a probe pattern activates the nearest stored pattern via energy minimization — the FFN's ReLU(ki⊤x)\text{ReLU}(k_i^\top x)ReLU(ki⊤​x) is a soft version of this threshold activation. Modern continuous Hopfield networks (Ramsauer et al., 2021) showed that transformer attention is equivalent to a single update step of a continuous Hopfield network with exponential interaction function — directly connecting FFN-like memory storage to attention mechanisms. In **enzyme catalysis** , an enzyme's active site acts as a key: only substrates with complementary shape (matching "query") bind and trigger the reaction (activate the "value" — a specific chemical transformation). The substrate-specificity of enzymes is essentially a biological key-value memory, refined by evolution rather than gradient descent. In **holographic memory** (optics), information is stored as interference patterns in a holographic medium; reconstruction occurs when an incomplete query pattern overlaps with stored information, and the retrieved hologram outputs the associated stored pattern — a continuous, distributed analog of the FFN's discrete key-value pairs.

* * *

### 23.5 Residual Connections

#### Basic Mechanism

Every sublayer has a residual (skip) connection:

output=x+SubLayer(x)\text{output} = x + \text{SubLayer}(x)output=x+SubLayer(x)

We already discussed residual connections in the context of ResNet (Chapter 5). Their role in the Transformer is deeper.

#### Residual Connections Create an Information Highway

Without residual connections in an NNN-layer encoder, a signal must pass through NNN sequential non-linear transformations:

x→f1(x)→f2(f1(x))→⋯→fN(⋯f1(x)⋯ )x \to f_1(x) \to f_2(f_1(x)) \to \cdots \to f_N(\cdots f_1(x)\cdots)x→f1​(x)→f2​(f1​(x))→⋯→fN​(⋯f1​(x)⋯)

With residual connections, a direct path through the network exists:

X(N)=X(0)+∑ℓ=1NΔ(ℓ)X^{(N)} = X^{(0)} + \sum_{\ell=1}^{N} \Delta^{(\ell)}X(N)=X(0)+ℓ=1∑N​Δ(ℓ)

where Δ(ℓ)\Delta^{(\ell)}Δ(ℓ) is the incremental contribution of sublayer ℓ\ellℓ. Each layer learns a **refinement** (residual) rather than a complete transformation — this is far easier to optimize.

The gradual refinement interpretation: deeper layers refine the representation rather than completely overwriting it. Early layers capture basic syntactic and positional structure; later layers build semantic and compositional relationships on top. The residual stream accumulates these refinements additively.

#### Gradient Propagation Analysis

The gradient of loss L\mathcal{L}L with respect to the first layer input X(0)X^{(0)}X(0):

∂L∂X(0)=∂L∂X(N)⋅(I+∂∂X(0)∑ℓ=1NΔ(ℓ))\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial X^{(0)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial X^{(N)}} \cdot \left(I + \frac{\partial}{\partial X^{(0)}} \sum_{\ell=1}^{N} \Delta^{(\ell)}\right)∂X(0)∂L​=∂X(N)∂L​⋅(I+∂X(0)∂​ℓ=1∑N​Δ(ℓ))

The identity matrix III ensures: even if all Δ(ℓ)\Delta^{(\ell)}Δ(ℓ) gradients vanish, ∂L/∂X(0)\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial X^{(0)}∂L/∂X(0) retains a nonzero component ∂L/∂X(N)\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial X^{(N)}∂L/∂X(N). **Gradients can never completely vanish** in a residual network, no matter how deep.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection — Incremental Refinement in Scientific and Engineering Systems**
> 
> The residual learning principle — "learn the correction, not the full mapping" — reflects a profound principle that appears in numerical methods, signal processing, and evolutionary biology. In **iterative numerical solvers** (Newton-Raphson, conjugate gradient), each iteration computes the residual error r(k)=b−Ax(k)r^{(k)} = b - Ax^{(k)}r(k)=b−Ax(k) and adds a correction Δx(k)\Delta x^{(k)}Δx(k) rather than recomputing the solution from scratch — identical in spirit to residual learning. In **control systems engineering** , integral control action accumulates corrections to persistent steady-state errors (e(t)=r(t)−y(t)e(t) = r(t) - y(t)e(t)=r(t)−y(t)), rather than computing the total control output from the reference signal — the controller "learns" the residual between desired and actual. In **evolutionary genetics** , the concept of genetic background and modifier genes is analogous: later mutations (sublayer corrections Δ(ℓ)\Delta^{(\ell)}Δ(ℓ)) act against a conserved background (the residual stream X(0)X^{(0)}X(0)), refining function incrementally rather than redesigning proteins from scratch. In **image compression and progressive encoding** (JPEG 2000, wavelet coding), the base layer encodes coarse structure (analogous to X(0)X^{(0)}X(0)) and enhancement layers encode residuals (analogous to Δ(ℓ)\Delta^{(\ell)}Δ(ℓ)); the receiver can reconstruct at any desired fidelity by accumulating corrections — the same additive structure as the residual stream.

### 23.6 Complete Information Flow: Translating "I love mathematics"

Tracing the full forward pass through encoder and decoder:

#### Encoder Side
    
    
    Input: "I love mathematics"
    
    1. Tokenize: ["I", "love", "mathematics"] → token IDs: [42, 1567, 8293]
    
    2. Embedding + Positional Encoding:
       x₁ = Embed(42) × √512 + PE₀    ∈ ℝ^512
       x₂ = Embed(1567) × √512 + PE₁  ∈ ℝ^512
       x₃ = Embed(8293) × √512 + PE₂  ∈ ℝ^512
    
       X^(0) = [x₁; x₂; x₃]          ∈ ℝ^{3×512}
    
    3. Encoder Layer 1 — Self-Attention:
       · "I" attends to "love" and "mathematics"
       · "love" attends to "I" and "mathematics" (identifies subject = "I")
       · "mathematics" attends to "I" and "love"
       → Each token's representation now incorporates context from all others
    
    4. Encoder Layer 1 — FFN:
       · Each position independently processes its aggregated representation
       · Factual patterns (e.g., "mathematics" → academic subject) activated
    
    5. Layers 2–6: Iterative refinement
       · Shallow layers: syntactic relationships (subject-verb-object)
       · Deep layers: semantic relationships, compositional meanings
    
    6. Output: H_enc ∈ ℝ^{3×512}
       Every position now encodes the full contextual meaning of its token
    

#### Decoder Side (Training with Teacher Forcing)
    
    
    Target input:  [<BOS>, "J'aime", "les", "mathématiques"]
    Target label:  ["J'aime", "les", "mathématiques", <EOS>]
    
    1. Embedding + PE: Y^(0) ∈ ℝ^{4×512}
    
    2. Decoder Layer 1:
    
       a) Masked Self-Attention:
          · <BOS>: attends only to itself
          · "J'aime": attends to <BOS> and itself
          · "les": attends to <BOS>, "J'aime", itself
          · "mathématiques": attends to all 4 positions
    
       b) Cross-Attention (the key step):
          · Q from decoder [4×64], K,V from encoder [3×64]
          · Attention matrix: [4×3]
    
          Position 1 (<BOS>→predict "J'aime"):   likely focuses on "I" + "love"
          Position 2 ("J'aime"→predict "les"):   likely focuses on "love"
          Position 3 ("les"→predict "mathémat."): likely focuses on "mathematics"
          Position 4 ("mathémat."→predict <EOS>): likely focuses globally
    
       c) FFN: independent processing per position
    
    3. Layers 2–6: iterative translation refinement
    
    4. Final output layer:
       Linear: [4×512] → [4×|V|]
       Softmax: probability distribution over vocabulary at each position
    
       Position 1: P("J'aime" | <BOS>, source) should peak
       Position 2: P("les" | <BOS> J'aime, source) should peak
       Position 3: P("mathématiques" | ..., source) should peak
       Position 4: P(<EOS> | full target, source) should peak
    

#### Autoregressive Generation at Inference
    
    
    Step 1: Input "<BOS>"
            → Cross-Attention queries encoder output
            → Probability distribution → argmax → "J'aime"
    
    Step 2: Input "<BOS> J'aime"
            → Masked Self-Attention (sees only <BOS> and J'aime)
            → Cross-Attention queries encoder output
            → Predict → "les"
    
    Step 3: Input "<BOS> J'aime les"
            → Predict → "mathématiques"
    
    Step 4: Input "<BOS> J'aime les mathématiques"
            → Predict → <EOS>
    
    Generation complete. Output: "J'aime les mathématiques"
    

**KV Cache** : at inference, each step requires reprocessing the full decoder input. **Key-Value Caching** stores the key and value tensors from previous steps, reusing them without recomputation. Only the new token's attention needs to be computed fresh. This reduces per-step computation from O(t2)O(t^2)O(t2) to O(t)O(t)O(t) and is critical for practical inference speed.

### 23.7 Parameter Count Analysis

For the base model (dmodel=512d_{\text{model}} = 512dmodel​=512, dff=2048d_{ff} = 2048dff​=2048, h=8h = 8h=8, N=6N = 6N=6):

Component | Formula | Parameters  
---|---|---  
Token Embedding | ∥V∥×dmodel=37000×512\|V\| \times d_{\text{model}} = 37000 \times 512∥V∥×dmodel​=37000×512 | 18.9M  
Positional Encoding (sinusoidal) | no parameters | 0  
Encoder MHA (per layer) | 4×dmodel2=4×51224 \times d_{\text{model}}^2 = 4 \times 512^24×dmodel2​=4×5122 | 1.05M  
Encoder FFN (per layer) | ≈2×dmodel×dff=2×512×2048\approx 2 \times d_{\text{model}} \times d_{ff} = 2 \times 512 \times 2048≈2×dmodel​×dff​=2×512×2048 | 2.10M  
Encoder LayerNorm (2 per layer) | 2×2×dmodel2 \times 2 \times d_{\text{model}}2×2×dmodel​ | 0.002M  
**Encoder total (6 layers)** | 6×(1.05+2.10+0.002)6 \times (1.05 + 2.10 + 0.002)6×(1.05+2.10+0.002) | **18.9M**  
Decoder Masked MHA (per layer) | 4×51224 \times 512^24×5122 | 1.05M  
Decoder Cross-Attention (per layer) | 4×51224 \times 512^24×5122 | 1.05M  
Decoder FFN (per layer) | 2×512×20482 \times 512 \times 20482×512×2048 | 2.10M  
Decoder LayerNorm (3 per layer) | 3×2×5123 \times 2 \times 5123×2×512 | 0.003M  
**Decoder total (6 layers)** | 6×(1.05+1.05+2.10+0.003)6 \times (1.05 + 1.05 + 2.10 + 0.003)6×(1.05+1.05+2.10+0.003) | **25.2M**  
Final Linear layer | shared with embedding | 0 (shared)  
**Total** |  | **~63M**  
  
63 million parameters — tiny by today's standards. GPT-3 has 175B (2,700× larger); reported GPT-4 estimates exceed 1T. Yet this 63M-parameter model achieved state-of-the-art translation in 2017, launching the entire large-model era.

**Note on weight sharing** : the final linear layer (Rdmodel×∣V∣\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times |V|}Rdmodel​×∣V∣) is typically tied to the transpose of the token embedding matrix Wemb⊤W_{\text{emb}}^\topWemb⊤​. This reduces parameter count and is theoretically motivated: the embedding layer learns to map tokens to vectors where similar tokens are nearby; the output layer should project from the same space back to token probabilities, making the same geometry useful in both directions.

### 23.8 Unified View: Three Attention Variants

The Transformer uses three attention types, all sharing the same Multi-Head Attention computational kernel, differing only in where Q, K, V originate and whether a mask is applied:

Attention Type | Q Source | K, V Source | Mask | Used In  
---|---|---|---|---  
Self-Attention | Same sequence | Same sequence | None | Encoder every layer  
Masked Self-Attention | Same sequence | Same sequence | Upper-triangle −∞-\infty−∞ | Decoder sublayer 1  
Cross-Attention | Decoder | Encoder output | None | Decoder sublayer 2  
  
This **unified design** is a core feature of the Transformer's elegance: one computational primitive (softmax(QK⊤/dk)V\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})Vsoftmax(QK⊤/dk​​)V) implements three qualitatively different functions through different input configurations. Implementation simplicity follows directly — a single multi-head attention module handles all three cases with minor parameter changes.

dk=dv=256/4=64d_k = d_v = 256/4 = 64dk​=dv​=256/4=64.

Each **row** ttt is a probability distribution over the 10 source positions — it describes how much decoder position ttt attends to each source position. Each **column** jjj collects all decoder positions' attention to source position jjj.

**(c)** Output per head: AV∈R15×64AV \in \mathbb{R}^{15 \times 64}AV∈R15×64. After concatenating 4 heads: R15×256\mathbb{R}^{15 \times 256}R15×256. After output projection WOW^OWO: R15×256=Rm×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{15 \times 256} = \mathbb{R}^{m \times d_{\text{model}}}R15×256=Rm×dmodel​.

**3.** Interpret the FFN as a key-value memory. Given W1∈Rdmodel×dffW_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{ff}}W1​∈Rdmodel​×dff​ and W2∈Rdff×dmodelW_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{ff} \times d_{\text{model}}}W2​∈Rdff​×dmodel​:

(a) Identify what plays the role of "keys," "values," and "queries" in this interpretation. (b) How does the ReLU activation determine which "memories" are retrieved? (c) Compare the FFN memory retrieval with the attention mechanism's retrieval. What is fundamentally different about their retrieval strategies?

Answer

**(a)** Keys: rows of W1W_1W1​ — each ki=W1[i,:]∈Rdmodelk_i = W_1[i,:] \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}ki​=W1​[i,:]∈Rdmodel​ is a "pattern detector." Values: columns of W2W_2W2​ — each vi=W2[:,i]∈Rdmodelv_i = W_2[:,i] \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}vi​=W2​[:,i]∈Rdmodel​ is the associated stored knowledge. Query: the input xxx to the FFN.

**(b)** Activation ai=ReLU(ki⊤x+b1,i)a_i = \text{ReLU}(k_i^\top x + b_{1,i})ai​=ReLU(ki⊤​x+b1,i​). When ki⊤x>−b1,ik_i^\top x > -b_{1,i}ki⊤​x>−b1,i​ (the pattern kik_iki​ matches the input xxx), ai>0a_i > 0ai​>0 and value viv_ivi​ contributes to the output with weight aia_iai​. When ki⊤x≤−b1,ik_i^\top x \leq -b_{1,i}ki⊤​x≤−b1,i​, ai=0a_i = 0ai​=0 and memory iii is completely silent. The hard threshold of ReLU makes this a **sparse** retrieval — typically only a fraction of the dffd_{ff}dff​ neurons activate for any given input.

**(c)** Fundamental differences:

| FFN Memory | Attention Memory  
---|---|---  
Keys | Learned parameters ki=W1[i,:]k_i = W_1[i,:]ki​=W1​[i,:] (fixed after training) | Inputs kj=hjWKk_j = h_j W^Kkj​=hj​WK (vary with current input)  
Retrieval mechanism | Hard threshold (ReLU: all-or-nothing) | Soft weighting (softmax: graded)  
Number of memories | dffd_{ff}dff​ (fixed, e.g., 2048) | nnn (varies with sequence length)  
What is retrieved | Fixed stored knowledge | Contextual information from current sequence  
  
FFN retrieves **static, learned world knowledge** (facts encoded during training). Attention retrieves **dynamic, contextual information** from the current input sequence. Together, they implement a system that both consults its training-time knowledge base (FFN) and integrates present context (attention) — a design with parallels to the distinction between semantic memory (general world knowledge) and episodic memory (current episode) in cognitive neuroscience.

#### Application

**4.** Consider an NNN-layer network with residual connections: X(ℓ)=X(ℓ−1)+Fℓ(X(ℓ−1))X^{(\ell)} = X^{(\ell-1)} + F_\ell(X^{(\ell-1)})X(ℓ)=X(ℓ−1)+Fℓ​(X(ℓ−1)).

(a) Show that ∂L∂X(0)\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial X^{(0)}}∂X(0)∂L​ contains a term that does not vanish even if all ∂Fℓ∂X(ℓ−1)→0\frac{\partial F_\ell}{\partial X^{(\ell-1)}} \to 0∂X(ℓ−1)∂Fℓ​​→0. (b) Compare this with a plain (no residual) NNN-layer network. Under the same conditions (∂Fℓ∂X(ℓ−1)→0\frac{\partial F_\ell}{\partial X^{(\ell-1)}} \to 0∂X(ℓ−1)∂Fℓ​​→0), what happens to ∂L∂X(0)\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial X^{(0)}}∂X(0)∂L​ in the plain network? (c) What does this imply for the minimum useful depth of a residual network vs. a plain network?

Answer

**(a)** By the chain rule for a residual network: ∂X(ℓ)∂X(ℓ−1)=I+∂Fℓ∂X(ℓ−1)\frac{\partial X^{(\ell)}}{\partial X^{(\ell-1)}} = I + \frac{\partial F_\ell}{\partial X^{(\ell-1)}}∂X(ℓ−1)∂X(ℓ)​=I+∂X(ℓ−1)∂Fℓ​​. Chaining over all layers:

∂L∂X(0)=∂L∂X(N)∏ℓ=1N(I+∂Fℓ∂X(ℓ−1))\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial X^{(0)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial X^{(N)}} \prod_{\ell=1}^{N} \left(I + \frac{\partial F_\ell}{\partial X^{(\ell-1)}}\right)∂X(0)∂L​=∂X(N)∂L​ℓ=1∏N​(I+∂X(ℓ−1)∂Fℓ​​)

When ∂Fℓ∂X(ℓ−1)→0\frac{\partial F_\ell}{\partial X^{(\ell-1)}} \to 0∂X(ℓ−1)∂Fℓ​​→0 for all ℓ\ellℓ, the product →IN=I\to I^N = I→IN=I, and ∂L∂X(0)→∂L∂X(N)\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial X^{(0)}} \to \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial X^{(N)}}∂X(0)∂L​→∂X(N)∂L​. The gradient does not vanish because the identity term is always present.

**(b)** For a plain network: ∂X(ℓ)∂X(ℓ−1)=∂Fℓ∂X(ℓ−1)\frac{\partial X^{(\ell)}}{\partial X^{(\ell-1)}} = \frac{\partial F_\ell}{\partial X^{(\ell-1)}}∂X(ℓ−1)∂X(ℓ)​=∂X(ℓ−1)∂Fℓ​​. Product: ∏ℓ∂Fℓ∂X(ℓ−1)\prod_{\ell} \frac{\partial F_\ell}{\partial X^{(\ell-1)}}∏ℓ​∂X(ℓ−1)∂Fℓ​​. When ∂Fℓ∂X(ℓ−1)→0\frac{\partial F_\ell}{\partial X^{(\ell-1)}} \to 0∂X(ℓ−1)∂Fℓ​​→0 for all ℓ\ellℓ, the product →0N=0\to 0^N = 0→0N=0. Gradients vanish completely — parameters in early layers receive zero gradient and do not update.

**(c)** In a residual network, adding more layers cannot make training strictly worse — if a layer learns Fℓ≈0F_\ell \approx 0Fℓ​≈0 (identity mapping), it contributes the identity transformation and the effective depth is that of previous layers. This is the **depth free lunch** of residual networks: depth never hurts, because each layer can always reduce to a no-op. In a plain network, adding unnecessary depth actively damages gradient flow. Therefore residual networks can usefully be made much deeper (e.g., 6–24 layers for Transformer base, or hundreds of layers for ResNet) while plain networks saturate at much shallower depths due to gradient vanishing.

**5.** The original Transformer uses encoder-decoder structure. Modern systems often drop the decoder and use encoder-only (BERT) or decoder-only (GPT) architectures.

(a) For encoder-only models (e.g., classification, representation learning): what masking strategy is appropriate? What is lost vs. gained? (b) For decoder-only models (e.g., language generation): how is the encoder-decoder interaction replaced? What component handles the role cross-attention played? (c) If a task requires both encoding a source document and generating a long target sequence, which architecture is most appropriate and why?

Answer

**(a) Encoder-only** : no masking required — the task is representation learning, not autoregressive generation. Every position can attend to every other position (bidirectional attention). Gain: each token's representation incorporates full two-way context, producing richer representations for downstream classification or retrieval. Loss: cannot autoregressively generate text of arbitrary length (no causal structure in the attention, so generating token ttt would have seen t+1t+1t+1 at training time).

**(b) Decoder-only** : there is no separate encoder. The "source" and "target" are concatenated into a single sequence with a separator token. The decoder's masked self-attention over the full concatenated sequence handles both "encoding" the context (early positions) and "generating" the completion (later positions). What encoder-decoder cross-attention achieved by separately storing source representations, decoder-only models achieve through the **KV cache of the context portion** — the source tokens' keys and values are cached and attended to by all generated tokens. This is less parameter-efficient for long contexts but simpler architecturally.

**(c) Encoder-decoder** : when source and target are long, distinct, and in different representational spaces (e.g., source document in English, target in French, or source = article, target = structured summary), encoder-decoder is most appropriate. Reasons: (1) encoder builds a rich bidirectional representation of the source without causal masking — all source tokens see each other, giving better source encoding; (2) decoder's cross-attention allows targeted access to specific source positions, which is more efficient than attending to all concatenated context; (3) the two sequences can have very different lengths without the O((n+m)2)O((n+m)^2)O((n+m)2) cost of full self-attention over a concatenated sequence.

* Total per encoder layer: ≈3,150,336≈3.15M\approx 3{,}150{,}336 \approx 3.15M≈3,150,336≈3.15M

**8.** The original Transformer uses post-norm placement: output=LayerNorm(x+Sublayer(x))\text{output} = \text{LayerNorm}(x + \text{Sublayer}(x))output=LayerNorm(x+Sublayer(x)). An alternative is pre-norm: output=x+Sublayer(LayerNorm(x))\text{output} = x + \text{Sublayer}(\text{LayerNorm}(x))output=x+Sublayer(LayerNorm(x)).

(a) In post-norm, show that the gradient ∂output/∂x\partial \text{output}/\partial x∂output/∂x includes a term from the LayerNorm Jacobian applied to the skip connection. Why might this complicate gradient flow for very deep Transformers? (b) In pre-norm, show that the gradient path through the skip connection is a clean identity: ∂output/∂x\partial \text{output}/\partial x∂output/∂x has an additive I\mathbf{I}I term that bypasses both LayerNorm and the sublayer. (c) Pre-norm Transformers are easier to train at depth >12 layers. Given your analysis, explain why. What is the trade-off (why did the original paper use post-norm)?

Answer

**(a)** Post-norm: y=LN(x+f(x))y = \text{LN}(x + f(x))y=LN(x+f(x)), so ∂y/∂x=JLN⋅(I+∂f/∂x)\partial y/\partial x = J_{\text{LN}} \cdot (\mathbf{I} + \partial f/\partial x)∂y/∂x=JLN​⋅(I+∂f/∂x), where JLNJ_{\text{LN}}JLN​ is the Jacobian of LayerNorm. The LayerNorm Jacobian is a non-identity matrix (it involves the centering and scaling operations), so even the skip-connection gradient JLN⋅I=JLNJ_{\text{LN}} \cdot \mathbf{I} = J_{\text{LN}}JLN​⋅I=JLN​ is modified. Over NNN layers, the gradient passes through NNN LayerNorm Jacobians, each of which can attenuate certain directions.

**(b)** Pre-norm: y=x+f(LN(x))y = x + f(\text{LN}(x))y=x+f(LN(x)), so ∂y/∂x=I+∂f/∂LN⋅JLN\partial y/\partial x = \mathbf{I} + \partial f/\partial \text{LN} \cdot J_{\text{LN}}∂y/∂x=I+∂f/∂LN⋅JLN​. The identity term I\mathbf{I}I passes gradients through the skip connection without any modification — exactly like ResNet's gradient highway. The LayerNorm Jacobian only appears in the sublayer branch, not in the skip path.

**(c)** Pre-norm preserves the ResNet gradient highway property: the identity path ensures gradients reach early layers without multiplicative degradation. For depth >12 layers, the accumulated LayerNorm Jacobian products in post-norm can cause training instability (requiring careful learning rate warmup). The trade-off: post-norm tends to produce slightly better final performance when training succeeds, because LayerNorm after the residual addition normalizes the combined representation (content + residual), potentially leading to better-calibrated layer outputs. The original paper used post-norm because it was sufficient for 6 layers; modern deep Transformers (e.g., GPT-3 with 96 layers) universally use pre-norm.
