* * *

**Introduction**

If the Transformer is a universal engine, the pre-training paradigm tells us how to drive it. The year 2018 was a watershed moment in the history of NLP: BERT and GPT-1 were published within months of each other, taking the Transformer's encoder and decoder down two sharply divergent technical paths. One path led toward deep language understanding; the other toward open-ended generation. The competition between these two paradigms, their divergence, and their eventual convergence define the most important narrative arc in AI over the past six years.

This chapter covers the conceptual foundations, mathematical details, and experimental results of the pre-training paradigm. We examine three pre-training objectives and the philosophies behind them, explain why self-supervised learning on text is so effective, trace the evolutionary lineage from Word2Vec to BERT/GPT-1, and provide close technical readings of both foundational papers. These topics form the substrate on which everything that follows—scaling laws, instruction tuning, in-context learning, chain-of-thought reasoning—is built.

* * *

### 25.1 From Task-Specific Models to Pre-train-then-Fine-tune

#### The Pre-training Era's Starting Point

Before 2018, the standard NLP workflow was: for every new task, train a new model from scratch. Sentiment analysis required one model, named-entity recognition another, and question answering yet another. These models shared almost no knowledge.

The inefficiency was obvious. More critically, many NLP tasks—legal text classification, biomedical relation extraction, clinical event detection—have extremely scarce annotated data. Training a competent model from random initialization on a few thousand labeled examples was barely feasible.

**Transfer learning** breaks this deadlock through a two-stage separation:

Large-scale unlabeled corpus⏟Pre-training ⟶ Small labeled dataset⏟Fine-tuning\underbrace{\text{Large-scale unlabeled corpus}}_{\text{Pre-training}} \;\longrightarrow\; \underbrace{\text{Small labeled dataset}}_{\text{Fine-tuning}}Pre-trainingLarge-scale unlabeled corpus​​⟶Fine-tuningSmall labeled dataset​​

Pre-training on massive unlabeled text teaches the model universal linguistic knowledge: syntax, semantics, coreference, world facts. Fine-tuning on a specific task's labeled data then specializes that general knowledge. The critical insight is that these two objectives are decoupled in cost: pre-training is performed once (at enormous computational expense) and fine-tuning is performed once per task (cheaply).

#### Computer Vision Established the Precedent

By 2012, AlexNet had demonstrated that features learned on ImageNet transferred remarkably well to nearly every visual task. The shallow layers of a pre-trained CNN learned general edge detectors, texture filters, and color patterns; these representations were equally useful for medical imaging, satellite scene classification, and autonomous driving. The standard workflow became: start from ImageNet weights, replace the final classification layer, and fine-tune with task-specific data. Transfer learning produced far better results than training from scratch, especially when target-domain data was scarce.

NLP lacked an equivalent. Word2Vec and GloVe provided static word-level embeddings, but a static representation cannot resolve polysemy: "bank" gets one vector whether it appears in "river bank" or "investment bank." RNN language models trained unidirectionally on modest corpora could not capture the rich contextual representations needed for difficult understanding tasks. NLP needed its own "ImageNet moment."

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> Transfer learning has deep analogues across scientific domains:
> 
> **Neuroscience — perceptual learning transfer** : Training on one visual discrimination task improves performance on structurally similar tasks, even without explicit exposure to the transfer target. Low-level feature detectors in early visual cortex (V1, V2) are reused across tasks, mirroring how shallow Transformer layers encode general linguistic features that transfer across downstream tasks. The specificity of transfer decreases as the tasks become more semantically dissimilar — the same gradient observed in NLP domain-adaptive pre-training.
> 
> **Evolutionary biology — exaptation** : Structures that evolve for one function are later co-opted for another. Feathers evolved for thermoregulation and were later exapted for flight; the mammalian inner-ear bones evolved from jaw structures. Pre-trained representations are similarly "exapted" from the pre-training objective (predict the next token) into capabilities never explicitly trained: coreference resolution, common-sense inference, mathematical reasoning. The functional reuse is genuine, not metaphorical — weight matrices used for masked-token prediction are literally reloaded into a sentiment classifier.
> 
> **Engineering — modular design** : High-reliability aerospace systems are built from certified, independently tested modules. A certified avionics component is validated once and deployed across multiple aircraft variants. Pre-trained language model weights play the same role: exhaustively trained at large cost, then instantiated in diverse applications. The economic structure is identical — high fixed cost, near-zero marginal deployment cost.

* * *

### 25.2 Three Pre-training Objectives

The central design choice of any pre-training system is the **pre-training objective** : what task does the model solve during pre-training? This single decision profoundly shapes which capabilities emerge. Three objectives have proved most important.

#### Masked Language Modeling (MLM)

MLM is BERT's core pre-training objective. A random subset of input tokens is masked, and the model must predict the original identities of the masked tokens from the surrounding (unmasked) context.

Input: The  [MASK]  sat  on  the  [MASK]\text{Input: The \; [MASK] \; sat \; on \; the \; [MASK]}Input: The  [MASK]  sat  on  the  [MASK] Target: cat,  mat\text{Target: cat, \; mat}Target: cat,  mat

Formally, given input sequence x=(x1,x2,…,xn)\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)x=(x1​,x2​,…,xn​), a random subset M⊂{1,…,n}\mathcal{M} \subset \\{1, \ldots, n\\}M⊂{1,…,n} (approximately 15% of positions) is selected. The training objective maximizes:

LMLM=−∑t∈Mlog⁡Pθ(xt∣x\M)\mathcal{L}_{\text{MLM}} = -\sum_{t \in \mathcal{M}} \log P_\theta(x_t \mid \mathbf{x}_{\backslash \mathcal{M}})LMLM​=−t∈M∑​logPθ​(xt​∣x\M​)

where x\M\mathbf{x}_{\backslash \mathcal{M}}x\M​ denotes the masked sequence.

**MLM's decisive advantage is bidirectionality.** For the second MASK above, the model can simultaneously exploit "the" (left) and the fact that the sentence ends there (right) to infer "mat." Predictions at every masked position exploit the full surrounding context — left and right together — rather than only what precedes the target.

#### Autoregressive Language Modeling

Autoregressive LM is GPT's pre-training objective: given all preceding tokens, predict the next one. The joint probability of a sequence is factored by the chain rule:

P(w1,w2,…,wn)=∏t=1nP(wt∣w1,w2,…,wt−1)P(w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} P(w_t \mid w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_{t-1})P(w1​,w2​,…,wn​)=t=1∏n​P(wt​∣w1​,w2​,…,wt−1​)

Training maximizes the sum of log-conditional probabilities over all positions:

LLM=−∑t=1Tlog⁡Pθ(wt∣w1,…,wt−1)\mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}} = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P_\theta(w_t \mid w_1, \ldots, w_{t-1})LLM​=−t=1∑T​logPθ​(wt​∣w1​,…,wt−1​)

This is **unidirectional** — the model sees only left context at each position. What appears to be a limitation actually grants a capability BERT lacks: **natural generation**. Because the training objective is literally "predict the next token," inference consists of repeating that operation autoregressively, producing arbitrarily long coherent text.

The intuitive contrast is crisp: MLM resembles filling in blanks on an exam — you can look anywhere in the passage, but you are not "writing" anything new. Autoregressive LM resembles writing in a journal — you can only build on what you have already written, but this precisely equips you to generate new text of arbitrary length.

#### Next Sentence Prediction (NSP)

NSP is BERT's auxiliary pre-training objective: given sentence pair (A,B)(A, B)(A,B), classify whether BBB is AAA's genuine next sentence in the original document.

Input: [CLS] A [SEP] B [SEP]\text{Input: [CLS] } A \text{ [SEP] } B \text{ [SEP]}Input: [CLS] A [SEP] B [SEP] Label: IsNext  or  NotNext\text{Label: IsNext \; or \; NotNext}Label: IsNext  or  NotNext

Training data construction: 50% of pairs are genuine consecutive sentences (label IsNext); 50% have BBB replaced by a randomly sampled sentence (label NotNext). The classifier operates on the [CLS] token's output representation:

P(IsNext∣A,B)=softmax(WNSP⋅h[CLS])P(\text{IsNext} \mid A, B) = \text{softmax}(W_{\text{NSP}} \cdot h_{[\text{CLS}]})P(IsNext∣A,B)=softmax(WNSP​⋅h[CLS]​)

The design intent was to teach the model inter-sentence coherence, which should benefit question answering and natural language inference. However, subsequent work — most decisively Liu et al. (2019) with RoBERTa — showed that NSP contributed little and removing it often improved performance. The reason: the random-sentence negatives differ from genuine next-sentences in _topic_ as well as _logical continuity_ , allowing the model to solve NSP by detecting topic mismatch rather than learning genuine logical entailment. Models that found this shortcut never learned the deeper inter-sentence reasoning the task was designed to elicit.

#### Comparing the Three Objectives

Dimension | MLM (BERT) | Autoregressive LM (GPT) | NSP (auxiliary)  
---|---|---|---  
Context direction | Bidirectional | Unidirectional (left-to-right) | Sentence-pair level  
Core capability | Contextual understanding | Text generation | Inter-sentence coherence (limited)  
Signal density | ~15% of positions | 100% of positions | One binary signal per pair  
Loss formula | −∑t∈Mlog⁡P(xt∣x\M)-\sum_{t \in \mathcal{M}} \log P(x_t \mid \mathbf{x}_{\backslash \mathcal{M}})−∑t∈M​logP(xt​∣x\M​) | −∑tlog⁡P(wt∣w<t)-\sum_t \log P(w_t \mid w_{<t})−∑t​logP(wt​∣w<t​) | −log⁡P(IsNext∣A,B)-\log P(\text{IsNext} \mid A, B)−logP(IsNext∣A,B)  
  
The signal-density difference warrants emphasis. MLM computes loss at only 15% of positions per training sequence; autoregressive LM computes loss at every position. Given equal data volume, autoregressive LM produces approximately 1/0.15≈6.7×1/0.15 \approx 6.7\times1/0.15≈6.7× more gradient signal per forward pass. This training-efficiency advantage accumulates at scale — it is one factor behind the eventual dominance of the decoder-only autoregressive paradigm.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> The NSP failure illustrates a general principle about task design in measurement and experimental science:
> 
> **Psychometrics — shortcut learning and construct validity** : A psychometric scale is said to have _construct validity_ when it measures what it purports to measure rather than a correlated proxy. NSP intended to measure inter-sentence logical coherence but actually measured topical overlap — a much easier proxy that correlates with coherence but is not the same thing. This is precisely the construct validity failure described in classical test theory (Cronbach & Meehl, 1955): the operational measure diverges from the theoretical construct.
> 
> **Medical diagnostics — test specificity** : A diagnostic test with low specificity generates many false positives by responding to confounders rather than the disease itself. NSP's random-negative construction created a "confounded test": the signal (topical change) was easy to detect and correlated with the target (IsNext/NotNext) but did not require learning the target capability. Later designs — notably ALBERT's Sentence Order Prediction (SOP), which uses same-document sentences with swapped order as negatives — improved specificity by removing the confounding topical signal.
> 
> **Signal processing — noise floor and dynamic range** : A sensor whose noise floor exceeds the signal of interest cannot measure that signal regardless of gain. NSP's discriminability from noise (topic difference) was so high that the task never operated above the noise floor for its intended capability (logical coherence). Effective pre-training objectives must have a noise floor below the target signal — easy enough to produce a gradient, hard enough to require genuine knowledge.

* * *

### 25.3 Why Pre-training Works: The Self-Supervised Rationale

#### "Predict the Next Token" Encodes Rich World Knowledge

Pre-training works because the language-modeling task — deceptively simple in description — requires far more than surface statistics to solve well. Consider what a model must learn to predict accurately across diverse texts:

**Syntax** : "The committees that oversee the agency ___" → "have" (not "has": the head noun "committees" governs agreement despite the intervening subordinate clause).

**Semantics** : "He deposited his paycheck at the ___" → "bank" (financial institution, not riverbank — context resolves polysemy).

**World knowledge** : "The Federal Reserve raises the federal funds ___" → "rate" (institutional knowledge about monetary policy).

**Causal reasoning** : "The experiment exceeded the pressure tolerance of the vessel, so the ___" → "reactor" (or "chamber", or "tank" — the model must track referents and causal chains across sentences).

A model trained on trillions of tokens to minimize prediction error at every position has no choice but to internalize all of these regularities. It need not be explicitly told that committees take plural verbs; it discovers this from the statistical regularity of the corpus. It need not read an economics textbook; it absorbs the institutional structure of monetary policy from thousands of news articles and policy documents.

This is the power of **self-supervised learning** : the labels are latent in the data itself. Every token is simultaneously a training signal and part of the context for predicting the next one. The internet contains on the order of 101310^{13}1013 tokens of text — essentially unlimited training data for this objective.

#### The Information-Theoretic Argument

Cross-entropy loss decomposes as:

LCE=−Ex∼Pdata[log⁡Pθ(x)]=H(Pdata)+DKL(Pdata∥Pθ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} = -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim P_{\text{data}}} [\log P_\theta(\mathbf{x})] = H(P_{\text{data}}) + D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\text{data}} \| P_\theta)LCE​=−Ex∼Pdata​​[logPθ​(x)]=H(Pdata​)+DKL​(Pdata​∥Pθ​)

where H(Pdata)H(P_{\text{data}})H(Pdata​) is the intrinsic entropy of natural language (a constant the model cannot affect) and DKLD_{\text{KL}}DKL​ is the KL divergence between model and true distributions. Minimizing cross-entropy is therefore equivalent to **minimizing the KL divergence between the model distribution and the true data distribution** — forcing the model to match the full statistical structure of language.

This is precisely Maximum Likelihood Estimation: given parameterized model PθP_\thetaPθ​, find θ∗=arg⁡max⁡θ∏tPθ(wt∣w<t)\theta^* = \arg\max_\theta \prod_t P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})θ∗=argmaxθ​∏t​Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​). Pre-training is MLE at an unprecedented scale.

The compression perspective offers a complementary view. Algorithmic information theory (Kolmogorov 1963; Solomonoff 1964) shows that optimal compression requires understanding. A model that achieves lower cross-entropy on a held-out corpus is, by definition, capturing more structure — not just memorizing training sequences. Better compression implies better understanding of the generative process. Shannon (1951) estimated English redundancy at approximately 50%, meaning that average per-token predictability is ∼1\sim 1∼1 bit below the theoretical maximum; a good language model exploits this redundancy through genuine linguistic knowledge, not statistical artifact.

#### Hierarchical Representations

Probing experiments — training a simple linear classifier on frozen intermediate-layer activations to predict linguistic properties — reveal that pre-trained Transformer layers encode different levels of linguistic structure:

* **Shallow layers (near input)** : lexical and morphological features, part-of-speech tags, local syntactic dependencies
* **Middle layers** : semantic roles (who did what to whom), coreference chains, entity types
* **Deep layers (near output)** : task-relevant abstract features, long-range logical dependencies

This layered representational structure means that fine-tuning is not merely recalibrating a feature extractor — it is selecting and adapting an entire linguistic knowledge hierarchy. Different downstream tasks draw on different layers: sequence labeling (NER) primarily uses middle-layer features; high-level reasoning benefits from deep-layer representations.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> The self-supervised pre-training principle appears in several scientific domains under different names:
> 
> **Geophysics — seismic tomography** : Tomographic reconstruction of Earth's interior uses travel-time residuals of seismic waves as self-supervised signal. No one drills to the Earth's core to label what is there; the constraints come from the physical laws governing wave propagation. The model (a velocity field) is updated so that predicted travel times match observed ones — exactly the structure of language model pre-training, where the model is updated so that predicted next-tokens match observed ones. In both cases, the "labels" are consequences of the data, not external annotations.
> 
> **Genomics — masked genome modeling** : Masked-sequence pre-training objectives analogous to MLM have been applied to DNA and protein sequences. Models such as ESM-2 (Lin et al., 2023) pre-train on protein sequences by masking residues and predicting their identities; the resulting representations encode structural and functional features that transfer to tasks like contact prediction and mutation effect scoring — structural properties never present in the training signal. The mechanism is identical to BERT: the model learns latent biological "language" by solving a local completion task.
> 
> **Fluid mechanics — latent variable discovery** : Reduced-order models (ROMs) of turbulent flow extract principal modes from simulation data without labeling which modes correspond to which physical phenomena. Koopman operator methods (Mezić, 2005) provide a self-supervised decomposition: eigen-functions learned from trajectory data span physically interpretable structures (vortices, shear layers) that generalize to prediction tasks. The hierarchy of modes discovered mirrors the hierarchy of Transformer representations — low-frequency globally coherent modes at deeper abstract levels, high-frequency local fluctuations in shallow representations.

* * *

### 25.4 Historical Lineage: Word2Vec to BERT/GPT

Pre-training did not emerge fully formed. It evolved through six years of incremental advances, each generation addressing the critical limitations of the one before.

#### Word2Vec (2013): Static Word-Level Pre-training

Mikolov et al.'s Word2Vec (Chapter 5) was the earliest NLP pre-training in the modern sense: train word vectors on large unlabeled text, then use them as features for downstream tasks.

**Critical limitation** : Word2Vec generates **static embeddings** — one fixed vector per word type, regardless of context. "Bank" receives the same representation whether it appears in "river bank" or "central bank." Furthermore, Word2Vec provides only word-level representations; there is no sentence-level or document-level contextual modeling.

#### ELMo (2018): Context-Sensitive Representations

Peters et al.'s ELMo (Embeddings from Language Models) took the essential next step: use a language model to generate **context-dependent** word representations.

ELMo trains a forward LSTM and a backward LSTM independently, then concatenates their per-layer hidden states:

ELMok=γ∑j=0Lsj[h→k,j;h←k,j]\text{ELMo}_k = \gamma \sum_{j=0}^{L} s_j \left[\overrightarrow{h}_{k,j}; \overleftarrow{h}_{k,j}\right]ELMok​=γj=0∑L​sj​[hk,j​;hk,j​]

where h→k,j\overrightarrow{h}_{k,j}hk,j​ and h←k,j\overleftarrow{h}_{k,j}hk,j​ are the forward and backward LSTM hidden states at layer jjj and position kkk, sjs_jsj​ are learnable layer weights, and γ\gammaγ is a scalar. Different downstream tasks learn different mixtures of layers.

ELMo demonstrated two critical facts: (1) contextual representations are vastly superior to static embeddings; (2) pre-trained LM representations improve downstream performance substantially even when used as frozen features.

**Critical limitation** : The two directions are trained **independently**. At every layer, the forward LSTM only sees left context and the backward LSTM only sees right context; they never interact within a layer. This "shallow fusion" (concatenate after independent computation) is fundamentally different from the "deep fusion" of BERT (left and right context interact within every attention head at every layer).

#### ULMFiT (2018): Systematizing Pre-train-then-Fine-tune

Howard and Ruder's ULMFiT was the first work to systematize the pre-train + fine-tune methodology itself. Three technical contributions became templates for subsequent work:

* **Discriminative fine-tuning** : assign smaller learning rates to lower layers (which hold general representations that should change little) and larger learning rates to higher layers (which hold task-specific representations that need more adaptation).
* **Slanted triangular learning rates** : linearly increase the learning rate during an initial warm-up phase, then decay it, preventing overshooting of the pre-training basin early in fine-tuning.
* **Gradual unfreezing** : unfreeze layers from top to bottom during fine-tuning, allowing each layer to adapt before the layer below it is released, mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

ULMFiT demonstrated stunning data efficiency: fine-tuning with 100 labeled examples matched performance that required 10,000 labeled examples from scratch. This quantified, for the first time, the "knowledge leverage" that pre-training provides.

#### BERT and GPT-1 (2018): Paradigm Consolidation

Two papers, published within months of each other, established the modern pre-training paradigm by replacing LSTM with Transformer:

* **GPT-1** (OpenAI, June 2018): Transformer **decoder** \+ autoregressive LM pre-training, then fine-tune.
* **BERT** (Google, October 2018): Transformer **encoder** \+ MLM pre-training, then fine-tune.

BERT simultaneously improved state-of-the-art on 11 NLP benchmarks, earning the descriptor "NLP's ImageNet moment." GPT-1's immediate benchmark performance was less dramatic, but it launched the decoder-only autoregressive paradigm that would ultimately dominate.

**Evolutionary summary** :
    
    
    Word2Vec (2013)     ELMo (2018)        ULMFiT (2018)       BERT / GPT (2018)
      │                   │                   │                   │
      Static vectors      Contextual repr.    Pre-train+finetune  Transformer +
      No context          Bidirectional LSTM  methodology         large-scale pre-training
      Word-level only     But: shallow fusion But: still LSTM     Paradigm established
      │                   │                   │                   │
      └───→ Pre-training ─→ Context matters ──→ Finetune method ──→ Scaled pre-training
             concept          proven             matures              standardized
    

Each generation solved the previous generation's key deficiency:

* Word2Vec → ELMo: static → contextual representations
* ELMo → ULMFiT: ad-hoc usage → systematic fine-tuning methodology
* ULMFiT → BERT/GPT: slow LSTM → parallelizable Transformer, enabling large-scale pre-training

* * *

### 25.5 BERT: Deep Bidirectional Transformers

#### The ImageNet Moment

On October 11, 2018, Devlin, Chang, Lee, and Toutanova posted "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding" to arXiv. The NLP community's reaction was unusual in its intensity because BERT did not improve on one task — it improved on **eleven tasks simultaneously** , across diverse categories:

* **GLUE benchmark** (8 tasks): the aggregate score jumped from 71.0 to 80.5 — a 9.5 point leap on a leaderboard that had advanced by ∼\sim∼1 point per year.
* **SQuAD v1.1** : BERT-Large's F1 of 90.9 approached human-level (91.2); with TriviaQA augmentation, it exceeded it at 93.2.
* **SWAG** (common-sense reasoning): from 75.1 to 86.3.

The name encodes its design philosophy: **B** idirectional **E** ncoder **R** epresentations from **T** ransformers.

* **Bidirectional** : the decisive innovation — simultaneous conditioning on left and right context
* **Encoder** : uses the Transformer encoder stack (no causal mask, no cross-attention decoder)
* **Representations** : learns universal language representations rather than task-specific models
* **Transformers** : Transformer rather than LSTM, enabling large-scale parallelism

#### True Bidirectionality via Masked Language Modeling

A fundamental tension existed before BERT: using a standard language model (predict the next token) with a Transformer encoder would cause **information leakage** — the model could attend directly to the token it is supposed to predict, making the task trivially solvable and the objective meaningless.

MLM dissolves this tension. The token to be predicted is replaced by [MASK] in the input; the model cannot attend to the original token because it is not there. With the prediction target hidden, bidirectional attention becomes safe and informative.

Comparing the three approaches precisely:

Standard LM: P(wt∣w1,…,wt−1)(left context only)\text{Standard LM: } P(w_t \mid w_1, \ldots, w_{t-1}) \quad \text{(left context only)}Standard LM: P(wt​∣w1​,…,wt−1​)(left context only) ELMo: P(wt∣w1,…,wt−1→)⊕P(wt∣wt+1,…,wn←)(two independent streams)\text{ELMo: } P(w_t \mid \overrightarrow{w_1, \ldots, w_{t-1}}) \oplus P(w_t \mid \overleftarrow{w_{t+1}, \ldots, w_n}) \quad \text{(two independent streams)}ELMo: P(wt​∣w1​,…,wt−1​​)⊕P(wt​∣wt+1​,…,wn​​)(two independent streams) BERT MLM: P(wt∣w1,…,wt−1,wt+1,…,wn)(truly bidirectional)\text{BERT MLM: } P(w_t \mid w_1, \ldots, w_{t-1}, w_{t+1}, \ldots, w_n) \quad \text{(truly bidirectional)}BERT MLM: P(wt​∣w1​,…,wt−1​,wt+1​,…,wn​)(truly bidirectional)

The ELMo representation of token ttt is a concatenation of two independently computed vectors that never interact within any layer. BERT's representation of token ttt is computed by attention heads that simultaneously attend to all other positions — left and right context participate in the same attention computation at every layer. This is deep fusion rather than shallow concatenation; it is the reason BERT's representations are qualitatively superior for understanding tasks.

#### The 15% Masking Rate and 80/10/10 Strategy

BERT's MLM design involves two nested choices: how many positions to mask, and what to do at masked positions.

**Why 15%?** Two opposing pressures constrain the masking rate:

* Too low (e.g., 5%): too few positions contribute to the loss per forward pass; training is slow and data-inefficient. In a 512-token sequence at 5% masking, only ~26 positions generate gradients.
* Too high (e.g., 50%): the remaining context is too sparse to support accurate predictions; the model cannot learn rich representations because the input is too degraded.

At 15%, a 512-token sequence yields ~77 masked positions — enough gradient signal while preserving sufficient context. The 15% figure is an empirically optimized equilibrium, not a theoretically derived optimum.

**The 80/10/10 replacement strategy** addresses a subtler problem: the **pre-train/fine-tune mismatch**. If every masked position were replaced by the [MASK] token, the model would learn representations conditioned on the presence of [MASK] — but [MASK] never appears at fine-tuning or inference time. To mitigate this distributional shift, Devlin et al. use a three-way randomized strategy at each selected position:

x~t={[MASK]with probability 0.80xrandom∼Uniform(V)with probability 0.10xtwith probability 0.10\tilde{x}_t = \begin{cases} \text{[MASK]} & \text{with probability } 0.80 \\\ x_{\text{random}} \sim \text{Uniform}(V) & \text{with probability } 0.10 \\\ x_t & \text{with probability } 0.10 \end{cases}x~t​=⎩⎨⎧​[MASK]xrandom​∼Uniform(V)xt​​with probability 0.80with probability 0.10with probability 0.10​

The training target is always the original xtx_txt​ regardless of what x~t\tilde{x}_tx~t​ is.

**Purpose of each component** :

* **80% [MASK]** : the core supervised signal; forces context-based prediction.
* **10% random substitution** : prevents a "laziness" strategy in which the model only exerts predictive effort when it detects [MASK] and ignores other positions. Random substitutions force the model to maintain high-quality representations everywhere, since any position might be "wrong."
* **10% unchanged** : closes the gap between pre-training and downstream inference where all tokens are authentic. Ensures the model learns to represent real tokens accurately in addition to predicting around [MASK].

This design can be understood through a mechanism-design lens: the 80/10/10 strategy eliminates "shortcuts" by making it impossible for the model to selectively attend only when signaled. Random audits (the 10% random substitutions) prevent strategic inattention, analogously to compliance monitoring in organizations.

#### Architecture and Input Representation

BERT was released in two sizes:

Hyperparameter | BERT-Base | BERT-Large  
---|---|---  
Transformer layers LLL | 12 | 24  
Hidden dimension dmodeld_{\text{model}}dmodel​ | 768 | 1024  
Attention heads hhh | 12 | 16  
FFN hidden dimension dffd_{ff}dff​ | 3,072 | 4,096  
Total parameters | 110M | 340M  
Max sequence length | 512 | 512  
  
BERT-Base was intentionally matched to GPT-1's 117M parameters to enable fair comparison between pre-training strategies rather than model capacities.

**Parameter verification for BERT-Base** (applying the formulas from Chapter 23):

Per encoder layer:

* Multi-head self-attention: 4dmodel2=4×7682≈2.36M4 d_{\text{model}}^2 = 4 \times 768^2 \approx 2.36\text{M}4dmodel2​=4×7682≈2.36M
* FFN: 2×dmodel×dff≈2×768×3072≈4.72M2 \times d_{\text{model}} \times d_{ff} \approx 2 \times 768 \times 3072 \approx 4.72\text{M}2×dmodel​×dff​≈2×768×3072≈4.72M
* LayerNorm (×2\times 2×2): 4dmodel≈0.003M4 d_{\text{model}} \approx 0.003\text{M}4dmodel​≈0.003M
* Per-layer total: ≈7.08M\approx 7.08\text{M}≈7.08M

12 encoder layers: 12×7.08≈85M12 \times 7.08 \approx 85\text{M}12×7.08≈85M

Embeddings:

* Token embedding: 30,522×768≈23.4M30{,}522 \times 768 \approx 23.4\text{M}30,522×768≈23.4M
* Position embedding: 512×768≈0.39M512 \times 768 \approx 0.39\text{M}512×768≈0.39M
* Segment embedding: 2×768≈0.001M2 \times 768 \approx 0.001\text{M}2×768≈0.001M

Total: ≈109M\approx 109\text{M}≈109M (matches reported 110M).

**Input representation** — each token's input vector is the elementwise sum of three embeddings:

Input(xi)=TokenEmb(xi)+SegmentEmb(xi)+PositionEmb(i)\text{Input}(x_i) = \text{TokenEmb}(x_i) + \text{SegmentEmb}(x_i) + \text{PositionEmb}(i)Input(xi​)=TokenEmb(xi​)+SegmentEmb(xi​)+PositionEmb(i)

* **Token Embedding** : maps each WordPiece token to a 768-dimensional vector (vocabulary size 30,522).
* **Segment Embedding** : two learnable vectors EAE_AEA​ and EBE_BEB​ that distinguish which of two sentences a token belongs to. Enables the model to encode sentence-pair structure for tasks like NLI and QA.
* **Position Embedding** : 512 learnable position vectors (contrast with the sinusoidal fixed encoding of the original Transformer). This choice trades generalization to out-of-distribution lengths (unavailable) for additional flexibility (possible); the trade-off is acceptable because BERT processes fixed-length input segments.

**Special tokens** :

* `[CLS]` prepends every sequence. Its final hidden state serves as a sequence-level representation used for classification tasks.
* `[SEP]` separates paired sentences and terminates sequences.

A complete input example:
    
    
    Tokens:   [CLS]  the  cat  sat  [SEP]  on  the  mat  [SEP]
    Segments:  A     A    A    A     A      B   B    B     B
    Positions: 0     1    2    3     4      5   6    7     8
    

#### The Fine-tuning Paradigm

BERT's most practically consequential design contribution is the uniformity of its fine-tuning recipe. Four structurally distinct task types all reduce to the same two-step procedure: load pre-trained BERT; add a shallow task-specific head; train end-to-end.

**Task type 1 — single-sentence classification** (sentiment analysis, grammaticality judgment): Input: `[CLS] sentence [SEP]` Take the [CLS] output h[CLS]∈Rdmodelh_{[\text{CLS}]} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}h[CLS]​∈Rdmodel​ and apply:

P(y∣x)=softmax(Wh[CLS]+b),W∈RK×dmodelP(y \mid x) = \text{softmax}(W h_{[\text{CLS}]} + b), \quad W \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times d_{\text{model}}}P(y∣x)=softmax(Wh[CLS]​+b),W∈RK×dmodel​

**Task type 2 — sentence-pair classification** (natural language inference, semantic similarity): Input: `[CLS] sentence_A [SEP] sentence_B [SEP]` Same [CLS]-based classifier; segment embeddings distinguish the two sentences.

**Task type 3 — sequence labeling** (named-entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging): Input: `[CLS] token_1 ... token_n [SEP]` Apply a per-token classifier to each output vector:

P(yt∣x)=softmax(Wht+b),for each position tP(y_t \mid x) = \text{softmax}(W h_t + b), \quad \text{for each position } tP(yt​∣x)=softmax(Wht​+b),for each position t

**Task type 4 — span extraction** (SQuAD-style reading comprehension): Input: `[CLS] question [SEP] passage [SEP]` Learn two vectors s\mathbf{s}s (start) and e\mathbf{e}e (end):

P(start=i)=exp⁡(s⋅hi)∑jexp⁡(s⋅hj),P(end=i)=exp⁡(e⋅hi)∑jexp⁡(e⋅hj)P(\text{start} = i) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{s} \cdot h_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\mathbf{s} \cdot h_j)}, \qquad P(\text{end} = i) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{e} \cdot h_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\mathbf{e} \cdot h_j)}P(start=i)=∑j​exp(s⋅hj​)exp(s⋅hi​)​,P(end=i)=∑j​exp(e⋅hj​)exp(e⋅hi​)​

The answer span score is s⋅hi+e⋅hj\mathbf{s} \cdot h_i + \mathbf{e} \cdot h_js⋅hi​+e⋅hj​ subject to j≥ij \geq ij≥i.

**Fine-tuning hyperparameters** are remarkably stable across tasks. Batch size ∈{16,32}\in \\{16, 32\\}∈{16,32}, Adam learning rate ∈{2e-5,3e-5,5e-5}\in \\{2\text{e-}5, 3\text{e-}5, 5\text{e-}5\\}∈{2e-5,3e-5,5e-5}, 2–4 epochs. This insensitivity reflects the pre-training's role in landing the model in a well-conditioned basin from which fine-tuning merely navigates locally. Fine-tuning typically completes in minutes to hours — negligible relative to pre-training's days-to-weeks cost.

The cost structure has a classical economic form. Pre-training is a **fixed cost** (BERT-Large: 16 Cloud TPUs × 4 days ≈ 2,048 TPU-hours); fine-tuning is a small **variable cost** per task. Total average cost per deployed task decreases monotonically with the number of downstream applications — textbook economies of scale. This explains why large organizations accept the enormous pre-training cost: each incremental application amortizes it further.

#### Key Experimental Results

**GLUE Benchmark** (selected tasks):

Task | Type | Data size | BERT-Base | BERT-Large | Prior SOTA  
---|---|---|---|---|---  
MNLI | NLI | 393K | 84.6 | 86.7 | 80.6  
SST-2 | Sentiment | 67K | 93.5 | 94.9 | 93.2  
CoLA | Grammaticality | 8.5K | 52.1 | 60.5 | 35.0  
RTE | NLI | 2.5K | 66.4 | 70.1 | 61.7  
  
Two patterns are diagnostic. First, the CoLA improvement (+25.5 points for BERT-Large) demonstrates that pre-training internalizes grammatical knowledge that small labeled datasets cannot teach directly — 8,500 examples cannot reliably teach subject-verb agreement from scratch, but billions of pre-training tokens already have. Second, improvements are larger for smaller datasets (RTE: +8.4 points; SST-2: +1.7 points). Pre-training's marginal value is highest precisely where labeled data is scarce.

**SQuAD v1.1** — BERT-Large single model achieves F1 = 90.9, approaching human performance (91.2). With TriviaQA-augmented training, F1 = 93.2, the first system to exceed human performance on a major reading-comprehension benchmark.

**Ablation study** (BERT-Base on three representative tasks):

Variant | MNLI | QNLI | SST-2  
---|---|---|---  
Full BERT-Base | 84.4 | 88.4 | 93.5  
Remove NSP | 83.9 | 84.9 | 93.5  
Replace MLM with left-to-right LM | 82.1 | 84.3 | 92.1  
Left-to-right LM + BiLSTM | 82.1 | 84.1 | 91.7  
  
Key findings: (1) Removing NSP has modest, inconsistent effects — confirming its limited contribution and foreshadowing RoBERTa's abolition of it. (2) Replacing MLM with unidirectional LM substantially degrades all tasks — directly demonstrating the value of bidirectionality for understanding. (3) Adding a BiLSTM on top of a unidirectional LM (the ELMo strategy) does not recover MLM's advantage — shallow fusion is materially inferior to BERT's deep bidirectional fusion.

* * *

### 25.6 GPT-1: Generative Pre-training

#### The Two-Phase Framework

GPT's full name — **Generative Pre-Training** — names its approach. Radford, Narasimhan, Salimans, and Sutskever (OpenAI, 2018) pursued a more direct route to pre-training: train a language model, then fine-tune it.

**Phase 1 — unsupervised pre-training** : on a large unlabeled text corpus U={u1,…,un}\mathcal{U} = \\{u_1, \ldots, u_n\\}U={u1​,…,un​}, maximize:

L1(U)=∑ilog⁡P(ui∣ui−k,…,ui−1;Θ)\mathcal{L}_1(\mathcal{U}) = \sum_{i} \log P(u_i \mid u_{i-k}, \ldots, u_{i-1}; \Theta)L1​(U)=i∑​logP(ui​∣ui−k​,…,ui−1​;Θ)

where kkk is the context window and Θ\ThetaΘ are the Transformer parameters.

**Phase 2 — supervised fine-tuning** : on downstream task dataset C\mathcal{C}C with inputs (x1,…,xm)(x_1, \ldots, x_m)(x1​,…,xm​) and label yyy, the input is passed through the pre-trained Transformer and the last token's final-layer hidden state hmLh_m^LhmL​ is sent through a linear classifier:

P(y∣x1,…,xm)=softmax(hmLWy)P(y \mid x_1, \ldots, x_m) = \text{softmax}(h_m^L W_y)P(y∣x1​,…,xm​)=softmax(hmL​Wy​)

GPT-1 fine-tuning is distinctive in retaining the language-modeling loss as an auxiliary objective:

L3(C)=L2(C)+λ⋅L1(C)\mathcal{L}_3(\mathcal{C}) = \mathcal{L}_2(\mathcal{C}) + \lambda \cdot \mathcal{L}_1(\mathcal{C})L3​(C)=L2​(C)+λ⋅L1​(C)

The motivation is regularization against **catastrophic forgetting** : fine-tuning on a small labeled dataset can overwrite the general language knowledge encoded during pre-training. The auxiliary LM loss λL1\lambda \mathcal{L}_1λL1​ provides a "restoring force" that penalizes the model for drifting too far from the pre-training basin. Ablation results confirm this: the auxiliary loss primarily benefits small-dataset tasks, where the risk of forgetting exceeds that of under-specializing.

#### Architecture: Decoder-Only Transformer

GPT-1 uses a **Transformer decoder with cross-attention removed**. The original Transformer's decoder has three sub-layers: masked self-attention, cross-attention (to encoder output), and FFN. GPT-1 eliminates the middle layer entirely, since there is no encoder:

hℓ=LayerNorm(hℓ−1+MaskedMHA(hℓ−1))h_\ell = \text{LayerNorm}(h_{\ell-1} + \text{MaskedMHA}(h_{\ell-1}))hℓ​=LayerNorm(hℓ−1​+MaskedMHA(hℓ−1​)) hℓ′=LayerNorm(hℓ+FFN(hℓ))h_\ell' = \text{LayerNorm}(h_\ell + \text{FFN}(h_\ell))hℓ′​=LayerNorm(hℓ​+FFN(hℓ​))

The causal mask ensures that position ttt attends only to positions {1,…,t}\\{1, \ldots, t\\}{1,…,t}, implementing the autoregressive constraint with the computational efficiency of the Transformer (all positions computed in parallel during training via matrix operations on the upper-triangular −∞-\infty−∞ mask).

**Architecture specification** :

Hyperparameter | GPT-1  
---|---  
Transformer layers | 12  
Hidden dimension dmodeld_{\text{model}}dmodel​ | 768  
Attention heads | 12  
FFN hidden dimension | 3,072  
Total parameters | 117M  
Activation | GELU  
Position encoding | Learnable  
Max sequence length | 512  
  
GPT-1 and BERT-Base have essentially identical architecture specifications (∼\sim∼110–117M parameters, same layer count, same dimensions), enabling attribution of performance differences to pre-training strategy rather than model capacity.

**Pre-training data** : BooksCorpus — approximately 7,000 unpublished books, ∼\sim∼800M words. The choice of books over web text was deliberate: books contain long, coherent, uninterrupted text conducive to learning long-range dependencies. Web text tends to be fragmented and topic-inconsistent.

By comparison, BERT used BooksCorpus + English Wikipedia ≈ 3.3B words — approximately 4× more data. This difference in pre-training scale accounts for a substantial fraction of BERT's benchmark advantage over GPT-1.

#### Task-Specific Input Transformations

GPT-1's most architecturally creative contribution is its unified method for adapting a single language model to structurally heterogeneous tasks through **input transformations** — reordering and concatenating task inputs into token sequences that the same Transformer processes identically:

**Classification** :
    
    
    [Start] text [Extract]
    

The [Extract]-position hidden state feeds the linear classifier.

**Entailment (Natural Language Inference)** :
    
    
    [Start] premise [Delim] hypothesis [Extract]
    

The [Delim] token separates the two components; attention across the [Delim] boundary builds the inference representation.

**Similarity** (symmetric relation):
    
    
    [Start] text₁ [Delim] text₂ [Extract]    and    [Start] text₂ [Delim] text₁ [Extract]
    

Both orderings are processed; their [Extract]-position representations are element-wise summed before classification. This symmetrization is necessary because the causal mask makes the model's representation of (A,B)(A, B)(A,B) different from its representation of (B,A)(B, A)(B,A) — the right-side member always has access to the left-side member's information but not vice versa. Averaging over both orderings restores the symmetry that the task requires.

**Multiple choice** (e.g., reading comprehension with NNN options):
    
    
    [Start] context [Delim] answer_i [Extract]    for each i = 1, ..., N
    

All options are scored independently; a softmax selects the highest-scoring answer.

This framework embodies a deep design principle: **task diversity reflects input format diversity, not architectural diversity.** A single inference engine with sufficient capacity handles all of these tasks; only the input presentation changes. GPT-2 would later push this principle to its limit: "all tasks are text generation," requiring not even a task head — just an appropriate prompt.

#### Experimental Results and the Zero-Shot Signal

GPT-1 achieved state-of-the-art on 9 of 12 evaluated tasks at its publication time. In comparison with prior work:

Task | GPT-1 | Prior SOTA | Change  
---|---|---|---  
MNLI | 82.1 | 80.6 | +1.5  
QNLI | 88.1 | 82.3 | +5.8  
CoLA | 45.4 | 35.0 | +10.4  
SST-2 | 91.3 | 90.2 | +1.1  
  
The CoLA improvement (+10.4 points) again stands out: grammaticality judgment from only 8,500 examples benefits enormously from the pre-training data's implicit encoding of syntactic regularities.

**Ablation study findings** :

* Removing the auxiliary LM loss: small effect on large datasets, larger effect on small datasets (confirms regularization interpretation).
* Replacing Transformer with LSTM: ∼\sim∼5-point average decline — Transformer architecture, not merely pre-training, is essential.
* No pre-training (train from scratch): ∼\sim∼14-point average decline — the most direct quantification of pre-training's value.

**Zero-shot performance analysis** : GPT-1 contains a largely overlooked but prescient experiment. The authors tracked several tasks' performance as a function of pre-training steps, _without any fine-tuning_. Zero-shot performance on sentiment analysis, question answering, and semantic similarity all increased monotonically as pre-training proceeded. This signal was small in GPT-1 but pointed directly at GPT-2 ("Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners") and GPT-3 ("Language Models are Few-Shot Learners"): the autoregressive language model internalizes task structure without explicit task supervision, and this capacity scales with both model size and pre-training data.

* * *

### 25.7 BERT vs. GPT-1: Architecture Comparison and Diverging Paths

#### Head-to-Head Specification

Dimension | BERT-Base | GPT-1  
---|---|---  
Architecture | Transformer Encoder | Transformer Decoder (no cross-attn)  
Attention direction | Bidirectional (no mask) | Unidirectional (causal mask)  
Pre-training objective | MLM + NSP | Autoregressive LM  
Pre-training data | BooksCorpus + Wikipedia (3.3B words) | BooksCorpus (0.8B words)  
Parameters | 110M | 117M  
Fine-tuning auxiliary loss | None | λLLM\lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}}λLLM​  
Generation capability | None (no joint P(x)P(\mathbf{x})P(x)) | Natural (autoregressively)  
Signal density | ~15% | 100%  
  
#### Who Won in 2018?

By benchmark metrics, BERT won decisively. Every GLUE task, SQuAD, SWAG — BERT-Base outperformed GPT-1 on nearly all of them, and BERT-Large widened the gap further.

But attributing this to BERT's architectural superiority requires care. The two most consequential confounds:

  1. **Data volume** : BERT used 4× more pre-training data.
  2. **Bidirectionality** : for NLU tasks, bidirectional context is structurally more informative.

Liu et al.'s RoBERTa (2019) addressed the data confound by training BERT with 10× more data, eliminating NSP, and training for longer. The result: BERT-style training vastly outperformed the original BERT — indicating that original BERT was significantly undertrained. Much of BERT's 2018 advantage over GPT-1 was data-scale advantage, not bidirectionality advantage.

#### Who Won in the Long Run?

GPT-1 launched a lineage that transformed the field: GPT-1 → GPT-2 → GPT-3 → GPT-4 → ChatGPT. The decoder-only autoregressive paradigm became the architecture of every frontier model, across labs and organizations: GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, Falcon.

BERT's encoder-only paradigm produced excellent successors (RoBERTa, ALBERT, DeBERTa) but remained confined to understanding tasks. No encoder-only model ever demonstrated competitive generative capabilities; the BERT lineage reached its natural limit around 2020–2021.

Why did GPT eventually dominate despite BERT's 2018 benchmark advantage?

  1. **Generation is a core capability** : deploying AI systems in practice almost always requires generating text — answers, summaries, translations, code. Encoder-only models cannot do this; decoder-only models can.

  2. **Unified task interface** : autoregressive models accept any task expressible as "given this prefix, generate the appropriate continuation." Instruction fine-tuning and RLHF leverage this uniformity at scale. BERT requires different heads for different tasks, creating a ceiling on generality.

  3. **Superior scaling properties** : the decoder-only architecture's training loss is more informative per unit of compute (100% signal density), and its capabilities scale more predictably with compute and data (Kaplan et al.'s scaling laws were established on GPT-style models).

  4. **In-context learning** : GPT-2 demonstrated that autoregressive models could perform tasks with only natural-language demonstrations as context, without any gradient update. This capability — absent from encoder-only models — became the foundation of zero-shot and few-shot deployment at scale.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> The BERT vs. GPT competition illustrates general principles of technological trajectory selection with parallels in several fields:
> 
> **Physics — spontaneous symmetry breaking** : A system poised near a bifurcation point evolves into one of two stable configurations depending on small initial perturbations. The 2018 NLP landscape was at such a bifurcation: encoder-bidirectional (BERT) or decoder-autoregressive (GPT) were both viable. BERT's early benchmark success created a perturbation that channeled substantial research investment toward the encoder branch. Yet the underlying "energy landscape" favored the decoder branch at larger scales — the final stable configuration was not determined by 2018 benchmarks.
> 
> **Industrial ecology — platform competition** : Arthur (1989) analyzed technology lock-in: a platform that achieves sufficient early adoption can dominate even if a technically superior alternative exists, through path-dependent network effects. BERT temporarily locked in a research ecosystem (massive publication activity around RoBERTa, ALBERT, ELECTRA, DeBERTa). GPT's ecosystem emerged later but with qualitatively different network properties: application developers could interact through a simple API, generating network effects that academic encoder-model papers did not create.
> 
> **Evolutionary biology — contingency and constraint** : Gould and Lewontin (1979) argued that evolutionary outcomes reflect both adaptive optimization and historical contingency — some outcomes are driven by selection pressure, others by initial conditions. BERT's 2018 victory was partly contingent (more pre-training data, earlier release of fine-tuning recipes) and partly adaptive (bidirectionality genuinely helps NLU). GPT's long-run dominance reflects a deeper selection pressure: the capacity for generation is more generally useful than the capacity for classification-without-generation. In evolutionary terms, the GPT lineage discovered an adaptive peak inaccessible to encoder-only models.

### 25.8 Exercises

#### Concept Checks

**1.** Explain why BERT's MLM achieves "true bidirectionality" while ELMo's bidirectional LSTM does not. What would go wrong if BERT used standard autoregressive language modeling instead of MLM while keeping the bidirectional Transformer encoder?

Answer

**ELMo's shallow bidirectionality** : ELMo trains a forward LSTM (h→k,j\overrightarrow{h}_{k,j}hk,j​) and a backward LSTM (h←k,j\overleftarrow{h}_{k,j}hk,j​) completely independently, then concatenates their hidden states:

hk=γ∑jsj[h→k,j;h←k,j]h_k = \gamma \sum_j s_j \left[\overrightarrow{h}_{k,j}; \overleftarrow{h}_{k,j}\right]hk​=γj∑​sj​[hk,j​;hk,j​]

At every layer jjj, the forward computation at position kkk uses only {x1,…,xk}\\{x_1, \ldots, x_k\\}{x1​,…,xk​} and the backward uses only {xk,…,xn}\\{x_k, \ldots, x_n\\}{xk​,…,xn​}. The two streams never interact within a layer — they are combined only in the final concatenation. This is "shallow fusion": two independent encoders whose outputs are pasted together.

**BERT's deep bidirectionality** : In BERT's Transformer encoder, every attention head at every layer computes:

ht(ℓ)=∑j=1nαtj(ℓ)Vj(ℓ)h_t^{(\ell)} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_{tj}^{(\ell)} V_j^{(\ell)}ht(ℓ)​=j=1∑n​αtj(ℓ)​Vj(ℓ)​

with no masking. Position ttt's representation at layer ℓ\ellℓ is a weighted combination of **all** positions' layer-(ℓ−1)(\ell-1)(ℓ−1) representations — left and right simultaneously. Each layer propagates integrated bidirectional information upward; representations become progressively richer through mutual conditioning across all positions at every layer. This is "deep fusion."

**Why standard LM + bidirectional Transformer fails** : Suppose we apply a standard "predict next token" objective to a Transformer encoder with no causal mask. To predict wtw_twt​, the model can directly attend to wtw_twt​ itself via the attention mechanism — zero effort required. The training loss becomes trivially small not because the model has learned anything useful but because it is memorizing by direct lookup. The model would never learn contextual representations at all; training would produce a system that "predicts" each token by attending to it directly. MLM forces genuine prediction by removing the target token from the input, so the model must use context to infer what was there.

Mathematically: with standard LM and bidirectional attention, ∇θL\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}∇θ​L drives the model to maximize Pθ(wt∣w1,…,wt−1,wt,wt+1,…,wn)P_\theta(w_t \mid w_1, \ldots, w_{t-1}, \mathbf{w_t}, w_{t+1}, \ldots, w_n)Pθ​(wt​∣w1​,…,wt−1​,wt​,wt+1​,…,wn​) — which can approach 1 trivially by assigning maximal attention weight to the ttt-th position. With MLM, the target is Pθ(wt∣w1,…,[MASK],…,wn)P_\theta(w_t \mid w_1, \ldots, \text{[MASK]}, \ldots, w_n)Pθ​(wt​∣w1​,…,[MASK],…,wn​), and wtw_twt​ is unavailable, so the model must genuinely infer from context.

* * *

**2.** The 80/10/10 substitution strategy contains three components (80% [MASK], 10% random token, 10% unchanged). Analyze what pathological behavior would emerge if each component were removed — i.e., consider: (a) 100% [MASK]; (b) 90% [MASK] + 10% random; (c) 90% [MASK] + 10% unchanged.

Answer

**(a) 100% [MASK] — no random substitution, no unchanged tokens** :

_Pre-training/fine-tuning mismatch_ : The model is trained on a distribution where ~15% of positions contain [MASK]; it is deployed on a distribution where 0% of positions contain [MASK]. The model learns representations partly conditioned on detecting [MASK] — features specific to the artificial masking setup that have no meaning in real text. Performance degrades at fine-tuning time because the input distribution is shifted.

Additionally, the model can adopt a lazy strategy: "I only need to produce informative representations at [MASK] positions; at all other positions I can output arbitrary garbage." The 10% random substitution prevents this by making any position potentially "wrong," forcing the model to attend carefully everywhere.

**(b) 90% [MASK] + 10% random — no unchanged tokens** :

The model never encounters authentic tokens during pre-training that require no prediction. Its representations are trained under the assumption that any token might be either [MASK] or a random replacement — never a trustworthy signal. At fine-tuning time, every input token is genuine, but the model has no mechanism for treating genuine tokens differently from potential random substitutions. Representations may be unnecessarily uncertain, reducing the quality of the task-specific features.

More precisely: the 10% unchanged component teaches the model that some positions' tokens are reliable signals to be encoded faithfully. Without it, the model never learns to "trust" any token, which degrades the encoding of genuine context.

**(c) 90% [MASK] + 10% unchanged — no random substitution** :

The model can now distinguish two input types: [MASK] (clearly needs prediction) and genuine tokens (clearly reliable). It learns to exert representational effort primarily at [MASK] positions and use genuine tokens as context passively. This encourages the same "lazy strategy" mentioned in (a): ignoring the possibility that non-[MASK] tokens could be wrong.

At fine-tuning time, the mismatch is smaller because the model sees genuine tokens everywhere (matching the 10% unchanged case). But the model's representations of non-masked positions are lower quality because they were trained under the assumption that those positions are always reliable, never requiring careful self-monitoring. The 10% random substitution specifically trains the model to watch its own context critically — a capability that improves representation quality at all positions.

**Summary** : Each component of 80/10/10 addresses a specific failure mode:

* 80% [MASK]: provides the core MLM training signal.
* 10% random: prevents lazy "attend only to [MASK]" strategy; forces high-quality everywhere.
* 10% unchanged: closes the pre-training/fine-tuning gap; teaches the model to represent genuine tokens faithfully.

* * *

#### Applications

**3.** The autoregressive LM provides 100% signal density (every token contributes to the loss), while MLM provides only ~15% signal density. Yet MLM is bidirectional.

(a) Define "training efficiency" precisely in terms of the expected information gain per forward pass.

(b) Argue whether bidirectionality compensates for lower signal density in terms of the total information extracted per token.

(c) Given that GPT-style models now dominate at scale, what does this suggest about the relative importance of signal density vs. bidirectionality in practice?

Answer

**(a) Training efficiency per forward pass** :

Formally, the gradient signal per forward pass is proportional to the number of positions that contribute to the loss and the magnitude of each contribution. Define per-token information gain as the reduction in DKL(Pdata∥Pθ)D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\text{data}} \| P_\theta)DKL​(Pdata​∥Pθ​) from one gradient update on that token. Then:

* Autoregressive LM: nnn positions contribute; expected total gradient norm is ∝∑t=1n∇θlog⁡Pθ(wt∣w<t)\propto \sum_{t=1}^n \nabla_\theta \log P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})∝∑t=1n​∇θ​logPθ​(wt​∣w<t​).
* MLM: ∣M∣≈0.15n|\mathcal{M}| \approx 0.15n∣M∣≈0.15n positions contribute; expected total gradient norm is ∝∑t∈M∇θlog⁡Pθ(xt∣x\M)\propto \sum_{t \in \mathcal{M}} \nabla_\theta \log P_\theta(x_t \mid \mathbf{x}_{\backslash \mathcal{M}})∝∑t∈M​∇θ​logPθ​(xt​∣x\M​).

For equal sequence length nnn and equal model size, the autoregressive forward pass produces ∼6.7×\sim 6.7\times∼6.7× more gradient terms. _Per forward pass_ , autoregressive LM is more training-efficient.

**(b) Bidirectionality and per-token information content** :

The information in a single MLM prediction is the conditional entropy H(xt∣x\M)H(x_t \mid \mathbf{x}_{\backslash \mathcal{M}})H(xt​∣x\M​) with full bidirectional context. The information in a single autoregressive prediction is H(wt∣w<t)H(w_t \mid w_{<t})H(wt​∣w<t​) with left-only context. Since right context typically reduces uncertainty:

H(xt∣x\M)≤H(wt∣w<t)H(x_t \mid \mathbf{x}_{\backslash \mathcal{M}}) \leq H(w_t \mid w_{<t})H(xt​∣x\M​)≤H(wt​∣w<t​)

Each MLM prediction is therefore more constrained (lower entropy) than each autoregressive prediction — it carries less uncertainty to be resolved, meaning the gradient contains less "surprise" per prediction. Bidirectionality and lower signal density partially offset each other.

However, this offset is at most 1/0.15≈6.7×1/0.15 \approx 6.7\times1/0.15≈6.7×, and only if right-context uncertainty reduction exactly compensates. In practice, right context does not eliminate that much uncertainty (English redundancy from right context is lower than from left context for many constructions), so the offset is partial. MLM remains less signal-dense than autoregressive LM even accounting for bidirectionality.

**(c) Implications of GPT dominance at scale** :

The empirical record (scaling law experiments, RoBERTa, GPT-2/3/4 performance) suggests that, at scale, **signal density matters more than bidirectionality** for general capability. Three reasons:

  1. _Compute constraint at scale_ : when training on trillions of tokens, the marginal token is never seen again (Kaplan et al. recommend ∼\sim∼1 pass through the dataset at optimal scale). Maximizing signal per token-pass is critical. Autoregressive LM extracts 6.7× more gradient signal per forward pass at the same token count.

  2. _Bidirectionality advantages are task-specific_ : bidirectional context primarily helps span-level understanding tasks (NER, NLI). For generation, reasoning, code, and instruction following — the dominant use cases for frontier models — autoregressive training is at least as appropriate.

  3. _Scale subsumes architectural inductive bias_ : at sufficient parameter counts and data volumes, the model can learn effective representations even from left-only context. The structural advantage of bidirectionality shrinks as the model becomes more powerful at generalizing from any incomplete context.

The conclusion is not that bidirectionality has no value — BERT-family models remain competitive on pure NLU benchmarks — but that, for general-purpose large-scale systems, autoregressive training's efficiency advantage outweighs bidirectionality's representational advantage.

* * *

**4.** BERT's ablation (Section 5.3 of Devlin et al.) shows that removing NSP affects QNLI far more than SST-2 (QNLI drops 3.5 points; SST-2 is unchanged). Explain this differential effect mechanistically. What does this reveal about what NSP learned?

Answer

**SST-2** (Stanford Sentiment Treebank-2): single-sentence binary sentiment classification. The model receives one sentence and must output positive/negative. No inter-sentence relationship is required; the entire task is resolved by attending to sentiment-bearing words within the single sentence ("excellent," "boring," "compelling").

**QNLI** (Question-answering Natural Language Inference): given a question and a passage, classify whether the passage contains the answer. This is a **sentence-pair task** — the model must determine whether a specific semantic relationship (question-answering entailment) holds between two distinct text units.

**Why NSP differentially affects QNLI** :

NSP trains the model on a binary classification of sentence-pair coherence. Although the specific relationship (next-in-document vs. random) is not identical to question-answering entailment, NSP develops the model's capacity to:

  1. Maintain a joint representation of two text segments via [CLS].
  2. Detect semantic dependencies between segments (coherence, topical continuity).
  3. Map cross-segment interactions to a global binary decision.

These capacities transfer partially to QNLI: both require detecting whether segment B is a semantically appropriate "response" to segment A. Removing NSP leaves the model without this sentence-pair reasoning training, causing performance degradation on QNLI.

For SST-2, none of these capacities are required — the task uses a single sentence. NSP's training signal contributes nothing to single-sentence representations. Its removal causes exactly zero effect.

**What this reveals about NSP** :

NSP did learn _something_ — a sentence-pair compatibility function transferable to other sentence-pair tasks. It failed to improve BERT's aggregate performance primarily because:

  1. Most GLUE tasks are single-sentence (SST-2, CoLA) or have alternative strong signals (MNLI, whose size makes NSP redundant).
  2. The NSP capability that does transfer (to QNLI) is narrow and could be achieved more efficiently.

RoBERTa's ablation complements this: removing NSP and replacing it with longer documents (ensuring the model always sees authentic document-consecutive sentences) actually _improves_ performance on sentence-pair tasks. This suggests NSP's random-negative design was the failure, not the sentence-pair objective itself — using within-document sentence pairs as context (without an artificial NSP task) trains better inter-sentence representations than the binary NSP classifier.

* * *

**5.** Verify BERT-Base's parameter count for its multi-head self-attention component. BERT-Base has dmodel=768d_{\text{model}} = 768dmodel​=768, h=12h = 12h=12 attention heads, and 12 encoder layers.

Compute:

(b) The per-head key dimensionality dkd_kdk​ and verify it satisfies the parameter-count formula from Chapter 22.

(c) The fraction of BERT-Base's 110M total parameters attributable to MHA layers.

Answer

**(a) MHA parameters per encoder layer** :

The four projection matrices each have shape Rdmodel×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}}Rdmodel​×dmodel​:

* WQW^QWQ: 768×768=589,824768 \times 768 = 589{,}824768×768=589,824 weights + 768768768 bias = 590,592590{,}592590,592
* WKW^KWK: same = 590,592590{,}592590,592
* WVW^VWV: same = 590,592590{,}592590,592
* WOW^OWO: same = 590,592590{,}592590,592

Total MHA parameters per layer: 4×590,592=2,362,368≈2.36M4 \times 590{,}592 = 2{,}362{,}368 \approx 2.36\text{M}4×590,592=2,362,368≈2.36M.

**(b) Per-head key dimensionality** :

From Chapter 22: dk=dmodel/h=768/12=64d_k = d_{\text{model}} / h = 768 / 12 = 64dk​=dmodel​/h=768/12=64.

In multi-head attention, each of the 12 heads operates on a 64-dimensional subspace. The combined projection WQ∈R768×768W^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{768 \times 768}WQ∈R768×768 can be decomposed into 12 head projections WiQ∈R768×64W_i^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{768 \times 64}WiQ​∈R768×64, and similarly for WKW^KWK, WVW^VWV. The full dmodel×dmodeld_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}dmodel​×dmodel​ matrix structure is equivalent to stacking hhh head projections:

WQ=[W1QW2Q⋮W12Q]∈Rdmodel×dmodelW^Q = \begin{bmatrix} W_1^Q \\\ W_2^Q \\\ \vdots \\\ W_{12}^Q \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}}WQ=​W1Q​W2Q​⋮W12Q​​​∈Rdmodel​×dmodel​

Parameter count formula: 4×dmodel2=4×7682=2,359,296≈2.36M4 \times d_{\text{model}}^2 = 4 \times 768^2 = 2{,}359{,}296 \approx 2.36\text{M}4×dmodel2​=4×7682=2,359,296≈2.36M (plus bias terms 4×768=3,0724 \times 768 = 3{,}0724×768=3,072). Total: 2,362,3682{,}362{,}3682,362,368. ✓ (consistent with (a)).

**(c) Fraction of 110M from MHA** :

* MHA per layer: ≈2.36M\approx 2.36\text{M}≈2.36M
* 12 layers: 12×2.36=28.3M12 \times 2.36 = 28.3\text{M}12×2.36=28.3M
* Fraction: 28.3/110≈25.7%28.3 / 110 \approx 25.7\%28.3/110≈25.7%

Cross-check with FFN:

* FFN per layer: 2×dmodel×dff=2×768×3072≈4.72M2 \times d_{\text{model}} \times d_{ff} = 2 \times 768 \times 3072 \approx 4.72\text{M}2×dmodel​×dff​=2×768×3072≈4.72M plus biases ≈0.004M\approx 0.004\text{M}≈0.004M
* 12 layers: ≈56.7M\approx 56.7\text{M}≈56.7M
* Fraction: ≈51.5%\approx 51.5\%≈51.5%

Parameter distribution:

Component | Parameters | Fraction  
---|---|---  
Token/Position/Segment Embeddings | ~23.8M | ~21.6%  
MHA (all 12 layers) | ~28.3M | ~25.7%

This breakdown reveals that the FFN dominates BERT's parameters (~51%), not the attention mechanism. The FFN's high parameter count (4× expansion ratio: 768→3072→768768 \to 3072 \to 768768→3072→768) makes it the primary storage medium for factual knowledge, consistent with Geva et al.'s (2021) finding that FFN layers act as key-value memories (Chapter 23).

* * *

**7.** Two approaches for adapting a pre-trained BERT model to a downstream classification task:

**Approach A (Feature extraction):** Freeze all BERT parameters. Extract the [CLS] token representation from the final layer. Train only a new linear classifier on top.

**Approach B (Full fine-tuning):** Initialize with pre-trained weights, then update ALL parameters (BERT + classifier) on the downstream task with a small learning rate.

(a) Compare the number of trainable parameters for each approach on a 2-class sentiment task (BERT-Base has 110M parameters). (b) For a downstream dataset of only 500 labeled examples, which approach would you recommend and why? (c) For a downstream dataset of 100,000 labeled examples, which approach would you recommend? (d) A third approach, **adapter tuning** , inserts small trainable bottleneck layers (e.g., 0.5M parameters) inside the frozen BERT model. What advantage does this have over both A and B?

Answer

**(a)** Approach A: trainable parameters = classifier only = 768×2+2=1,538768 \times 2 + 2 = 1{,}538768×2+2=1,538 (linear layer from [CLS] dimension to 2 classes). Approach B: trainable parameters = 110M+1,538≈110M110M + 1{,}538 \approx 110M110M+1,538≈110M. Approach B has ~71,000× more trainable parameters.

**(b)** For 500 examples: **Approach A** (feature extraction). With only 500 examples, fine-tuning 110M parameters risks severe overfitting — the model can memorize the training set without learning generalizable patterns. Feature extraction is more robust: BERT's pre-trained representations are already rich, and a linear classifier can find a good decision boundary with limited data. This is analogous to the bias-variance tradeoff (Chapter 2): fewer trainable parameters = lower variance = better generalization when data is scarce.

**(c)** For 100,000 examples: **Approach B** (full fine-tuning). With sufficient data, overfitting is less of a concern, and fine-tuning allows BERT's representations to adapt to the specific task distribution. The pre-trained weights serve as a strong initialization (low bias), and the large dataset provides enough signal to update without overfitting (manageable variance). Empirically, full fine-tuning outperforms feature extraction when data is sufficient.

**(d)** Adapter tuning combines the benefits: (1) Like A, most parameters are frozen → low overfitting risk, efficient storage (one BERT copy + small adapter per task). (2) Like B, the adapter layers can adapt the representation nonlinearly → better than pure linear classification. (3) For multi-task deployment: store one frozen BERT + one adapter per task, vs. one full BERT copy per task. With 10 tasks: adapter = 110M + 10×0.5M = 115M total, vs. fine-tuning = 10×110M = 1.1B total.

* * *

#### Think Deeper

**6.** GPT-1 demonstrated zero-shot performance improvements on multiple tasks as a function of pre-training steps — without any fine-tuning. This signal was small in 2018 but proved highly predictive.

(a) From an information-theoretic perspective, why should zero-shot performance on any task TTT be a monotonically non-decreasing function of pre-training loss improvement?

(b) If the zero-shot capability of an autoregressive LM on a specific task TTT is a function of model parameters θ\thetaθ, and pre-training loss is a function of θ\thetaθ, what theoretical condition is required for the GPT-1 zero-shot observation to hold?

(c) GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) showed "emergent" zero-shot capabilities that appeared discontinuously as scale increased. Reconcile this with the smooth monotonic argument from (a).

Answer

**(a) Monotonicity argument** :

Pre-training loss L(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta)L(θ) is related to the KL divergence from the true language distribution: L(θ)=H(Pdata)+DKL(Pdata∥Pθ)\mathcal{L}(\theta) = H(P_{\text{data}}) + D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\text{data}} \| P_\theta)L(θ)=H(Pdata​)+DKL​(Pdata​∥Pθ​). Lower loss → smaller DKLD_{\text{KL}}DKL​ → PθP_\thetaPθ​ more closely approximates PdataP_{\text{data}}Pdata​.

For any task TTT that can be expressed as a conditional distribution over text (classification P(y∣x)P(y \mid x)P(y∣x), generation P(answer∣question)P(\text{answer} \mid \text{question})P(answer∣question)), the correct behavior on TTT is a property of PdataP_{\text{data}}Pdata​ — the distribution of natural language produced by competent humans. A model whose distribution is closer to PdataP_{\text{data}}Pdata​ will, by continuity, produce outputs that more closely approximate correct task behavior, at least in expectation over many instances.

Formally: if task performance πT(θ)\pi_T(\theta)πT​(θ) is a continuous functional of PθP_\thetaPθ​, and Pθ→PdataP_\theta \to P_{\text{data}}Pθ​→Pdata​ monotonically as training proceeds, then πT(θ)\pi_T(\theta)πT​(θ) is monotonically non-decreasing. The condition is continuity of πT\pi_TπT​ as a functional — reasonable for any task whose correct outputs are typical under PdataP_{\text{data}}Pdata​.

**(b) Required theoretical condition** :

The zero-shot observation requires that task performance is a **monotone function of the model's language modeling accuracy**. This holds under:

  1. **Task consistency** : the correct output for task TTT is consistently expressed in the pre-training corpus (e.g., question-answer patterns appear frequently in books and web text). If TTT's correct behavior is rare or absent in the pre-training distribution, better language modeling need not improve TTT.

  2. **No competing signal** : the pre-training distribution does not contain systematically incorrect task demonstrations that could improve LM loss while degrading task performance.

  3. **Sufficient capacity** : the model has enough parameters to simultaneously improve LM performance and improve latent task-relevant features. For small models, there may be trade-offs between compression for LM loss and preservation of task-relevant representations.

If these conditions hold, the map L(θ)→πT(θ)\mathcal{L}(\theta) \to \pi_T(\theta)L(θ)→πT​(θ) is monotone non-decreasing, and the GPT-1 observation follows.

**(c) Reconciling emergence with smooth monotonicity** :

The apparent contradiction dissolves by distinguishing between two levels:

**Continuous at the level of representations** : The internal representations of the model improve continuously with pre-training and with scale. Probing experiments confirm that task-relevant features (syntactic structure, entity coreference, factual knowledge) are present in the representations at all scales, and become progressively stronger at larger scale.

**Discontinuous at the level of task performance metrics** : Tasks like multi-step arithmetic, chain-of-thought reasoning, and multi-hop question answering have high "capability thresholds" — they require the composition of many sub-capabilities, all of which must be sufficiently reliable for the end-to-end task to succeed. Each sub-capability improves smoothly; but the composed task performance, being roughly the product of sub-capability reliabilities, undergoes a rapid transition near the threshold where all sub-capabilities exceed some minimum. This is a **phase transition in a product of probabilities** : if p1,p2,…,pkp_1, p_2, \ldots, p_kp1​,p2​,…,pk​ each increase smoothly from 0 toward 1, their product ∏ipi\prod_i p_i∏i​pi​ increases slowly until all pip_ipi​ are near 1, then increases rapidly. Observed task performance appears to "emerge" discontinuously even though the underlying sub-capabilities grow smoothly.

This reconciliation implies that emergence is not a fundamental property of the system but an artifact of measuring end-to-end performance on high-threshold tasks. Wei et al. (2022) provide empirical support: "emergent" capabilities can sometimes be made continuous by switching to smoother evaluation metrics.

* * *

**8.** The Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task in BERT was later shown to be unnecessary (RoBERTa, Liu et al. 2019 achieved equal or better performance without it).

(a) The NSP task constructs negative examples by pairing sentence A with a random sentence B from the corpus. What confound does this introduce? (Hint: consider what features distinguish a random sentence from the true next sentence.) (b) An alternative pre-training objective, **Sentence Order Prediction (SOP)** , uses actual consecutive sentences but swaps their order for negative examples. Why does SOP avoid the NSP confound? (c) Design a thought experiment to test whether BERT's NSP head learns inter-sentence coherence (as intended) or merely topic similarity (the confound). Describe your experimental setup and what results would confirm each hypothesis.

Answer

**(a)** The confound: a random sentence B is likely from a completely different document and therefore a different topic. The model can distinguish "true next" from "random" simply by checking whether A and B share vocabulary and topic — without learning anything about logical coherence or discourse structure. The NSP head learns a topic classifier, not a coherence classifier. This is a **construct validity** problem: the task measures the wrong thing.

**(b)** SOP uses consecutive sentences in both positive (correct order: A→B) and negative (swapped: B→A) examples. Since both orderings contain the same two sentences from the same document, they share identical topics and vocabulary. The only signal for discrimination is the logical flow and discourse markers ("however," "therefore," "after that"). SOP forces the model to learn genuine coherence, not topic matching.

**(c)** **Setup** : Take 1000 sentence pairs from a test corpus. Create three conditions: (i) True consecutive pairs (A, B); (ii) Same-document random pairs (A, B' where B' is from the same document but not adjacent); (iii) Cross-document random pairs (A, B'' from a different document). Run BERT's NSP head on all three. **Prediction if NSP learns coherence** : (i) high "IsNext" score, (ii) low score (same topic but not coherent), (iii) low score. **Prediction if NSP learns topic** : (i) high score, (ii) high score (same topic), (iii) low score. The discriminating condition is (ii): if same-document non-adjacent pairs score high, NSP is detecting topic, not coherence. Empirical results (Shi & Demberg 2019) confirm the topic hypothesis — validating the confound.

### Chapter Summary

Concept | Key Idea  
---|---  
Transfer learning | Pre-train on large unlabeled corpus; fine-tune on small labeled data; knowledge learned in pre-training transfers to downstream tasks  
MLM (Masked LM) | BERT's core objective; mask 15% of tokens, predict them from bidirectional context; enables true deep fusion of left and right information  
Autoregressive LM | GPT's objective; predict the next token from left context only; 100% signal density; natural generation capability  
NSP | BERT's auxiliary task; limited benefit because negative samples are too easy (topic-distinguishable) without requiring genuine logical inference  
Self-supervised learning | Labels come from the data itself; enables training on trillion-token corpora without annotation cost  
Information-theoretic foundation | Minimizing cross-entropy ≡\equiv≡ minimizing DKL(Pdata∥Pθ)D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\text{data}} \| P_\theta)DKL​(Pdata​∥Pθ​) ≡\equiv≡ MLE; better LM loss implies better language model  
80/10/10 strategy | 80% [MASK] for signal; 10% random token to prevent lazy attention; 10% unchanged to close pre-train/fine-tune gap  
BERT fine-tuning | One pre-trained model → four structurally different task types → same two steps (load weights; add linear head; train end-to-end)  
GPT-1 input transformations | All task types reduced to token sequences via special delimiters; same Transformer handles all  
Signal density vs. bidirectionality | Autoregressive LM: 100% signal, left-context only; MLM: 15% signal, bidirectional; at scale, signal density advantage dominates  
BERT won 2018 | By benchmark metrics; but confounded by 4× more pre-training data  
GPT won long run | Generation, unified task interface, superior scaling, in-context learning; decoder-only paradigm now universal at frontier scale  
Zero-shot emergent capability | GPT-1 showed monotonic zero-shot improvement with pre-training; GPT-2/3 showed discontinuous emergence from task-composition thresholds
