**Introduction**

This final chapter closes the circle that began in Chapter 1. We have built up the mathematical machinery — gradient descent, backpropagation, attention — and watched it crystallize into the Transformer architecture and the pre-training paradigm. Now we go back to first principles and ask: what exactly is a language model doing, in precise probabilistic terms? What does it mean for a language model to be "good"? How does raw text become the token sequences that flow through a Transformer? And why have decoder-only models come to dominate the field over encoder-only and encoder-decoder alternatives?

These questions have rigorous answers grounded in probability theory, information theory, and algorithmic design. The mathematics here is not decorative — it determines what loss functions to use, how to interpret evaluation metrics, how to control text generation at inference time, and why certain architectural choices scale better than others. Understanding these foundations enables you to read and evaluate any technical paper in the field, design experiments, and reason about model behavior in deployment.

* * *

### 26.1 The Autoregressive Decomposition

#### Chain Rule of Probability: An Exact Identity

The mathematical core of autoregressive language modeling is the **chain rule of probability**. For any sequence of random variables w1,w2,…,wTw_1, w_2, \ldots, w_Tw1​,w2​,…,wT​:

P(w1,w2,…,wT)=∏t=1TP(wt∣w1,w2,…,wt−1)P(w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(w_t \mid w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_{t-1})P(w1​,w2​,…,wT​)=t=1∏T​P(wt​∣w1​,w2​,…,wt−1​)

Using the shorthand w<t=(w1,…,wt−1)w_{<t} = (w_1, \ldots, w_{t-1})w<t​=(w1​,…,wt−1​):

P(w)=∏t=1TP(wt∣w<t)P(\mathbf{w}) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(w_t \mid w_{<t})P(w)=t=1∏T​P(wt​∣w<t​)

This is an **exact identity with no approximation**. It follows from the definition of conditional probability applied recursively: P(A,B)=P(A)P(B∣A)P(A, B) = P(A) P(B \mid A)P(A,B)=P(A)P(B∣A), extended to TTT variables. Any autoregressive language model that approximates each conditional P(wt∣w<t)P(w_t \mid w_{<t})P(wt​∣w<t​) with a parameterized function Pθ(wt∣w<t)P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​) is simply approximating this factored form.

**Why left-to-right?** The chain rule permits factoring in any order — right-to-left, even random permutation order (as explored by XLNet). Left-to-right is the natural choice because it matches the order in which text is written and read, and — crucially — it produces models that can generate new text by repeating the operation: predict token ttt given tokens 1,…,t−11, \ldots, t-11,…,t−1; append the prediction; advance ttt.

#### Parameterizing Each Conditional

In a Transformer language model, each conditional is computed as:

Pθ(wt=v∣w<t)=softmax(Whead⋅htL+b)[v]P_\theta(w_t = v \mid w_{<t}) = \text{softmax}(W_{\text{head}} \cdot h_t^L + b)[v]Pθ​(wt​=v∣w<t​)=softmax(Whead​⋅htL​+b)[v]

where:

* htL∈Rdmodelh_t^L \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}htL​∈Rdmodel​ is the final-layer Transformer hidden state at position ttt
* Whead∈R∣V∣×dmodelW_{\text{head}} \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d_{\text{model}}}Whead​∈R∣V∣×dmodel​ is the language model head projection
* ∣V∣|V|∣V∣ is the vocabulary size
* The output is a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary

The intermediate vector z=Whead⋅htL+b∈R∣V∣\mathbf{z} = W_{\text{head}} \cdot h_t^L + b \in \mathbb{R}^{|V|}z=Whead​⋅htL​+b∈R∣V∣ is called the **logit vector**. Each element zvz_vzv​ represents an unnormalized score for vocabulary item vvv. Softmax converts scores to probabilities:

Pθ(wt=v∣w<t)=exp⁡(zv)∑v′=1∣V∣exp⁡(zv′)P_\theta(w_t = v \mid w_{<t}) = \frac{\exp(z_v)}{\sum_{v'=1}^{|V|} \exp(z_{v'})}Pθ​(wt​=v∣w<t​)=∑v′=1∣V∣​exp(zv′​)exp(zv​)​

This is identical to the multinomial logit model in discrete choice theory — the model assigns a "utility" zvz_vzv​ to each vocabulary item and converts utilities to choice probabilities via the logit transformation.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> Autoregressive decomposition and its analogues appear across several quantitative sciences:
> 
> **Statistical physics — Markov chain factoring** : The Boltzmann probability of a spin configuration σ1,σ2,…,σN\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \ldots, \sigma_Nσ1​,σ2​,…,σN​ in an Ising model can be factored via the transfer matrix method into a product of conditional probabilities, one per site, analogous to the language model's per-token factoring. The "energy" of each spin configuration given its neighbors corresponds to the logit contribution of each token given its context. Exactly as language model training minimizes cross-entropy to match the empirical text distribution, statistical mechanics equilibrium distributions minimize free energy to match the thermal distribution.
> 
> **Signal processing — autoregressive (AR) processes** : A linear AR(p) process models each sample as a linear combination of the ppp most recent samples plus noise: xt=∑k=1pakxt−k+εtx_t = \sum_{k=1}^p a_k x_{t-k} + \varepsilon_txt​=∑k=1p​ak​xt−k​+εt​. This is a Gaussian-linear special case of the general autoregressive language model — the Transformer is a highly nonlinear, discrete-vocabulary generalization of AR processes with effectively infinite order (p=t−1p = t-1p=t−1). Yule-Walker equations for fitting AR models are the early-1900s analogue of modern gradient-descent training for language models.
> 
> **Psycholinguistics — incremental sentence processing** : Human sentence comprehension is incremental: readers process words sequentially, building a probabilistic prediction of upcoming words before they appear (surprisal theory, Hale 2001; Levy 2008). The cognitive "processing difficulty" at word ttt is proportional to −log⁡P(wt∣w<t)-\log P(w_t \mid w_{<t})−logP(wt​∣w<t​) — the same quantity language models minimize. This parallel is not metaphorical: neural language model surprisal correlates with human reading times and EEG responses, suggesting that both biological and artificial language processors implement variants of the same autoregressive prediction objective.

* * *

### 26.2 Cross-Entropy Loss: Complete Derivation

#### Starting Point: Maximum Likelihood Estimation

Given training corpus D={w1,w2,…,wT}\mathcal{D} = \\{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_T\\}D={w1​,w2​,…,wT​} (treated as a single token sequence for simplicity), we seek parameters θ\thetaθ that maximize the probability of the observed data:

max⁡θ Pθ(D)=max⁡θ ∏t=1TPθ(wt∣w<t)\max_\theta \; P_\theta(\mathcal{D}) = \max_\theta \; \prod_{t=1}^{T} P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})θmax​Pθ​(D)=θmax​t=1∏T​Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​)

Taking logarithms (which preserves the arg⁡max⁡\arg\maxargmax and converts products to sums):

max⁡θ log⁡Pθ(D)=max⁡θ ∑t=1Tlog⁡Pθ(wt∣w<t)\max_\theta \; \log P_\theta(\mathcal{D}) = \max_\theta \; \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})θmax​logPθ​(D)=θmax​t=1∑T​logPθ​(wt​∣w<t​)

Equivalently, minimizing the **negative log-likelihood (NLL)** :

LNLL(θ)=−1T∑t=1Tlog⁡Pθ(wt∣w<t)\mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})LNLL​(θ)=−T1​t=1∑T​logPθ​(wt​∣w<t​)

The 1/T1/T1/T normalization gives a per-token average loss that enables fair comparison across sequences of different lengths.

#### Why This Is Cross-Entropy

At position ttt, the training data provides one observed word wtw_twt​. We can represent this as a **one-hot distribution** over the vocabulary:

P∗(v∣w<t)={1v=wt0v≠wtP^*(v \mid w_{<t}) = \begin{cases} 1 & v = w_t \\\ 0 & v \neq w_t \end{cases}P∗(v∣w<t​)={10​v=wt​v=wt​​

The **cross-entropy** between true distribution P∗P^*P∗ and model distribution PθP_\thetaPθ​ is defined as:

H(P∗,Pθ)=−∑v∈VP∗(v∣w<t)⋅log⁡Pθ(v∣w<t)H(P^*, P_\theta) = -\sum_{v \in V} P^*(v \mid w_{<t}) \cdot \log P_\theta(v \mid w_{<t})H(P∗,Pθ​)=−v∈V∑​P∗(v∣w<t​)⋅logPθ​(v∣w<t​)

Substituting the one-hot P∗P^*P∗:

H(P∗,Pθ)=−∑v∈V1[v=wt]⋅log⁡Pθ(v∣w<t)=−log⁡Pθ(wt∣w<t)H(P^*, P_\theta) = -\sum_{v \in V} \mathbf{1}[v = w_t] \cdot \log P_\theta(v \mid w_{<t}) = -\log P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})H(P∗,Pθ​)=−v∈V∑​1[v=wt​]⋅logPθ​(v∣w<t​)=−logPθ​(wt​∣w<t​)

Since all terms except v=wtv = w_tv=wt​ are zero. Averaging over TTT positions:

LCE(θ)=1T∑t=1TH(P∗,Pθ)=−1T∑t=1Tlog⁡Pθ(wt∣w<t)=LNLL(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} H(P^*, P_\theta) = -\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}}(\theta)LCE​(θ)=T1​t=1∑T​H(P∗,Pθ​)=−T1​t=1∑T​logPθ​(wt​∣w<t​)=LNLL​(θ)

This establishes the fundamental equivalence:

Maximum Likelihood Estimation ⟺ Minimize Cross-Entropy ⟺ Minimize Negative Log-Likelihood\boxed{\text{Maximum Likelihood Estimation} \;\iff\; \text{Minimize Cross-Entropy} \;\iff\; \text{Minimize Negative Log-Likelihood}}Maximum Likelihood Estimation⟺Minimize Cross-Entropy⟺Minimize Negative Log-Likelihood​

#### The KL Divergence Connection

The cross-entropy decomposes as:

H(P,Q)=H(P)+DKL(P∥Q)H(P, Q) = H(P) + D_{\text{KL}}(P \| Q)H(P,Q)=H(P)+DKL​(P∥Q)

**Proof** :

H(P,Q)=−∑vP(v)log⁡Q(v)=−∑vP(v)log⁡P(v)+∑vP(v)log⁡P(v)Q(v)=H(P)+DKL(P∥Q)H(P, Q) = -\sum_v P(v) \log Q(v) = -\sum_v P(v) \log P(v) + \sum_v P(v) \log \frac{P(v)}{Q(v)} = H(P) + D_{\text{KL}}(P \| Q)H(P,Q)=−v∑​P(v)logQ(v)=−v∑​P(v)logP(v)+v∑​P(v)logQ(v)P(v)​=H(P)+DKL​(P∥Q)

For the one-hot training distribution, H(P∗)=−1⋅log⁡1=0H(P^*) = -1 \cdot \log 1 = 0H(P∗)=−1⋅log1=0, so H(P∗,Pθ)=DKL(P∗∥Pθ)H(P^*, P_\theta) = D_{\text{KL}}(P^* \| P_\theta)H(P∗,Pθ​)=DKL​(P∗∥Pθ​) — minimizing cross-entropy loss is exactly minimizing the KL divergence from the training data to the model.

At the level of the full data distribution PdataP_{\text{data}}Pdata​:

LCE(θ)=H(Pdata)+Ew<t[DKL ⁣(Pdata(⋅∣w<t) ∥ Pθ(⋅∣w<t))]\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(\theta) = H(P_{\text{data}}) + \mathbb{E}_{w_{<t}}\left[D_{\text{KL}}\\!\left(P_{\text{data}}(\cdot \mid w_{<t}) \;\|\; P_\theta(\cdot \mid w_{<t})\right)\right]LCE​(θ)=H(Pdata​)+Ew<t​​[DKL​(Pdata​(⋅∣w<t​)∥Pθ​(⋅∣w<t​))]

The first term H(Pdata)H(P_{\text{data}})H(Pdata​) — the intrinsic entropy of natural language — is a constant independent of θ\thetaθ. The second term is the expected KL divergence, the part the model can reduce.

**Training interpretation** : every gradient step reduces DKL(Pdata∥Pθ)D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\text{data}} \| P_\theta)DKL​(Pdata​∥Pθ​). The theoretical minimum of the loss is H(Pdata)H(P_{\text{data}})H(Pdata​) — reached only when the model perfectly replicates the statistical structure of natural language. In practice, the model reaches some point above this floor, and the gap measures the quality of the learned distribution.

**Directionality** : the forward KL DKL(Pdata∥Pθ)D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\text{data}} \| P_\theta)DKL​(Pdata​∥Pθ​) penalizes the model whenever PθP_\thetaPθ​ assigns low probability to a location that PdataP_{\text{data}}Pdata​ assigns high probability. This "mode-covering" behavior forces the model to represent all observed linguistic patterns, which is exactly what we want in a language model.

### 26.3 Perplexity: Definition, Interpretation, and Use

#### Definition

**Perplexity (PPL)** is the standard evaluation metric for language models. It is the exponential of the per-token cross-entropy:

PPL(w)=exp⁡ ⁣(LCE)=exp⁡ ⁣(−1T∑t=1Tlog⁡Pθ(wt∣w<t))\text{PPL}(\mathbf{w}) = \exp\\!\left(\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}\right) = \exp\\!\left(-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})\right)PPL(w)=exp(LCE​)=exp(−T1​t=1∑T​logPθ​(wt​∣w<t​))

#### Three Equivalent Forms

Using the laws of exponents and logarithms:

**Form 1 — geometric mean of inverse probabilities** :

PPL=[∏t=1T1Pθ(wt∣w<t)]1/T\text{PPL} = \left[\prod_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})}\right]^{1/T}PPL=[t=1∏T​Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​)1​]1/T

**Form 2 — normalized inverse sequence probability** :

PPL=Pθ(w)−1/T\text{PPL} = P_\theta(\mathbf{w})^{-1/T}PPL=Pθ​(w)−1/T

where Pθ(w)=∏tPθ(wt∣w<t)P_\theta(\mathbf{w}) = \prod_t P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})Pθ​(w)=∏t​Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​) is the model's probability of the full sequence.

**Form 3 — effective branching factor** (the intuitive interpretation):

Suppose at every position the model assigns equal probability 1/B1/B1/B to BBB candidate words. Then:

Pθ(wt∣w<t)=1/B for all t⇒PPL=[∏tB]1/T=BP_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}) = 1/B \;\text{ for all } t \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{PPL} = \left[\prod_t B\right]^{1/T} = BPθ​(wt​∣w<t​)=1/B for all t⇒PPL=[t∏​B]1/T=B

Perplexity equals the uniform branching factor that produces the same sequence probability. More generally: **a model with PPL = BBB behaves as if it is choosing uniformly among BBB equally plausible candidates at each step.**

#### Boundary Cases

Model type | PPL | Interpretation  
---|---|---  
Perfect model (Pθ(wt∣w<t)=1P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}) = 1Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​)=1 always) | 1 | No uncertainty; impossible for natural language  
Uniform random (Pθ=1/∥V∥P_\theta = 1/\|V\|Pθ​=1/∥V∥ always) | ∥V∥\|V\|∥V∥ | Equally lost at every position  
n-gram (trigram) | 200–500 | Captures local statistics only  
LSTM language model | 50–100 | Learns grammar and some semantics  
GPT-2 (1.5B parameters) | 15–25 | Near-human prediction on broad text  
GPT-3 (175B parameters) | 8–15 | Approaches and sometimes exceeds Shannon's bound  
Shannon (1951) theoretical lower bound | ~32–181 | Based on human prediction experiments  
  
**Why do modern models beat Shannon's estimate?** Shannon (1951) had human subjects predict text one character at a time and estimated entropy from their success rates. Humans do not maintain context effectively beyond ~20 words and cannot access the internet's worth of world knowledge. Modern LLMs with long context windows, large vocabularies, and extensive world knowledge systematically exploit more of the available information, achieving lower perplexity than human predictors.

#### Numerical Example

Consider 4-token sequence "The cat sat down" with predicted probabilities:

Position ttt | Token wtw_twt​ | Pθ(wt∣w<t)P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​) | −log⁡Pθ-\log P_\theta−logPθ​  
---|---|---|---  
1 | The | 0.05 | 2.996  
2 | cat | 0.01 | 4.605  
3 | sat | 0.15 | 1.897  
4 | down | 0.08 | 2.526  
LCE=2.996+4.605+1.897+2.5264=12.0244=3.006\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} = \frac{2.996 + 4.605 + 1.897 + 2.526}{4} = \frac{12.024}{4} = 3.006LCE​=42.996+4.605+1.897+2.526​=412.024​=3.006 PPL=e3.006≈20.2\text{PPL} = e^{3.006} \approx 20.2PPL=e3.006≈20.2

Verification via Form 1: (1/0.05×1/0.01×1/0.15×1/0.08)1/4=(20×100×6.67×12.5)0.25=166,7500.25≈20.2(1/0.05 \times 1/0.01 \times 1/0.15 \times 1/0.08)^{1/4} = (20 \times 100 \times 6.67 \times 12.5)^{0.25} = 166{,}750^{0.25} \approx 20.2(1/0.05×1/0.01×1/0.15×1/0.08)1/4=(20×100×6.67×12.5)0.25=166,7500.25≈20.2 ✓

The model behaves as if it is choosing among approximately 20 equally plausible words at each step. The "cat" position dominates (probability 0.01 = 1/100), pulling the geometric mean up substantially.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> Perplexity as an effective branching factor has exact structural analogues in three fields:
> 
> **Information theory — compression ratio** : Shannon's source coding theorem states that the minimum average code length per symbol equals the source entropy. Perplexity measures how far a model is from this theoretical minimum: PPL=2bits-per-token\text{PPL} = 2^{\text{bits-per-token}}PPL=2bits-per-token, so PPL = 20 means each token requires log⁡220≈4.32\log_2 20 \approx 4.32log2​20≈4.32 bits, whereas a perfect model achieving Shannon's lower bound would need only the irreducible entropy (~3–4 bits). The gap between current PPL and Shannon's bound is literally the compression overhead of model imperfection.
> 
> **Ecology — species diversity indices** : Shannon's diversity index H=−∑ipilog⁡piH = -\sum_i p_i \log p_iH=−∑i​pi​logpi​ and Hill numbers (effective number of species =eH= e^H=eH) are structurally identical to language model perplexity. An ecosystem with diversity equivalent to BBB uniformly abundant species has eH=Be^H = BeH=B — exactly the perplexity formula. In ecology, this "effective species count" is used because it is interpretable without requiring knowledge of the underlying probabilities. Ecologists and NLP practitioners arrived at the same interpretive trick — exponentiate the entropy to get an effective count — independently and for the same reason: intuitive interpretability.
> 
> **Search theory — average branching factor in game trees** : In combinatorial search (chess, Go), the **average branching factor** bbb describes the average number of legal moves per position; a tree of depth ddd has approximately bdb^dbd nodes. Perplexity is the autoregressive language model's equivalent: it describes the average number of plausible "next moves" (next words) at each depth (position). Just as a Go AI with access to better evaluation reduces its effective branching factor by pruning implausible moves, a language model with better context representations reduces perplexity by concentrating probability on plausible continuations.

### 26.4 Tokenization: From Text to Token Sequences

#### Why Tokenization Matters

Language models do not operate on character strings — they process sequences of discrete **tokens**. The mapping from raw text to token sequences, called **tokenization** , is a foundational design decision with far-reaching consequences:

* **Vocabulary size** : determines the embedding layer's parameter count (∣V∣×dmodel|V| \times d_{\text{model}}∣V∣×dmodel​)
* **Sequence length** : the same text yields different sequence lengths under different tokenization schemes, affecting the O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) attention cost
* **Out-of-vocabulary handling** : whether unseen words can be represented
* **Cognitive granularity** : whether the model "thinks" in characters, subwords, or words
* **Task performance** : arithmetic ability, multilingual equity, and API cost all depend on tokenization choices

Three granularity levels exist, each with fundamental trade-offs.

**Character-level** : minimal vocabulary (~100 tokens for English), no OOV problem, but sequences are very long ("understanding" → 13 tokens) and the model must learn word structure from scratch at every position.

**Word-level** : natural for humans, but vocabulary is enormous (>100K for English), OOV is pervasive (proper nouns, neologisms, misspellings), and the embedding layer becomes prohibitively large.

**Subword-level** : the universal choice in modern systems. Common words remain whole; rare words decompose into meaningful sub-units; vocabulary stays manageable; OOV is structurally impossible.

#### BPE: Byte-Pair Encoding

BPE (Gage 1994; adapted for NLP by Sennrich et al. 2016) is GPT's tokenization algorithm. The algorithm is elegant: start from single characters, repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair.

**Full algorithm trace** on a small corpus:

Initial word frequencies (end-of-word marked as `_`):
    
    
    "low_"    × 5
    "lower_"  × 2  
    "newest_" × 6
    "widest_" × 3
    

Initial vocabulary: all single characters {l,o,w,e,r,n,s,t,i,d,_}\\{l, o, w, e, r, n, s, t, i, d, \\_\\}{l,o,w,e,r,n,s,t,i,d,_}

**Round 1** — count all adjacent pair frequencies:

Pair | Frequency  
---|---  
(e, s) | 6 + 3 = **9**  
(s, t) | 6 + 3 = **9**  
(t, _) | 6 + 3 = **9**  
(w, e) | 2 + 6 = 8  
(l, o) | 5 + 2 = 7  
... | ...  
  
Highest frequency (tie): select **(e, s)** → merge to `es`.

Updated representations:
    
    
    l o w _          (×5)
    l o w e r _      (×2)
    n e w es t _     (×6)
    w i d es t _     (×3)
    

**Round 2** — highest frequency pair is now **(es, t)** at 9 → merge to `est`.

**Round 3** — highest is **(est, _)** at 9 → merge to `est_`.

**Round 4** — highest pair is either **(l, o)** at 7 → merge to `lo`.

Continuing until vocabulary reaches target size (e.g., 50K): high-frequency words like "the", "and" eventually become single tokens; rare words like "transformerization" decompose into multiple subword units.

**Key properties of BPE** :

* Deterministic (no randomness)
* Frequency-driven: reflects corpus statistics
* Composable: any string expressible as some sequence of vocabulary tokens
* Length compression: common sequences represented by fewer tokens

#### WordPiece: Likelihood-Based Merging

BERT's tokenization algorithm. The core difference from BPE: **the merge criterion is PMI (pointwise mutual information) rather than raw frequency**.

For candidate merge (a,b)(a, b)(a,b), WordPiece computes:

score(a,b)=freq(ab)freq(a)×freq(b)\text{score}(a, b) = \frac{\text{freq}(ab)}{\text{freq}(a) \times \text{freq}(b)}score(a,b)=freq(a)×freq(b)freq(ab)​

This is the PMI in un-logged form: it measures how much more often aaa and bbb co-occur than expected if they were independent. A pair with high PMI (like "q" and "u" in English, which almost always co-occur) would be merged even if its absolute frequency is moderate.

**BPE vs. WordPiece on a concrete example** : Suppose "t" appears 10,000 times, "h" 8,000 times, "th" 5,000 times; "q" appears 100 times, "u" 200 times, "qu" 95 times.

* BPE score("th") = 5,000; BPE score("qu") = 95 → BPE merges "th"
* WordPiece score("th") = 5000/(10000×8000)=6.25×10−55000/(10000 \times 8000) = 6.25 \times 10^{-5}5000/(10000×8000)=6.25×10−5; WordPiece score("qu") = 95/(100×200)=4.75×10−395/(100 \times 200) = 4.75 \times 10^{-3}95/(100×200)=4.75×10−3 → WordPiece merges "qu"

WordPiece recognizes that "qu" is an almost obligatory unit in English (q appears without u only in borrowings), while "th" is merely frequent. In practice, BERT marks continuation sub-tokens with `##`: "unhappiness" → ["un", "##happi", "##ness"].

#### SentencePiece: Language-Agnostic Tokenization

BPE and WordPiece both assume that whitespace marks word boundaries — a valid assumption for English but not for Chinese, Japanese, Thai, or many other languages. Kudo & Richardson (2018) developed **SentencePiece** to operate directly on raw character streams, treating whitespace as an ordinary character (represented as `▁`).
    
    
    Input: "Hello world"
    SentencePiece: ["▁Hello", "▁world"]
    
    Input: "今天天气很好"
    SentencePiece: ["▁今天", "天气", "很好"]
    

The `▁` prefix encodes "this token begins a new word." This design works for any script without language-specific preprocessing. SentencePiece supports two underlying algorithms: BPE (applied at the character level directly) and Unigram Language Model (starts from a large candidate vocabulary and iteratively prunes low-contribution tokens, using EM). Most modern multilingual models (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen) use SentencePiece with BPE or Unigram.

**Practical consequences of tokenization choices** :

_Arithmetic difficulty_ : GPT-series models tokenize numbers non-intuitively: "42195" might become ["421", "95"]. The model has no access to individual digits within "421", making column-by-column arithmetic structurally impossible. Character-level or byte-level tokenization improves arithmetic substantially.

_Multilingual inequity_ : English text at comparable semantic density typically requires 1.5–2× fewer tokens than Chinese or Arabic text under English-dominant tokenizers. Since API cost scales with token count and context length is fixed, non-English users are systematically disadvantaged. Multilingual-optimized tokenizers (e.g., trained with language-balanced corpora) partially mitigate this.

_Information density per token_ : vocabulary size trades off with average tokens per concept. Larger vocabularies (100K+) reduce average sequence lengths but require more embedding parameters. Smaller vocabularies produce longer sequences with higher attention cost. The optimal vocabulary size is approximately 32K–100K for most modern systems.

> **Cross-Disciplinary Connection**
> 
> Tokenization design raises fundamental questions about units of representation that appear throughout computational and cognitive science:
> 
> **Molecular biology — codon decomposition** : The genetic code maps triplets of nucleotide bases (codons) to amino acids. The choice of triplet (rather than singlet or doublet) was "discovered" by evolution rather than designed — it balances specificity (4³ = 64 codons for 20 amino acids, providing some redundancy) against sequence length. BPE-style subword tokenization converges on a similar trade-off: common amino-acid-like "conceptual units" (words) are assigned single tokens; rare composites decompose like codon sequences. The Unigram LM algorithm in SentencePiece even has a formal parallel to the maximum-parsimony principle in phylogenetics — choose the segmentation that maximizes the probability of the observed sequence under the simplest underlying model.
> 
> **Data compression — entropy coding** : Huffman coding assigns shorter codes to more frequent symbols, minimizing average code length. BPE approximates Huffman coding at the vocabulary level: frequent substrings become single vocabulary items (short codes), rare substrings decompose into multiple items (longer codes). The difference is that BPE builds the vocabulary greedily by frequency, while Huffman coding builds the code tree by minimizing expected code length explicitly. Both are attempts to exploit the same statistical regularity: natural language data is highly non-uniform, and non-uniform sources are compressible.
> 
> **Morphological linguistics — morpheme discovery** : Unsupervised morphological analysis (Goldsmith 2001; Creutz & Lagus 2005) attempts to segment words into morphemes ("re-", "transform", "-ation") from statistical regularities alone. BPE and WordPiece are computationally simpler but perform similar statistical segmentation. The "learned vocabulary" of a BPE tokenizer trained on English approximates a morphological lexicon: prefixes ("un-", "re-"), suffixes ("-ing", "-tion"), stems ("transform", "play"), and common words are all represented. The alignment between BPE segments and morphological units is not perfect but is systematically better than random — the statistical signal that BPE exploits is largely the same signal that morphological structure creates.

### 26.5 Architecture Variants: Encoder-Only, Decoder-Only, Encoder-Decoder

#### Encoder-Only (BERT Family)

**Attention pattern** : fully bidirectional — no masking, every token attends to every other token. The attention matrix is a full n×nn \times nn×n matrix:

Menc=(11⋯111⋯1⋮⋱⋮11⋯1)M_{\text{enc}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\\ 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\\ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\\ 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \end{pmatrix}Menc​=​11⋮1​111​⋯⋯⋱⋯​11⋮1​​

**Pre-training objective** : MLM (plus optional NSP).

**Strengths** : deep bidirectional context at every layer; maximally informative representations for understanding tasks.

**Fundamental limitation** : cannot naturally generate text. MLM does not learn to produce coherent left-to-right sequences; generating from a masked-LM model requires iterative heuristics that are slow and produce low-quality output.

**Representative models** : BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT, ELECTRA, DeBERTa.

**Best-fit tasks** : text classification, NER, semantic similarity, extractive question answering — any task reducible to "classify or extract from a fixed input."

#### Decoder-Only (GPT Family)

**Attention pattern** : causal lower-triangular mask — position ttt attends only to positions {1,…,t}\\{1, \ldots, t\\}{1,…,t}:

Mdec=(10⋯011⋯0⋮⋱⋮11⋯1)M_{\text{dec}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\\ 1 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\\ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\\ 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \end{pmatrix}Mdec​=​11⋮1​011​⋯⋯⋱⋯​00⋮1​​

**Pre-training objective** : autoregressive LM.

**Strengths** : natural generation, unified task interface, in-context learning, KV cache efficiency, 100% training signal density.

**Limitation** : left-context only at each position; theoretically less information for tasks requiring right-context disambiguation at specific positions.

**Representative models** : GPT-1/2/3/4, LLaMA, Mistral, Claude, Gemini.

**Best-fit tasks** : all generative tasks; all tasks expressible as "given this prefix, continue with the correct answer."

#### Encoder-Decoder (T5 / BART Family)

**Attention pattern** : encoder uses full bidirectional attention; decoder uses causal masked self-attention plus cross-attention to all encoder positions. Three distinct attention types:

  1. Encoder self-attention: nenc×nencn_{\text{enc}} \times n_{\text{enc}}nenc​×nenc​ full matrix
  2. Decoder self-attention: ndec×ndecn_{\text{dec}} \times n_{\text{dec}}ndec​×ndec​ lower triangular
  3. Cross-attention: ndec×nencn_{\text{dec}} \times n_{\text{enc}}ndec​×nenc​ full matrix (decoder queries, encoder keys/values)

**Pre-training objectives** : T5 uses span corruption (mask consecutive spans of text, predict them); BART uses denoising (delete, shuffle, or infill spans).

**T5's text-to-text formulation** : every task is reframed as producing an output text from an input text, with the task specified by a prefix:
    
    
    "sst2 sentence: this movie is great"        → "positive"
    "translate English to German: That is good" → "Das ist gut"
    "summarize: [long document]"                → "[short summary]"
    

**Strengths** : dedicated encoder for understanding, dedicated decoder for generation; parameter specialization matches the information flow of seq2seq tasks.

**Limitation** : parameters are split between encoder and decoder; both halves are smaller than a same-total-parameter decoder-only model. Cross-attention adds inference complexity.

**Representative models** : T5, Flan-T5, BART, mT5, mBART.

**Best-fit tasks** : machine translation, abstractive summarization, document-question-answering (long document → short answer).

#### Systematic Comparison

Dimension | Encoder-Only | Decoder-Only | Encoder-Decoder  
---|---|---|---  
Self-attention direction | Fully bidirectional | Causal (unidirectional) | Encoder: bidirectional; Decoder: causal  
Pre-training target | MLM | Autoregressive LM | Span corruption / denoising  
Core capability | Understanding | Generation (+ understanding via prompt) | Understanding + generation  
Parameter utilization | All parameters for encoding | All parameters for generation | Parameters split between encoder/decoder  
Inference cost | Single forward pass | Autoregressive (sequential) | Encoder once + decoder sequential  
KV Cache benefit | Not applicable | Large benefit | Partial (encoder cacheable; decoder sequential)  
In-context learning | Difficult | Natural | Possible but less smooth  
Scaling simplicity | Moderate | High (single module type) | Lower (encoder/decoder balance required)  
  
* * *

### 26.6 Why Decoder-Only Dominates at Scale

By 2023, every frontier large language model — GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, LLaMA, Mistral — uses the decoder-only architecture. This convergence is not accidental. Four complementary factors explain it.

**Factor 1 — Generation covers understanding**. Any classification or comprehension task can be reformulated as generation: "sentiment analysis: [text] Answer:" → "positive". This reformulation works well at scale because the model's generative capability already encodes the task's necessary representations. Encoder-only models require dedicated task heads and fine-tuning; decoder-only models can tackle new tasks with only a prompt string. The unified interface dramatically simplifies deployment.

**Factor 2 — In-context learning**. When a decoder-only model is large enough, it learns to recognize patterns in the input prompt and generalize them to the prediction. GPT-3 demonstrated this at 175B parameters: providing a few (input, output) examples in the prompt context allows the model to perform novel tasks without any gradient updates. This capability — in-context learning — is structurally tied to the autoregressive training objective, which trains the model to continue any prefix including "demonstration → completion" patterns. Encoder-only models, trained to classify representations, cannot naturally perform this operation.

**Factor 3 — KV cache inference efficiency**. During autoregressive generation, the key (KKK) and value (VVV) vectors for all previously generated tokens need not be recomputed at each step — they can be cached from earlier forward passes. Generating the ttt-th token requires only computing QQQ, KKK, VVV for the new token and attending against cached KV from positions 1 through t−1t-1t−1. Per-step compute is O(t⋅d)O(t \cdot d)O(t⋅d) with naive computation but O(d)O(d)O(d) with KV cache — a factor-ttt speedup that becomes critical for long generations. Encoder-decoder models can also cache encoder outputs, but the decoder's cross-attention adds additional compute and memory overhead.

**Factor 4 — Scaling simplicity**. The decoder-only architecture consists of a single repeated module type: masked self-attention + FFN. There are no design decisions about encoder/decoder parameter ratios, no cross-attention layer count choices. When scaling to 70B, 100B, 1T+ parameters, architectural uniformity improves training stability and predictability. Kaplan et al.'s scaling laws were primarily validated on decoder-only models; the most reliable guidance for compute-optimal training (Chinchilla) applies specifically to autoregressive LMs with this architecture.

**Encoder-decoder is not obsolete**. Encoder-decoder models retain advantages in specific settings: (1) when inputs are long documents requiring deep understanding before generation begins (e.g., long-form abstractive summarization); (2) machine translation, where the encoder's bidirectional view of the source language genuinely helps; (3) speech recognition (Whisper uses encoder-decoder: audio encoder + text decoder); (4) moderate-scale deployments (Flan-T5 remains competitive on many tasks at 11B parameters or less). The architecture choice should be driven by task structure, not fashion.

* * *

Pτ(wt=v)=exp⁡(zv/τ)∑v′exp⁡(zv′/τ)P_\tau(w_t = v) = \frac{\exp(z_v / \tau)}{\sum_{v'} \exp(z_{v'} / \tau)}Pτ​(wt​=v)=∑v′​exp(zv′​/τ)exp(zv​/τ)​

τ\tauτ | Effect on zv/τz_v / \tauzv​/τ | Distribution shape | Text character

since (zj−z∗)/τ→−∞(z_j - z^*)/\tau \to -\infty(zj​−z∗)/τ→−∞ for all j≠i∗j \neq i^*j=i∗. Simultaneously Pτ(i)→0P_\tau(i) \to 0Pτ​(i)→0 for all i≠i∗i \neq i^*i=i∗.

**Numerical example** — logits z=[2.0,1.0,0.5,−1.0]z = [2.0, 1.0, 0.5, -1.0]z=[2.0,1.0,0.5,−1.0]:

At τ=1.0\tau = 1.0τ=1.0: ez=[7.389,2.718,1.649,0.368]e^z = [7.389, 2.718, 1.649, 0.368]ez=[7.389,2.718,1.649,0.368], sum = 12.124 → P=[0.609,0.224,0.136,0.030]P = [0.609, 0.224, 0.136, 0.030]P=[0.609,0.224,0.136,0.030]

At τ=0.5\tau = 0.5τ=0.5: ez/0.5=e[4.0,2.0,1.0,−2.0]=[54.60,7.389,2.718,0.135]e^{z/0.5} = e^{[4.0, 2.0, 1.0, -2.0]} = [54.60, 7.389, 2.718, 0.135]ez/0.5=e[4.0,2.0,1.0,−2.0]=[54.60,7.389,2.718,0.135], sum = 64.84 → P=[0.842,0.114,0.042,0.002]P = [0.842, 0.114, 0.042, 0.002]P=[0.842,0.114,0.042,0.002]

At τ=2.0\tau = 2.0τ=2.0: ez/2.0=e[1.0,0.5,0.25,−0.5]=[2.718,1.649,1.284,0.607]e^{z/2.0} = e^{[1.0, 0.5, 0.25, -0.5]} = [2.718, 1.649, 1.284, 0.607]ez/2.0=e[1.0,0.5,0.25,−0.5]=[2.718,1.649,1.284,0.607], sum = 6.258 → P=[0.434,0.263,0.205,0.097]P = [0.434, 0.263, 0.205, 0.097]P=[0.434,0.263,0.205,0.097]

Halving the temperature concentrates ∼\sim∼23 additional probability mass on the top token (0.609 → 0.842); doubling it redistributes that mass to lower-ranked tokens.

#### Top-k Sampling

**Algorithm** : retain only the kkk highest-probability tokens; renormalize; sample.

  1. Compute full P(v∣w<t)P(v \mid w_{<t})P(v∣w<t​) for all v∈Vv \in Vv∈V
  2. Sort by probability; take top-kkk subset VkV_kVk​
  3. Renormalize: P′(v)=P(v)/∑v′∈VkP(v′)P'(v) = P(v) / \sum_{v' \in V_k} P(v')P′(v)=P(v)/∑v′∈Vk​​P(v′)
  4. Sample from P′P'P′

**Limitation** : kkk is context-independent. In "The United States of ___", almost all probability mass is on "America"; fixing k=50k = 50k=50 includes 49 nearly-zero-probability candidates unnecessarily. Conversely, in "The hero walked into the ___" (many plausible continuations), k=10k = 10k=10 might exclude reasonable options.

#### Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling

Holtzman et al. (2019) proposed **top-p sampling** , which dynamically adapts the candidate set size:

Select the minimum set Vp⊆VV_p \subseteq VVp​⊆V such that ∑v∈VpP(v∣w<t)≥p\sum_{v \in V_p} P(v \mid w_{<t}) \geq p∑v∈Vp​​P(v∣w<t​)≥p, where tokens are added in descending probability order. Renormalize and sample within VpV_pVp​.

**Example** with p=0.90p = 0.90p=0.90:

_High-certainty context_ : P=[0.85,0.05,0.03,0.02,…]P = [0.85, 0.05, 0.03, 0.02, \ldots]P=[0.85,0.05,0.03,0.02,…]. Cumulative after 1st token: 0.85 < 0.90; after 2nd: 0.90 ✓. Nucleus = 2 tokens.

_Low-certainty context_ : P=[0.18,0.15,0.14,0.12,0.10,0.09,0.08,0.05,…]P = [0.18, 0.15, 0.14, 0.12, 0.10, 0.09, 0.08, 0.05, \ldots]P=[0.18,0.15,0.14,0.12,0.10,0.09,0.08,0.05,…]. Cumulative sums: 0.18, 0.33, 0.47, 0.59, 0.69, 0.78, 0.86, 0.91 ✓. Nucleus = 8 tokens.

**Adaptive advantage** : when the model is certain, the nucleus contracts; when it is uncertain, the nucleus expands. Top-k's fixed cutoff is insensitive to context; top-p matches the natural variability of linguistic predictability.

#### Beam Search

**Greedy decoding failure** : at each step, selecting the highest-probability token can lead to globally suboptimal sequences.

Example: P("I")=0.6P(\text{"I"}) = 0.6P("I")=0.6, P("The")=0.4P(\text{"The"}) = 0.4P("The")=0.4; given "I", P("am"∣"I")=0.3P(\text{"am"} \mid \text{"I"}) = 0.3P("am"∣"I")=0.3; given "The", P("cat"∣"The")=0.8P(\text{"cat"} \mid \text{"The"}) = 0.8P("cat"∣"The")=0.8.

Joint probabilities: "I am" = 0.6×0.3=0.180.6 \times 0.3 = 0.180.6×0.3=0.18; "The cat" = 0.4×0.8=0.320.4 \times 0.8 = 0.320.4×0.8=0.32. Greedy selects "I" (locally optimal) but misses "The cat" (globally optimal).

**Beam search** maintains the BBB (beam width) highest-scoring partial sequences at each step. At step ttt, each of the BBB existing beams is expanded by all vocabulary items; the best BBB of the resulting B×∣V∣B \times |V|B×∣V∣ candidates advance. Final output is the highest-scoring complete sequence.

**Length bias** : since all log-probabilities log⁡P(wt∣w<t)≤0\log P(w_t \mid w_{<t}) \leq 0logP(wt​∣w<t​)≤0, each additional token makes the cumulative score non-increasing. Beam search systematically favors shorter sequences. Standard remedy: length normalization,

score(Y)=log⁡P(Y)∣Y∣α,α∈[0,1]\text{score}(Y) = \frac{\log P(Y)}{|Y|^\alpha}, \quad \alpha \in [0, 1]score(Y)=∣Y∣αlogP(Y)​,α∈[0,1]

with α=0.6\alpha = 0.6α=0.6 common in NMT.

**Use cases** : beam search suits tasks requiring "faithful" generation (translation, summarization), where the globally most-likely sequence is a good proxy for quality. It performs poorly for open-ended generation (dialogue, creative writing) because it produces repetitive, generic text — the "most probable" sequences tend to be high-frequency templates.

#### Summary: Decoding Strategy Selection

Strategy | Deterministic | Diversity | Best for  
---|---|---|---  
Greedy | Yes | Minimal | Fast prototyping  
Beam search (B≥2B \geq 2B≥2) | Yes | Low | Translation, summarization  
Temperature sampling | Adjustable | Adjustable | General text generation  
Top-k sampling | No | Medium | General generation  
Top-p (nucleus) sampling | No | Medium-high | General generation (adaptive)  
Temperature + top-p | No | Adjustable | Modern LLM default  
  
Modern production LLMs (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini) use temperature + top-p as their default decoding configuration, with task-specific tuning: lower temperature (τ≈0.3\tau \approx 0.3τ≈0.3) for code completion and factual Q&A, higher temperature (τ≈0.9\tau \approx 0.9τ≈0.9) for creative writing.

#### Conceptual and Computational (CC)

**1.** (Derivation). Prove the following claims from first principles:

(a) Show that minimizing cross-entropy LCE(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(\theta)LCE​(θ) is equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence Ew<t[DKL(Pdata(⋅∣w<t)∥Pθ(⋅∣w<t))]\mathbb{E}_{w_{<t}}[D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\text{data}}(\cdot \mid w_{<t}) \| P_\theta(\cdot \mid w_{<t}))]Ew<t​​[DKL​(Pdata​(⋅∣w<t​)∥Pθ​(⋅∣w<t​))].

(b) Show that perplexity is the geometric mean of the per-token inverse probabilities: PPL=[∏t=1T1/Pθ(wt∣w<t)]1/T\text{PPL} = \left[\prod_{t=1}^{T} 1/P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})\right]^{1/T}PPL=[∏t=1T​1/Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​)]1/T.

(c) For a model that assigns uniform probability 1/∣V∣1/|V|1/∣V∣ to every token, compute PPL and verify it equals ∣V∣|V|∣V∣.

Answer

**(a) Cross-entropy = KL divergence up to a constant** :

The expected cross-entropy across all contexts is:

LCE(θ)=Ew<t∼Pdata[H(Pdata(⋅∣w<t), Pθ(⋅∣w<t))]\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{w_{<t} \sim P_{\text{data}}} \left[ H(P_{\text{data}}(\cdot \mid w_{<t}),\; P_\theta(\cdot \mid w_{<t})) \right]LCE​(θ)=Ew<t​∼Pdata​​[H(Pdata​(⋅∣w<t​),Pθ​(⋅∣w<t​))]

Using the decomposition H(P,Q)=H(P)+DKL(P∥Q)H(P, Q) = H(P) + D_{\text{KL}}(P \| Q)H(P,Q)=H(P)+DKL​(P∥Q):

LCE(θ)=Ew<t ⁣[H(Pdata(⋅∣w<t))]+Ew<t ⁣[DKL ⁣(Pdata(⋅∣w<t)∥Pθ(⋅∣w<t))]\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{w_{<t}}\\!\left[H(P_{\text{data}}(\cdot \mid w_{<t}))\right] + \mathbb{E}_{w_{<t}}\\!\left[D_{\text{KL}}\\!\left(P_{\text{data}}(\cdot \mid w_{<t}) \| P_\theta(\cdot \mid w_{<t})\right)\right]LCE​(θ)=Ew<t​​[H(Pdata​(⋅∣w<t​))]+Ew<t​​[DKL​(Pdata​(⋅∣w<t​)∥Pθ​(⋅∣w<t​))]

The first term is H(Pdata)H(P_{\text{data}})H(Pdata​) — the intrinsic conditional entropy of natural language, a constant independent of θ\thetaθ. Therefore:

arg⁡min⁡θLCE(θ)=arg⁡min⁡θ Ew<t ⁣[DKL ⁣(Pdata(⋅∣w<t)∥Pθ(⋅∣w<t))]\arg\min_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(\theta) = \arg\min_\theta \;\mathbb{E}_{w_{<t}}\\!\left[D_{\text{KL}}\\!\left(P_{\text{data}}(\cdot \mid w_{<t}) \| P_\theta(\cdot \mid w_{<t})\right)\right]argθmin​LCE​(θ)=argθmin​Ew<t​​[DKL​(Pdata​(⋅∣w<t​)∥Pθ​(⋅∣w<t​))]

Minimizing cross-entropy is equivalent to minimizing expected KL divergence. ■\blacksquare■

**(b) Geometric mean form** :

Starting from the definition:

PPL=exp⁡ ⁣(−1T∑t=1Tlog⁡Pθ(wt∣w<t))\text{PPL} = \exp\\!\left(-\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})\right)PPL=exp(−T1​t=1∑T​logPθ​(wt​∣w<t​))

Rewrite the exponent using −log⁡x=log⁡(1/x)-\log x = \log(1/x)−logx=log(1/x):

PPL=exp⁡ ⁣(1T∑t=1Tlog⁡1Pθ(wt∣w<t))\text{PPL} = \exp\\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log \frac{1}{P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})}\right)PPL=exp(T1​t=1∑T​logPθ​(wt​∣w<t​)1​)

Use ∑log⁡at=log⁡∏at\sum \log a_t = \log \prod a_t∑logat​=log∏at​:

PPL=exp⁡ ⁣(log⁡(∏t=1T1Pθ(wt∣w<t))1/T)=(∏t=1T1Pθ(wt∣w<t))1/T\text{PPL} = \exp\\!\left(\log \left(\prod_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})}\right)^{1/T}\right) = \left(\prod_{t=1}^{T} \frac{1}{P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})}\right)^{1/T}PPL=exp​log(t=1∏T​Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​)1​)1/T​=(t=1∏T​Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​)1​)1/T

This is the geometric mean of the TTT values 1/Pθ(wt∣w<t)1/P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})1/Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​). ■\blacksquare■

**(c) Uniform model** :

If Pθ(wt∣w<t)=1/∣V∣P_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}) = 1/|V|Pθ​(wt​∣w<t​)=1/∣V∣ for all ttt:

LCE=−1T∑t=1Tlog⁡1∣V∣=log⁡∣V∣\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} = -\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T \log \frac{1}{|V|} = \log|V|LCE​=−T1​t=1∑T​log∣V∣1​=log∣V∣ PPL=elog⁡∣V∣=∣V∣ ✓\text{PPL} = e^{\log|V|} = |V| \;\checkmarkPPL=elog∣V∣=∣V∣✓

This confirms the intuition: a model with no linguistic knowledge, assigning equal probability to all vocabulary items, has perplexity equal to the vocabulary size — it must "choose" from all ∣V∣|V|∣V∣ tokens equally at every step.

**2.** (BPE trace). Given the following corpus frequencies:
    
    
    "ab_"   × 10
    "abc_"  × 8
    "bc_"   × 5
    

Perform the first 3 rounds of BPE. After each round, state: (a) the selected pair, (b) the merged symbol, (c) the updated representations.

Answer

**Initial representations** :

* "ab_" → `a b _` (×10)
* "abc_" → `a b c _` (×8)
* "bc_" → `b c _` (×5)

**Round 1 — count all adjacent pairs** :

Pair | Frequency  
---|---  
(a, b) | 10 + 8 = **18**  
(b, _) | 10  
(b, c) | 8 + 5 = 13  
(c, _) | 8 + 5 = 13  
  
Selected pair: **(a, b)** → merged symbol: `ab`

Updated:

* `ab _` (×10)
* `ab c _` (×8)
* `b c _` (×5)

**Round 2 — recount** :

Pair | Frequency  
---|---  
(ab, _) | 10  
(ab, c) | 8  
(b, c) | 5  
(c, _) | 8 + 5 = **13**  
  
Selected pair: **(c, _)** → merged symbol: `c_`

Updated:

* `ab _` (×10)
* `ab c_` (×8)
* `b c_` (×5)

**Round 3 — recount** :

Pair | Frequency  
---|---  
(ab, _) | **10**  
(ab, c_) | 8  
(b, c_) | 5  
  
Selected pair: **(ab, _)** → merged symbol: `ab_`

Updated:

* `ab_` (×10) — single token
* `ab c_` (×8) — two tokens
* `b c_` (×5) — two tokens

**Summary** : after 3 rounds, new vocabulary items are `{ab, c_, ab_}`. The word "ab_" is now a single token; "abc_" segments into [ab, c_]; "bc_" segments into [b, c_].

#### Application (App)

**4.** (Design reasoning). Compare decoder-only and encoder-only architectures for the following tasks. For each, state which architecture you would choose and provide a specific technical justification:

(a) Named-entity recognition (NER) on medical records

(b) Open-domain conversational question answering (e.g., ChatGPT use case)

(c) Machine translation from English to Chinese for a business application requiring consistent, high-quality output

(d) Code completion in an IDE (suggest the next token or few tokens as a developer types)

Answer

**(a) NER on medical records — Encoder-only (BERT-style)**

NER requires per-token classification: for each token in the input, predict a label from a fixed set (B-PER, I-PER, B-ORG, …, O). The quality of each token's representation determines classification quality. Encoder-only models provide bidirectional context at every layer — token ttt's representation reflects both preceding and following tokens. This is crucial in medical NER: "Dr. Smith prescribed aspirin for Jones" — recognizing "Dr. Smith" requires attending to "prescribed" (following context confirms professional role). A decoder-only model at position "Dr." only sees "Dr." — it cannot yet see "prescribed." Encoder-only is strictly better for this task given equal model size.

**(b) Open-domain conversational QA — Decoder-only (GPT-style)**

This use case requires generating multi-sentence answers, handling follow-up questions, performing in-context reasoning, and adapting to user intent expressed in natural language. All of these are fundamentally generative. Encoder-only models cannot generate; they can answer span-extraction questions but not generate explanations, lists, code, or nuanced responses. Decoder-only with instruction fine-tuning (e.g., the GPT/Claude/Gemini family) is the correct choice. The unified "text-in, text-out" interface accommodates any conversational pattern without task-specific architecture.

**(c) English-to-Chinese machine translation, high quality — Encoder-Decoder (T5 / BART-style) or Decoder-only**

For formal business translation where consistency and faithfulness matter over creativity, encoder-decoder is the traditional choice: the encoder builds a bidirectional, rich representation of the full English source sentence before decoding begins, ensuring no source information is missed. The cross-attention mechanism in the decoder explicitly aligns Chinese output tokens with relevant English source tokens — a well-understood mechanism with interpretability advantages for quality auditing.

However, large decoder-only models with adequate Chinese representation (e.g., GPT-4, Qwen) now achieve competitive or superior translation quality, because scale compensates for the architectural advantage. For a new purpose-built system at moderate scale (≤11B), encoder-decoder is the defensible choice; for a large-scale system using existing pretrained models, decoder-only with fine-tuning is pragmatic.

**(d) Code completion in IDE — Decoder-only**

IDE code completion is an archetypal autoregressive generation task: the developer has typed prefix code; the model must predict the most likely continuation one or a few tokens ahead. This is precisely the decoder-only architecture's pre-training task. The causal mask ensures that the model's completion depends only on the code that the developer has already written — semantically correct. Real-time latency is critical (completions must appear within ~100ms); decoder-only inference with KV cache is highly optimized for this. Encoder-only models (e.g., BERT) cannot produce continuations; encoder-decoder would add the overhead of encoding the prefix separately. GitHub Copilot, CodeGemma, StarCoder, and similar systems all use decoder-only.

**(c) Top-p = 0.90 on τ=1.0\tau = 1.0τ=1.0 distribution**:

Sort descending: A(0.831), B(0.112), C(0.041), D(0.015)

Cumulative: 0.831 < 0.90; 0.831 + 0.112 = 0.943 ≥ 0.90 ✓

**Nucleus = {A, B}** , total mass = 0.943.

Renormalized: P′(A)=0.831/0.943=0.881P'(A) = 0.831/0.943 = 0.881P′(A)=0.831/0.943=0.881; P′(B)=0.112/0.943=0.119P'(B) = 0.112/0.943 = 0.119P′(B)=0.112/0.943=0.119.

**(d) Top-k = 2 on τ=1.0\tau = 1.0τ=1.0 distribution**:

Two highest-probability tokens: A(0.831), B(0.112). Total = 0.943.

Renormalized: P′(A)=0.881P'(A) = 0.881P′(A)=0.881; P′(B)=0.119P'(B) = 0.119P′(B)=0.119.

**Comparison** : in this case, top-p = 0.90 and top-k = 2 produce exactly the same nucleus {A, B}. This is not generally true:

* If A had probability 0.60 and B had probability 0.35 (sum = 0.95 > 0.90 already at k=1k=1k=1), top-p = 0.90 would include only A, while top-k = 2 would include both A and B.
* If A had probability 0.25 and B through E each had probability 0.15 (sum reaches 0.90 at k=5k=5k=5), top-p = 0.90 would include 5 tokens, while top-k = 2 would include only 2.

Top-p adapts to the actual probability mass; top-k is insensitive to it.

* * *

**6.** (Top-p vs top-k boundary cases). Consider a language model predicting the next token with the following probability distribution over a vocabulary of 5 tokens:

Token | a | b | c | d | e  
---|---|---|---|---|---  
P | 0.40 | 0.25 | 0.20 | 0.10 | 0.05  
  
(a) Apply top-k sampling with k = 2. What tokens are in the candidate set? What are their renormalized probabilities? (b) Apply nucleus (top-p) sampling with p = 0.7. What tokens are in the candidate set? What are their renormalized probabilities? (c) Now consider a different distribution: P = [0.85, 0.05, 0.04, 0.03, 0.03]. Apply top-k with k = 2 and top-p with p = 0.7. Which method produces a more appropriate candidate set for this "confident" distribution? (d) In general, when does top-p outperform top-k? Explain using the concept of entropy of the distribution.

Answer

**(a)** Top-k = 2: select the 2 highest-probability tokens: {a, b}. Renormalized: P(a) = 0.40/(0.40+0.25) = 0.615, P(b) = 0.25/0.65 = 0.385.

**(b)** Top-p = 0.7: sort by probability and accumulate until cumulative ≥ 0.7. a: 0.40 (cumulative 0.40). b: 0.25 (cumulative 0.65). c: 0.20 (cumulative 0.85 ≥ 0.7). Include {a, b, c}. Renormalized: P(a) = 0.40/0.85 = 0.471, P(b) = 0.25/0.85 = 0.294, P(c) = 0.20/0.85 = 0.235.

**(c)** For [0.85, 0.05, 0.04, 0.03, 0.03]: Top-k = 2: {a, b} with P(a) = 0.85/0.90 = 0.944, P(b) = 0.05/0.90 = 0.056. This unnecessarily includes token b (very low probability). Top-p = 0.7: a alone has P = 0.85 ≥ 0.7, so candidate set = {a}. Top-p correctly recognizes that the model is confident and restricts to the single dominant token. Top-p is more appropriate here — it adapts to the distribution's entropy.

**(d)** Top-p outperforms top-k when the model's confidence varies across positions. In low-entropy distributions (model is confident), top-p shrinks the candidate set to 1–2 tokens, avoiding sampling from the noisy tail. In high-entropy distributions (model is uncertain), top-p expands to include more tokens, maintaining diversity. Top-k uses a fixed candidate size regardless of confidence — it under-samples when uncertain (cutting plausible tokens) and over-samples when confident (including implausible tokens). Top-p dynamically adapts to the effective vocabulary size at each step, which is the operational definition of entropy.

* * *

**7.** (SentencePiece multilingual fairness). SentencePiece treats whitespace as an ordinary character (using the metaspace symbol ▁), making it truly language-agnostic. Consider training a single SentencePiece tokenizer on a bilingual corpus of English and Chinese text.

(a) English text averages ~4.5 characters per word, while Chinese averages ~1.5 characters per "word" (morpheme). If the tokenizer achieves an average of 1.2 tokens per English word, estimate the average tokens per Chinese morpheme, assuming the tokenizer allocates vocabulary proportionally to character frequency. (b) A sentence conveying the same information requires ~15 words in English and ~10 words in Chinese. Compute the token counts for each language. What is the ratio? (c) This token count ratio means Chinese text uses more of the model's context window for the same information. Propose two modifications to the tokenization strategy that would reduce this asymmetry. (d) Why does this tokenization asymmetry matter for language model perplexity comparisons across languages?

Answer

**(a)** English characters are high-frequency in a balanced bilingual corpus (Latin alphabet has ~26 letters used very frequently). Chinese characters are individually less frequent (thousands of unique characters). BPE/SentencePiece merges the most frequent pairs first, so English subwords benefit more from merging. Estimate: English achieves ~1.2 tokens/word (good compression). Chinese, with less merging opportunity per character, might achieve ~1.5–2.0 tokens/morpheme. A reasonable estimate is ~1.8 tokens per Chinese morpheme.

**(b)** English: 15 words × 1.2 tokens/word = 18 tokens. Chinese: 10 morphemes × 1.8 tokens/morpheme = 18 tokens. In this estimate the counts are roughly equal, but in practice Chinese often uses 1.3–1.5× more tokens than English for equivalent content, because Chinese characters are less compressible by BPE (each character carries more information in fewer bytes).

**(c)** Two modifications: (1) **Character-level fallback for Chinese** : use individual Chinese characters as tokens (each character is already a meaningful unit), avoiding the overhead of subword merging that doesn't help for Chinese. (2) **Language-balanced vocabulary allocation** : reserve a fixed fraction of the vocabulary for each language (e.g., 50/50 for bilingual), rather than letting frequency-based merging favor the higher-frequency-character language.

**(d)** Perplexity is computed per token: PPL=exp⁡(−1T∑tlog⁡P(wt))\text{PPL} = \exp(-\frac{1}{T}\sum_t \log P(w_t))PPL=exp(−T1​∑t​logP(wt​)). If Chinese uses more tokens for the same content, each token carries less information on average, making each token easier to predict → lower per-token perplexity. This makes Chinese perplexity appear artificially lower than English, even if the model understands both languages equally well. Fair cross-lingual comparison requires bits-per-character or bits-per-byte normalization, not bits-per-token.

#### Thought and Discussion (TD)

**8.** (Synthesis). This chapter and this book conclude with a question that unifies several themes.

The central narrative of this textbook traces a path: scalar functions → gradient descent → multi-layer networks → backpropagation → CNNs → sequence models → attention → Transformer → pre-training → scaling. At each step, a key bottleneck was removed.

Identify the **single most important bottleneck removed at each of the following transitions** , and state in one sentence how its removal enabled the next step:

(a) Multi-layer networks → Backpropagation

(b) RNN/LSTM → Attention Mechanism

(c) Attention Mechanism → Pre-training Paradigm

(d) Pre-training Paradigm → Scaling Laws

Answer

**(a) Multi-layer networks → Backpropagation**

_Bottleneck removed_ : No scalable algorithm existed to compute gradients through multiple layers.

_How removal enabled the next step_ : Backpropagation (Rumelhart et al. 1986) provided an O(∣θ∣)O(|\theta|)O(∣θ∣) algorithm for computing exact gradients through arbitrarily deep networks, making deep learning trainable in principle. Without it, deeper networks could not be optimized; the entire edifice of learned feature hierarchies (CNNs, LSTMs, Transformers) would have been inaccessible.

**(b) RNN/LSTM → Attention Mechanism**

_Bottleneck removed_ : Sequential computation enforced an O(n)O(n)O(n) information path between distant tokens, causing effective information loss over long sequences and preventing parallel training.

_How removal enabled the next step_ : Attention collapsed the maximum information path length from O(n)O(n)O(n) to O(1)O(1)O(1), simultaneously enabling parallelism (no sequential dependency) and direct long-range interaction. This made the Transformer possible: a uniformly deep, highly parallelizable architecture that could be trained on massive datasets at scale. Without O(1)O(1)O(1) path length, pre-training on billion-token corpora would have been computationally infeasible.

**(c) Attention Mechanism → Pre-training Paradigm**

_Bottleneck removed_ : No universal, efficient method existed for extracting transferable representations from large unlabeled corpora; every task required training from scratch on its own labeled data.

_How removal enabled the next step_ : MLM and autoregressive LM objectives provided self-supervised targets that exploited the Transformer's O(1)O(1)O(1) path length to learn deeply bidirectional or causally sequential representations from unlabeled text. By establishing that "predict the masked/next token" is a proxy objective that encodes syntax, semantics, and world knowledge, the pre-training paradigm decoupled representation learning (cheap, with unlimited data) from task learning (expensive, with limited labeled data). This made all subsequent scaling efficient: scale the model and data for pre-training; amortize the cost across all downstream tasks.

**(d) Pre-training Paradigm → Scaling Laws**

_Bottleneck removed_ : No principled guidance existed for how to allocate compute budget between model size, training data, and training compute; practitioners relied on heuristics and ablations.

_How removal enabled the next step_ : Kaplan et al. (2020) and Hoffmann et al. (2022 / Chinchilla) empirically established power-law relationships L(N,D)∝N−α+D−βL(N, D) \propto N^{-\alpha} + D^{-\beta}L(N,D)∝N−α+D−β relating loss to parameter count NNN and token count DDD, with an optimal allocation formula: N∗∝C0.5N^* \propto C^{0.5}N∗∝C0.5, D∗∝C0.5D^* \propto C^{0.5}D∗∝C0.5 (where CCC is compute budget). This transformed scaling from art to engineering: given a compute budget, the optimal model size and dataset size are calculable. Scaling laws enabled the systematic construction of GPT-3, PaLM, LLaMA, and their successors — not by trying all sizes, but by principled extrapolation of the power-law curves measured at smaller scale.
